News.title: El Nino forecast 'off the charts' as weather event linked to more snow in UK
News.content:
El Nino forecast 'off the charts' as weather event linked to more snow in UK

Weather experts say this year's El Nino could be 'off the charts', with potential cold snaps threatening to unleash snow, flooding, power cuts and damage from high winds

View 5 Images A map shows where sea-surface temperatures were above average as of October 22 (Image: ElNinoLive)

Britain could face a spell of extreme winter weather as a powerful El Nino threatens to smash records, with the UN warning the event could be stronger than anything seen in four decades.

‌



‌



The developing weather phenomenon has been branded "off the charts" by the head of the UN's World Meteorological Organization (WMO), as ocean temperatures across the tropical Pacific climb above the long-term average.

‌



Experts say it could bring wetter and stormier conditions to the UK, with potential "cold snaps" threatening to unleash snow, flooding, power cuts and damage from high winds.

‌



Maps tracking sea-surface temperatures show vast areas of unusually warm water, a key sign of El Nino gaining strength.

View 5 Images El Nino could bring extreme conditions this winter (Image: Getty)

Met Office urges Brits in 26 areas to prepare emergency kit for 18 hours – list READ MORE :

It comes as new figures from the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) found an estimated 2,200 deaths were linked to cold weather last winter.

‌



The data, which covers five "cold weather episodes" from winter 2025/26, suggests the cold-associated deaths happened in all regions of England except the North East, with people aged over 85 were most at risk.

Last winter there were five cold episodes, which are defined as a period of two or more consecutive days during which the average daily temperature falls below 2C. Health officials suggested that the population in England may have had a "greater vulnerability to cold weather and its impacts" in the most recent five-year period.

‌



View 5 Images An estimated 2,200 deaths were linked to cold weather in the UK last winter (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

BBC Weather issues verdict on El Nino and polar vortex bringing major snow to UK READ MORE :

They found that in the five winters from 2014/15 to 2018/19 low temperatures were "associated with a less rapid increase in mortality" compared with the most recent five year period – 2020/21 to 2025/26. "This may indicate that the population had greater vulnerability to cold weather and its impacts in the more recent five-year period," the UKHSA said.

‌



The WMO has warned temperatures in the central and eastern tropical Pacific could reach record levels between October and December, as the phenomenon approaches its expected peak.

El Nino develops when sea temperatures in this region rise at least 0.5C above average, disrupting atmospheric circulation and shifting weather patterns across the world. Its effects can range from scorching heat and drought to torrential rain, flooding and powerful storms.

‌



View 5 Images El Nino could spark damage caused by high winds (Image: PA)

While the UK is thousands of miles from the Pacific, Britain could still feel the effects this autumn and winter. The Met Office warned in August that El Nino could bring wetter, stormier conditions across north-west Europe, including the UK, during autumn and early winter.

‌



The British Red Cross has highlighted the potential for "cold snaps" while there are also fears that a weakening of the stratospheric polar vortex could bring heavy snow and allow freezing Arctic air to push further south.

The Met Office has previously identified this as one possible outcome during a strong El Nino, but stressed it was too early to say whether it would affect the UK.

‌



View 5 Images The Met Office says the weather phenomenon could bring wetter and stormier conditions to parts of the UK (Image: PA)

El Nino is already being linked to extreme weather in other parts of the world. Heavy rain has caused rivers to swell in parts of Argentina, Paraguay and Uruguay, forcing thousands of people from their homes and sending ranchers scrambling to move cattle to higher ground.

Article continues below

Meanwhile, wildfires on Indonesia's island of Borneo have worsened during a prolonged dry season, threatening endangered orangutans and other wildlife.

News.title: Kate Middleton admits she's missed Prince George at Eton and 'can't wait' to have him home for holidays
News.content:
Kate Middleton admits she's missed Prince George at Eton and 'can't wait' to have him home for holidays

The Princess of Wales visited a joint charity shop and cafe in Norfolk today, where she talked about Prince George, who starts his half-term holiday from Eton College tomorrow

View 7 Images The Princess of Wales on a visit to Cafe 98 in Norfolk today (Image: Ben Stanstall/Press Association)

The Princess of Wales has admitted she has missed eldest son Prince George since he started boarding school and is looking forward to him returning home for the holidays.

‌



‌



Thirteen-year-old George started at Eton College last month and will return home for his first “long leave” tomorrow. His younger siblings, Princess Charlotte, 11, and Prince Louis, eight, also break up from Lambrook School tomorrow for a two-week half term.

‌



Today, Kate, who visited a joint charity shop and cafe in Norfolk for East Anglia Children’s Hospices (Each), chatted with surprised customers and was asked how her children were getting on.

‌



Kate serenaded by 'brilliant' teenager with rare condition on moving hospice visit READ MORE :

View 7 Images Kate and Prince William take Prince George to his first day at Eton College (Image: POOL/AFP via Getty Images)

And Denise Ashton, 68, who was sat with two friends when the princess came over for a chat, said: "She said she's looking forward to George coming home - she's missed him.” She added: "They may be going somewhere (during the break).”

It was just last month that Kate and husband Prince William were seen dropping George off for his first day at the prestigious Eton College, which sees him following in the footsteps of his father.

‌



While chatting to locals who had gathered outside the shop after word quickly spread of the royal visit today, the princess asked children if they were on half term.

One youngster told her that it was his last day today, and she replied: “My children break up tomorrow and I can’t wait to have them all home.”

‌



View 7 Images Kate surprised customers in the charity cafe today (Image: Ben Stanstall/Press Association)

Kate’s visit to Café 98 in Hoveton, East Anglia’s Children’s Hospices' first and only café located within one of the charity’s retail stores, was kept under wraps due to the café's small size.

‌



And when she walked in, locals enjoying a cup of tea and browsing the rails couldn’t believe the future Queen had stopped by. As she headed over to the counter to greet catering Manager Morgan Neary, a group of ladies called her over asking: “Do you want to see our shopping?”

“Oh yes please,” Kate said, darting over to them. “Do you come in here quite a bit?” Essie Landsborough, 75, who sat opposite Ms Ashton, said “yes” as she rifled through her carrier bag and pulled out a box of two port sippers.

‌



Looking at the boxes, the future queen said: “You never know what you’re going to find [in a charity shop]. That’s what’s so nice. If feels a bit more like a treasure hunt.”

View 7 Images Kate helps fold donations in the hospice charity shop (Image: Ben Stanstall/Press Association)

‌



Interrupting with a tone of surprise, Ms Landsborough said: “Do you go to charity shops?” “Yes I do,” the princess said. “I love going round a charity shop. When I was up at university in St Andrews there were a lot of charity shops.”

Kate also met helpers in an upstairs sorting area where clothes were examined and graded, and when one volunteer told her with the “cost-of-living” crisis shoppers bought “party wear” the princess replied “So much just goes to waste – should be given another life.”

‌



She was given the task of helping volunteer Christine Rich sort through some items and when she discovered an expensive looking coat had been attacked by moths said “that’s a shame” and was told to put it in the “imperfect” pile.

Kate asked about the background of helpers and was told young people, as well as the retired, donated their time. She said: “I sometimes think people want to volunteer but they don’t know how…(we) need to make it a bit easier if they want to volunteer.”

‌



View 7 Images Kate greets locals outside the cafe (Image: Getty Images)

Earlier in the day, the princess had spent nearly an hour talking to children and families who are receiving care during an emotional visit to The Treehouse hospice in Ipswich.

‌



The unit provides short breaks and palliative support for children and young people with life-limiting conditions, and bereavement support for families. During her visit Kate, who previously opened the hospice in March 2012, toured its music therapy room and a sensory room with special lighting, a water bed and a projector.

Among those the princess met at the Treehouse was 13-year-old Charlotte Freegard, who has a rare genetic muscle disorder called nemaline myopathy.

‌



Kate sat with Charlotte at the piano as the youngster sang the Ed Sheeran hit Perfect, with the princess breaking out in a round of applause and telling her she was ‘brilliant’ after her performance. The princess told her: “Charlotte, that was beautifully sung. Well done, you.”

View 7 Images The Princess of Wales with 13-year-old Charlotte Freegard on a visit to The Treehouse Children's Hospice (Image: Getty Images)

‌



Kate said it was good for the children to have so much musical equipment and asked Charlotte: “You’re able to express yourself and really enjoy yourself?” to which the girl replied: “Definitely.”

The future queen also met four-year-old Primrose Harvey, who has a rare congenital heart defect called hypoplastic right-heart syndrome, and her parents who regularly bring her to The Treehouse.

‌



The little girl’s mother, Katie, told the princess that Primrose has had three heart surgeries, including one at six days old and another only two weeks ago. Kate told Primrose’s mother: “Super brave girl and brave parents too.”

Mrs Harvey said it was “lovely” to speak to the Princess of Wales about her daughter and the support they receive.

‌



View 7 Images The princess joins with a music therapy session (Image: Chris Radburn/Press Association)

She said: “It was really lovely just to talk about, you know, how amazing Each is for us as a family. It’s really nice for her to come here and see first-hand how much they do for families.”

‌



Meanwhile, Freddie Ormrod, 11, who has the mitochondrial genetic disorder Leigh syndrome, which causes epileptic seizures and profound physical disability, played chimes and a tambourine during Kate’s visit.

Freddie’s father, James, jokingly told the princess there was only so long he could listen to the chimes, to which she replied: “It is noisy. Often in our household, the noisier the instrument the better.”

‌



Content cannot be displayed without consent

Kate also met a group of bereaved parents, who are still supported by the hospice, and she listened to their stories while giving one of them a hug.

Article continues below

Earlier, the princess, who was wearing a dark green blazer and trousers, donned a white hard hat and orange hi-vis vest to visit a construction site where the hospice is being expanded, including a new hydrotherapy pool, a wellbeing and therapies suite, and a new bedroom that will be completed in 2028.

News.title: Starting a pension for your baby could lead to £1.77million nest egg
News.content:
With the cost of living crisis hitting families across the country, it can be a struggle to pay the bills - so putting cash away for your kids might seem impossible.

But because baby pensions allow for years of growth, sticking a few quid aside each month could build into a golden nest egg in retirement. A Junior Self-Invested Personal Pension can be opened by parents, legal guardians, or relatives for a child until they turn 18.

You can be flexible with what you put in depending on what you can afford, but £50 a month from birth could be worth around £368,000 by the time they turn 65. 18 The total annual limit of how much can be paid into a Junior SIPP is £3,600.

View 4 Images The number of parents opening Junior SIPPS for their children at the start of the 2026 tax year was 158% higher than last year (Image: Getty Images)

‌



This is made up of £2,880 from an individual and £720 from the government through tax relief. As with an adult pension, the child cannot access the funds until later life – currently, you can access a personal pension from the age of55, though this is rising to 57 from April 2028.

If you did the maximum paid into pot from birth until their 18th birthday, you would contribute £51,840, with tax relief taking the total to £64,800.

Assuming the pot grows at 6% a year after charges, it could be worth £1.77million when they hit 65. Allowing for inflation of 2% a year, that is around £488,000 in today's money.

Molly Haylett, 30, of Essex, is a financial adviser and a mum of two daughters, aged two and five. She started paying into a pension for each of her children as soon as they were born and saves into Junior ISAs.

‌



She said: "I wanted them to have options. You give your kids money all the time through presents, so having pots that aren't for today is really important.

"It's a gift that I might not see them use, but I am very confident it's going to make a huge impact on them. It's just really nice to know that I'm being sensible and building some pots up in different places that can help them at different stages of life."

View 4 Images Junior SIPPs are popular with some parents, as they know their child will be older and wiser when they receive a large sum of cash (Image: Getty Images)

Molly has adjusted the amount she puts into the Junior SIPPs over the years. So far, her youngest has a pension pot worth £3,000 and her eldest has £12,000 stashed away.

‌



She said: "I was putting about £20 a month in, then I increased it to about £60 a month. Now I'll do about £200 a month and then they'll get tax relief on that as well. I did it based on what I could afford at any given time.

"The reason I love the idea of doing a pension is that you can't put loads in. So the cost, to me, is relatively affordable. I just put money in a direct debit each month that comes out. Even if you did £20, small steps make such a big difference because it's invested - there's growth and compound interest over time."

Junior SIPPs are popular with some parents, as they know their child will be older and wiser when they receive a large sum of cash. But you need to consider how they will pay for other life milestones along the way. The money cannot be used for big events like a first home, driving lessons, or university fees.

Sarah Coles, Head of Personal Finance at AJ Bell, says this is why some parents choose to have multiple ways of saving for their children. You also need to be able to afford to part with the money and do not neglect your own finances.

‌



She said: "Life is increasingly expensive for this generation, so there will be times throughout their lives that support from family can be a lifeline.

"It's why some people will pay into a Junior ISA and a Junior SIPP alongside one another, so the money is there for important stages in life."

View 4 Images The number of parents opening Junior SIPPS for their children at the start of the 2026 tax year was 158% higher than last year (Image: Getty Images/Maskot)

Junior ISA savings can be accessed when the child turns 18. You can save up to £9,000 a year and it does not affect your own ISA allowance.

‌



But research from Octopus Money shows only 22% feel comfortable giving their children access to long term savings at 18. More than half (51%) would prefer to delay access, with 25 the most popular age.

Research from Hargreaves Lansdown suggests some families may be using Junior SIPPs to cut their Inheritance Tax bill by making the most of gifting allowances.

The number of parents opening Junior SIPPS at the start of the 2026 tax year was 158% higher than 2025. Most unused pension funds and death benefits will be included in the value of a deceased person's estate for Inheritance Tax purposes from April.

Hargreaves Lansdown suggests this means some families may be trying to get ahead with planning. Under current rules, if you die before the age of 75, the person inheriting your pension does not have to pay tax on your retirement savings.

‌



If you die after the age of 75, those who inherit your pension pay Income Tax when they draw from it. But for Molly, she says investing into a pension is about giving her peace of mind for her children.

She contributions from said: "Think about to age 18 when you want them to have the money, because pensions have got a lock on the door.

"If they do make bad decisions, which I hope they don't, they've still got money there that I've given them when they're going to be much wiser and older."

News.title: 'Royal British Legion saved my life after 12 years in the RAF - and it gave my daughter her dad back'
News.content:
'Royal British Legion saved my life after 12 years in the RAF - and it gave my daughter her dad back'

As The Royal British Legion kicks off its Poppy Appeal for 2026, a hero dad reveals how the charity saved his family after spending 12 years in the RAF

View 5 Images Poppy with her veteran dad who says he owes his life to the Royal British Legion (Image: © Royal British Legion. Photo by Matt Alexander)

An RAF veteran says the Royal British Legion saved his life and gave his little girl her dad back.

‌



‌



Now he is trying to pay the charity back by joining its annual Poppy Appeal, as it tries to raise £50million.

‌



Dad Neil Fellingham, 38, served for more than 12 years in the RAF as a Senior Aircraftsman Technician, working on ejection seats for Tornado aircrafts.

‌



He was passionate about serving in the military, but his career was cut short after he sustained a serious leg break when he was run over by a car he was helping to repair in August 2018. He is now waiting for his left leg to be amputated after living with chronic pain.

Reflecting on his life after the accident, he said: “I can be brutally honest when I say this, I wouldn't be here without the Royal British Legion. The car accident was horrific. Our entire lives were turned upside down. I went from being able-bodied to a wheelchair user."

To see more of the stories you love from The Mirror and to find them easily in Google then make us your preferred source. Free and easy-to-do, just click on the link here to find more from The Mirror at the top of your feed.

‌



View 5 Images Neil said he was in a 'dark place' after a horrific accident but has now found joy again (Image: © Royal British Legion. Photo by Matt Alexander)

Royal British Legion poppy appeal kicks off with a one-day mission READ MORE :

The dad said of the accident: "I attempted to jump up and get out of the way but unfortunately I was dragged underneath the car and snapped my tibia just below my left knee."

‌



Medics discovered Neil from Ipswich had a neuroma growing inside his leg and he endured multiple surgeries. He has been left with complex regional pain syndrome.

The injury has had a huge impact on his physical and mental health which left him struggling to leave his home he shares with wife Lauren and their five-year-old daughter Poppy.

‌



“I was in a very dark place. I did try to do something and I got to a point where I finally realised I needed help, so I did reach out," he said.

“Without the RBL’s support, for all of us, I quite honestly don’t believe I will be here right now. There would have been nothing to live for.

‌



"Because of the Royal British Legion, I have been able to spend more time with my wife, my wife has got her husband back and I've been able to spend time with Poppy, and she has been able to get her dad back. We've been able to go and do fun things together.

View 5 Images Neil with his wife and daughter who have also received support from Britain's biggest military charity (Image: © Royal British Legion. Photo by Matt Alexander)

‌



“The support is not just for a serving member, when a donation is made to the RBL it doesn’t just go to a serving person or a veteran, it can go to their families, it can go to whatever support is needed."

Neil, who experienced PTSD following his accident, participated in an RBL recovery program in 2024, which involved a multi-activity course at the charity’s Battle Back Centre in Shropshire.

‌



There, Neil rediscovered his love of sports, and ended up part of Team UK for the Invictus Games in Canada in 2025. He was selected and went on to compete in Wheelchair basketball and Alpine skiing.

“It gave me a reason to keep going. Attending the first training camp at the Battle Back Centre was incredible. I can't describe it as anything other than just feeling safe and reassured.

‌



“Everybody was just so kind and I needed that because I was in a very bad place mentally. It was my first time out of the house in two years on my own, without my usual support network.

“But it was just a really positive experience that I look back on now and I’m so grateful I was able to go because it helped me get selected for Team UK which is mind-blowing.”

‌



View 5 Images The RBL is hoping to raise £50m this year with its Poppy Appeal (Image: UK Press via Getty Images)

On Thursday he returned to Battle Back centre in Shropshire, which helped turn his life around, to receive a special poppy from the RBL, made from a former war-time Spitfire.

‌



With their help he went from despair to competing in the Invictus Games in Canada and has recently applied for the next games.

“The RBL have been fantastic. Because of them I am doing this fun thing with my family.

‌



"We have received an inordinate amount of both physical and mental support over the years and because of that we have been able to take part in lots of positive activities".

Neil said his wife and daughter and his parents, Graham and Hazel Fellingham, have also been supported by Britain's biggest military charity.

‌



“Because of their help we have been able to do fun activities together, things that we would never have been able to have done without their support."

About his involvement in the Invictus Games, he said: “I was dumbstruck and it was incredible. I loved it. I learnt so much, not just about winning medals - I didn't do that well! I was able to learn so much about what I can still do.

‌



'I thought I was done, washed up'

“I spent an awful long time thinking that was kind of going to be it. I was washed up, I was done, there was nothing else to be done. I then went from that to doing sit-ski for example, something that I’d never done before in my life.

“To go from this is your first wheelchair into ‘okay we are going to try wheelchair basketball’. I learnt so much of what I could still do, it changed everything. It showed me what I could do and not what I could no longer do.

‌



“It was the same for my family too. The RBL supported them at the games, they helped me have a sense of a normal life again by having those guys with me when I needed them most. It just made life that little bit easier.”

View 5 Images There's expected to be about 40,000 Poppy Appeal volunteers this year (Image: Getty Images)

‌



About his wait for his leg to be amputated, he has explained he needs a spinal stimulator fitted which will help him control some of the nerve pain going down my leg.

And hopefully that means he will be able to reduce a lot of the medication he’s “which I really, really want because the brain fog is awful.

‌



“In the long term my surgical team have agreed that amputation is the best option to give me better mobility and an improved quality of life, which is all I want. I want to be more mobile, to be able to do more stuff. And to not be on the medication which just turns me into a zombie.

“I’m still in the process of waiting for that to be done because I am a complex case because of a lot of nerve damage that was undetected for a long time.

‌



“I don't know if I can take a prosthetic but this will hopefully drive me forward and the RBL’s continued support helps me progress with my life knowing there are activities that make life worth living. Knowing as a family we can still do wonderful things. I just have to think of things differently.

“I’ve met some incredibly wonderful people on this recovery journey. The RBL supports everyone.”

Article continues below

The dad says they are “incredibly grateful” for the donations made by the public to the nation’s beloved charity.

“The donations received have helped me, my wife and my parents. People don’t give up on you, you can still do amazing things even when you are not okay, even when you are struggling.”
