News.title: AI documentary warns unchecked greed will trigger next global crash
News.content:
A chilling new documentary predicts that AI will be responsible for the next global financial crash - but says people, not technology, will be to blame. “AI is dangerous, but not in the way people think,” says movie director Valerie Veatch. “The real dangers are playing out now, and they’re nothing to do with technology - they’re being driven by the people behind it.”

Valerie has spent years exploring the topic, and her latest film, Ghost in the Machine, saw her interview dozens of scientists, researchers and philosophers, who helped her reach the devastating conclusion. She said: “They keep saying that we are going to lose control of the future, that AI is going to run the world - but I want to ask, how?

“The idea that they can think for themselves is science-fiction. The reality is that people are behind software and they are using it for their own ends.”

View 7 Images A chilling new documentary predicts that AI will be responsible for the next global financial crash (Image: Getty Images)

‌



Valerie says the real danger is playing out now - not with a Skynet-style superintelligence, but with a dangerous spending bubble, exploited workers, environmental damage, and a terrifying impact on the way children learn. “The people driving it are not accountable,” she warned.

This year, US senator Elizabeth Warren said the scale of AI investment had ‘striking parallels’ to the 2008 financial crash. Four tech giants - Alphabet, Amazon, Meta and Microsoft - plan to spend a combined $725 billion (£543.22 billion) on capital expenditure in 2026, up 77% on last year - much of it driven by the AI boom.

View 7 Images A data centre for AI, such centres have been found to use an incredible amount of water (Image: Getty Images/Cavan Images RF)

Nikkei Asia estimates that five major tech firms Alphabet, Microsoft, Amazon, Meta and Oracle - hold about $1.65 trillion (£1.23 trillion) in off-balance-sheet obligations tied to AI, including data centre leases and chip supply contracts, on top of about $1.35 trillion (£1.01 trillion) of debt on their balance sheets.

‌



Concerned that the AI bubble may burst, Valerie said: “Ultimately, it’s the banks - those folks profit from the hype and a lot of retail investors lose their money. These funds that are meant to be safe places for retirement will be gutted because of this. There’s no good outcome here.”

Valerie’s film also exposes the workforce few users ever see - behind the chatbots - following them to Nairobi. Kenyan workers employed by an outsourcing firm for an AI research and deployment company took home between $1.32 (99p) and $2 (£1.49) an hour, for sifting through graphic text - including descriptions of child sexual abuse and self harm - so the material could be filtered out of an AI chatbot’s training data, according to a 2023 Time investigation.

View 7 Images This year, US senator Elizabeth Warren said the scale of AI investment had ‘striking parallels’ to the 2008 financial crash. (Image: ETIENNE LAURENT/EPA-EFE/Shutterstock)

“The great sadness is that those communities are targeted for daily work,” Valerie said. “With no training, often the work becomes harmful and there’s no infrastructure or labour rules, labour laws to protect this kind of work. When I started making the film, I didn’t have a clear understanding of the scale of what we’re talking about. Now I do.”

‌



As well as the human cost, there is evidence of damage to the environment in the name of AI - with water use a particular issue.

Valerie said: “One of the things we should be talking about is access to water. For example, England has been through a serious drought. And these AI data centres say, ‘well, we don’t use that much water. We recycle our water.’

“But they never tell us how much water they actually use. I’m pretty sure that someone with a hosepipe ban, or struggling to access a water supply, would be pretty curious to find that out. We [Great Britain] are not an energy rich island. We’re not a resource rich island.”

View 7 Images Valerie Veatch is an acclaimed independent documentary filmmaker. (Image: Ghost in the Machine)

‌



Calling the use of resources ‘greedy,’ Valerie warned that once farmland and nature gives way to data centres, it’s gone forever. She said: “You can’t have a tourism industry, but you do have this data centre that does not enrich anybody.”

She also warns that the promise that data centres will bring jobs is hollow. Research by the environmental thinktank Verdant estimates that planned UK data centres will create around 10,400 direct jobs - about a quarter of the more than 40,000 new jobs by 2035 forecast by industry body TechUK.

But Valerie said: “By the time all of that plays out, the politicians who put these things in place will be gone. The companies will have sold, sold, sold. So even the companies who created the data centres will be gone. And they will leave us with nothing.”

View 7 Images (Image: Getty Images)

‌



The roots of the film are deeply personal for Valerie, who was inspired to research AI by something a boy said in her daughter’s class. Her daughter told her: “Oh, this boy in my class says that he doesn’t need to try to learn this maths because AI is just going to do it.”

Valerie said: “That actually was this deep catalyst for this project, because I was like, ‘there’s a misunderstanding of what we’re even talking about here.’

“We’re telling children that the magic and discovery of the learning process can be circumvented by using a chat bot. Come on, that is horrible.”

A study of 405 pupils, aged 14 and 15, across seven English secondary schools, published in November 2025, found note-taking beat AI chatbots for comprehension and memory when measured three days later - even though more pupils said they preferred the chatbot to taking notes.

‌



View 7 Images Ghost in the Machine is available on Amazon Prime Video from November 13 (Image: Ghost in the Machine)

Valerie said: “AI is not this new magical thing. This is just an extension of what the big tech companies have been doing for a long time. They will approach school systems and say, ‘put in our product and we’ll give you a couple hundred thousand dollars.” For a school, that’s amazing. They can make a football pitch, whatever they want. But the cost to our children in the long-term is not worth it.”

Keen not to be seen as someone advocating a return to the dark ages, she added: “I don’t want to sound like I’m anti-tech. I’m absolutely not. I think that there’s wonderful ways that we can implement technology that actually works for our social goals, that will help us reduce our carbon emissions.”

But she believes ordinary people have the power to stop AI excesses. She said: “We, as people, can decide we do not need this technology. We can refuse the active use 100%. We refuse normalising it within our realm, within whatever your realm is.

‌



“It promotes this intensely dehumanising idea that your craft, your talent, your imagination, is not valuable and not unique. And that’s the thing I hate most about this technology. If you’re a journalist, if you’re a teacher, if you’re a writer, if you’re a filmmaker, we can push back on the intrusion of these technologies and also the idea that comes along with it - the idea that machines can think. Because they can’t.”

*Ghost in the Machine is available on Amazon Prime Video from November 13. Info on screenings and further info can be found HERE

News.title: Second Australian female politician 'threatened' days after alleged car attack on MP Helen Haines
News.content:
Second Australian female politician 'threatened' days after alleged car attack on MP Helen Haines

A man entered the office of an Australian politician with nunchucks just days after an MP lost both of her legs in a 'car attack'

View 4 Images A man entered the office of Australian state politician Hannah Beazley with nunchucks (Image: Richard Wainwright/AAPIMAGE via)

A man has been charged with threatening an Australian politician's staff with nunchucks just days after a MP had both of her legs amputated after an alleged car attack.

Police said a man, 56, entered the electoral office of Hannah Beazley, a Western Australian state government minister, brandishing nunchucks and making verbal threats, on Wednesday. Beazley was not in the office, in suburban Perth, at the time of the incident. The man was arrested and charged with being armed in a way that may cause fear and with threatening to perform an unlawful act. He spent the night in police custody and will appear in a Perth court later on Thursday, police said.

This comes after MP Helen Haines, 65, was left critically injured after she was "rammed twice" by a 4x4 on Monday.

To see more of the stories you love from The Mirror and to find them easily in Google then make us your preferred source. Free and easy-to-do, just click on the link here to find more from The Mirror at the top of your feed.

View 4 Images MP Helen Haines was 'attacked' on Monday (Image: Mick Tsikas/AAPIMage via AP)

Man accused of 'ramming' MP Helen Haines pictured leaving court for first time READ MORE :

There was no allegation the man's behaviour was connected to the driver who hit Ms Haines with his car in the east coast state of Victoria.

Ms Beazley said she was in the state parliament when the man entered her electorate office demanding to see her. She said two members of her staff had been "rattled" but had remained safe behind a security screen. On Wednesday she told reporters: "We don't know his motives at all."

View 4 Images Ms Haines's husband Phil Haines said both of her legs were amputated (Image: Mick Tsikas/AAP Image via AP)

These incidents comes as concerns are heightened over the safety of female politicians' in Australia, where politicians are highly accessible to the public.

Ms Haines's alleged attacker, Brendan Nugent, appeared in court on Wednesday charged with intentionally causing serious injury, dangerous driving causing serious injury and causing harm to a federal official. He did not enter pleas and remains in custody and police are still searching for a motive.

The independent MP's husband, Phil Haines, shared an update on his wife saying both of her legs were amputated after she was airlifted to Melbourne but "two most important parts of Helen", her heart and her mind, were in "good shape".

View 4 Images Brendan Nugent was charged after the MP was critically injured (Image: Anita LESTER/AFP via Getty Images)

Just under 50% of federal politicians and a majority of Prime Minister Anthony Albanese’s cabinet are women. Mr Albanese said the fact that the threat to Ms Beazley came so soon after the alleged attack on Ms Haines was "just heartbreaking". Ms Beazley is the daughter of Mr Albanese's former federal colleague, Kim Beazley.

Mr Albanese, speaking to the Australian Broadcasting Corporation, said: "We can have debate and disagreement, but do it in a way without descending into the sort of violence that we have seen in too many parts of the world. It's certainly not who we are as Australians."

Article continues below

The Prime Minister attended an online security briefing this week for female politicians in his Labour Party. Security agencies addressed misogynistic threats directed at them.

Mr Albanese said: "Of course people are concerned. They're anxious. There has been a normalisation of behaviour that can be very aggressive in a way that wasn't happening a couple of decades ago."

News.title: Lost village hidden for decades under reservoir reappears after horrific UK drought
News.content:
Lost village hidden for decades under reservoir reappears after horrific UK drought

The village of Derwent, in Derbyshire, was lost for decades after it was deliberately flooded to make way for a reservoir that would service cities in South Yorkshire and the Midlands

View 4 Images The ruins of the village of Derwent have been exposed after a prolonged drought (Image: Getty Images)

A lost village hidden under a reservoir for decades has reappeared as a lengthy drought continues.

‌



‌



The village of Derwent, in Derbyshire, was deliberately flooded in the 1940s during the construction of Ladybower Reservoir, which was built between 1935 and 1943. Ladybower reservoir's water levels now stand at just 32 per cent capacity following a lengthy dry spell that led to a drought being declared in the East Midlands in August.

‌



Churches, cottages and a pump house were lost when the Derwent Valley was flooded. Locals strongly hit out against the plan at the time, which was aimed at serving the nearby cities of Derby, Sheffield, Nottingham and Leicester.

‌



View 4 Images People have been asked to stay along the paths at the reservoir (Image: Getty Images)

Lost village lies beneath beautiful reservoir after it was drowned in the war READ MORE :

Now new overhead images shows what remains of the village with some still retaining many of their key features. While the ruins of the lost village have been exposed due to the flood, visitors have been asked to keep to the nearby paths as the reservoir bed is "extremely muddy and not safe to walk on".

Figures from the Environment Agency show a majority of regions in England are in drought conditions following record-breaking heatwaves over the summer. Some 82 per cent of the country is in a drought with 18 reservoir groups under half capacity. They would require significant rainfall over the autumn and winter to replace the amount lost.

‌



View 4 Images The village was deliberately flooded in the 1940s (Image: Getty Images)

"We've seen six months of below-average rainfall and above-average temperatures so reservoir levels will take time to recover, but overall, across our region we've more stored than this time last year," said Doug Clarke, Severn Trent's water resources lead, reports the BBC.

‌



"Reservoirs make up around a third of our water supplies, with the rest coming from rivers and groundwater, and our teams are continuing to work around the clock to treat more water and fix leaks at record levels.

View 4 Images The old pump house has now been revealed following a drought (Image: Getty Images)

Article continues below

"But we're also asking customers to continue using water wisely all year round, to help ensure there is always enough to go around."

Ladybower Reservoir can retain an impressive 2,869 mega litres of water and underwent major refurbishment in the 1990s to raise and increase the strength of the dam's wall to reduce the risk of "over-topping" in a major flood.

News.title: AI discovered a massive cyber-security flaw - here's what happened
News.content:
Governments and cyber-security agencies around the world are scrambling to contain a massive flaw in internet technology, after AI discovered issues that could be exploited by hackers.

Developers of the PHP platform - which powers more than 70% of websites, including Wikipedia and digital shopping sites - rolled out patches to fix the vulnerabilities that had been lurking in their software for years.

Cyber-security firm Wiz described the issue as the "most severe" ever detected, while OpenAI, whose technology was used to find the flaws, called the discovery "one of the most impactful security issues in recent memory".

But how did AI discover a massive cyber-security risk in the internet, and what does it mean for you? The BBC's technology correspondent Joe Tidy reports.

Read more on the cyber-security threat here.

News.title: Barclays cutting 5,000 jobs as it increases reliance on AI
News.content:
Barclays is cutting around 5,000 staff as it introduces more artificial intelligence (AI) into its work processes.

The banking group said 1,000 posts had already been closed and it expects a further reduction of 4,000 to be complete by the end of this year, amounting to around 5% of its global workforce.

The bank's cost reductions are focused on its UK retail bank, but some back office functions for the UK are done in India, where a significant proportion of the job cuts are expected to fall.

Barclays said the changes were the result of an ongoing modernisation plan, with the use of AI being the "icing on the cake" of its strategy.

Although not all of the cuts are due to AI, their scale will prompt further concern over the impact of the new technology.

Company spending on AI is increasing along with claims new tools can replace some of the basic tasks currently done by staff such as administrative and programming work.

HSBC, Standard Chartered and Danske Bank have also flagged AI-related job cuts this year.

"It is a hot button topic," said AJ Bell investment analyst, Russ Mould.

However, banks had not yet made big moves towards the widespread introduction of AI and they would be considering the implications for security and customer service before implementing AI technology to make financial savings, he said.

"Any company at any time needs to keep on top of its cost base," he said.

"It will be intriguing to see what other banks say in their results in the coming weeks.

Sharon Graham, general secretary of the Unite union that represents banking sector workers said the company was "using AI as an excuse to discard its loyal and long-suffering workforce".

"Employers should be focussed on upgrading employees' skills so that they remain employed as new technology changes the workplace. Instead, Barclays is guilty of taking a short-term, kneejerk approach," she said.

Barclays is reaching the end of a three year cost-cutting programme focused primarily on its UK retail banking arm, although the investment banking division is also affected.

AJ Bell's Russ Mould said despite "reaching for the AI lever" Barclays had failed to match expectations with its financial results.

Barclays also revealed it made Â£2.3bn profit in the three months to September, higher than the same period a year ago, but slightly less than forecast.

Barclays Group chief executive CS Venkatakrishnan said the job cuts were the result of significant investment it is making in technology to simplify and improve its business.

"AI has an important role to play and may have a more important role to play in the future.

"We will employ the AI at scale," he said. "But AI is the icing on the cake not the cake.

"Because you need to do the infrastructure build to get the benefits of AI."

Barclays said around 60% of the job cuts will fall within its support functions, including among developers.

Will Howlett, financials analyst at Quilter Cheviot said the cuts illustrated "how significantly AI and automation could reshape the banking industry over the next few years".

"Banks have spent heavily on technology for years, but we are increasingly reaching the point where that investment translates into fewer people being required to run the business," he said.

Barclays said it expects its efficiency measures to deliver a further Â£1.1bn of savings in 2027.

News.title: Russell Brand accuser said alleged rape 'really hurt', court hears
News.content:
Warning - this report contains graphic content

The friend of a woman claiming to have been raped by Russell Brand told a jury the complainant had told her after the alleged attack that it had "really, really hurt".

The witness who spoke via video link at his trial said she had attended the Hammersmith Apollo theatre in London with the alleged victim in 2009, where they had been invited to the defendant's dressing room after his comedy show.

Statements from the woman's parents were also heard in court, saying their daughter had told them about the alleged attack, and that she had been "very worried about HIV".

Brand, 51, has pleaded not guilty to all seven charges in the trial - three counts of rape, three charges of sexual assault and one of indecent assault.

The allegations span a 10-year period from 1999 to 2009 and involve six female complainants.

The witness said the woman had told her she had visited Brand's house in London soon after meeting at the theatre, and that he then sent a car to collect the woman, which took her to his place in Hampstead.

She said when they spoke about it "quite soon after", she said she "was just crying - really upset".

The witness said Brand had forced her into having anal sex at the end of an encounter that started off consensually.

"He was quite aggressive," she said her friend had told her.

"He forcibly put it in my bum and "it really really hurt".

The witness says she remembers specifically asking the complainant if she had said no to Brand when the alleged attack started.

News.title: Moment man rescued from sinking car by Australian TV reporter
News.content:
A man in a sinking car has been saved by a TV journalist after driving into deep flood water.

Will Murray was at the scene reporting for the Australian Broadcasting Corporation in Morayfield, Queensland, when he saw a vehicle drive past him into the water.

Murray, and a bystander, rushed to help the driver as the SUV sank.

Murray says when it became clear the car was sinking very fast "there was no thinking involved", because the man might have drowned.

"Better that you jump in and give it a crack", Murray tells BBC News.

News.title: Two storms in two days as Austen and Boelo head for UK
News.content:
Gusts of wind will widely reach 60-70mph, and perhaps 80mph in exposed locations.

Winds of this strength will blow some trees over, bringing a significant risk of transport disruption and there may also be some power cuts.

Some buildings could potentially be damaged by the strongest winds, leading to a risk of flying debris at the height of the storm.

Yellow wind warnings cover most of England and Wales with gusts of wind on Friday forecast to reach 45-60mph, with 70mph gusts likely in some places.

As strong as these winds are, the most damaging winds will run to the south of the low pressure centre.

That puts north-west France firmly in the firing line and parts of Brittany could see gusts close to 90mph.

The Channel Islands are also expecting severe gales with gusts up to 80mph.

All schools have been told to close on Friday because of the high winds predicted to be caused by Storm Austen, the Government of Jersey has said.

Heavy rain in Scotland may cause some localised flooding with a Met Office yellow warning for 20-40mm of rain forecast with up to 80mm accumulating in a few areas through Friday.

News.title: Retired decorator's Pokémon cards sell for £1.5m after years in attic
News.content:
A retired decorator has become a millionaire after selling a collection of PokÃ©mon cards at auction.

The man, from Woking, said he had no idea the cards had any value until he read in his local newspaper about a single card fetching more than Â£6,000.

His collection, which had been in an attic for 15 years, was auctioned off at Ewbank's on Wednesday for Â£1.56m.

The Surrey auction house claimed it was the UK's most valuable trading cards auction ever and suggested it could be a European record.

"I know people always talk about finding treasure in the attic, but in my case that is literally true," said the man, who asked not to be identified.

"When my son was young, in the late 1990s, he started getting cards and swapping them at school.

"I thought they looked nice and wondered whether they might be a good investment.

"He had his own cards, but he never got to touch these, I'm glad to say."

PokÃ©mon is a Japanese franchise best known for its trading cards, video games and animated television series.

The man said he had bought some complete sets of the cards from someone in Malaysia on eBay.

One set which cost him Â£300 at the time went for Â£75,000 at Wednesday's auction.

The cards, all filed into bespoke PokÃ©mon binders while still sealed, were stored in the attic after his son lost interest in the franchise.

News.title: Dame Judi Dench: 'I can't do a play, a film or read anymore'
News.content:
Dench also discussed meeting American actor Sidney Poitier, who became the first black man to win the Academy Award for best actor in 1964.

She was appearing in Amy's View in New York when Poitier came backstage after a performance. She recalled that director Richard Eyre was in her dressing room, giving her notes, when there was a knock at the door.

Dench said she felt as if she were in a wind tunnel when Poitier walked in, adding: "It was thrilling."

Asked what she had said to him, Dench replied: "Not much, a bit of an open mouth. So charming. Very tall."

The conversation then turned to Dench's love of Shakespeare. She recalled watching her brother play King Duncan in Macbeth when she was nine and said the moment sparked her passion for the playwright.

"He walked on and he said 'What bloody man is that?' I thought, 'oh my God, this is for me'. He said 'bloody', did you hear that?"

She also admitted to being " besotted" by Shakespeare's sonnets: "I just love them."

"It's the rhythm of it. It's the rhythm of your heart," she added, "it's the way he's summed up so simply the way that any of us feel about, well, anything."

News.title: Tommy Robinson hired detectives to find journalists, court told
News.content:
Political activist Tommy Robinson has told a court he hired private detectives to track down and photograph two reporters to "put pressure" on them.

The 43-year-old from Bedfordshire, real name Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, told Southwark Crown Court he was "shocked and scared" when the Daily Mail published a story accusing him of "stoking race riots from his sunbed".

He has denied two charges of harassment causing fear of violence to reporters Andrew Young and Jacob Dirnhuber after the 2024 Southport attacks.

Robinson is accused of writing posts on X, sending direct messages and making phone calls that made the two journalists fear the risk of vigilante attacks.

He denied wanting to expose the journalists to threats of violence, and said he felt his actions were "totally reasonable... under the circumstances".

News.title: UK's gaps in Arctic defence leave it open to Russian attacks, committee warns
News.content:
The UK has "glaring gaps" in its ability to defend the Arctic region, leaving it vulnerable to potential Russian attacks, a report by MPs has warned.

The Commons Defence Committee said a shortage of Royal Navy warships and submarines was leaving the country's critical infrastructure in the High North, including undersea cables and energy supplies, exposed.

In the event of a conflict, the report added that Russia could threaten the UK's population, civilian and military infrastructure and vital supply routes across the Atlantic from the US.

The Ministry of Defence (MoD) said it is "clear-eyed about the threat Russia posed" and is investing heavily to protect Britain's undersea cables.

Former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer previously warned that Russia could attack Nato by the end of the decade.

The High North - which includes the Arctic circle and areas adjacent to it - has become central to the UK's defence concerns in recent years.

Earlier this year, the MoD said Russian submarine activity in the North Atlantic is now back to the same levels as the Cold War era.

In the new report, MPs highlighted a "shockingly low availability" of submarines and said there was a temporary loss in ability to operate them beneath Arctic ice.

"Russia can then use the ice to conceal and protect its own submarines while threatening Nato sea lanes, UK critical infrastructure and the UK's nuclear deterrent," it added.

Chair of the Defence Committee, Tan Dhesi, said: "This is a demanding, hostile environment, and one that our greatest adversary, Russia, is seeking to dominate for military advantage."

The work to address these gaps "cannot start soon enough," he added.

In light of uncertainty over US support for Nato, the report said the UK should consider whether the British-led Joint Expeditionary Force (Jef), a UK-led military coalition of northern European nations, should focus more on the High North.

An MoD spokesperson said the Jef was already "strengthening Nato's northern flank and increasing our ability to respond rapidly to emerging threats".

Conservative shadow minister for war readiness Stuart Anderson said: "If Nato could be at war with Russia as soon as 2030, as the former prime minister warned, that means time is just as important as money.

"To deter war we must be ready for it, that means spending money now, not kicking the can down the road until it's too late".

News.title: Diabetes and ADHD drugs to be tested on Alzheimer's patients in new study
News.content:
A clinical trial has been launched in the UK which scientists hope could cut years from the search for new treatments for Alzheimer's disease.

It will test multiple drugs simultaneously, starting with two repurposed medicines already used to treat type 2 diabetes and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD).

The study will examine whether the drugs can lessen symptoms such as memory and thinking problems, and help people maintain their quality of life.

Angela Bucksey, 67, from Cambridgeshire, was diagnosed with Alzheimer's in January and is the first person to begin treatment on the trial, called AD-SMART.

"We have Alzheimer's in the family," she told the BBC.

"My mother had it and my aunts, so it was a disappointment rather than a shock when I was diagnosed because I knew it would restrict my life.

"But I was determined that it wasn't going to define me."

Angela said she felt empowered joining the trial because "at least you are doing something".

"Instead of just sitting there, you're standing up and saying, I will fight back."

Alzheimer's is the most common type of dementia, affecting around 600,000 people in the UK.

News.title: TV star's brother 'never recovered' from her death
News.content:
The brother of TV presenter Caroline Flack took his own life having "never recovered" after his sister's death, an inquest heard.

Paul Flack, 55, was found unresponsive at his home in Sandringham Road, Norwich, on 21 June, and died later in hospital.

His partner told Norfolk Coroner's Court how he had struggled with his father developing dementia and his younger sister's death in 2020.

Area Coroner Johanna Thompson gave a narrative conclusion, stating Paul Flack died while under the influence of alcohol and that his "intent in doing so is unknown".

He was described as "everyone's favourite person" by his partner Joanna Millington, but she said this "took its toll".

His sister, the ex-Love Island and X Factor host, was found dead at her home in Stoke Newington, east London, on 15 February 2020.

"We then went into lockdown for Covid," said Millington, who provided a written statement to the court.

"I do not think Paul ever recovered from this."

An inquest later established Caroline Flack took her own life, aged 40, having feared press intrusion ahead of her trial accused of assaulting her boyfriend.

News.title: 'I wasn't thinking straight' says five jobs civil servant
News.content:
In the spring of 2023, he was employed by the Defra, the UK Health Security Agency, the Food Standards Agency, the Department for Business and Trade and the Home Office.

The jury was told that throughout this period he was contracted to work 183 hours a week - more than the number of hours that exist in seven days. Each job paid a full-time wage, with Chowdhury paid Â£11,000 for a single month's work in 2023.

Prosecutors say Chowdhury "exploited" the work-from-home culture which began during the Covid-19 pandemic to hide his multiple jobs and took sick leave from some employers to manage the workload.

But Chowdhury told the court he had not wanted the jobs at the DHSC, Department for Business and Trade and the Home Office.

He told the jury: ''I sent out a flurry of these applications. The offers for these jobs came all at once. I had discussions with my line managers saying that I did not want these jobs and explained my circumstances. These were all short term and probationary and my priority was to look after my mother.''

He added that around May and June 2022, his mother's health "deteriorated".

He said: "That overwhelmed me at the time. It just destroyed me."

Chowdhury described the jobs as his "lifeline at the time".

"They gave me a link to the outside world and were a distraction from what was going on in my personal life, looking after my mum at that time."

The prosecution alleges Chowdhury managed to keep his overlapping jobs secret because he worked entirely remotely. He told his employers he was the sole carer for his elderly mother and the prosecution alleges he "exploited this opportunity".

The trial continues.

News.title: Big Brother fans still not happy as housemate called out on behaviour
News.content:
A Big Brother housemate who prompted more than 7,000 complaints has been spoken to about his on-screen behaviour - but some fans say the show's not doing enough.

Viewers and women's safety charities had been calling on ITV to intervene in Omar El Mayer and Rhianna Collins' relationship after several heated exchanges between the pair.

He was called into Big Brother's Diary Room during Wednesday's episode and told his language and behaviour "could cause offence". He denied dismissing Rhianna's feelings.

ITV has been contacted for comment. The broadcaster previously said "welfare and safeguarding are prioritised throughout the production".

Big Brother contestants live together for 24 hours a day, seven days a week, with almost everything they do captured on camera.

The popular reality show format sees divides form and tensions build as housemates try to avoid being eliminated in weekly votes.

Collins and El Mayer struck up a relationship after entering the Big Brother house but concerns about his alleged "toxic" behaviour had grown among fans.

Monday's episode, which showed a heated exchange between the pair, generated 7,138 complaints, according to broadcast watchdog Ofcom.

Viewers saw Collins break off the relationship before being called to the Diary Room, where she told Big Brother she and El Mayer "have not been good over the last few days".

"Sometimes I don't like the way he speaks to me."

Later, Collins was seen telling El Mayer she didn't want to argue, to which he replied: "Then don't say mad things that you don't mean. It's not fair... sort it out, get it together."

Both Women's Aid and Refuge allege the 21-year-old behaviour towards Collins is concerning and say ITV should do more to protect contestants.

News.title: Mystery of man found dead in wetsuit deepens as inquest questions ethnicity
News.content:
An unidentified man whose body was discovered in a reservoir in mid Wales two years ago may not have been of white ethnicity as previously thought, an inquest heard.

The body of the man, who was wearing an open water swimming wetsuit, was found by a dogwalker at the Claerwen Reservoir near Rhayader, Powys, in October 2024.

Despite a major international police appeal and the use of ground-breaking facial reimaging techniques, his identity and the cause of his death remain a mystery.

Coroner Patricia Morgan told detectives to analyse a liver sample given to the police two years ago which was never tested, adding she wanted to explore "this further line of inquiry" before reaching a conclusion.

The inquest heard the man's remains could have been in the water for more than three months before they were found.

News.title: Tougher punishments for criminals who refuse to attend sentencing backed by victim's family
News.content:
Tougher punishments for offenders who refuse to attend their sentencings will "rebalance the power" in the justice system, the aunt of murder victim Zara Aleena has said.

From next year, prisoners could be blocked from prison visits and confined to their cells for weeks on end if they do not follow orders to go to court.

This builds on an existing law that orders criminals to attend sentencing or face being fined or jailed for another two years.

"A year or two added to a life sentence wouldn't make any difference to an offender. But taking away these privileges would," Farah Naz said.

Naz said the refusal of the man who murdered her niece to go to his sentencing "left a sense that justice was not quite complete".

Aleena, an aspiring lawyer, was murdered by Jordan McSweeney as she walked home from an east London bar in June 2022.

McSweeney remained in his cell when he was sentenced to life in prison at the Old Bailey later that year.

He was jailed for at least 38 years, which was later reduced to 33 years after he won a Court of Appeal challenge.

Naz said Zara's Aleena's family had hoped that by reading their victim impact statement in front of her murderer, he would see "the consequence of his actions, of what he'd done, the devastation that he had caused".

She added that the new measures would "bring accountability and rebalance the power in the justice system from offender to victim."

Offenders who refuse to attend sentencing can already face a fine or up to two years additional imprisonment for contempt of court.

But the Ministry of Justice has acknowledged that longer jail time alone is unlikely to deter those already behind bars.

The new measures mean offenders could be confined to cells for up to three weeks, while social visits could be banned for 27 days and other prison privileges revoked for longer.

Judges will also be able to restrict social visits further to once every four weeks for a period of almost three months.

For criminals aged 18-20, similar restrictions could be handed down, but for shorter periods of time, the Ministry of Justice said.

However, visits from prisoners' children will be exempt from the new sanctions.

"Criminals should not be able to pick and choose when they face justice," Prisons Minister Catherine McKinnell said.

"Refusing to turn up to sentencing is an insult to victims and their families, and offenders must face the consequences," she added.

News.title: Former Scotland rugby international to go on trial charged with rape
News.content:
A former Scotland rugby international is to go on trial accused of controlling, abusing and raping a woman.

The charges against Tim Visser span a 14-year period and are alleged to have happened in Edinburgh and elsewhere between 2010 and 2024.

Two of the four charges state that the 39 year-old, who has been capped 33 times by Scotland, raped the woman on various occasions.

These include claims he had sex with her after consent had been withdrawn.

A separate charge alleges that the ex-Newcastle Falcons, Edinburgh and Harlequins player repeatedly behaved in a threatening and abusive manner towards the woman.

Among the accusations are that Visser "took intimate images" of her without her consent.

He was said to have been aggressive, sent her unwanted calls and texts, demanded to know where she was and controlled her appearance, finances and what she wore and ate.

News.title: Vivek Ramaswamy attack ad is so reviled that even CNN’s Scott Jennings blasted it — and Vance’s defense of it
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Conservative commentator Scott Jennings has joined the growing chorus of Republican voices denouncing Vivek Ramaswamy for running an attack ad featuring the estranged mother of his Democratic opponent — and blasted Vice President JD Vance for defending it.

Jennings warned that the ad, which dredged up Amy Acton’s traumatic childhood, would “blow up” in the Republican Party’s face and harm Ramaswamy’s chances in the Ohio gubernatorial race. Ohio Governor Mike DeWine is the latest Republican to condemn Ramaswamy for the ad and on Thursday urged him to take it down.

Vance defended Ramaswamy Wednesday, saying he was “disgusted” by GOP backlash and accused Republicans of “whining” about the ad that featured Donna Arthur, Acton’s estranged mother. Arthur lost custody of her children after her husband, Cledith Arthur, was indicted for raping Acton. He was never prosecuted for the rape charge, and the couple fled Ohio.

The ad makes no mention of the family’s past, but featured Arthur smearing her daughter as “a liar.” Jennings berated the vice president Wednesday on CNN’s NewsNight and said that Vance “could’ve just ignored” the issue.

“This issue of whining, I don’t see people whining about this,” Jennings told CNN’s Abby Phillip. “I think they are warning about this. There’s a heck of a lot of Republicans in Ohio and elsewhere who would love to see a Republican get elected governor of Ohio, who do not believe that this is a defensible ad, nor do they believe it’s a good strategy.”

open image in gallery Conservative pundit Scott Jennings has blasted the Republican Party - and Vice President JD Vance - for the attack released by Ohio GOP gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy. The ad features his opponent’s estranged mothermother ( CNN )

“Whether you take it from the moral view or you take it just from the political strategy view, there’s a lot of concern,” Jennings continued. “That’s not whining. That’s warning.”

“From what I’ve heard from my people in Ohio, it’s warning that this may have actually been a backfire,” the pundit concluded. “It’s gonna blow up in their face.”

Vance complained about his fellow Republicans’ reaction to the ad after a reporter asked him whether he thought it was appropriate to feature Arthur. “I have to admit that I’m a little bit disgusted when I see Republicans across the country who are whining more about that  than they are about what the congressional Democrats and other Democrats want to do to the United States of America,” he said.

But after Ramaswamy and the vice president doubled down on the ad, more Republican figures have spoken out against it.

DeWine, Ohio’s sitting GOP governor, said the ad was “deeply, deeply troubling” and urged Ramaswamy to take it down.

“I want to stay focused on this ad, and I’m still hopeful that they will take this ad down,” he told reporters Thursday, but declined to withdraw his endorsement of Ramaswamy.

Republican Lydia Mihalik, a member of DeWine’s Cabinet, said that the ad had crossed a line in a post on X.

“I don’t have to agree with Amy Acton’s politics to believe that exploiting someone’s childhood trauma is wrong,” Mihalik said. “There are lines we shouldn’t cross, and this is one of them.”

open image in gallery Ramaswamy, an ally of President Donald Trump, faced fierce backlash for the ad, which Acton’s campaign called a ‘disgusting smear’ using her ‘estranged, abusive mother’ ( Getty )

Ohio Republican Sen. Jon Husted said, “I would not have run that ad,” in his campaign against Democrat Sherrod Brown.

Conservative commentator Meghan McCain said the ad was “dastardly” and “never never should have been created.”

Former South Carolina Governor Nikki Haley, who ran against Ramaswamy for the Republican nomination in the 2024 presidential primaries, labeled her former opponent “a bad guy,” and added, “It's a shame he continues to get away with it.”

Dan Hauser, a Republican strategist for Utah Sen. Mike Lee, apologized for sharing the ad on social media. “I posted the video of Amy Acton’s mother without understanding the details behind their relationship and the very serious accusations that caused their issues,” Hauser said.

Privately, GOP strategists lamented the decision to run with the attack ad. “We’ve lost the plot,” a Republican strategist told TIME. “We had a real good chance and then we do this two weeks out.”

“We now deserve to lose this race,” another told the outlet.

open image in gallery Ramaswamy has doubled down on the ad despite calls from Republicans, including Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine, that he should take it down ( Reuters )

On the campaign trail and as the director of the Ohio Department of Health, Acton has discussed what she described as a troubled childhood, including surviving homelessness and sexual abuse from her stepfather.

In 2019, she told the Ohio newspaper The Vindicator that she was sexually abused between the ages of 9 and 12, when, in 1978, her stepfather was charged with rape and indicted by a grand jury. He pleaded not guilty.

A statement from Acton’s campaign called the “platforming” of her “estranged and abusive mother” a “despicable low.”

Arthur has denied that her husband, who died in 2004, sexually abused Acton but acknowledged in a separate 2020 interview that she supported him during the proceedings, borrowed money to hire an attorney — and then left town with him after his indictment.

Alex Woodward contributed to this report

News.title: Father and son charged with illegal gold mining in California: ‘This is not 1849’
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

The latest headlines from our reporters across the US sent straight to your inbox each weekday Your briefing on the latest headlines from across the US Your briefing on the latest headlines from across the US Email * SIGN UP I would like to be emailed about offers, events and updates from The Independent. Read our Privacy notice

A father and son have been sentenced to county jail for illegal gold mining in California, with the district attorney declaring: “This is not 1849.”

​Gregory Arnoldi Jr., from Nevada City, and his father, Gregory Arnoldi Sr., from Browns Valley, constructed an illegal dirt road along Keystone Creek near Loganville in Sierra County, prosecutors say.

​An image released by the Sierra County Sheriff’s Office shows one of the two defendants driving a digger. The sheriff’s office says the vehicle was used to make alterations to a historic carriage route in order to allow passage for their truck and mining equipment.

The work resulted in rock and soil tumbling into Keystone Creek, which flows into the Yuba River, they added.

​“In this case, the defendants’ illegal mining scheme vandalized private and public property and caused significant damage to those properties and to the natural resources that make Sierra County a desirable place to live and visit, including damage to mining artifacts (sic),” Groven said. “This is not 1849.

“Accordingly, they were sentenced to jail time for those decisions and will have to restore what they damaged at their expense.”

open image in gallery ​Gregory Arnoldi Sr and Jr were sentenced to jail time ( Sierra County Sheriff's Office )

​District Attorney Sandra Groven told CBS News Sacramento said the father and son were first charged in May after a local raised concerns about their activities.

​The gold miners were handed a number of charges by Groven’s office, including felony vandalism of public land managed by the United States Forest Service and adjacent private property, felony criminal conspiracy, and misdemeanor charges alleging water pollution.

​They were also charged with alteration of a stream without first notifying the California Department of Fish and Wildlife, mining without a Reclamation Plan and without a Sierra County Conditional Use Permit, and grading without a permit.

​Both Arnoldi Jr. and Sr. entered pleas of no contest to charges of felony vandalism of public and private properties, as well as misdemeanor water pollution and stream alteration charges.

open image in gallery Sierra County was a major hub during the California Gold Rush. This image shows gold found in 2025 in El Dorado County ( AFP/Getty )

The Arnoldis were each sentenced to 30 days in a county jail, to pay a fine of $8,135 and to establish a restoration plan for the areas that they vandalized. The associated costs of permitting, design and construction are to be borne by the pair.

​If they fail to carry out the restoration by August 1, 2027, the pair will be sentenced to an additional eight months in county jail and will need to pay $30,000 each in fines. ​The father and son were also placed on felony probation for three years and are banned from mining during this period.

​Sierra County was a hub for miners during the California Gold Rush, with around 16,000 miners arriving in the area between 1848 and 1860.

​Speaking to CBS News Sacramento, Groven said that protecting such a historic area can be difficult.

​“We are a small county with a lot of public lands which are remote, so enforcement can be difficult,” Groven said. “We prosecute the cases which are reported and substantiated by sufficient evidence. In this case, damage done to the environment was extensive.”

News.title: As Nobody Wants This returns, couples share their religious conversion experiences
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

When 29-year-old Ben met his Jewish boyfriend Liam* seven years ago, religion hadn’t played a role in his life before. Ben was raised in an atheist home and attended a secular school, but he would occasionally attend Jewish festivals as Liam’s guest. All of this changed when Liam moved abroad three years ago to study to become a rabbi, and the distance left Ben missing both his boyfriend – and his newfound religious community.

“When he was gone [and] there was no longer any reason for me to keep going as a guest, that's when I began to seriously consider converting,” says Ben. From there, he got in touch with the rabbi at Liam’s Reform synagogue – which practices progressive Judaism, a major denomination that adapts traditional Jewish practices to modern life and culture – and completed a two-year conversion process. Ben took conversion classes and had final interviews with three rabbis, completing his conversion a year ago this month.

Choosing religion for – or inspired by – a romantic partner is the focal point of Netflix’s hit romcom series Nobody Wants This, which follows agnostic sex podcaster Joanne (played by Kristen Bell) and the “hot rabbi” Noah (Adam Brody) as they repeatedly break up over their religious differences, along with Noah’s family’s disapproval and Joanne’s reluctance to convert. In the latest installment out this week (warning: spoilers follow), their relationship gets more serious – and Joanne finally embarks on the conversion process that the past two seasons have built up to.

In Nobody Wants This, which is based on series writer Erin Foster’s experience of converting to Judaism when she married her husband Simon Tikhman, Joanne initially has to convert in order to reinstate Noah’s reputation as a rabbi. But when she attends her first conversion class, she is confronted with the weight of her decision.

When the participants begin to describe their connection to Judaism, Joanne kicks things off by gushing over her handsome boyfriend, rather than speaking about the religion itself. She immediately faces disapproval from the other participants, since converting solely for a partner is discouraged in Judaism (Rabbis typically look for an independent commitment to Jewish life instead). But, as the series progresses, Joanne seems to find her own journey with the religion.

open image in gallery ‘Nobody Wants This’ follows agnostic sex podcaster Joanne (played by Kristen Bell) and the ‘hot rabbi’ Noah (Adam Brody) as they repeatedly break up over their religious differences ( KATRINA MARCINOWSKI/NETFLIX )

Debra Feinberg, a therapist and founder of Maplewood Counseling in New Jersey, says that couples should have honest, open conversations before a partner chooses to convert. She suggests partners ask, “What does this mean to you?”, to figure out if the decision comes from “family pressure, fear of losing the relationship, or trying to please your partner.” Another question she urges asking is: “What happens if, down the road, one of us feels differently?”

Feinberg adds that the person who chooses to convert can feel acute pressure. “Interfaith couples I've worked with can struggle with the expectations about how it will feel to say ‘I will convert,’ and how it actually feels to go through the process.” Lots of couples can handle it, she says, but those who struggle more are the ones that are “rigid and inflexible about how it has to go, especially around raising children and dealing with in-laws.”

The decision to convert to any religion is never straightforward and often requires deep soul-searching. Very early on in his conversion process, Ben found that his classes had nothing to do with his relationship because converting is meant to be such an independent experience. “I had introduced myself to the rabbi and to the team at the synagogue and I said, well, ‘My partner’s moved away to study to become a rabbi’. But they couldn't care less what my partner was doing. They wanted to know what I was doing and what I wanted,” he says. “There were a couple of people in my class who were converting, who had Jewish partners, but the vast majority of people either didn't have a Jewish partner or didn't feel [it was] worth mentioning, because it was such an individual thing to do.”

Greg, a 26-year-old graphic designer who was raised an atheist, converted to Islam before marrying his wife Hubbah, who he met during his first year of college. He found it was a natural step in their relationship, and he took his Shahada – the Islamic declaration of faith – in 2024 with Hubbah’s grandfather. Greg began with small lifestyle changes, like giving up pork, and then alcohol further down the line. “We obviously had lots of conversations and then I started doing it in bits and pieces as I went,” he says.

open image in gallery In the latest season of ‘Nobody Wants This,’ Joanne starts taking conversion classes and is confronted with the weight of her decision ( COURTESY OF NETFLIX )

Greg’s family were supportive of his decision and his relationship. “I guess for other people on the outside, it might have looked strange but it felt really natural and normal,” he says. “My parents were pretty on board and they're very open-minded. And obviously I had been with my partner for four years at that point, so they saw it coming and I had already started to make lifestyle changes.”

At the start, Greg’s partner’s mom was rightly curious about where the relationship was going. “[Her mom] might have been a bit worried that she was going to be with someone from a different culture. It all worked out in the end – her family has been very welcoming. I think they can see that I'm the right person.”

Ben also had positive reactions from his family when he began his conversion. “My mom said, ‘Can I be Jewish too?’ Because all she had heard from me about it is like the amazing food and these lovely dinners that I've been having with these really hospitable people,” he says, adding that his dad was supportive too. As a gay man in a Progressive synagogue, he felt welcomed. “The answer might be unexpected, but nobody has ever even raised an eyebrow about it at all,” he says. “The only people who have raised an eyebrow are non-Jewish people when I explain the situation to them.”

open image in gallery Therapist Debra Feinberg advises new couples with religious differences (like Joanne and Noah) to be open-minded and curious ( Netflix )

For both Ben and Greg, practicing the same religion as their partners has strengthened their respective relationships. Ben says that practicing the same religion has helped him and Liam communicate better and stay connected. “It helped us develop a more common language,” he says. “And I find less and less that I have to ask, okay, what exactly is that?”

Feinberg, too, has seen the benefits for couples who practice the same religion. “Practicing the same religion can bring couples together by sharing rituals, holidays, common values and things to look forward to together,” she says. Still, she says it should not be seen as a substitute for a lack of communication. “Connection comes from respect and curiosity, not from having the same beliefs,” she says.

The therapist advises new couples with religious differences to be open-minded and curious. “Ask about the meaning behind certain traditions, or build a blend of traditions…. alternate them, or even create new ones,” she says. “Remember to respect your differences rather than trying to avoid or erase them.” It’s solid advice for all couples, from Joanne and Noah in Nobody Wants This to Greg and Hubbah.

From his experience, Greg encourages new couples to talk openly about religion, rather than ignoring the elephant in the room. “We had a conversation about it early on and if I wasn’t as into it, the relationship could have crumbled if I wasn’t willing to go through with it,” he says. “You’ve just got to be honest with each other.”

*names have been changed

News.title: Doctor suspended after injuring patient in surgery and drinking alcohol on duty
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

A surgeon who was accused of consuming alcohol while on duty and injuring a patient’s bowel during an operation has been suspended for 12 months.

Dr Aleksandras Uzkalnis was practising as a Surgical Consultant in General Surgery at University Hospital Lewisham at the time of the accusations.

A Medical Practitioners Tribunal Service misconduct hearing revealed Dr Uzkalnis was issued with a warning by the General Medical Council, which regulates doctors, in September 2023 after he was convicted of drink driving.

Six months later, in February 2024, Dr Uzkalnis was accused of “smelling of alcohol during the surgery” by another doctor. He was also accused of abandoning surgeries and causing harm to patients that same day.

open image in gallery Dr Uzkalnis was suspended for 12 months following the tribunal ( PA )

The misconduct hearing revealed Dr Uzkalnis was supervising a junior colleague while he was conducting a laparoscopic cholecystectomy — surgery to remove the gallbladder. It was alleged by the GMC that Dr Uzkalnis failed to scrub in and take over from the junior colleague before making the decision to abandon the procedure.

The tribunal indicated that the consultant surgeon should have taken over if the procedure was deemed too difficult for the specialist registrar and that abandoning the procedure without taking over, when only a camera port had been inserted, was “inadequate”.

Later that day, Dr Uzkalnis was supervising another doctor who was operating on a patient listed for a spigelian hernia repair.

Another junior colleague who was present said Dr Uzkalnis took over the surgery but failed to stop when it became clear that the patient did not have a spigelian hernia, instead continuing and opening the peritoneal cavity that lines the abdominal wall. The patient then suffered an injury to the small bowel.

Dr Uzkalnis then passed on the procedure to the doctor he was supervising and said “this is your operation” before leaving the theatre.

Evidence given against Dr Uzkalnis suggested he did not take “adequate care” during the procedure and highlighted that due to the complexity of the case, and the fact that he had personally caused the injuries to the small bowel, Dr Uzkalnis should have stayed to complete the operation or stayed to supervise.

Dr Uzkalnis admitted he left the doctor he was supervising to finish the surgery, saying: “When I left [Dr D] to finish the surgery, I went to my office then I made coffee…”

Following the surgery, the hearing found Dr Uzkalnis did not discuss the complications with the patient or their family, or apologise to them. A witness said: “This represents care seriously below the expected standard.”

Dr Uzkalnis also admitted to drinking alcohol whilst on duty that day. In his Trust investigation interview, he said he went into his office and put “brandy in his coffee”, which he consumed after leaving the doctor he was supervising to complete the surgery.

However, other doctors gave witness statements indicating they could smell alcohol during the surgery. The tribunal noted this could possibly be explained by other events such as alcohol consumption the day before. There was also no evidence he had consumed alcohol prior to operating; only that he drank alcohol on duty, the tribunal heard.

Allegations that Dr Uzkalnis drank alcohol on duty, injured a patient’s bowel, abandoned a procedure and left the operating theatre during a surgery were proven by the tribunal panel. Following the findings, Dr Uzkalnis has been suspended for 12 months from 15 October.

News.title: Tiger Woods set for 2027 return to golf and tipped to play two tournaments
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Tiger Woods has been tipped to return to golf in 2027 after reclaiming a place on his TGL team at the expense of Kevin Kisner.

Woods, who fronts the Jupiter Links Golf Club, is preparing for the third season of the indoor golf league, with five players making up each team’s roster.

And the 15-time major champion is recovering from injury after playing just one match in Season 2 before returning to play in the TGL Finals, with Jupiter Links eventually losing to Los Angeles Golf Club.

"Well, obviously, I'm not on the team anymore," Kisner said on the Fore Play podcast. "I had a two-year contract with Jupiter Links and then they, Tiger wants to play. And then they wanted to sign Keith Mitchell, which is totally fine with me.

“And I'm sure I'll still be involved in some sort of fashion at some point. Go down there and do some stuff for them. You know, the Bad News Bears are still going to be a part of my life, and hopefully they continue to win."

Woods will be joined by Max Homa, Tom Kim and Akshay Bhatia, with the newly-signed Mitchell also on board.

“Rob, Tiger's guy, he text me a long text last week, I think. Just telling me what they did on their decisions, how they were moving around and what players were going to do and that Tiger wanted to play a full schedule.”

And Kisner outlined how Woods could target The Hero World Challenge and PNC Championship in 2027 to complement his TGL commitments.

It's the best two nights of the week: The Celebrity Traitors is back on our screens, and we're fully invested in the latest round of secret plotting and accusations. While the A-listers are busy trying to work out who's lying and who’s faithful, there's another thing altogether keeping us glued to the screen: the outfits.

If Stephen Libby's wardrobe from the last series is anything to go by, we're not the only ones paying attention to what everyone wears in the castle. News.title: Oikos maker has an interesting use for its wasted yogurt
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Danone, the maker of Oikos yogurt, has an interesting use for its wasted products — converting them into renewable energy.

With a protein craze that has taken over the internet, more Americans are turning to yogurt as a snack or even a meal. As yogurt makers ramp up production, they are also increasing greenhouse gas emissions.

But now, Danone, a leading global food and beverage company known for its dairy products, has a solution to keep up with yogurt demand while helping the environment.

PurposeEnergy announced Monday that it has partnered with Danone on a $40 million facility in Minster, Ohio, to convert yogurt residuals into renewable energy through anaerobic digestion.

open image in gallery PurposeEnergy announced Monday that it has partnered with Danone on a new million facility in Minster, Ohio, to convert yogurt residuals into renewable energy through anaerobic digestion ( AFP via Getty Images )

Anaerobic digestion is a process in which bacteria break down organic matter, like food waste, without oxygen. The process produces biogas, which can be used as an energy source for electricity, heating, or fuel.

The new facility is located in the same village as Danone’s largest U.S. yogurt manufacturing plant. Wastewater and organic food residuals are piped directly from the Danone plant to the new facility, which then converts them into biogas.

The biogas is then piped to a dedicated boiler back at the Danone plant, where it will be used instead of conventional natural gas.

PurposeEnergy estimates that the new facility can displace about 3,200 tons of carbon dioxide equivalent per year.

open image in gallery PurposeEnergy estimates that the new facility can displace about 3,200 tons of carbon dioxide equivalent per year ( Getty Images )

"The PurposeEnergy facility is an example of our Danone Impact Journey in action and part of our wider Re-Fuel energy excellence program, helping turn organic material from our Minster plant into renewable biogas that can be piped back to the plant and used through a new biogas boiler,” Heiko Gerling, chief operating officer of Danone Americas, said in a press release.

“It is a powerful example of how operational growth and environmental stewardship can go hand in hand.”

The new facility is already operational, and it will have a grand opening next spring.

"Food manufacturers shouldn't have to choose between growing production and meeting their environmental commitments,” Eric Fitch, founder and CEO of PurposeEnergy, said.

“With this facility anchored near Danone's Minster plant, we can give our partner a solution that supports both their goals."

News.title: Construction on Trump’s beloved arch could start in just a few weeks, court documents reveal
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Construction on President Donald Trump’s proposed 250-foot victory arch could break ground in just two weeks, shortly after Election Day, according to court documents.

In a court filing Wednesday, the Department of Justice said that the National Capital Planning Commission is scheduled to meet November 5 to consider approving the final plans. The Department of Interior and the National Parks Service could then issue authorization.

“NPS may publish such notice as early as November 5, 2026, and construction could commence as early as November 5, 2026,” the Justice Department said. The court filing comes as a federal judge considers whether to halt construction in response to a lawsuit.

The proposed monument, which echoes the Arc de Triomphe in Paris, France, is set to be erected in Memorial Circle, located across the Potomac River from the Lincoln Memorial. Plans indicate it will include gilded statues and an observation deck, with the words “One nation under God” emblazoned across its white stone facade.

Trump said last month that the arch would also double as a “top grade Military Complex,” but plans released last week by the administration do not appear to include a national security purpose.

open image in gallery Construction on President Donald Trump’s proposed 250-foot arch could start in just a few weeks, according to court documents ( @RealDonaldTrump, Truth Social )

The president has said the towering monument is meant to commemorate the 250th anniversary of the signing of the Declaration of Independence. But when asked by a journalist last year who the arch was for, he replied: “Me — it's going to be beautiful.”

At 250 feet, the arch would eclipse the U.S. Capitol Building, the Lincoln Memorial, the White House and even the Arc de Triomphe. “I'd like it to be the biggest one of all,” Trump told reporters in February. “We're the biggest, most powerful nation.”

It’s unclear how much the project will cost. The White House has said it will likely rely on both private and public funds, according to The New York Times. The National Endowment for the Humanities has set aside $15 million.

The proposed arch has sparked debate since Trump unveiled plans to build it last October. Several lawsuits have been filed to stop the monument from being erected, including one by a group of Vietnam veterans. They argue the arch lacks the required congressional approval and would obstruct views of Arlington National Cemetery, where over 400,000 people are buried.

open image in gallery Democrats have derided the construction effort as a vanity project, and a number of protests have been held in Memorial Circle

Democrats have derided the construction effort as a vanity project, and a number of protests have been held in Memorial Circle.

According to an April Ipsos survey, 52 percent of Americans oppose the arch, while 21 percent favor it.

If built, the riverside monument would join a growing list of construction and restoration projects undertaken by Trump in Washington, D.C., including his $400 million White House ballroom and the Trump-Kennedy Center renovations.

News.title: Telegraph Fantasy Football tips: Game Week 8
News.content:
As the Telegraph Fantasy Football season heads further into 2026-27, the award-winning experts at Fantasy Football Hub ccontinue to bring you the very best in fantasy football knowledge, tips and tools to help you rise up the ranks and win your mini-leagues.

Join the Hub and get access to all their great resources and expert tips.



Telegraph Fantasy Football: last week's insights



1-0 to the Arsenal



The reigning champions put in a resolute performance at the City Ground to keep the pressure on leaders Manchester City, grinding out a narrow victory thanks to a late Noni Madueke (£3.8m) strike. While Gunners attackers aren’t currently on the menu, the upcoming fixture run and style of play should see further defensive returns. News.title: Health authorities race to investigate first human death linked to Shamonda virus
News.content:
A French man has become the first person to contract Shamonda virus, a disease previously only found in animals and spread through midges.

The patient, who had a weakened immune system, has since died, according to the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC).

Shamonda virus was first identified in Nigeria in the 1960s and has this year been detected in farm animals all across Europe.

It was confirmed to have spread to the British Isles in September, after being found in a cattle herd on the island of Jersey. There have also been cases in Ireland.

The French patient, who was immunocompromised, died earlier this month while infected with the virus, but it is unclear if the infection contributed to his death, the ECDC said in a statement.

Investigations into whether the virus caused or contributed to the patient’s death and how the infection was acquired are ongoing.

Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, the director of the World Health Organization (WHO) said in a statement on X that he was “in contact with French authorities, who are collecting information to better understand the source of infection.”

He added the patient was “immunocompromised, which made them more vulnerable to infection and severe disease.”

There was “no health risk to the general public identified at this time”, the French health and agriculture ministries said in a joint statement.

Dr Ben Brennan, Group Leader and Senior Lecturer, MRC-University of Glasgow Centre for Virus Research, University of Glasgow, said: “This is an important scientific finding, as it is the first reported human infection with Shamonda virus [..] at present, there is no evidence that Shamonda virus causes widespread human disease, although further investigation is needed to understand its ability to infect people.”

In animals, Shamonda virus attacks the central nervous system and can lead to severe inflammation and haemorrhage. It can also lead to miscarriages.

Affected horses have been reported to exhibit seizures, lethargy, fever, muscle twitching, and difficulty walking.

Authorities are also still trying to ascertain whether the man himself was infected by a biting midge – the route of transmission between animals – or if he could have been infected by close contact with livestock.

It is thought he was infected in eastern France, where the virus had been circulating in midges and animals earlier in the year.

“Despite decades of circulation of the Shamonda virus in Africa and Asia, no human cases had been documented until now. This is therefore an exceptional case occurring in a severely immunocompromised patient,” French health authorities said in a statement.

The UK Plant and Health Agency said some of the neurological signs of the disease in horses resemble West Nile fever, human cases of which reached a record high on mainland Europe this year.

News.title: What happens when you get malaria during pregnancy?
News.content:
Huge strides have been made in recent years in combating malaria but one group is more at risk than ever before: pregnant women.

They are uniquely vulnerable to the disease and because sub-Saharan Africa shoulders the burden of global cases the continent’s rapidly growing population means far more women are exposed today than at the turn of the millennium.

According to a recent study, 52 million pregnant women in Africa face the threat of malaria each year, up from 37 million in 2000.

And the toll is heavy: malaria in pregnancy kills at least 10,000 mothers and 210,000 infants every year.

Malaria in pregnancy is uniquely dangerous, and the disease acts very differently to how it does in someone who is not pregnant.

“Pregnant women are one of the most vulnerable groups to malaria, it can lead to severe anaemia, immune suppression, and in the worst cases, mortality,” Lottie Renwick, global campaign director at Malaria No More UK told The Telegraph.

Malaria parasites infect and feed on red blood cells, dividing and multiplying in the bloodstream. This makes them easily detectable through a simple blood test, which allows life-saving treatment to be administered quickly.

But in pregnancy, the parasites are notoriously evasive.

Instead of floating in the bloodstream, they colonise in the placenta – the organ that feeds and sustains the baby.

News.title: Harry Kane proves there is only one Ballon d’Or winner
News.content:
After Arsenal were beaten by Bayern Munich in a Champions League quarter-final two years ago, Mikel Arteta bemoaned a lack of “magic moments” in attack.

Arsenal have since progressed to a Champions League semi-final and final, while ending a 22-year wait for a Premier League title.

The upward trajectory has translated to tangible success, but Arsenal are still searching the level-raising attacker they lacked on their last visit to the Allianz Arena in 2024.

Back then, Arsenal’s offensive game revolved around Kai Havertz, Bukayo Saka and Martin Odegaard and that remains the case, which makes one wonder if Arsenal’s forward options have been adequately renewed.

A pair of stodgy performances (in victory) against Leeds United and Nottingham Forest have amplified those questions, though some of Arsenal’s slicker football in the season’s early weeks has been forgotten a little hastily.

They have made another strong start to another European campaign with six points from six, but this is undoubtedly their hardest fixture of the league phase.

Their chances of matching last season’s eight wins from eight could well hinge on the outcome of tonight’s game, but there are worse times to face Bayern.

Vincent Kompany’s team looks as formidable as ever, having scored 22 goals from six Bundesliga games so far this season. Their rotational approach is hard to track, with runners from deep breaking beyond Harry Kane who wanders into deep midfield positions.

However, they are without Michael Olise (suspension) and Jamal Musiala (injury) while Joshua Kimmich will miss the game on compassionate grounds following the death of his father.

With the exception of William Saliba, Christos Tzolis and Piero Hincacpie, Arsenal have a pretty clean bill of health and the strength of their bench was crucial against Leeds, Lille and Forest last week.

For Arteta, there are some interesting selection calls to make. It is anticipated that Jurrien Timber will replace Ben White at right-back, and first-choice left-back Riccardo Calafiori has been rested for the Champions League games so far. Should Arteta continue that policy, Myles Lewis-Skelly will fill the position, which will likely mean a midfield start for Bruno Guimarães or Mikel Merino.

Arsenal’s manager must also decide between Noni Madueke and Eberechi Eze on the left, and Viktor Gyokeres and Kai Havertz up front. Havertz is Arteta’s preference, but he also has to consider a relatively short turnaround before Saturday’s league game against Everton.
