World.title: Preview | Kaizer Chiefs take aim at Red Arrows
World.content:
Kaizer Chiefs will be desperate to keep their continental campaign alive when they face Zambia’s Red Arrows in Durban on Friday, 23 October. Image: Kaizer Chiefs website

Kaizer Chiefs will be desperate to keep their continental campaign alive when they face Zambia’s Red Arrows in the second leg of their CAF Confederation Cup second preliminary round tie in Durban on Friday, 23 October.

Kick-off at the Moses Mabhida Stadium is 18:00.

Amakhosi head into the encounter trailing 1-0 on aggregate after suffering a narrow defeat in the first leg in Ndola, Zambia.



The stakes are clear: Kaizer Chiefs must win by at least two goals to secure automatic qualification for the 2026/27 CAF Confederation Cup group stage.

Kaizer Chiefs need a strong response

The first leg was decided in the 76th minute when Alassane Diarra headed home from a corner, handing Red Arrows a crucial advantage ahead of the return fixture.

Kaizer Chiefs will now have home support behind them as they attempt to overturn the deficit and progress in the competition for a second consecutive season.



A two-goal victory, such as 2-0 or 3-1, would see Amakhosi advance on aggregate.

A 1-0 win would take the tie to a penalty shoot-out, with no extra-time played in two-legged CAF knockout matches.

However, if Kaizer Chiefs win by a single goal while conceding, Red Arrows will progress under the away-goals rule. A draw or defeat would also eliminate the Soweto giants.



Home record offers hope

Kaizer Chiefs can draw confidence from their recent record in African club competitions.

Amakhosi are unbeaten in their last 11 home matches in continental competition, having recorded seven victories and four draws across the 2020/21 CAF Champions League and last season’s CAF Confederation Cup campaigns.

Their overall home record in the CAF Confederation Cup stands at six wins, one draw and two defeats in nine matches. Kaizer Chiefs have scored in all nine of those games.



Their record against Zambian opposition is less encouraging, however.

In seven previous matches against Zambian clubs in African competitions, Kaizer Chiefs have managed two wins, one draw and four defeats.

Their only home victory against a Zambian opponent in three matches came against Zesco at Moses Mabhida Stadium during last season’s CAF Confederation Cup group stage.



Can Amakhosi repeat last season’s comeback?

Kaizer Chiefs have previously lost the first leg of a continental tie eight times, progressing only once.

That successful comeback came last season against Kabuscorp in the CAF Confederation Cup preliminary round. After losing the first leg 1-0 away from home, Kaizer Chiefs won the return match 1-0 before advancing on penalties.

It remains the club’s only continental tie decided by a penalty shoot-out.



Kaizer Chiefs will hope to draw on that experience as they look to overcome Red Arrows, avoid an early exit and secure another opportunity to compete in the CAF Confederation Cup group stage.

Tickets are available through Computicket and at Shoprite and Checkers outlets nationwide for R80, while hospitality tickets are available at R1 699 and R2 899.

Suite tickets can be purchased through the Moses Mabhida Stadium hospitality team by emailing MMS.Hospitality@durban.gov.za or calling 031 322 3115.



Will Kaizer Chiefs do enough to progress to the CAF Confederation Cup group stage?

World.title: House hunting: Is South Africa cheaper than Botswana?
World.content:
Home buyers comparing property prices in Southern Africa may find significant differences between the markets in South Africa and Botswana, particularly when looking at advertised prices in their largest cities.

A comparison of property listings in Johannesburg and Gaborone offers an indication of how much buyers could expect to pay, although prices vary according to location, property size and condition.

South Africa house prices

In Johannesburg, the median asking price for a house stood at R1.48 million in October 2026, according to property platform ImmoAfrica.



The platform’s data covered more than 4 100 active listings, with half of the advertised properties priced between R970 000 and R2.25 million.

Three-bedroom houses had a median asking price of R1.399 million, while four-bedroom properties had a median of R2.1 million.

These figures indicate the range of options available to buyers in Johannesburg, although the final price depends on the suburb and features of the property.

The advertised prices are not necessarily the amounts buyers ultimately pay when a sale is concluded.

Botswana house prices

In Botswana, Gaborone had a median asking price of P1.65 million across 29 houses in an October 2026 property market snapshot published by Sam Associates Botswana.

Using the Bank of Botswana’s exchange rate of P1.2287 to R1 on 21 October 2026, this translates to approximately R2.03 million.



The difference between the two cities’ median asking prices is therefore about R548 000, with Gaborone recording the higher figure.

However, the comparison covers houses of different sizes and types rather than identical properties, so it should be treated as an indication of advertised prices rather than a definitive measure of affordability.

Where can buyers find cheaper houses?

The figures suggest that Johannesburg has the lower median asking price for houses compared with Gaborone.

However, Botswana’s property market also varies considerably by location.

Sam Associates reported a median asking price of P875 000 for houses outside Gaborone, equivalent to approximately R1.07 million at the same exchange rate.

This suggests buyers willing to look beyond Botswana’s capital may find lower-priced properties.

Ultimately, buyers should consider more than the advertised price. Property condition, location, financing costs, legal fees and other purchase expenses all affect the total cost of buying a home.

The comparison is based on October 2026 asking-price data and does not establish which country is cheaper across the entire housing market.

World.title: Head’s dismissal opens the door: Proteas win second Test in Gqeberha
World.content:
Travis Head and Scott Boland are unable to help Australia win the second Test against South Africa. Image: @cricketcomau, @proteasmencsa (X).

The Proteas have drawn level in their Test series against Australia.

South Africa bowled the Baggy Greens out on day 5 to win by an innings and 31 runs.

This leaves everything to play for in the final Test at Newlands later this month.



Rain washes out opening days of second Test

Day 1

Only 12.2 overs were bowled as the rain in Gqeberha brought play to an early close.

The Proteas were on 20/2, with Marques Ackerman and Temba Bavuma at the crease.

Aiden Markram and David Bedingham both fell to a Scott Boland bowling masterclass.



Day 2

Rain continued to fall at St George’s Park, limiting play to a single session.

South Africa ended on 97/5, with Bavuma and Wiaan Mulder in the middle.

Boland continued his path of destruction, with Mitchell Starc also getting in on the action.



Day 3

With play finally going again, Bavuma anchored a massive scoring effort for the Proteas.

He was eventually dismissed by Starc for a captain’s innings of 179 runs.

South Africa declared late in the day on 425/9.

In reply, Australia ended the third day on 3/1 as Kagiso Rabada marked his return by claiming Nic Maddinson’s wicket.



Where the Test match stood at day 4

The opening sessions saw Rabada and Marco Jansen tear through the Australian lineup.

The Baggy Greens were dismissed for just 99 runs, forcing the follow-on.

Jansen was the pick of the Proteas bowling attack, claiming a five-wicket haul.



A major concern is Anrich Nortje, who left the match with a suspected groin injury.

According to ESPN Cricinfo, he played no further part in the second Test.

Australia’s second innings stood at 156/4 at close of play on day four.



Travis Head scored a crucial 87 runs and was the clear danger man.

The Proteas needed 6 wickets to seal a win in the unlikeliest of circumstances.

🚨 MATCH RESULT 🚨



What a phenomenal game, what an incredible display from #TheProteas! An absolutely heart-stopping performance! 🤩



Bavuma led the way with the bat, and our bowlers ran riot with the ball! 💪🔥#TheProteas level the series 1-1 with a comprehensive victory by… pic.twitter.com/E89Ki6tyIj  October 22, 2026

Proteas vs Australia: How Day 5 played out

Rain once again threatened to spoil the action in Gqeberha.

The morning session was delayed from its initial 10:30 start due to a wet outfield.

Once play resumed, Head remained anchored, with Boland his unlikely partner in the middle.



He was eventually dismissed by Mulder for a stellar 121.

Boland’s heroic stand finally ended after 166 balls, leaving the tail-enders to make up a 70-run shortfall.

Alex Carey made a 37-run cameo at the end, but was ultimately the last man standing.



The Proteas bowled the visitors out for 295, sealing a win by an innings and 31 runs.

South Africa and Australia are now 1-1 in the Test series, ahead of the decider starting next week.

According to Cricket South Africa, the match will take place at Newlands in Cape Town from 27-31 October.

World.title: Proteas complete innings victory over Australia in 2nd Test
World.content:
GQEBERHA - South Africa wrapped up a brilliant innings-and-31-run win over Australia in the second Test at St George's Park on Thursday, levelling the three-match series.

Despite another session being washed out on the fifth day of a rain-hit game, the Proteas took the remaining six second-innings wickets needed to complete victory.

South Africa, who suffered a heavy defeat in the opening game in Durban last week, recovered from 110-6 in the first innings to post 425-9 declared, thanks largely to captain Temba Bavuma's career-best 179.

Marco Jansen took five wickets as the Aussies were then skittled for 99 and forced to follow on for the first time since 2019.

Travis Head's 121 and a 166-ball 40 from nightwatchman Scott Boland held up the South African charge on the final day, as did persistent morning rain, but Wiaan Mulder removed both and the tourists were bowled out for 295.

Jansen took the final wicket by dismissing Josh Hazlewood, as reigning world Test champions South Africa set up a series decider next week in Cape Town.

World.title: CheckPoint Podcast | Did Joseph Kabila Betray South Africa? The M23 Questions That Won't Go Away | 22 October 2026
World.content:
When Yesterday's Enemy Becomes Today's Ally, Who Pays the Price in Congo?

Political alliances can change overnight. For people caught in the Democratic Republic of Congo's conflict, the consequences can last for generations.

In a war that has drawn in neighbouring governments, international mediators and armed movements, political loyalty can be difficult to distinguish from political survival. The reported alignment between former Democratic Republic of Congo president Joseph Kabila and the M23 movement exposes one of the conflict's most troubling contradictions: the people who once stood on opposing sides can find themselves pursuing common interests, even while the human cost of their earlier confrontations remains unresolved.

That contradiction has particular significance for South Africa. Its soldiers took part in operations against M23 while Kabila was president. South African troops have subsequently died during the conflict. Questions about Kabila's relationship with the movement therefore extend beyond Congolese domestic politics to the obligations political leaders owe countries that have committed people and resources to supporting them.

The problem with shifting alliances

Political analyst Dr Claude Kabemba offers a stark description of how quickly relationships can change: "Your enemy today can be your ally tomorrow." His explanation centres on political interest and personal security, rather than any assumption that the objectives of former adversaries have become identical.

The distinction matters. An alliance formed out of immediate political necessity may resolve a problem for its participants while creating new problems for everyone else. A political leader may regard a former opponent as a source of protection or leverage. Citizens and soldiers affected by that opponent's actions may see the same development as a profound breach of trust.

This does not establish that Kabila secretly supported M23 during earlier fighting. Such questions require evidence, and allegations must remain separate from findings. But the absence of a final answer does not make the question irrelevant. South Africa has a legitimate public-interest reason to seek clarity about the conduct and allegiances of those involved in a conflict in which its soldiers have served.

The wider issue is how governments respond when their security commitments become entangled with political relationships that later change. Diplomacy requires dialogue, sometimes with deeply compromised actors. Accountability requires that the pursuit of negotiations does not erase legitimate questions about past conduct.

Why replacing leaders may not deliver peace

Congo's political dilemma also reaches beyond Kabila and M23. In Kabemba's assessment, the country faces a choice between entrenched political power and armed groups seeking influence through force. Neither route necessarily produces legitimate or accountable government.

Peace negotiations frequently bring powerful participants together because they have the ability to stop fighting. Yet that practical necessity contains a risk. An agreement may reward the possession of political or military power without creating stronger institutions to constrain its future use.

The result can be a recurring cycle. Those who obtain authority become dependent on the factions that supported them, while citizens remain without reliable mechanisms for holding leaders accountable. Agreements change the balance of power, but not necessarily the rules governing it.

For a population living with insecurity and poverty, the most important test of any settlement is not simply who signs it. It is whether the agreement creates a credible

path towards functioning institutions, public oversight and political participation without violence.

Resources raise the stakes

Congo's mineral wealth complicates this struggle. Cobalt, copper and coltan are strategically valuable, creating commercial and political interests that extend far beyond the country's borders. Where governance is contested, competition over resources can become inseparable from competition for influence.

It would be simplistic to attribute the entire conflict to minerals alone. Leadership disputes, insecurity and regional relationships also play important roles. Nevertheless, decisions about who controls valuable resources can affect which political actors attract support and how alliances develop.

For South Africa, the lesson is not that engagement with Congo should end whenever political loyalties change. Regional stability and the protection of civilians remain important objectives. The lesson is that diplomatic relationships need continuous scrutiny, clear strategic goals and a willingness to ask difficult questions, even of former partners.

Kabemba's most consequential observation is that shifting allegiances carry a human price. The lasting question is whether those exercising power will ever be held responsible for that price.

References

· CheckPoint: The Podcast, Nkepile Mabuse in conversation with Dr Claude Kabemba, 22 October 2026. Source transcript, particularly the exchanges at approximately (00:00–02:36), (12:43–14:41), (17:14–20:25) and (23:24–25:54).

World.title: Woman accused of staging own kidnapping remains in custody
World.content:
KWA-THEMA - The case against a woman accused of staging her own kidnapping in an attempt to extort R40,000 from her cousin has been postponed to 29 October for bail application.

The 37-year-old woman made a brief appearance before the Kwa-Thema Magistrate’s Court on Thursday, where she faces charges of defeating the ends of justice.

Her co-accused, a man believed to be her accomplice, appeared in absentia since he has been detained in hospital.

Gauteng National Prosecuting Authority (NPA) spokesperson, Lumka Mahanjana said the man sustained injuries during his arrest.

“The state intends to oppose the accused person's release on bail. However, today, because it was a short appearance, the matter was postponed to the 29th of October for bail investigations, and also for the co-accused who is currently in hospital to join this accused,” she said.

Mahanjana said at this stage, they cannot delve into evidence against the accused because the docket still needs to be disclosed to the defence.

However she mantained that the state has a strong case against the accused.

The woman was reported missing by her family on 7 October, amid the discovery of women’s bodies in various parts of Ekurhuleni.

Her alleged captors demanded R40,000 for her safe return.

Her family also received threatening messages and a video showing her naked and injured, pleading with her mother for help.

The woman was dropped off near a cemetery on 10 October.

Investigations subsequently raised suspicions that the kidnapping had been staged.

World.title: Carrim to spend another weekend behind bars
World.content:
MUSINA - The vehicle smuggling case against controversial businessman Suliman Carrim has been postponed to 30 October for a formal bail application.

Carrim made a brief appearance at the Musina Magistrate’s Court on Thursday.

His lawyer argued that the bail application should proceed, saying Carrim has a constitutional right to apply for bail at his first court appearance.

READ | Carrim expected in court over alleged vehicle smuggling

But the court cited a congested roll and a lack of capacity as reasons for the delay.

Prosecutors are expected to add him as an accused in two cases involving vehicles allegedly taken across the Beitbridge border using fraudulent documentation.

Carrim is already facing charges under the Commissions Act for repeatedly failing to appear before the Madlanga Commission.

World.title: New local govt policy aims to improve service delivery within 18 months - Hlabisa
World.content:
JOHANNESBURG - South Africans could begin to see changes in municipal service delivery within the next 18 months under a revised local government policy.

President Cyril Ramaphosa is expected to unveil the new White Paper on Local Government in Boksburg on Thursday, as government moves towards a new approach to municipal governance and service delivery.

Cooperative Governance and Traditional Affairs Minister Velenkosini Hlabisa, along with Cabinet colleagues and other local government stakeholders, is discussing the policy ahead of its official launch.

Hlabisa said the timing is significant, with new municipal councils expected to take office following the November local government elections, including several municipalities likely to be governed through coalition arrangements.

READ | Ramaphosa to unveil revised White Paper on local government

He said the process will begin with the constitution of new councils, followed by an induction programme for councillors in January.

The minister said the first 90 days of the transition will be used to identify key areas requiring change, with the aim of ensuring that the White Paper delivers visible improvements within a relatively short period.

“This is the right timing for the White Paper because we are launching a new approach in the local government space and how services must be delivered, and this comes at a time when we are going to have new councillors.

“We are going to have a 90-day transition period. In the 90 days, we are going to identify key things that must change so that the White Paper can be seen bringing change within a short space of time.

“And thereafter, 18 months, which is one year, six months, in that period, people of South Africa must start to feel the change.”

World.title: Joburg Water warns of possible contamination in Bezuidenhout Valley
World.content:
JOHANNESBURG - Johannesburg Water has warned of possible water contamination in Bezuidenhout Valley following repairs to a damaged pipeline.

The pipeline was repaired on Wednesday after a tree stump fell onto it during excavation work by a contractor replacing a sewer pipe.

The bulk water supplier said it was collecting water samples for laboratory testing to ensure the water met the required quality standards.

Residents have been advised not to use the water until further notice.



“An alternative water supply will continue to be provided while restrictions remain in place. Johannesburg Water will notify affected customers once laboratory tests have confirmed that the water meets the required quality standards and normal water supply can safely resume,” it said.

The affected areas include 8th Avenue and the intersections of 4th, 5th, 6th and 7th streets.

World.title: England and France face do-or-die clash at Rugby League World Cup
World.content:
LONDON - England hooker Brad O'Neill says there is a "real belief" the team can pull off a convincing victory over France on Saturday to keep their Rugby League World Cup hopes alive.

After being stunned 30-12 by Tonga in their tournament opener, the world number three must beat the French in Perth and by a big margin.

Only two of the six nations across Pools B and C from the 10-team tournament in Australia, Papua New Guinea and New Zealand progress to the final four.

"Despite the result, I feel like the way that we wanted to play was on show," said Wigan star O'Neill. "There was just maybe a bit of lack of execution, and credit to Tonga's defence as well.

"But I felt like the way we wanted to play was shown and we've just got to keep working on that.

"There is a real belief in our team."

On paper, England should have little problem, winning their last 23 meetings with France.

Coach Brian McDermott has kept faith with the squad that faced Tonga, naming an unchanged side for the Pool B clash.

France, who also need a big win to stay alive after crashing 78-4 to Samoa in an abysmal display, appear to have little hope.

But fullback Arthur Mourgue is adamant they can improve.

"We do have speed and some great forwards but compared with top-quality nations we are still a bit under them," he said. "But we're not going away."

After a mid-week pause, round two of the World Cup gets underway on Friday in Sydney with Tonga looking to build on their England upset when they face Lebanon.

Tonga playmaker Isaiya Katoa said the result might have surprised outsiders, but not within the squad.

"Within our four walls, we had that belief already," he told reporters.

"We understand the potential of this group and I think internally we've just got a bit of a quiet confidence about us."

Papua New Guinea take on Samoa at home in the other Pool B clash with confidence high after thrashing Lebanon 42-18 to get their tournament started.

Holders Australia face Fiji in Brisbane on Saturday, with the Pacific islanders currently topping Pool A after a dominant 40-12 win over the Cook Islands.

The 12-time champion Kangaroos are fresh from a thrilling 24-22 win over New Zealand in the World Cup's opening game, and coach Kevin Walters has shuffled his starting side with James Tedesco, Bradman Best, Sam Walker, Blayke Brailey and Lindsay Smith all coming in.

New Zealand are looking to bounce back against the Cook Islands in Christchurch without star fullback Kalyn Ponga who has a broken arm, opening the door for Keano Kini to start.

World.title: Tesla profits fall on higher spending as 'Elon Inc.' talk builds
World.content:
NEW YORK - Tesla reported lower third-quarter profits as near-trillionaire Elon Musk's electric vehicle maker ramped up huge investments in artificial intelligence and other envelope-pushing technologies.

Besides marginally lower car sales, Tesla saw a drop in revenues from regulatory credits and energy and storage, while spending on research and development more than doubled as the company engages in a spending binge on AI, robotics and autonomous transport.

The earnings were arguably upstaged by Musk's disclosure Tuesday that special committees of independent directors at both SpaceX and Tesla have been set up to discuss a merger of the two companies. Musk, who leads both companies, declined to offer further details Wednesday.

The potential merger -- which some have dubbed "Elon Inc." -- boosted shares of both companies on Wednesday, lifting Musk's wealth back near $1 trillion at $989 billion, according to Forbes' real-time billionaires index.

In the third quarter, Tesla reported profits of $787 million, down 42.7 percent from the year-ago period. Revenues were essentially flat at $28 billion.

Analysts had been cautious about Tesla's latest results heading into Wednesday's release.

While third-quarter auto sales topped estimates, due in part to an uptick in European markets amid high gasoline prices, better sales have not always translated to Tesla's bottom line.

The company has faced questions about the rollout of Tesla's robotaxi venture that has progressed much more slowly than hoped.

Musk has repeatedly made overly rosy forecasts about self-driving technology, as in 2019 when he predicted there would be more than a million robotaxis the following year.

In Texas, where Tesla has focused its robotaxi launch, there are currently about 800 robotaxis, according to FSD Database.

Tesla's release highlighted the September 3 launch of robotaxi service in Austin and said "cumulative unsupervised Robotaxi miles grew eightfold quarter over quarter."

Company officials said Wednesday that if the current pace of robotaxi growth continues, the venture could be meaningful financially as early as next year. The ramp-up is guided by a strong desire to avoid safety problems, company officials said.

For much of this year, Tesla has also encountered scrutiny over swelling capital spending to fund ambitious programs in artificial intelligence, robotics and autonomous driving.

Capital spending more than doubled in the third quarter to $4.7 billion, but the company lowered its capital spending plans compared with earlier in the year.

Chief Financial Officer Vaibhav Taneja, who in July had projected 2026 spending of more than $25 billion, said Wednesday the company expects to spend $20 billion, adding that the company managed "our capital deployment efficiently."

That is still more than double Tesla's 2025 capital budget of $8.5 billion.

Besides robotaxi and AI, Tesla is heavily investing in Musk's "Optimus" humanoid robots as well as the buildout jointly with SpaceX of a large chip factory in Austin.

The chip factory, called Terafab, was the object of some of Musk's most effusive and self-boosting language on Wednesday.

"Terafab I think will be the most valuable building in the world, and will probably have an economic value that will place it in the top 20 of countries," he said.

Musk is also eyeing auto growth, projecting production of five million in 2030 compared with 1.7 million in 2025.

"After many years of sort of grind and things being fairly flat, I think we're now headed for a lot of fun and significant growth," Musk said.

- Looming SpaceX merger? -

But questions about Tesla's future loomed larger with talk of the potential SpaceX tie-up. The companies have a combined equity value of more than $3.5 trillion.

"We think it's a matter of when, not if" the two companies combine, said CFRA Research equity analyst Garrett Nelson.

"That's the whole issue," Nelson said of a potential megadeal. "Tesla as we know it today may not exist in six to 12 months."

On SpaceX's conference call Tuesday night, Musk said the committees have not agreed on the terms of any deal and there is no guarantee they will.

Musk said the two companies could gain from working together on AI software, chip design, robotics and space-based computing.

Talk of the deal heaps additional attention on Musk as the billionaire's latest cash infusion into US political elections fuels fresh criticism. Musk has steered at least $276 million to allies of President Donald Trump in the Republican Party.

Musk is also under scrutiny over a report he ordered a reduction in Starshield telecom services for Ukraine, adding to pressure on the country at the same time Trump has criticised Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and called for him to be replaced.

Shares of Tesla initially rose in after-hours trading, but were down 3.3 percent near 0050 GMT.

World.title: Ruto hands over COMESA chairmanship, pushes for levy to fund regional programmes
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

President Ruto and Zimbabwean President Emmerson Mnangagwa during the handover of the Common Market for Eastern and Southern Africa chairmanship at the bloc’s 25th Summit of Heads of State and Government in Harare, Zimbabwe, on Thursday, October 22, 2026. [PCS]

President William Ruto has handed over the Common Market for Eastern and Southern Africa (COMESA) chairmanship to Zimbabwean President Emmerson Mnangagwa.

Ruto took over the one-year chairmanship from Burundi’s President Évariste Ndayishimiye at the 24th COMESA Summit in Nairobi on October 9, 2025.

His tenure focused on using digital technology to deepen regional integration, expand trade and promote inclusive growth.

He handed over the role on Thursday, October 22, during the 25th Comesa Summit of Heads of State and Government in Harare, Zimbabwe, where he urged the regional bloc to fast-track a market levy to finance its programmes and institutions.

“We cannot be ambitious in our plans and timid in our financing. Every programme we agree upon must be matched by the resources to deliver it. Otherwise, our communiqués will promise what our budgets cannot pay for,” Ruto said.

He urged the Comesa Secretariat to fast-track Article 168 of the COMESA Treaty, which provides for the Comesa Market Levy, as the organisation seeks sustainable and predictable financing.

The treaty establishes the levy to generate resources for financing the bloc’s activities.

Ruto said officials from finance ministries, central banks and other relevant agencies would meet to consider a draft COMESA Resource Mobilisation Strategy aimed at strengthening member states’ ownership of regional programmes and finding new ways to raise funds.

He called on member states to make financing central to their discussions, warning that the bloc’s institutions and integration agenda would depend on their ability to fund agreed commitments.

“Can we finance what we commit, and deliver what we finance?” he asked.

Ruto also urged African countries to channel more of their domestic financial resources into African institutions rather than leaving funds in foreign accounts while development projects lack capital.

He said Africa holds more than $4 trillion in domestic financial assets, arguing that regional financial institutions could mobilise more of these resources to support trade, infrastructure and development.

Ruto named the Trade and Development Bank (TDB), the African Trade and Investment Development Insurance (ATIDI) and ZEP-RE among the institutions that could mobilise capital for regional priorities.

He urged African governments to place more reserves with these institutions, finance more projects through them and support their bonds and guarantees.

The outgoing Comesa chairperson said the bloc needed stronger regional value chains and more trade among member states as global supply chains faced disruption and protectionism returned.

“Regional integration is no longer a dream we discuss. It is an economic and strategic necessity,” he noted.

Ruto said Comesa’s economic growth rose from 5.6 per cent in 2024 to 6.4 per cent in 2025, while inflation fell from 31 per cent to 13.2 per cent.

Exports among member states increased by 10.5 per cent to $14.7 billion, their highest level between 2020 and 2025, while exports to global markets rose by 6 per cent to $212 billion, he said.

He argued that African countries needed to process more raw materials locally instead of exporting them and importing finished products.

“To every partner who seeks our minerals, our markets and our young workforce, our offer is clear: invest with us, process with us, build with us,” Ruto added.

He called for partnerships based on mutual benefit and equal treatment, saying African countries should have a greater role in determining how their resources and markets contribute to economic development.

World.title: Judge certifies fresh bid to jail Sakaja, Charles Kerich over Sh76.7m debt as urgent
World.content:
Nairobi Governor Johnson Sakaja. [File, Standard]

The High Court has certified as urgent a fresh application seeking to have Nairobi Governor Johnson Sakaja, former Finance Executive Charles Kerich and two other county officials jailed over an alleged breach of a court-approved payment plan in a Sh106.7 million legal fees dispute.

Justice Francis Gikonyo certified the application by Kwengu & Company Advocates seeking to reinstate a three-month jail sentence previously imposed on Kerich and hold Sakaja, current Finance County Executive Committee Member Ibrahim Auma Nyangoya and Chief Officer for Finance Asha Abdi accountable for the alleged failure to pay Sh76.7 million.

World.title: Kenya confirms third Ebola case
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Kenya has confirmed a third case of Ebola involving a 65-year-old woman who is a close relative of the first two patients.

The Ministry of Health, in a statement, said the woman developed a fever, sore throat and malaise while in quarantine, prompting her isolation and testing.

Her samples tested positive for Ebola at both the National Virology Reference Laboratory and the Kenya Medical Research Institute (KEMRI).

According to the Health Director-General Patrick Amoth, the patient has been transferred to an infectious disease unit, where she is receiving supportive care and being monitored.

“Having been in quarantine, she was diagnosed early and is currently receiving supportive care, improving her chances of recovery while limiting the risk of further spread of the disease,” the statement read.

The second patient, on the other hand, is in stable condition and responding well to supportive care.

The latest case brings the number of confirmed Ebola infections in Kenya to three.

According to the Ministry, of the 130 contacts identified so far, 127 had been traced and placed in quarantine, with efforts ongoing to trace the remaining three.

World.title: Motorists, households face fresh fuel price hikes
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

EPRA attributed the price increases to the escalating conflict in the Middle East. [FIle, Standard]

The Energy and Petroleum Regulatory Authority (EPRA) has increased fuel prices, raising the cost of super petrol by Sh12.93 per litre, diesel by Sh9.90, and kerosene by Sh28.49.

The new prices, effective from October 15 to November 14, 2026, will see motorists in Nairobi pay up to Sh226.96 per litre for super petrol, Sh227.76 for diesel, and Sh219.85 for kerosene.

EPRA Director-General Edward Mwirigi Kinyua attributed the price increases to the escalating conflict in the Middle East, which has disrupted petroleum supply chains and driven up the cost of importing fuel.

The rise in kerosene prices is likely to hit low-income households that rely on the fuel for cooking and lighting.

Meanwhile, higher diesel prices could raise the cost of transporting goods and operating public service vehicles, potentially driving up fares and commodity prices.

Diesel is a key fuel for the country's freight transport sector and a significant portion of public service vehicle operations, meaning the increase could have a ripple effect across the economy.

The latest review comes after EPRA maintained pump prices during the September 15 to October 14 pricing period, despite a decline in the cost of importing petrol.

World.title: Oburu Oginga to leave hospital soon - ODM
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

ODM SG Catherine Omanyo criticised bloggers spreading unverified information about the veteran politician.

ODM Secretary General Catherine Omanyo has dismissed social media reports about the health of party leader Oburu Oginga, saying he is recovering well and is expected to be discharged from hospital either today or tomorrow.

Omanyo criticised bloggers spreading unverified information about the veteran politician, accusing them of exploiting his health condition to attract online attention and increase engagement.

“It's unfortunate what I've been reading on social media. Those people who are seeking to have more likes or viewers, they will be disappointed because he's up, he's well, he's fine. In fact, he's headed home either today or tomorrow,” she said.

Omanyo insisted that the reports had exaggerated his situation, dismissing claims of his death and assuring the public that he was doing well.

She noted that health conditions could fluctuate, saying Oburu's position as ODM party leader had made his well-being a subject of heightened public interest.

“Everybody, everybody, including you and me, our health is not static. You can be under the weather any time. It's just that he's a party leader, and it makes breaking news,” Omanyo said.

She urged social media users to exercise restraint when discussing the health of public figures, warning against spreading unverified reports, particularly claims of death, before confirmation from credible sources.

Her remarks come amid growing speculation on social media about Oburu's health, with some users circulating unverified claims about his condition.

World.title: Kenya declares Ebola a formidable epidemic disease, sets new rules
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Health Cabinet Secretary Aden Duale, who declared Ebola caused by the Bundibugyo virus a formidable epidemic disease under the Public Health Act. [File,Standard]

Kenya has declared Ebola virus a formidable epidemic disease, introducing new rules governing screening, isolation, quarantine, contact tracing and the handling of bodies.

Health Cabinet Secretary Aden Duale issued the declaration through a legal notice published in the Kenya Gazette on Monday, October 12, under Section 35 of the Public Health Act.

The declaration follows Kenya’s confirmation of its first imported case of Bundibugyo Ebola virus disease on October 6, after a Kenyan citizen who had been living in the Democratic Republic of Congo travelled through Uganda to Nairobi. The patient died despite receiving supportive treatment.

The case prompted health authorities to trace people who may have come into contact with the patient and strengthen screening at points of entry.

In an update on October 12, the World Health Organization (WHO) said Kenya had listed 127 contacts, with 94 in quarantine, and screened more than 665,000 travellers at points of entry.

WHO also supplied protective equipment and testing materials worth about US$70,000 to support the response.

The government published two legal notices on October 12. Legal Notice No. 203 declares the disease a formidable epidemic, while Legal Notice No. 204 establishes the Public Health (Ebola Disease) Rules, 2026.

The regulations provide for screening at points of entry, medical assessment, isolation, referral, quarantine and monitoring.

They also assign responsibilities to transport operators, health facilities, medical practitioners and laboratories.

Health authorities will conduct investigations and contact tracing, while designated health facilities will manage suspected and confirmed cases. The rules also provide for the inspection and decontamination of premises.

The regulations cover the safe and dignified disposal of bodies, burial procedures, record-keeping, transportation and repatriation. They also address public communication, media houses’ responsibilities in public sensitisation and assistance from enforcement agencies.

The rules provide for offences and penalties, although the Gazette extract does not specify the penalties for individual violations.

What the declaration means

Bundibugyo virus disease is a form of Ebola that spreads through direct contact with the blood or other bodily fluids of an infected person or contaminated materials.

Contact with the body of someone who has died from the disease can also expose people to infection during unsafe burial practices.

Symptoms can include fever, fatigue, muscle pain, headache and sore throat, followed by vomiting and diarrhoea. The incubation period ranges from two to 21 days.

WHO says no approved vaccine or specific treatment currently exists for the Bundibugyo strain, making early detection, isolation, supportive care and contact tracing central to controlling its spread.

The health agency has advised against travel or trade restrictions on Kenya, Uganda and the Democratic Republic of Congo based on the information available.

The new rules establish a legal framework for managing the disease, from identifying suspected infections and monitoring contacts to caring for patients and preventing exposure during burials.
