World.title: Liberia’s Billion-Dollar Budget: 0.58% for the Capital’s Public Schools
World.content:
Monrovia — Thousands of students in school uniforms marched on Liberia’s legislature on Tuesday, chanting “We want to learn too.” They were protesting months of disruption in the public schools of the capital, Monrovia, where unpaid teachers have repeatedly walked out of classrooms.

By Rodney D. Sieh

The students’ anger has a paper trail. Liberia’s own 2026 budget documents show that the Monrovia Consolidated School System (MCSS), which runs the city’s public schools, receives US$7.23 million. That is 0.58 percent of a national budget the government celebrates as the largest in the country’s history.



The same documents show that schools in the system get US$65,000 a year for educational materials — less than they get for stationery. They also show that three-quarters of the money recorded as the system’s capital spending last year was booked against an airport, a Finance Ministry headquarters and electoral reform.

A billion-dollar milestone

Liberia, a West African nation of about 5.2 million people, is still rebuilding from 14 years of civil war that ended in 2003. Its national budget crossed US$1 billion for the first time this year. Lawmakers approved US$1.25 billion for 2026, up 41.9 percent from the year before, according to an analysis by the budget-monitoring group BudgIT.

President Joseph Boakai’s development plan, known as the ARREST Agenda, names six priorities. The “E” stands for education. The “A” stands for agriculture, which receives about 1.19 percent of the budget even though the Agriculture Ministry’s own target is 10 percent.

The Monrovia Consolidated School System was created by law in 1964 to run public schools in the capital and surrounding communities. Families who cannot afford private fees depend on it. It is where the gap between budget promises and classroom reality is easiest to see.

“Our patience must not be mistaken for weakness”

Tuesday’s march, organized by the MCSS Students Union, lasted more than two hours. It followed a 24-hour ultimatum that expired the same day. Students gathered between the University of Liberia and the Capitol, the seat of the legislature, and handed lawmakers a petition with four demands.

They want the government to carry out a March 27 agreement with the school system on teachers’ pay and status. They want an investigation into alleged intimidation of student leaders. They want the dismissal of an assistant superintendent, Emmanuel Kyne Robertson, whom they accuse of disrupting classes and threatening students. And they want a bigger school budget and more transparency in how it is spent. The allegations have not been independently verified.

“Our patience must not be mistaken for weakness,” the union wrote, “and our commitment to peace must not be used to justify continued inaction while students’ education remains at risk.”

The House of Representatives read the petition in plenary and gave its education and petitions committees one week to report back.

Hours after the march, the government said it would add the remaining 201 volunteer MCSS teachers to the national payroll from October. That brings the number of verified MCSS volunteers absorbed to 409. Back pay is promised one week after October salaries. Teachers’ demands for higher pay were deferred to a government-wide salary reform, for which no date was given.

Where the money goes instead

Education receives US$136.3 million in 2026, or 10.9 percent of the budget. Security and rule of law receive US$154.9 million, about US$18.6 million more than education. Debt service takes US$230 million, 1.7 times the entire education sector.

Capital spending tells a similar story. Of the US$289.7 million set aside for investment projects, education gets 5.3 percent. Roads and energy together take about 61 percent.

Then there is the legislature. The draft budget gave lawmakers US$51.7 million, up from US$41.3 million in 2024. Their travel, goods and services line alone rose to US$14.6 million.

Put differently: the legislature’s running costs for travel and supplies are 38 times what the capital’s public schools get to run their classrooms for a year.

Stationery over science

The school system’s own pages in the 2026 budget book show how little reaches the classroom.

Salaries take 67 percent of the MCSS budget. Capital projects take 28 percent. Everything needed to actually run schools — books, chalk, cleaning, repairs, fuel — gets 5.3 percent, or US$380,000 for a whole year.

Within that sliver:

• Educational materials: US$65,000, down 35 percent from US$100,000 in 2025. That is less than the US$70,000 budgeted for stationery.

• Laboratory supplies: US$5,000 for every science lab in the system, cut from US$25,000.

• Generator fuel: US$54,500, up from US$2,000 — a 27-fold increase. It now nearly equals the entire budget for learning materials.

• ⁠

The outlook gets worse, not better. The government’s own projections cut the system’s operating budget by another 44 percent in 2027, to US$212,112. Educational materials would fall to US$36,282.

The budget also files every dollar of the school system under a single program: “Administration and Management.” There is no separate line for teaching.

The system’s payroll of US$4.85 million covers 1,088 staff, an average of about US$372 a month. That figure includes non-teaching staff. The budget keeps that headcount frozen through 2028, even as hundreds of volunteer teachers are added to the payroll.

An airport, a ministry and an election law

The most striking entry is on page 294 of the budget book. It lists the school system’s estimated capital spending for 2025 at US$388,691.

Only US$94,320 of that — 24 percent — is labeled as school renovation. The remaining US$294,371 is recorded under projects with no apparent link to schools: electoral legal reform (US$117,865), support for small and medium enterprises (US$84,306), a new Finance Ministry headquarters (US$82,135) and an upgrade of Robert International Airport (US$10,065).

The budget book contradicts itself. Elsewhere it records the system’s 2025 capital spending as US$320,150, all on furniture and fixtures, and none under the investment plan at all.

The entries may reflect a coding error rather than diverted money. But either way, the official record of what Liberia spent on its capital’s schools cannot be trusted as published.

For 2026, the budget promises US$2 million for renovating and furnishing MCSS schools. The system’s own list of 2025 achievements, however, claims only that it completed the procurement process to renovate four campuses — not the renovations themselves.

A school system running on volunteers

In December, Finance Minister Augustine Kpehe Ngafuan returned to his old school in Monrovia and announced a 60 percent increase for the capital’s schools, including a US$2 million fund to fix them. On paper, the promise holds: the MCSS budget rose from US$4.52 million to US$7.23 million. Take out the US$2 million capital line, much of it not yet delivered, and the increase is about 16 percent.

The teacher shortage the students are protesting is national. The Education Ministry says Liberia relies on 6,198 volunteer teachers who work without government salaries. In October, the ministry said it had removed more than 1,000 teachers who had abandoned their classrooms from the payroll. Lawmakers have also pressed officials over the U.S.-dollar portion of teachers’ salaries, unpaid since October 2025.

A mid-year supplementary budget, approved in May, added US$7.25 million for education. About 73 percent of it goes to closing payroll gaps and absorbing volunteers — paying for the past rather than building classrooms. MCSS received US$514,510. That includes US$200,000 for its volunteer teachers, roughly US$995 for each of the 201 now being added.

That money is fragile. About nine of every ten dollars in the supplementary package came from the World Bank, not Liberian revenue. BudgIT warned that moving volunteers onto the payroll creates permanent salary costs a one-off top-up cannot sustain. Meanwhile, the government projects total spending will fall to US$1.02 billion in 2027.

The largest share of that mid-year package — 27.8 percent — went not to schools or clinics but to public administration. It included an ambassador’s residence lease in Accra and Independence Day celebrations.

Who lives on the budget

The students did not cite budget codes on Tuesday. But their demands — pay the teachers, fix the classrooms, show where the money goes — line up closely with what the government’s own figures reveal.

The pattern echoes agriculture. A government that puts farming first in its slogan gives it about 1 percent of the budget. A government that puts education among its pillars gives the capital’s public schools less than 1 percent, and less for learning materials than for stationery.

The House committees have until next Tuesday to report on the students’ petition. The salary reform teachers were promised has no start date. The 2027 budget, now being prepared, is projected to be smaller.

For the students who marched, the question is simpler than any budget table. When a country spends US$1.25 billion in a year, why are they still waiting for a teacher to show up?

World.title: MoE staff urged to make cleanliness an everyday work culture
World.content:
Ministry of Education Permanent Secretary for Administration, Noriana Muneku, has implored the ministry staff to make cleanliness an everyday work culture rather than limiting it to national commemorations.

Ms Muneku says cleanliness should be embraced as a way of life rather than a temporary activity, stressing that everyone has a role to play in keeping the environment clean.

Speaking during a cleaning exercise at the Ministry’s premises in Lusaka today ahead of Zambia’s 62nd Independence Anniversary, Ms Muneku emphasised that the ministry’s surroundings should remain clean and presentable at all times.

Ms Muneku urged the administration department to take the lead in maintaining high standards of cleanliness, stressing that staff must demonstrate their commitment through consistent action.

And Lusaka Mayor, Chitambala Mwewa, called on members of the public to take responsibility for maintaining cleanliness around their premises and trading in designated market places.

Mr Mwewa expressed concern over the disposal of plastic waste into drainage systems, which he attributed to trading activities conducted in undesignated areas.

He said traders should operate from markets to promote proper waste management and ensure that business activities are conducted in appropriate environments.

Mr Mwewa further called for high standards of cleanliness along the road between the Ministry of Education and the Ministry of Finance, saying the area should be spotless.

He urged the public to support efforts to relocate traders to designated markets, emphasising that the initiative represents a permanent change in the way trading and environmental cleanliness are managed.

World.title: Govt. recommits to reforming Zambia’s pension system
World.content:
Government has reaffirmed its commitment to reforming Zambia’s pension system to expand coverage, strengthen regulatory oversight and improve retirement income security, particularly for workers in the informal sector.

Speaking at the official opening of the 2026 Annual Pension Conference, held under the theme “Building Sustainable Pension Innovation, Governance and Policy Reform,” Ministry of Labour and Social Security Secretary Zachariah Luhanga said pension reforms were essential to safeguarding workers’ contributions, enhancing benefits and positioning pension funds to contribute to national economic development.

Mr Luhanga said government remained committed to building a sustainable pension system that protects members’ savings, provides adequate retirement income and supports families in old age.

“Pension is more than a monthly payment,” the Permanent Secretary said, describing retirement benefits as recognition of workers’ years of service and sacrifice.

Mr Luhanga added that pension funds could also contribute to economic development by directing capital towards productive sectors, including infrastructure, housing and capital markets.

“The true measure of success is when the system protects members, provides adequate retirement benefits and reaches those who need it most,” Mr Luhanga said.

The Permanent Secretary also highlighted government’s ongoing efforts to improve the pension system through legislative reforms.

He further identified digital technology as an important tool for modernising pension administration, reducing operational costs and improving access to information.

Mr Luhanga, however, warned that technological advancement must be accompanied by strong data management, cybersecurity safeguards and adequate protection of members’ personal information.

He reiterated government’s commitment to expanding pension coverage, particularly among workers in the informal sector, many of whom remain outside formal pension arrangements.

Speaking earlier, Pension and Insurance Authority Registrar and Chief Executive Officer, Namakau Ntini, called for stronger governance, greater transparency and expanded pension coverage to ensure a sustainable retirement system capable of protecting contributors and supporting national economic development.

Ms Ntini stressed that pension systems could no longer rely on traditional approaches alone, particularly as demographic changes increase the need for sustainable retirement planning.

On governance, the Registrar emphasised the importance of competence, accountability, effective risk management and transparent investment decisions in protecting contributors’ savings and maintaining public confidence in pension institutions.

She said strengthening governance structures was essential to addressing weaknesses in pension administration and ensuring that the interests of contributors and retirees remained central to industry operations.

And Zambia Association of Pension Funds (ZAPF) Chairperson, Collina Halwampa, urged pension industry to embrace innovation, strengthen member engagement and promote policy dialogue to ensure the long-term sustainability of pension schemes amid changing membership demographics.

Meanwhile, Pan African Fund Managers Association Programme Manager, Oguche Aguda, called for reforms in pension systems to ensure retirement income security, promote sustainable contributions and channel pension funds into investments capable of driving economic growth.

Mr Aguda, said pension administrators and regulators must strike a balance between innovation, investment security and the long-term sustainability of retirement savings.

He also urged stakeholders to pay greater attention to younger workers, saying pension systems must become more relevant and understandable to younger generations to encourage early and consistent contributions.

World.title: Petauke senior citizens, freedom fighters receive hampers
World.content:
Senior citizens and freedom fighters in Petauke District have received assorted hampers from the District National Events Committee (DNEC), with support from Dealer’s Corner Millers. ‎

The gesture, which is part of this year’s Independence celebrations, is an appreciation gesture, also aimed at enabling beneficiaries to share in the country’s Independence celebrations.

The hampers were presented by Petauke District Commissioner Wachepa Phiri, who said the initiative was intended to share the Independence spirit with less privileged members of society.

‎

‎ “To share the Independence celebration with others who are not as privileged as some of us might be,” he said.

‎

Meanwhile, Dealer’s Corner Millers Director Ibrahim Phiri said the donation was part of the company’s Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR).

‎

‎Mr Phiri said he valued the partnership and support from the public, which had contributed to the growth of his business.

‎

‎ “We are a Christian nation, so with the little we have, we thought of sharing,” he said.

‎

‎Meanwhile, 83-year-old Alifat Tembo said the gesture reminded him of the celebrations in the early days of Zambia’s Independence.

‎

‎ “With this parcel you have given me, I am reminded of the old days and reassured that we are still remembered. Government should continue to remember freedom fighters,” he said.

‎

‎Another senior citizen, Esnart Mbewe, thanked the organisers for the gesture and appealed for continued support towards senior citizens and freedom fighters.

‎

‎ “I am grateful that you have helped me during this year’s Independence celebration. As a parent, I feel that you have truly thought of me. The honour and respect you have shown us are greatly appreciated. May this continue,” she said.

The hampers included mealie meal, cooking oil and salt, among other items.

World.title: Chama commends Luanshya council for CDF projects
World.content:
Cabinet Office Permanent Secretary for Special Duties, Fumba Chama, has commended Luanshya Municipal Council for implementing community-driven projects under the Constituency Development Fund (CDF).

Mr Chama said the council has demonstrated that implementation challenges could be overcome through effective leadership and collaboration among government institutions.

Speaking after touring selected CDF projects in Luanshya District, he cited the ongoing rehabilitation of sewer lines in Roan constituency as an example of the fund responding to community needs.

“What we’ve seen here is exactly that CDF is supposed to achieve development that is conceptualised by the local people, prioritised by the local people and then funded by the local people,” he said.

Mr Chama said the sewer problems could have gone unnoticed at national level without community involvement in identifying development priorities, adding that the intervention reflected President Hakainde Hichilema’s vision of placing communities at the centre of development.

However, he expressed concern that some completed health facilities remained non-operational because of staffing and accommodation challenges.

Mr Chama urged district authorities to plan for staff accommodation and other operational requirements alongside the construction of health facilities.

“I’ve spoken to the TC, I’ve spoken to the DC and challenged them to sit with the people that are working on these projects and let’s have houses for the staff that should be working there,” he said.

He said communities should not be denied healthcare services because accommodation for health workers had not been provided.

Meanwhile, Kafubu Water and Sanitation Company Manager Felix Nsonde disclosed that 350 metres of damaged sewer pipes had been replaced and more than one kilometre of blocked sewer lines cleared under the CDF-supported sanitation works.

He said the intervention had relieved communities where sewage previously flooded residential surroundings.

The manager said vandalism of manhole covers remained a major challenge, as debris entering the sewer system during the rainy season caused repeated blockages.

He added that the company was raising manholes and installing protective covers to prevent further blockages.

Mr Chama praised the council’s collaboration with Kafubu Water and Sanitation Company, describing it as a practical demonstration of the One Government approach.

He said the Cabinet Office was conducting monitoring visits across the country to assess the actual impact of CDF projects on communities beyond reports submitted by implementing institutions.

“This trip to Luanshya was basically to be eyewitnesses of what CDF is doing,” he said.

Mr Chama said the monitoring exercise had revealed both successes and challenges, adding that the Government would continue reviewing areas requiring improvement to ensure the fund delivered its intended benefits.

World.title: BoZ donates laundry equipment to UTH Adult Hospital
World.content:
The Bank of Zambia (BoZ) has donated industrial laundry equipment valued at K1.5 Million to the University Teaching Hospital (UTH) Adult Hospital to strengthen infection prevention and improve patient care.

The donation comprises two sheet ironers, two hydro extractors, three industrial pressing machines and two industrial digital scales.

Speaking during the official handover ceremony in Lusaka today, Ministry of Health Permanent Secretary of Donor Coordination, George Sinyangwe, said the donation demonstrated the important role of partnerships between public institutions in strengthening the country’s healthcare system.

Dr Sinyangwe noted that good health is both a contributor to national development and an outcome of development, adding that a country could not achieve meaningful development without a healthy population.

“Laundry services are essential in controlling the spread of infections and promoting patient safety in health facilities,” he said.

Dr Sinyangwe commended the bank for extending its corporate social responsibility efforts to the health sector and encouraged other public and private institutions to support similar initiatives.

He also urged UTH management to ensure that the equipment was properly installed, maintained and accounted for to maximise its benefits.

Speaking at the same event, Bank of Zambia Deputy Governor-Administration, Rekha Mhango, said a clean and well-maintained hospital environment is important in reducing healthcare-associated infections, supporting patient recovery and improving the working conditions of healthcare professionals.

Ms Mhango said the donation is part of the central bank’s corporate social responsibility initiatives aimed at supporting communities and improving people’s welfare.

She noted that good health is an important pillar of economic development because a healthy population strengthens human capital, improves productivity and reduces the financial burden on the government.

“We trust that this equipment will contribute significantly to improving laundry services at the hospital and support your continued efforts to provide quality healthcare in a clean, safe, and dignified environment for all patients,” she added.

And UTH Adult Hospital Senior Medical Superintendent, Charles Mbewe, said the equipment would improve laundry services and contribute to maintaining a clean and safe hospital environment.

Dr Mbewe said laundry services are an essential component of healthcare delivery because they help control the spread of infections and ensure that hospital textiles are properly cleaned and processed.

He thanked BoZ for the donation, describing it as an investment in patient safety, comfort and the overall quality of healthcare services.

Lusaka District Commissioner and Chairperson for UTH Adult Hospital Facelift Taskforce, Rosa Kayuni expressed gratitude to the Bank of Zambia for supporting the government’s efforts to improve healthcare delivery.

She said the K1.5 Million donation of laundry equipment is a significant contribution to the ongoing UTH facelift project and a demonstration of government’s commitment, under the leadership of President Hakainde Hichilema, to improving the country’s healthcare system.

World.title: Stammering Association calls for increased awareness on stammering
World.content:
Stammerers Association of Zambia Programmes Coordinator, Shepherd Mwanza, has called for increased public awareness and support for people who stammer to help them overcome stigma and build confidence in communication.

Mr Mwanza says people who stammer often face challenges in schools, workplaces and public settings, where they may be subjected to ridicule or discrimination because of their speech difficulties.

Speaking during the International Stammering Awareness Day at East Park Mall in Lusaka today, Mr Mwanza said the association is working to sensitise the public and provide encouragement to individuals and families affected by stammering.

“We are here to bring awareness to society and to offer help to people who stammer,” he said.

He stated that the association was also committed to linking parents of children who stammer with speech therapists and other support services to help them manage the condition.

Mr Mwanza, who also experiences stammering, called for engagement with school authorities and employers to ensure that people who stammer were not disadvantaged in education and employment opportunities.

Meanwhile, Stammering Association of Zambia Executive Secretary, Jacob Kwanwa, has urged people who stammer to seek support, adding that the association is committed to helping them overcome communication challenges and build confidence.

Mr Kwanwa said there was a need to educate the public about stammering and the challenges faced by people who experience the condition.

“We want people who stammer to know that we are there for them and that they can reach out to us for support,” he said.

The International Stammering Awareness Day is commemorated annually on October 22 to raise awareness about stammering and promote understanding and support for people who experience the speech condition.

World.title: President Hichilema arrives in Zimbabwe for COMESA Summit
World.content:
President Hakainde Hichilema has arrived in Harare, Zimbabwe where he is attending the 25th COMESA Summit of Heads of State and Government.

President Hichilema arrived this morning at nine hours, local time and was welcomed by Zimbabwean Minister of Finance, Mthuli Ncube and Zambia’s Minister of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation, Mulambo Haimbe.

Zimbabwean Ambassador to Zambia, Charity Charamba was also among other dignitaries who welcomed the Head of State.

Shortly after arrival, the President inspected a Guard of Honour, Mounted by Zimbabwe’s defence force, before proceeding to the New Zimbabwe Parliament building where the Summit is taking place.

This year’s Summit is being held under the theme “One Market, One Future: Advancing Inclusive Industrialisation, Investment and Regional Integration in COMESA”.

The President joins several other Heads of State and their representatives from 21 COMESA member states at the meeting.

During the Summit, President Hichilema and other leaders will witness the handover of the Chairmanship of the Bureau of the COMESA Authority from Kenyan President, William Ruto, to the Summit host, Zimbabwe’s Emmerson Mnangagwa.

Zambia, which houses the headquarters of COMESA, has held the rotating Chairmanship of the COMESA Authority twice, since its establishment in 1994.

President Frederick Chiluba was Chairperson of COMESA from 1997 to 1999. In 2023 when Zambia hosted the 22nd COMESA Summit, President Hichilema took over the position, succeeding President Abdel Fattah El-Sisi of Egypt.

President Hichilema last attended a COMESA Summit at the 23rd COMESA Heads of State and Government Summit in Bujumbura, Burundi, on October 31, 2024, where he handed over the chairmanship to President Évariste Ndayishimiye.

The 25th COMESA Summit will focus on deepening regional integration, inclusive industrialisation and value addition, leveraging digitalisation as well boosting intra-regional trade and investment.

Another area of focus includes empowering women and youth by integrating them into cross-border economic networks and regional supply chains.

On the sidelines of the Summit, President Hichilema is expected to hold bilateral talks with other member countries on mutually beneficial matters.

The Head of State is later today expected to return to Zambia, at the conclusion of his engagements

World.title: 17 hospitalised over suspected well poisoning
World.content:
Seventeen people, including a 10-month-old baby, have been admitted to Lundazi District Hospital following suspected water poisoning in Chasefu District.

Lundazi District Hospital Acting Medical Superintendent Chota Phiri confirmed that the victims presented with abdominal pain and diarrhoea but were in stable condition.

Dr Phiri said the patients allegedly drank water from a community well suspected to have been contaminated with a poisonous substance.

He said a team of toxicologists was conducting tests on water and human samples to establish the cause of the incident.

The person suspected of contaminating the well, which reportedly affected about 38 people, is also receiving treatment after allegedly ingesting the suspected poisonous substance.

One of the victims, Oscar Zimba, told the media from his hospital bed that he saw one of his relatives hurriedly leaving the community water point on Monday evening.

Zimba said when the relative was confronted, he allegedly ingested the substance suspected to have been used to contaminate the well.

The suspect is among those admitted to Lundazi District Hospital.

The admitted patients include 10 children, two men and seven women.

By press time, police had not yet issued a statement on the incident.

World.title: Duo arrested over smuggled South African vehicle

Two Beitbridge men have been arrested for allegedly smuggling a vehicle from neighbouring South Africa.

Korombi Muleya (29) and Elelwanni Mbedzi (36) were arrested on October 18 by members of the Zimbabwe Republic Police (ZRP) Support Unit deployed in Beitbridge under Operation “No to Cross Border Crimes”.

World.title: WHO says weak studies holding back new TB tests
World.content:
By THE World Health Organisation (WHO) has flagged new tuberculosis (TB) diagnostic studies as weak, incomplete, and inconsistent to inform policy decisions.

This emerged as the world health body published its first guidelines on how such evidence should be gathered.

The document, Guidance on Evidence Generation for New Tuberculosis Diagnostics, sets out what researchers, test developers and funders must do if their work is to inform WHO recommendations on new TB tests, sample types and testing strategies.

World.title: Shumba takes basketball leadership fight to High Court as FIBA demands fresh BUZ elections
World.content:
JOHNSON Shumba has gone to the High Court in a bid to hold on to his position at the Basketball Union of Zimbabwe, setting up a collision with FIBA, which has told the association to hold fresh elections to end its leadership dispute.

In a letter dated 19 October, FIBA said the co-presidency arrangement agreed after Shumba and David Pick tied in the last elections no longer has the support of all parties. The world governing body noted that the BUZ constitution provides for a single president serving a four-year term, and directed the association to hold fresh elections in line with that constitution and the position of the Sports and Recreation Commission.

World.title: Navaya closes in on Golden Boot as Scottland trio lead chasing pack
World.content:
HARDROCK FC striker Washington Navaya is closing in on the Castle Lager Premier Soccer League Golden Boot after taking his tally to 17 goals at the end of Matchday 31, opening up a five-goal lead over his nearest challengers.

With the season entering its closing stages, Navaya is firmly in the driving seat, with Herentals College forward Ralph Kawondera and Dynamos striker Frank Agyemang his closest rivals on 12 goals apiece.

Kawondera and Agyemang face an uphill task to catch the Hardrock marksman, who has established a commanding advantage with only a handful of matches remaining.

World.title: Senegal: General Strike Continues Amid Protests Against New Labour Laws
World.content:
Dakar — Senegal's labour unions have called for a 72-hour general strike, from October 21 to 23, 2026. The government disputes the legality of the strike, saying the notice filed by the unions doesn't comply with the procedures. This standoff comes amid ongoing tensions surrounding the reform of the Labor Code and the Social Security Code.

The confrontation between the government and the trade unions has entered a new phase. At the call of the Trade Union Front for the Defense of Labor (FSDT) and the mobilized trade union federations, workers are invited to observe three days of strike action to protest, in particular, against the conditions under which the new labor and social protection laws were adopted.

For several months, unions have been denouncing a process they deem insufficiently consultative. On July 10, the FSDT had already announced a general strike to express its opposition to the approach taken by the authorities. Despite this protest, the two texts were promulgated on September 3, 2026, under laws no. 2026-18 and no. 2026-19, before their publication in the Official Journal on September 18th.

A disagreement over the legality of the movement



Faced with this new call for mobilization, the Ministry of Public Service, Labor, and Public Service Reform considers the strike order unlawful. According to information reported by PressAfrik, the administration contests the use of a single strike notice to cover the public, semi-public, and private sectors, which are subject to separate procedures.

In the private and semi-public sectors, the Labor Code stipulates that the dispute must be notified to the Labor and Social Security Inspector or the relevant Director General, as applicable. If no agreement is reached, or in the event of partial conciliation, a thirty-day notice period may then be given to the company's management.

For civil servants, the ministry reminds them that written notice must specify the reasons for and duration of the strike, with one month's notice given before the action begins. Local government employees, for their part, must notify the president of the departmental council or the mayor concerned of their strike notice.

The administration warns that failure to comply with these formalities may result in salary deductions for days not worked and disciplinary action. It also mentions potential consequences for the right to compensation and damages in the event of termination of the employment contract.

For more, read the original story in French.

World.title: Ethiopia: Drone Strikes Kill Schoolchildren in Amhara, Civilians in Tigray Regions As Conflicts Show No Sign of Abating
World.content:
Addis Abeba — Drone strikes in Ethiopia's Amhara and Tigray regions killed schoolchildren and other civilians on Tuesday, 20 October, according to eyewitnesses and local residents who spoke to Addis Standard, adding to mounting civilian casualties amid renewed fighting between federal forces and armed opponents in both regions.

In South Gondar Zone of Amhara, a drone strike hit Sana Elementary School in Dera Woreda, killing at least six schoolchildren and injuring more than 20 others, according to preliminary reports.

Separately, a drone strike in Finaruo village, in Saharti Samre Woreda of Tigray's Southeastern Zone, killed four people and injured six others as they loaded livestock onto a truck, local residents said.

The strikes occurred as drone attacks increasingly affect civilian areas and infrastructure in both regions, raising fresh concerns about civilian protection amid expanding aerial warfare.



In Amhara, the strike on Sana Elementary School occurred between 10:00 and 11:00 a.m. on Tuesday, 20 October, in Sana Kebele, according to preliminary accounts. The injured children were taken to a local clinic, although their conditions were not immediately known.

Casualty figures remain uncertain. While initial reports put the death toll at six, other accounts circulating publicly have reported between seven and ten students killed and more than 25 wounded. Addis Standard could not independently verify the total number of fatalities.

An elementary schoolteacher who spoke to Addis Standard disputed claims circulating on social media that the strike targeted a nearby hideout used by Fano armed groups.

"This was a school with more than 150 students attending the morning shift; there was no armed people in the school or nearby," the teacher said. "There was not conflict in nearby areas. Many of our students came back to school after three- or two-years interruptions. We don't know why the school was targeted."

The teacher said more than 20 students had been wounded and that parts of two classrooms had been damaged, adding that the full extent of the destruction had yet to be assessed.

Videos circulating on social media showed parents rushing into the school compound and carrying children away as pupils fled in different directions. Some children appeared disoriented, while teachers attempted to direct them to safety. Others could be heard calling for the wounded to be taken for medical treatment.

Alemtshay, whose name has been changed for security reasons, told Addis Standard that her 11-year-old son, Dagim, had stayed home that morning because he was unwell.

"He was having fever and was down with a terrible cold. I was pushing to go to school because he has already missed two years of school due to the war and school closures," she said.

She recalled hearing screams from the neighborhood around 10:30 a.m., during the school's tea break, before families began rushing their injured children to a local clinic.

"It was a complete chaos; mothers were crying and wailing," she said. "When we heard there was a bomb dropped from a helicopter, some men started to go around shouting for people to not leave their houses because they were afraid there might be another attack."

Reflecting on her son's absence from school, she added: "I was unhappy when my son failed to go to the school but now, I know God was protecting him."

In Tigray, the strike in Finaruo occurred at around 9:00 p.m. on Tuesday, 20 October, while a group of people were loading livestock onto an Isuzu truck, according to residents who spoke to Addis Standard.

Four people were killed, including the livestock owner and three people assisting him, while an unspecified number of animals also died, the residents said.

"What is most distressing is that the three of them were close relatives who were helping the owner," one resident told Addis Standard.

The six injured people were taken to different hospitals for treatment. Three were admitted to Samre Hospital, while the other three, who sustained severe injuries, were taken to Ayder Comprehensive Specialized Hospital in Mekelle, according to the residents. Some of the wounded were aged between 13 and 17.

One resident said there had been no military movements involving either federal forces or Tigrayan forces in the area in the days preceding the attack.

"It has been almost days since the town was free of military movements from both sides," the resident said.

The latest attack follows a series of drone strikes in Tigray that have killed and wounded civilians and damaged schools and humanitarian infrastructure. The attacks have continued amid renewed fighting between Ethiopian federal forces and Tigrayan forces, which intensified on 23 September.

Earlier this month, a drone strike reportedly hit a shelter housing internally displaced people (IDPs) in Shiraro, in Tigray's Northwestern Zone, killing nine people and wounding 14 others, including a newborn baby. In Adwa, in the Central Zone, residents reported civilian deaths after drone strikes hit several locations in the city, although the exact toll could not be independently verified.

Other reported drone attacks have damaged residential neighborhoods, hotels, schools and media facilities. In September, a drone strike destroyed a Catholic Relief Services truck carrying more than 41 metric tons of food assistance intended for an IDP camp in northwestern Tigray. The United States condemned the attack and called for a transparent public investigation.

The renewed fighting follows the breakdown of the November 2022 Pretoria Cessation of Hostilities Agreement, which ended two years of devastating war in Tigray, and a sustained drone attacks . The latest escalation has displaced tens of thousands of people, with humanitarian organizations estimating that at least 150,000 people have been displaced across Tigray and neighboring Afar.

Close 

In Amhara, federal forces have been fighting Fano armed groups since 2023, with drone strikes becoming a recurring feature of the conflict. Previous attacks reported by Addis Standard have hit residential areas, health facilities and religious sites, causing civilian casualties and damaging civilian infrastructure. The army has also targeted fighters on their own side killing at least 40.

In July this year, a drone strike on Saint Kirikos Monastery drew condemnation from the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church and the World Council of Churches, which called for impartial investigations. Earlier attacks have also killed children and other civilians in residential communities across the region.

The two latest strikes on Tuesday underscore the risks facing civilians as Ethiopia's conflicts increasingly involve aerial attacks by federal forces in populated areas.

Addis Standard could not independently establish the circumstances of either strike, determine the intended targets or obtain an official response from the Ethiopian military.

The casualty figures in both regions remain subject to independent verification.

World.title: Kenya: Kenya Searches for Missing Ugandan Contact As Ebola Cases Rise
World.content:
Kenyan authorities are searching for a Ugandan national who came into contact with the country's first Ebola patient in Nairobi, as the number of confirmed cases linked to the initial cluster rises to nine.

Kenya's director general of health, Patrick Amoth, says authorities have been unable to locate the contact case, despite having his passport and telephone numbers.

The man is suspected of having crossed the border using an unofficial route to avoid border checks, Amoth said on Tuesday. Ugandan authorities have been notified.

The current Ebola outbreak was first declared in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) in mid-May.



On Tuesday evening, Kenya announced a ninth case. Nairobi said it was "still linked to the first cluster". The patient is being held in isolation, along with the other 129 people identified as contacts by health authorities.

Earlier this week, the United States State Department advised Americans to reconsider travel to Kenya and raised its travel advisory level for the country because of health risks.

A race against time to prevent an outbreak follows Kenya's first Ebola death

Quarantine centre concerns

The authorities maintain that the situation remains under control, but their handling of the outbreak has come in for criticism.

Opponents accuse the government of a lack of transparency in its response.

"It is clear that quarantine centres are turning into incubation units for the Ebola virus," said David Maraga, a former chief justice and candidate in Kenya's 2027 presidential election.

After days of pressure, the doctors' union was included in the national Ebola response task force on Tuesday.

France earmarks a further €7m to help fight DRC's worst-ever Ebola crisis

Regional threat

Nigeria on Tuesday became the latest country to be affected by the recent Ebola outbreak, when a woman who arrived from Uganda around two weeks ago was diagnosed in the capital Abuja.

Health Minister Muhammad Pate said authorities had begun tracing 44 people identified as contacts of the patient and were "doing everything possible to contain this case".

Caused by the rare Bundibugyo strain of the virus, for which there is no approved vaccine or treatment, the outbreak has killed at least 4,600 of the 9,500 people affected in DRC.

However, drug trials suggest there may be "reasons for hope". The first clinical trial of a potential vaccine is expected to begin by the end of October, the World Health Organization said on 13 October.

Close 

Nigeria Ebola case matches DR Congo strain

Uganda recorded 20 cases and two deaths before declaring the outbreak over in its territory in late August.

Jean Kaseya, head of Africa CDC - the African Union's health agency in charge of disease control and prevention - warned on Tuesday of "an extremely serious threat" and called for international mobilisation.

France in June confirmed a positive case of Ebola in a doctor traveling back from DRC, making it the only country outside Africa so far to have recorded a case in the current outbreak.

World.title: Rwanda: Rwandans in France Decry Unresolved Genocide Case of Ex-French Captain
World.content:
The Rwandan Community of France (CRF) has criticised French justice authorities for failing to bring former French gendarmerie captain Paul Barril to justice over allegations of complicity in the 1994 Genocide against the Tutsi.

Barril died on Tuesday, October 21 at the age of 80. The former head of the anti-terrorism unit at the Élysée Palace was accused of maintaining close ties with Rwanda's interim government during the Genocide that claimed more than one million lives. In 2013, French prosecutors launched an investigation into the allegation.

ALSO READ: Ex-French captain faces probe over Genocide

In a statement on Wednesday, the CRF said Barril died without being tried over allegations that he helped sustain the government responsible for the Genocide.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

The CRF said his death should not end efforts to establish the facts surrounding his alleged activities and the role of other individuals who may have been involved.

"This outcome constitutes a serious failure in the search for truth and accountability," the statement said.

ALSO READ: Safari Madjaliwa: Who is the Genocide suspect facing trial in France?

The community also called for an examination of the obstacles that hampered investigations into Barril's activities, including difficulties accessing archives that could have shed light on his dealings with Rwandan and French officials.

It further questioned whether Barril had received any form of protection that prevented the allegations against him from being fully examined in court.

"How can we accept that accusations of such gravity were never examined in a trial?" the statement asked.

His death ends the criminal proceedings against him personally, but the CRF insists that efforts to establish the truth must continue.

The community called on French authorities to make relevant archives accessible and ensure that investigations into other possible perpetrators and accomplices are not abandoned.

Complaint filed in 2013

In June 2013, three French human rights organisations, the International Federation for Human Rights (FIDH), the French Human Rights League (LDH) and Survie, filed a complaint against Barril over his alleged complicity in the genocide.

The complaint, lodged at the Tribunal de Paris, concerned allegations that Barril had entered into an agreement with Jean Kambanda, then prime minister of Rwanda's interim government, to provide arms, ammunition, military training and supervision.

The organisations sought to establish whether his alleged assistance had contributed to the interim government's efforts to remain in power as the genocide unfolded.

Close 

The complaint led to the opening of a judicial investigation, paving the way for an independent inquiry into the allegations. However, Barril died without the case reaching trial.

In 2013, Rwanda's then National Commission for the Fight against Genocide (CNLG) welcomed the investigation. Its executive secretary at the time, Jean de Dieu Mucyo, and then Ibuka president Jean-Pierre Dusingizemungu described the move as an important step towards justice.

Dusingizemungu, however, said accountability should extend beyond Barril to other French officials who held senior military positions during the Genocide.

Barril's alleged involvement had attracted attention following reports about a military assistance contract signed with Kambanda on May 28, 1994, after the United Nations had imposed an arms embargo on Rwanda.

French media also reported that a letter dated April 27, 1994, from then Rwandan Defence Minister Augustin Bizimana requested weapons and 1,000 mercenaries to help the interim government fight the Rwandese Patriotic Front (RPF).

The allegations concerning the supply of arms, mercenaries and military assistance have remained central to questions about Barril's activities during the genocide.

The CRF said that, more than three decades after the Genocide against the Tutsi, victims and their families were still owed the truth.

"Paul Barril's death must not close the case," the community said, urging French authorities to pursue every available avenue to establish responsibility and ensure accountability.

World.title: Africa: Are Bilateral Ties the Route to Renewed West African Security Cooperation?
World.content:
Chiefs of Staff of the Armed Forces of the Alliance of Sahel States (AES) - Mali, Burkina Faso, and Niger. (File photo)

analysis

Pending the outcome of ECOWAS-AES talks, cooperation between neighbouring states offers a starting point for rebuilding regional security ties.

Despite tensions between the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS) and the Confederation of Sahel States (AES), recent advances reflect a broader regional trend. In August, Ghana and Burkina Faso signed a defence agreement, while Mali and Côte d'Ivoire agreed to delimit their shared border.

The withdrawal of Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger from ECOWAS in January 2025 deeply fragmented West Africa's institutional architecture, but did not end cooperation between individual states. Instead, relations are being pragmatically reorganised around countries' security priorities, mainly through bilateral deals. This shift has been underway since 2025 and offers a concrete way to manage divisions without waiting for ongoing ECOWAS-AES negotiations to produce a political agreement.

Across several ECOWAS-AES fault lines, states are reactivating or deepening bilateral cooperation frameworks, agreements, joint commissions, or operational mechanisms, some of which predate the current regional crisis.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Joint patrols launched by Senegal and Mali in the Kayes region in 2025 build on a cooperation framework established in 2021. Mali and Guinea's shared military commission met in April 2025 and June 2026, producing a memorandum of understanding that provides for intelligence sharing. And in August 2026, Ghana and Burkina Faso signed a defence pact after relaunching their Permanent Joint Commission for Cooperation and signing seven cross-border cooperation agreements.

These initiatives show that institutional fragmentation has not paralysed security cooperation altogether, even if the effectiveness of agreements is yet to be demonstrated. They also challenge the notion of a standstill, as bilateral mechanisms play an increasingly prominent role, enabling states to maintain or rebuild relations around their immediate security interests.

This window of opportunity should be maximised while ECOWAS and the AES negotiate a framework for future security cooperation. Talks could drag on, or even stall, given how politically and symbolically charged relations between the two blocs remain. Meanwhile, armed groups continue to exploit gaps in cooperation.

Rather than waiting for a new institutional agreement, regional actors and their partners could reverse the sequence. They could encourage states to cooperate where their interests converge, facilitate rapprochement where political tensions stand in the way, and over time, connect bilateral arrangements through flexible regional mechanisms.

Two of West Africa's border areas need priority attention.

The first is northern Benin, where jihadist groups exploit gaps in neighbouring countries' collaboration. Around the W-Arly-Pendjari complex, where Benin, Burkina Faso and Niger meet, violence remains intense. Further east, in the Benin-Niger-Nigeria triangle, weak coordination is enabling armed groups to expand. Discussions between Nigeria and Benin remain incomplete without Niger, and the rapprochement launched by Beninese President Romuald Wadagni during his June visit to Niamey has yet to reopen the border.

The second is the Sikasso-Korhogo-Bobo-Dioulasso (SKBo) cross-border area, where Mali, Côte d'Ivoire and Burkina Faso meet. Political distrust between Abidjan and Ouagadougou continues to hinder cooperation on the ground, and progress between Côte d'Ivoire and Mali has yet to translate into joint security efforts commensurate with the risks.

Other regional actors could help unblock cooperation in these priority border areas. The Conseil de l'Entente, which brings together Benin, Burkina Faso, Côte d'Ivoire, Niger and Togo, with Mali as an observer, already has a dialogue framework on security and border management. It could discreetly facilitate rapprochement among its members, particularly around the W-Arly-Pendjari complex and the SKBo area, in a format less exposed to ECOWAS-AES political tensions.

In the Benin-Niger-Nigeria zone, the African Union (AU) Mission for Mali and the Sahel (MISAHEL) could offer a complementary entry point. Its mandate, which will extend to Benin and Togo from 2027, and its AU affiliation independent of both ECOWAS and AES, make it well placed to facilitate dialogue among the three countries. The aim would be to gradually restore trust and help states identify concrete ways to restart joint security initiatives.

MISAHEL could share lessons from the Nouakchott Process, launched by the AU in 2013 to strengthen security cooperation in the Sahelo-Saharan region, with the priority border areas. Although the process is largely inactive, the mechanisms it promoted - intelligence sharing, cross-border coordination, joint patrols and regular exchanges between security officials - are precisely those that several states want to revive on an ad hoc basis in their bilateral cooperation.

This approach should remain flexible enough to adapt to the needs that states themselves identify. On one border, the main requirement may be restoring contact between military officials; on another, establishing intelligence-sharing protocols. Elsewhere, political conditions might allow states to go further, with more frequent joint patrols or more formal coordination between countries.

Close 

The goal would not be to replicate a regional mechanism, but to tailor these tools to the needs and possibilities specific to each border area. This variable-geometry approach is increasingly taking shape through the 'coalition of the willing' proposed by Ghana. Rather than waiting for a regional consensus that would require countries to progress at the same pace, the approach is moving towards implementation among states ready to move forward.

In the long run, an ECOWAS-AES framework could develop from working relations established on the ground, rather than from the top down through an institutional agreement. The resulting regional architecture may be less orderly than before, but more solid - precisely because it would be anchored in states' concrete security interests and their need to cooperate.
