Djiby Sow, Senior Researcher, ISS Regional Office for West Africa and the Sahel

World.title: South Africa: Black Market Weight-Loss Drug Sellers Are Moving Fast. South Africa's Regulators Are Struggling To Keep Up
World.content:
Why is South Africa struggling to stop the sellers of illegal weight-loss injections, and how can consumers tell whether the medicines they're buying are safe?

South African regulators have won an important court battle against a pharmacy making its own versions of popular weight-loss injections. But illegal and experimental drugs are still being sold openly, while new rules to crack down on the trade are months away. Why is the country struggling to stop the sellers — and how can consumers tell whether the medicines they're buying are safe?

South African pharmacies are allowed to make up medicines for patients with specific needs. But some are producing weight-loss injections in large quantities without the licences required to manufacture medicines.

In June, the Gauteng High Court ordered Tshwane-based compounding pharmacy iDexis to stop producing medicines containing semaglutide, the substance that makes Ozempic work.

Yet experimental weight-loss drugs such as retatrutide, which are still being studied and haven't been approved for sale anywhere in the world, are still being sold openly in South Africa.

Regulators say clearer rules for pharmacies that make their own medicines are on the way, but these are only expected by February or March 2027. The pharmaceutical industry warns that the delay gives illegal sellers more time to operate.

Australia has banned pharmacy compounding of weight-loss jabs, citing such drugs as "potentially unsafe and dangerous". So why are South African so-called compounding pharmacies still making their own versions of blockbuster weight-loss drugs such as Ozempic and Mounjaro , and selling them to the public?

The reality is that such activity is illegal in South Africa as well, at least in instances where the pharmacies make up copycat weight-loss jabs — which dampen appetite and make people feel full for longer — in large quantities, or use unregistered or illegally imported ingredients to make them.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

But as demand has soared, some pharmacies have turned the niche practice of compounding into a lucrative business. In June, the Gauteng High Court ordered iDexis, a compounding pharmacy in Tshwane, to stop producing medicine containing semaglutide — the active ingredient of Ozempic — after large quantities of compounded weight-loss jabs had been confiscated on its premises.

The court order was an important legal victory for the country's regulators, including the South African Health Products Regulatory Authority (Sahpra), Stavros Nicolaou , chairperson of the Pharmaceutical Task Group , an umbrella organisation for the pharmaceutical industry in South Africa, said during a panel discussion held in Sandton last week.

But he said the momentum built by the court order could be lost if Sahpra and the South African Pharmacy Council (SAPC) don't follow up on it quickly with clearer guidelines for compounding pharmacies about what they can, and cannot legally do. "You can go and win these court cases, and have people on the back foot, but all of that can unravel because we're just not acting swiftly enough as a country," he said.

Illegal drugs in plain sight

The panel gathered representatives from Sahpra and the SAPC, as well as the police service, border control, revenue service and the pharmaceutical industry, to explain to the public how they are working together to stop the trade in fake drugs.

Sahpra says it has received around 600 complaints so far this financial year relating to illegitimate and fake medicines being sold through informal supply chains, reaching the public via online portals, gyms, or even local hairdressers.

"We are worried that the scourge is getting out of control," said Daphne Fafudi , the body's head of regulatory compliance. And it's the public that can pay the ultimate price, she added. "People do die, and it doesn't even come to our attention," she said.

Some fake or illegitimate drugs are sold covertly. Others are traded in plain sight. One of them is retatrutide , a weight-loss injection that is still being tested in studies and therefore hasn't been licensed for sale by a drug regulatory anywhere in the world. Yet, it is sold "openly and brazenly" around the world, including in South Africa, said Nicolaou.

In the July episode of Bhekisisa 's TV programme, Health Beat, we reported how a Johannesburg woman's doctor sold her retatrutide, telling her it's safe because he "had it tested", while making her sign a waiver to release him of any responsibility for what might go wrong .

Earlier this year, a man reportedly died in the United States after taking injections sold as retatrutide on the black market — although the British Medical Journal said the evidence for the drug causing the fatality was "less clear cut" than media reporting suggested.

Nicolaou urged the police service and the Hawks to make an example of those who sell retatrutide in South Africa, as a deterrent to others. "The public needs to know that our enforcement agencies are actually enforcing the law," he told the meeting last week.

Vincent Tlala , CEO of the SAPC , said revised guidelines for compounding pharmacies were underway, a process Sahpra is leading, with input from the SAPC. However, Tlala said, these were not expected to be ready until February or March next year.

According to Nicolaou, this is too late. "The regulations are taking too long," he says. Regulators in other countries have introduced bans and restrictions on compounding pharmacies specifically for weight-loss jabs, to prevent the kind of products that have flooded South Africa. "Why are we not doing the same thing?"

What South African law says about compounding

Compounding medicines is lawful in South Africa, but only under specific conditions . Compounding requires a healthcare professional's prescription, generally for a formulation that is not available as a registered medicine — for instance, if a patient requires a medication as an oral liquid that is only normally sold as a pill.

As for compounding in bulk, the law says that a pharmacy may prepare stock in advance if they can show that patients regularly need the medicine — such as repeat prescriptions for the same person.

But some pharmacies produce large quantities without that evidence, Sahpra chief executive Boitumelo Semete-Makokotlela told Bhekisisa. This means "you're not compounding, you are manufacturing", which requires a good manufacturing practice licence that compounding pharmacies do not hold.

A good manufacturing practice licence shows that a company has met the safety and quality standards required to manufacture medicines.

A second concern is where ingredients come from. Active pharmaceutical ingredients — the substances in medicines that make them work — must be registered in South Africa and imported by a licensed entity, says Semete-Makokotlela. A pharmacy's operational licence does not authorise it to import unregistered ingredients, she says, yet some have arrived in travellers' luggage.

Another loophole that needs to be closed, Semete-Makokotlela notes, is where people sell experimental drugs (meds still being studied) or medicinal products directly to the public that are authorised for "research purposes" only. This includes some peptide products that are neither registered medicines nor experimental drugs in formal trials (like retatrutide), yet are still widely bought and sold as lifestyle or wellness drugs to do things like lower inflammation and boost energy.

Peptides are short chains of amino acids — small building blocks that the body uses to make proteins. Insulin is a peptide , as is semaglutide , the active ingredient in Ozempic. Both are registered medicines in South Africa.

However, there are other peptides, such as BPC-157 , which are being sold online and in gyms as solutions to specific health problems, such as tissue repair. These peptides aren't technically medicines, nor are they actively being studied in drug trials. Yet, they are sold as healthcare products, without evidence that they are safe or effective at treating humans.

Then there is the battle for public opinion, which is proving to be another hurdle. Semete-Makokotlela admits regulators are "on the back foot" when consumers see people losing weight while official warnings struggle to compete.

Close 

The answer, she believes, includes offering people registered alternatives at different prices — including cheaper generics — and working with healthcare professionals to steer patients towards safe, registered medicines.

South Africa's first generic weight-loss drug, containing semaglutide, hit the shelves in August .

How the public can keep safe

During the panel discussion, South African Revenue Service official Gene Ravele called the lack of coordination between enforcement agencies "the number one problem that organised crime is taking advantage of", and that this is also true for counterfeit and illegitimate drugs.

Border Management Authority head Nakampe Masiapato added that police detectives and prosecutors are often generalists, ill-equipped for specialised pharmaceutical cases. "They have no idea what this is about," he said.

For consumers, the advice from regulators is to use authorised channels and check that medicines are registered. Common signs that a drug is not legitimate is that it has unusual or blank packaging, no printed expiry date on the box or container, or that it doesn't have a normal insert detailing how to take it and the common side effects. Broken or dented packaging is another big 'tell', the Sandton meeting heard last week.

The bottom line is that a product's online availability, or a seller's claim that it is equivalent to a registered medicine, is not proof that it has been assessed or approved, said Fafudi. "If you cannot trust the source, do not trust the medicine."

This story was produced by the Bhekisisa Centre for Health Journalism.

World.title: Africa: All of Africa Today - October 22, 2026
World.content:
Cameroon Train Disaster Survivors Still Await Justice 10 Years Later

Ten years after Cameroon's deadliest rail disaster killed 79 people and injured more than 500, survivors are still dealing with serious injuries, while some victims have not received compensation and legal proceedings remain unresolved. The Camrail train derailed near Eseka on 21 October 2016 while travelling from Yaoundé to Douala. An investigation found that it was travelling at 96km/h in a section with a 40km/h speed limit. Overloading, defective brakes and the addition of extra carriages also contributed to the crash. Survivors continue to suffer from chronic pain and lasting disabilities. In 2018, Camrail and 11 employees were convicted of involuntary manslaughter and causing unintentional injuries. The company's former managing director received a suspended sentence, while other officials were also given suspended sentences. The train driver was sentenced to five years in prison. However, Camrail appealed the ruling, and the appeal has yet to be heard. Victims' lawyers say compensation has been inadequate, with some payments still outstanding.

Burkina Faso Restores Death Penalty Amid Crackdown on Critics

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Burkina Faso's unelected parliament has unanimously adopted a new penal code restoring the death penalty for offences including high treason, terrorism, espionage, parricide and importing expired or prohibited products. The death penalty for ordinary crimes was abolished in 2018. Human Rights Watch warns that reinstating capital punishment could further threaten civil liberties under the military junta, which took power in a 2022 coup. Authorities have restricted media outlets, suspended civil society organisations and unions, and targeted critics through arrests and enforced disappearances. The government said that the measure will help combat terrorism. Rights advocates argue that weaknesses in the justice system increase the risk of wrongful convictions and irreversible injustice.

Nearly 200,000 Zimbabweans Returned From South Africa

Nearly 200,000 Zimbabweans have returned home from South Africa amid anti-migrant protests and attacks targeting foreign nationals, according to the government. Cabinet was told that 197,294 people had returned, including 42,553 repatriated through government assistance and 154,741 who returned independently. The government deployed buses to collect stranded nationals, including those in Cape Town. The protests, involving groups such as Operation Dudula and March and March, have targeted Zimbabweans and other African migrants. Authorities said the number of returnees has declined but are continuing to monitor the situation. Zimbabwe is also screening deportees arriving from South Africa, including 700 people received from the Lindela Repatriation Centre.

Gambia to Compensate Victims With Proceeds From Jammeh's US Mansion

The Gambia's Reparations Commission has received more than US$2.57 million from the sale of a Maryland mansion belonging to former president Yahya Jammeh. The funds will be used to compensate victims of abuses committed during his more than two decades in power. US authorities secured the right to sell the property in 2022, arguing that it had been acquired using criminal proceeds and misappropriated public funds. Jammeh seized power in a 1994 coup and was accused of overseeing torture, forced disappearances, rape and extrajudicial killings. He lost the 2016 election to Adama Barrow but initially refused to step down. He eventually left office in 2017 and went into exile in Equatorial Guinea. A national inquiry found that he had amassed hundreds of properties and misappropriated more than US$300 million.

Latin American Drug Cartels Expand Operations Across Africa

Latin American drug trafficking organizations are expanding into Africa, using the continent as a transshipment point for cocaine and as a new production base for methamphetamine. Global demand is rising, and enforcement efforts are harder to maintain in the Americas, so criminal groups have tried to link up with African networks. Methamphetamine labs have been found in South Africa, Nigeria, Kenya, and Mozambique. It is still common for cocaine to travel through West Africa on its way to Europe. They generate revenue by engaging in money laundering and drug trafficking. They achieve this by capitalizing on corruption, porous borders, and a scarcity of police officers. Nevertheless, the drug trade is gaining popularity, which is a cause for concern as it undermines government institutions and results in a rise in crime, addiction, and violence. The authorities have increased the number of arrests and seizures. Experts warn that criminal networks will continue to thrive where oversight and law enforcement remain weak.

Close 

Kagame Urges Rwanda's Youth to Put Health Before Ambitions

Rwandan President Paul Kagame has called on the youth to prioritise their health and well-being as they chase their personal and professional aspirations. Speaking at a youth engagement event at BK Arena on October 21, he stressed the importance of developing healthy habits from childhood. Kagame warned against alcohol and drug abuse, saying such behaviours can worsen personal difficulties rather than solve them. He also encouraged young people to exercise, continue learning, work hard and make responsible decisions. He called on them to challenge harmful practices in their communities instead of allowing them to become normalised. Kagame said young people should recognise their potential, distinguish right from wrong and take responsibility for shaping their futures.

World.title: Nigeria: Ebola Outbreak - Lawmakers Move to Amend Nigeria's 100-Year-Old Quarantine Act
World.content:
A tent used to isolate Ebola patients is disinfected in Bunia, DR Congo (file photo).

The senators resolve to treat the proposed amendment as an urgent matter to strengthen the country's response to the Ebola outbreak and prevent further spread of the disease.

The Senate on Wednesday resolved to engage the presidency on the review of Nigeria's Quarantine Act to bring it in line with modern public health legislation and the International Health Regulations.

The Senate President, Godswill Akpabio, directed the Senate Committee on Judiciary to liaise with the executive arm of government and relevant health agencies to develop proposals for amending the law.

Mr Akpabio gave the directive during Wednesday's plenary while lawmakers debated a motion on the need to enforce mandatory health screening at all international airports and other entry points to prevent the spread of Ebola and other epidemic-prone diseases.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

The motion was sponsored by Francis Faduyile (APC, Ondo South).

Mr Akpabio said the proposed amendment should be treated as an urgent matter to strengthen the country's response to the Ebola outbreak and prevent further spread of the disease.

"We should take the issue very seriously and we should invite the Senate Committee on Judiciary to start contact with the health authorities in view to amending this Quarantine Act of 1926. This should be immediate, we should consult with the executive arm of government and all relevant agencies.

"We should not attempt to wait for them to bring an Act to us, we should go to them to get their inputs. That is what I think we should do in order to be able to nip this in the bud. Otherwise, if it spreads, there'll be a major problem."

Ebola case in Nigeria

Nigeria confirmed an Ebola case on Tuesday. The patient, a woman who recently arrived in the country on an international flight from Uganda, is receiving medical care in isolation at a private hospital in Abuja.

The Coordinating Minister of Health and Social Welfare, Muhammad Pate, said 44 people had been identified as contacts of the patient and that authorities were tracking them for monitoring and possible isolation.

Senate's resolutions

After Mr Akpabio's remarks, the lawmakers rejected a proposal for senators to visit the entry points through which the woman travelled before being isolated in Abuja.

Instead, the upper chamber urged the federal government to immediately release emergency funds from the Service Wide Vote to prevent the spread of the Ebola virus.

The Senate also urged the Federal Ministry of Health and Social Welfare, the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC) and the Port Health Services to make health screening compulsory for all international arrivals at airports, seaports and designated land borders.

Close 

The lawmakers called for enhanced screening of passengers who had been in or transited through affected areas within the preceding 21 days, regardless of their nationality or country of departure.

They further urged the Federal Airports Authority of Nigeria (FAAN) and the Nigeria Immigration Service (NIS) to ensure that all entry points were adequately staffed and equipped with trained port health officers, thermal scanners, protective equipment and isolation rooms.

World.title: Trump pushback, Biden 'disaster' and gender surprise: 5 key moments from Kansas Senate debate
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Sen. Roger Marshall, R-Kan., and Democratic challenger Adam Hamilton sparred over President Donald Trump, immigration, Iran, transgender athletes, artificial intelligence and personal controversies during a contentious Kansas Senate debate Wednesday night.

The hourlong showdown came less than two weeks before Election Day as Marshall seeks a second term and Hamilton, a longtime pastor, tries to become the first Democrat elected to the U.S. Senate from Kansas since 1932.

The race has drawn increased national attention as Republicans and Democrats battle for control of the Senate, with Trump traveling to Kansas earlier this week to campaign for Marshall â a topic touched on during the debate.

Here are five moments that stood out from Wednesday night's debate.

SLEEPER SENATE RACE EMERGES AS UNEXPECTED HEADACHE FOR REPUBLICANS AHEAD OF MIDTERMS

Debate opens with candidates confronted over personal controversies

The debate wasted little time getting contentious, opening with questions about controversies that have fueled attacks against both candidates.

Marshall was confronted with a New York Times review that found his former medical practice sued more than 700 patients over unpaid bills.

"Every year we gave away $3 to $4 million of charity, but we also had a business," Marshall responded. "We had 300 employees, we had a mortgage payment, we had electric."

Hamilton, meanwhile, was questioned about his handling of allegations involving a volunteer at his church's summer camp who was accused of sexual abuse.

Hamilton acknowledged that he should have ensured the individual did not return to the camp following an initial investigation.

FROM 'THIRD REICH' TO âNOT THAT INFORMEDâ: SENATE DEBATES DELIVER FIREWORKS BEFORE MIDTERMS

"I should have checked to make sure that he wasn't going back," Hamilton said. "That was a mistake on my part."

Marshall says 'President Trump is not always right'

Trump became part of the debate after moderators played footage from the president's campaign appearance for Marshall in Kansas earlier in the week.

"And at this election, I'm asking you to pretend, please, that I'm on the ballot. Just pretend," Trump told the crowd.

Marshall was then asked whether Trump's support meant Kansans should expect him to back every part of the president's agenda.

"No," Marshall responded, saying there had been "multiple times" when he objected to Trump.

Pressed to identify a specific disagreement, Marshall pointed to recent immigration enforcement in southwest Kansas and Trump's approach to beef imports.

"Just like with my wife, I can disagree with her. My wife is always right," Marshall joked. "And President Trump is not always right."

Marshall nevertheless urged Trump voters to turn out for him, arguing that electing Hamilton could help Democrats capture the Senate.

Both candidates say there are 'two genders'

The two rivals found themselves in agreement when the moderator asked each candidate how many genders there are.

"There's two. There's a boy and there's a girl," Marshall said. "I delivered 5,000 of them and almost half were boys and half were girls."

"There are two genders, male and female," Hamilton responded.

TOP TAKEAWAYS FROM JD VANCE TOWN HALL: COSTLY GAS, DC CORRUPTION, IMMIGRATION HOT TAKES AND THE WAR

The candidates then turned to the debate over transgender participation in women's sports.

Hamilton said decisions over athletic eligibility should generally be made locally but was unequivocal about whether biological males should compete against females.

"I have a 12-year-old granddaughter. I don't want biological men or boys competing against her that could harm her," Hamilton said. "It's not a fair, fair fight."

Marshall argued that by high school, "boys need to be in boys sports, girls in girls sports," while accusing national Democrats of pushing "transgender ideology."

Hamilton later accused Marshall of using the issue to "pick on" and "bully" people.

Hamilton calls AI an 'existential threat' â but can't name regulations he'd support

Hamilton called for greater federal oversight of artificial intelligence and compared the emerging technology to the development of nuclear power and nuclear weapons.

"We developed a Nuclear Regulatory Commission. We need to do the same thing with AI," Hamilton said.

But when the moderator pressed him to identify specific federal regulations he would support, Hamilton acknowledged he did not yet have an answer.

"You know what? I'm not sure, to be honest," Hamilton said, arguing that even experts are struggling to understand the technology's potential dangers.

Marshall advocated a "light touch" approach focused on national security, transparency, protecting children and privacy, while slamming a one-size-fits-all global order for artificial intelligence advancement.

Hamilton pushed back sharply.

"This is an existential â potential existential threat to the human race," Hamilton said. "We can't just go with a light touch and hope everybody does their best."

BIDEN CONSPICUOUSLY ABSENT FROM CAMPAIGN TRAIL AS OBAMA, HARRIS STEP UP FOR MIDTERM PUSH

Hamilton calls Biden's border policies a 'disaster'

Hamilton sought to put distance between himself and former President Joe Biden when moderators challenged the Democrat over his claim that he would "lead from the middle."

The moderator pointed to Hamilton's past donations to Democrats, including Biden, former Vice President Kamala Harris and Rep. Sharice Davids, D-Kan., before asking him to identify a progressive policy he opposed.

"The Biden policies when it came to the border were a disaster," Hamilton responded. "I believe in strong and secure borders."

"I'm not somebody who favors the Socialist Party," Hamilton added. "I'm somebody who stands in the middle."

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Hamilton also reiterated during the debate that he would not support Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer for majority leader if Democrats capture control of the chamber.

World.title: Slotkin's viral 'threat' to conservatives takes new twist as student moves to hold her accountable: 'Shocking'
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

FIRST ON FOX: Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.) is facing an ethics complaint filed to the United States Senate over comments she made earlier this month that many characterized as a "threat" to conservatives who are thinking about working for the Trump administration.

During an Oct. 13 University of Chicago event, Slotkin drew criticism after a clip went viral showing her saying she wants to pursue "signature cases" against people who "enabled" President Donald Trump and push a "deterrence message" for young people.

"I want young people coming out of school to say, 'Should I go work for the Trump administration? Like, that sounds fun, I might get an opportunity.' I want them to be like, 'Lord, that might be buying myself a ton of problems that I don't want, and so let me avoid participating in that,'" she said. "I want that deterrence message sent," Slotkin said.

Slotkin is now facing an ethics complaint filed Thursday by Michael Bicksel, a University of Chicago student who first reported her remarks. The complaint was submitted to the Senate Select Committee on Ethics and argues that Slotkin proposed using congressional investigations and potential prosecutions to frighten young people away from serving in a Republican administration.

FORTY-FIVE PERCENT OF COLLEGE STUDENTS SAY VIOLENCE CAN BE JUSTIFIED TO STOP HATE SPEECH, POLL FINDS

"Recently at an event at my college, the University of Chicago, Senator Slotkin laid out a legislative-oversight agenda that involved using the legal process to terrorize members of the Trump administration in order to âdeterâ young people from going to work for it," Bicksel wrote.

The complaint asks the committee to determine whether Slotkin's comments amounted to "improper conduct which may reflect upon the Senate," a standard described in the Senate Ethics Manual as applying to conduct that may be unethical even if it does not violate a specific law or Senate rule.

"As a college student and a conservative, this was a shocking thing to hear," Bicksel's complaint reads. "A prominent U.S. Senator came to my college and laid out a goal that I and my peers should be afraid to serve our country in the executive branch. This is well below the standard of conduct expected of a U.S. Senator and deserves investigation by the Senate Select Committee on Ethics and appropriate subsequent disciplinary action."

ELISSA SLOTKIN TELLS STUDENTS LIKE ME NOT TO WORK IN GOVERNMENT. DON'T LISTEN TO HER

Bicksel argued that Slotkin's comments were directed at students considering government service, rather than exclusively at people who commit crimes or engage in unethical conduct.

"The substance of the âdeterrence messageâ is clear as day," Bicksel wrote. "Her target was âyoung people coming out of schoolâ (like me and my classmates) who are debating whether they should âgo work for the Trump administration.â"

"We are obviously not debating â as she subsequently tried to clarify â whether to go commit crimes or behave unethically," he continued. "Those who commit crimes should be punished for doing so. No one disagrees with that. All we are debating is public service, pure and simple, and Senator Slotkin says we should think twice about doing so because it might provoke the full power of the United States Senate."

Slotkin, when pressed on the response to her comment on CNN, referred to the controversy as "manufactured outrage."

"I think the thing that I've heard from my own Republican colleagues and peers, including interns and folks who work around the Hill who come to our events, they'll tell you, âI was worried,â" Slotkin added. "My parents were worried, you know. It's really messy. I'm not sure what to get involved in.' Politics, in general, has become messy."

The Justice Department is currently facing calls to investigate Slotkin over her remarks, Washington Examiner reported on Wednesday.

Slotkin's communication director pointed Fox News Digital to a statement made by the senator on Tuesday when reached for comment.

"Now, if you take a breath, this is all pretty crazy. A president from the Oval Office is weaponizing our justice system against an American who clearly gets under his skin. And if he can do it to me, he can do it to anyone," Slotkin said. "His supporters use a coordinated play to threaten, intimidate, and silence anyone who speaks up. It's a play to distract us from his failed economy, high gas prices, and the disastrous war he started with Iran. But if I've learned one thing from this past year, it's that you have to push back."

World.title: Washington foster parents score legal victory after state demanded they use children's preferred pronouns
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

A Christian couple who spent more than a decade caring for foster children is celebrating a major legal victory after Washington state agreed to change its licensing rules following a dispute over requirements that foster parents use children's preferred pronouns and comply with gender identity policies, even when those requirements conflicted with their religious beliefs.

Shane and Jennifer DeGross told Fox News Digital in an interview Wednesday that the dispute began in 2022, when they attempted to renew their foster care license and discovered the state had changed its requirements concerning gender identity.

The couple said they were willing to love and care for any child placed in their home but could not agree to certain state-imposed requirements they believed violated their Christian faith.

"We were made aware that the state had updated and changed some of their requirements," Jennifer DeGross told Fox News Digital. "While we agreed that we would love and care for any child in our home, they had specific things that we could not agree to as Christians."

DOJ BACKS NUNS CARING FOR DYING CANCER PATIENTS IN FIGHT AGAINST NEW YORK TRANS IDEOLOGY MANDATE

Shane DeGross said the state required them to affirm the state's views on gender identity and human sexuality.

"Those views directly conflict with the biblical worldview of human sexuality," Shane DeGross said. "So, as Christians, we just couldn't accept that. Our allegiance is to God and the truth of Scripture. And we just couldn't abide by what they were requiring us to affirm."

Washington's licensing policies required foster parents to affirm and support LGBTQ children, including expectations concerning gender identity and the use of preferred names and pronouns. The DeGross family challenged the requirements on religious freedom grounds. Jennifer said the state eventually partially reinstated their license but restricted the ages of children they could foster.

AUTISM PROVIDERS WARN FOSTER KIDS AT RISK FROM UNINTENDED CONSEQUENCES OF TRUMP'S MEDICAID FRAUD CRACKDOWN

"We felt like even when they reinstated a partial license to us that they were still discriminating against us," she said.

"When a child reached 5, they had to be removed from our home," Jennifer said. "So not only was that upsetting to us, but that's not good for kids, right?"

Jennifer argued that such a restriction could disrupt a child's placement even if the child had already spent years living with a foster family.

PATRIOTS RB TREVEYON HENDERSON SLAMS STATE OVERREACH AFTER CATHOLIC FAMILY LOSES CUSTODY IN GENDER CASE

"If we had had a child for a couple of years, and then they have to be removed just because they turned or reached a certain age, it's definitely not in the interest of children," she said.

The legal battle resulted in a settlement under which Washington agreed to revise its foster care licensing rules, addressing the conflict between the state's gender identity requirements and foster parents' religious freedom claims.

Johannes Widmalm-Delphonse, senior counsel at Alliance Defending Freedom, told Fox News Digital that the DeGross' case should serve as a lesson for the rest of the country.

"These foster care agencies, they have to respect the First Amendment rights of foster parents, as well as the children in the system and everyone that they work with," Widmalm-Delphonse said.

"So, states should be on notice from this settlement, as well as some of the other cases that we've seen like the Bates v. Pakseresht decision, that they have to respect First Amendment rights, they have to respect free speech rights, and the way you do that is you invite as many foster parents into the system as possible on the front end, and then you match at the back end according to children's individual needs or family's abilities, comfort level, things like that, which is what they've been doing for decades, and this settlement shows that they can continue doing that now," Widmalm-Delphonse added.

WASHINGTON FATHER SUES SCHOOL DISTRICT FOR DENYING RELIGIOUS OPT-OUT FOR 5TH GRADER FROM LGBTQ INSTRUCTION

Widmalm-Delphonse said that since the settlement, Washington State has a new proposed regulation, WSR 26-20-103, currently undergoing the public notice and comment process which would in part give foster parents like Shane and Jennifer DeGross a religious exemption.

"This new rule, in part, would give foster parents like the DeGross's a religious exemption from any rule requiring them to violate their religious beliefs on gender or sexuality," Widmalm-Delphonse said.

Shane DeGross told Fox News Digital, "It's a great victory in the sense that more Christians can be available to love and care for foster kids without fear of being excluded because of their religious beliefs."

"It's a huge victory for kids that need a loving home," he added.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"We are proud of the diversity of our foster parent and kinship caregiver community who have different cultures, religious beliefs, and lived experience," the Washington State Department of Children, Youth, and Families said in a news release on the settlement. "We are grateful that they all open their doors and provide a loving home to children and youth in foster care."

"This settlement agreement respects the religious beliefs of foster parents, while ensuring LGBTQIA+ youth are placed in an environment that is safe and supports their well-being," DCYF Secretary Tana Senn said.

Fox News Digital reached out to the Washington DCYF for further comment.

World.title: 'The Terminal List' season two features new Kip Moore track inspired by special operations world
World.content:
Country music star Kip Moore dropped new music for the hit series "The Terminal List."

The popular series is based on a book series written by Jack Carr. It follows Navy SEAL James Reece on the hunt for revenge.

Season one came out in 2022 with Pratt playing the lead character. Season two premiered on Oct. 21, and is based on Carr's "True Believer."

'THE TERMINAL LIST' SEASON 2 FIRST PREVIEW DROPS WITH CHRIS PRATT RETURNING AS NAVY SEAL JAMES REECE

It also includes fresh music from Moore.

Kip Moore releases new song for season two of "The Terminal List."

Moore announced Wednesday on Instagram that he made a new song â "The Wolf" â for the second season of Pratt's series.

"I was on a surf trip in Central America in January of 2024 when I got a call from Jared Shaw, who I now consider a friend, about The Terminal List. I hadnât seen the first season at the time, but he asked if I'd read some of the scripts they were working on for season two and consider writing something for the main character. I immediately dove into season one and was hooked," Moore explained.

He continued, "I've always been fascinated by the world of special operations and I have a tremendous amount of respect for anyone willing to endure that level of training, and the sacrifices it takes. As I started reading through the scripts, I kept coming back to something Jared had scribbled in his notes: âIt's like the battle between two wolves.â"

"That idea really stuck with me. Iâve always been drawn to exploring the more complex, human side of those experiences rather than simply celebrating the heroism. I wanted to dig into the internal battles, the weight of what these individuals carry, and the toll those experiences can take on a person's mind and spirit. I tried to put myself in the character's shoes and write from that place, exploring what he might be wrestling with on a deeper level. That's really where âThe Wolfâ came from," Moore finished.

World.title: Leavitt opens up on helping Trump find new press secretary after Zacharia debacle: 'Was not for her'
World.content:

MANCHESTER, N.H. - Former White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt says she is helping President Donald Trump choose his next press secretary after his first pick for the job lasted just five days.

"I've offered my help to the president to help him select someone who can serve him and the country well," Leavitt said Wednesday evening in an exclusive interview with Fox News Digital.

Leavitt served as Trump's press secretary from the start of the president's second term until Aug. 27, when she stepped down from the demanding role to spend more time with her two young children, including a daughter who was born in May.

Her successor, political commentator Katie Zacharia, took over earlier this month, but lasted just five days in the role, making her the shortest-serving White House press secretary in U.S. history.

TRUMP'S NEW PRESS SECRETARY OUT OF A JOB JUST DAYS AFTER ROCKY DEBUT

"White House press secretary is a tough job. I know that because I did it, obviously for almost two years, and many people say it's one of the hardest jobs in politics," Leavitt emphasized.

She noted that the job "takes a lot of preparation and sometimes you don't know how someone will perform until they go out there."

"We wish Katie the best. The job obviously was not for her, but we wish her and her family well," Leavitt added.

When it comes to whom Trump will choose next for the position, Leavitt said the president "is continuing to look over options. There's a lot of people who want that job. It's an amazing job. It provides you with incredible opportunities."

SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER

Asked what advice she's offered to Trump, Leavitt said, "I'll keep my private counsel to the president private, but I do obviously talk to him about what the job entails, and he knows it very well."

"Nobody understands the press better than Donald Trump. He knows he needs someone who is tough, who is smart, who understands his policies, who is loyal, and who can go out there and put up a fight," she added.

Leavitt, a New Hampshire native, served as an intern in the Trump White House after graduating from Saint Anselm College in 2019. She later became an assistant White House press secretary at the end of Trump's first term.

After Trump's defeat in the 2020 presidential election, Leavitt worked as communications director for Republican Rep. Elise Stefanik of New York. She then served as spokeswoman for the Trump-aligned super PAC MAGA Inc. before taking over as press secretary for Trump's 2024 presidential campaign.

After being named White House press secretary following the 2024 election, Leavitt made history as the youngest person ever in the role.

World.title: LaMelo Ball gets away with egregious travel during Timberwolves season opener, immediately trash-talks fans
World.content:
If NBA referees called every travel they saw, games would never end, but blowing the whistle every now and again to remind players that they can't take an infinite number of steps would be appreciated by all involved. Unfortunately, the exact opposite precedent was set during the season opener between the Minnesota Timberwolves and Miami Heat on Wednesday.

LaMelo Ball put on an impressive performance in his official debut for Minnesota, scoring 21 points and dishing out six assists in his team's 131-106 victory on the road, but three of his 21 points should not have counted.

Just over three minutes into the first quarter, Ball dribbled around a well-set screen that got his defender off balance. Instead of driving towards the basket, he opted to pick his spot beyond the three-point line, but forgot to put the ball on the floor on his way there.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

Ball appeared to take every bit of four full steps without taking a dribble. The carry was so egregious that each of the announcers on the broadcast couldn't help but call out how bad the no-call was.

The 25-year-old guard immediately talking trash to some courtside fans after he made the three made the whole scene that much worse. Then again, Ball and essentially every other player in the league have gotten away with traveling with the basketball throughout their NBA careers.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW-UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Oftentimes, the missed travel calls take place with players driving to the basket and getting away with an extra half-step while carrying the basketball. For Ball not to get whistled while standing well beyond the three-point line is a bit of a surprise, even by NBA standards.

As for the contest itself, the Timberwolves looked as good and entertaining as expected with their new two-headed monster of Anthony Edwards and Ball in the 25-point win over Giannis Antetokounmpo and the Heat.



Edwards finished the night with 45 points, including nine made three-pointers, to go along with 10 rebounds.

While the duo of Ball and Edwards combining for 66 points stands out, maybe the most promising stat line to look at if you're a Minnesota fan is that the two only turned the ball over five times total in the win.

World.title: NASCAR fans have changed the channel for good, and the alarming trend just hit a boiling point
World.content:
The numbers are in, and they paint a disturbing picture for NASCAR as the series barrels toward its championship race in three short weeks.

Bottom line? Fans are leaving the sport ... in droves.

Nobody is watching. And those who are watching, are complaining. A lot. About the car. About the tracks. About the lack of drama, and personality, and, frankly, about the TV channel.

HAS NASCAR LOST THE SOUTH? EX-DRIVER UNLOADS AFTER SEEING "100,000 EMPTY SEATS"

Most folks have turned it off completely. Those who have stayed aren't thrilled.

I don't need to tell you guys, but that's not a great place to be.

Take a look:

Why are fans leaving NASCAR? It's simple.

Last Sunday's NASCAR Cup Series race at Phoenix drew a pathetic audience of just 1.2 million viewers. That number is alarming, folks. I've seen a lot of bad TV numbers for NASCAR over the years. Believe me.

It's not like they're hard to find.

But that's a low number. It's an unfathomable number given the series is smack dab in the middle of its playoffs. I never thought we'd see the day where a NASCAR Cup Series race drops below the Mendoza line (1 million), but we're getting close. Too close.

For comparison's sake, NASCAR averaged more than 4.5 million viewers per race in 2016, which was a really bad time for the sport. That's when viewers were fleeing left and right. Jeff Gordon had retired. Tony Stewart was on his way out. Dale Jr. was right behind him.

NASCAR RACE LOOKS PATHETIC WITH EMPTY SEATS, DRIVER GIVES THE FINGER & THE MOST EMBARRASSING COMMAND EVER?

There's been a nearly 50% drop-off in viewership since then! Through 33 races this season, the Cup Series is averaging 2.3 million viewers per race. Through seven Chase races (that's what we're calling the playoffs this season), the number drops to 1.5 million.

So, yeah â I'd imagine alarms are going off in the big glass building across from Daytona International Speedway this morning. At least they should be.

NASCAR MAKES MAJOR CHANGE TO 2027 DAYTONA 500 WEEK, FANS FURIOUS WITH ANOTHER CHANGE & RACE WIFE IN COSTA RICA

Now, the obvious question they'll be asking themselves is ... why? Why is this happening? Where are fans going? Why are they leaving?

To me, it's a fairly simple answer if everyone is just honest with themselves for 30 seconds. I'll go in order from what I consider most pressing, to least:

The TV deal stinks. It brought in a lot of money, but it's really poor for exposure. Do you know how many races have been on network TV this season? Seven. Seven! Six on FOX, one on NBC. That means there has been one race on network TV since the spring (Daytona in August). That's awful. Asking folks to hunt down the USA Network, and TNT, and then download Amazon Prime, and also find FS1 for 26 of your 33 races is a slap in the face. The schedule stinks. I don't mean the tracks themselves, I mean the time of year. NASCAR is putting its 10-race "Chase" right up against college football and the NFL. That's like taking a knife to a gun fight. No sport is going to win that fight, much less NASCAR. Chase Elliott said it years ago, and it's still true today: The season needs to end around Labor Day weekend. There's no upside in going up against the NFL. The Next Gen car has been a bigger turnoff than a Kamala Harris cackle. Fans despise it. Drivers despise it. You can't pass. You can't push the car. God forbid you try to run in "dirty air." Folks aren't stupid. They've seen what it's done to these races, and they've lost interest. To steal a phrase from the great Rick Pitino, "Dale Jr. is not walking through that door." There's no real personality in the garage anymore, beyond Carson Hocevar. Like him or hate him, Carson has moved the needle all season. Nobody else does. Chase Elliott is your "Most Popular Driver" year in and year out, and he was supposed to be NASCAR's Dale Earnhardt Jr. replacement. That hasn't worked out. Chase has no interest in carrying that torch.

Jeff Gordon is gone. Dale Jr. is gone. Tony Stewart is gone. Kyle Busch, tragically, died. He was, perhaps, the last of the "old guard" when it came to NASCAR. Beyond hoping someone goes viral and physically attacks Carson Hocevar every week, I'm not sure who NASCAR is looking at to bring in new fans. He doesn't exist.

And finally ...

Let's be honest, the drama isn't there anymore. At least it's not what it's been over the past decade. Yes, the shift back to The Chase format was popular amongst hardcore NASCAR fans. I get it. But the sport gave up elimination races in the process, which is naturally going to hurt interest from casual fans. People like drama. Having an elimination race every third race in the fall certainly helped with interest. Those are gone now.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

Now, let's try to fix NASCAR ...

OK, that was a long-winded "30 seconds" of honesty, but you get the picture. You add all those up, and I think it's fairly easy to see how the series has cratered in terms of viewership over the past few years.

As for the answers? I don't know. I'd shorten the season and own the summer. That's probably atop my list. Utilize midweek races in June and July. End the regular season in July, and end the postseason on Labor Day weekend.

That's probably the quickest and easiest fix.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOWâUNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

The TV deal is done, so I'm not sure you're changing that any time soon. A new-era car would take a while to build, so that's probably a ways off, too. As for the lack of personalities in the garage ...

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Yeah, I wouldn't hold your breath. Carson Hocevar is gonna need to keep rattling cages for years to come, I fear.

So start with the schedule, and go from there. That's my best suggestion ...



Because right now we live in a world where a WNBA Finals game is outdrawing a NASCAR postseason race.

And nobody wants to live in that world, folks.

World.title: On Main Street, Goldman Sachs makes a big bet on AI
World.content:
Artificial intelligence is already a huge business for Wall Street. But how is it playing on Main Street?

Goldman Sachs, as part of a philanthropic effort, is spending big in an attempt to help ensure smaller employers get in on it. The bank announced Thursday that it has launched the Small Business AI Institute as part of a $500 million expansion of its 10,000 Small Businesses, a program geared toward educating and supporting entrepreneurs. It said it would partner with Google, Anthropic, OpenAI and Meta to provide AI training and tools to small businesses.

“You’ve got to embrace new technology always, because if you’re not embracing it, trying to figure out how it can make your businesses better, there’s a real chance that you can fall behind,” Goldman Sachs CEO David Solomon said in an exclusive interview for NBC News’ Business in America series.

It’s a pivotal moment for the AI wave and its financial backers, including Goldman. The technology is broadly available to consumers, and U.S. economic growth increasingly depends on the buildup of data centers.

“We believe AI will create the greatest boom in entrepreneurship and small businesses that the world has ever seen,” Sam Altman, CEO and co-founder of OpenAI, said in an announcement from Goldman Sachs. “This is an incredible moment for anyone with an idea for a new endeavor because the gap between imagining it and bringing it to life is getting much smaller.”

Yet the growth that AI is already driving has also helped push up prices for inflation-weary Americans. Anger at data centers is a rare point of bipartisan agreement among voters, and the midterm elections are days away.

In the finance world, critics say AI is an investment bubble that could burst and potentially wipe out companies and jobs. Cracks are forming in the AI trade in markets after Big Tech firms drove much of stocks’ recent surge to record highs.

Goldman Sachs, like much of Wall Street, is in the thick of it all.

The bank’s share price has approximately tripled over the past three years while AI-related companies pushed the stock market to record highs. Goldman helped lead the much-ballyhooed, record-breaking initial public offering for Elon Musk’s SpaceX, which counts xAI and Grok among its core businesses. Goldman is also reportedly working on the IPO of Anthropic, the startup behind the AI chatbot Claude.

“There is going to be a lot of financing to do,” Solomon said last week on an earnings call, “and we’re going to be in the middle of that.”

Goldman and other big firms are counting on small businesses, which make up more than 90% of all U.S. companies and drive most of America’s job growth, to buy in. It won’t be easy getting everyone on board, though.

A recent NBC News poll found that 79% of respondents believe the government isn’t doing enough to regulate AI use. Sixty-seven percent disapprove of how President Donald Trump is handling the technology. Trump has said he favors lax AI regulation from the government.

Meanwhile, some small businesses that already embraced AI have faced backlash from the public, including restaurants that used AI-generated images of food that critics denounced as “slop.”

Still, according to Goldman, entrepreneurs are adopting the technology at a fast clip. A survey this year of more than 2,400 graduates of the company’s small business program found that 86% of respondents were using AI in their businesses, up from just 56% in 2024.

Rechelle Balanzat, founder of the laundry services app Juliette and an alumna of the 10,000 Small Businesses program, told NBC News she sees AI as a tool to help her gin up more business with limited resources.

Rechelle Balanzat, founder of the laundry services app Juliette. Kayla Steinberg / NBC News

“I really treat my AI as my consigliere,” Balanzat said. “They are not there to replace your accountant and lawyer. They are not there to replace humans. However, it does help prep me to have much more meaningful questions when I am meeting with my accountant and with my lawyer.”

Despite the widespread use of AI among the Goldman program alumni, just 15% of them said they had fully integrated AI into their core operations, according to Goldman.

Mike DiMarino, who heads Linda Tool in Brooklyn, New York, was part of the inaugural class of Goldman’s program in 2010. The company makes precision machine components for the military and aerospace industries, and DiMarino thinks AI can help with planning, management and processes.

“I’m sure there’s a lot more it can do that I don’t know yet,” he said.

But DiMarino is also cautious about how Linda Tool uses the technology, especially given how much sensitive information the company handles for its work in defense, aerospace and manufacturing.

Mike DiMarino heads Linda Tool. Kayla Steinberg / NBC News

His concerns mirror broader cybersecurity fears about AI. In July, a swarm of about 700 AI agents created by OpenAI hacked into the open-source platform Hugging Face. Last month, Google said Chinese hackers are using AI to automate their attacks.

In addition to the security risks, company leaders are also increasingly raising concerns about the cost of AI, especially relative to its concrete impact on the bottom line. After spending on AI tokens exploded in the past year, companies from Uber to Microsoft to Meta have all taken steps to limit or re-evaluate how their employees use AI compute power.

Americans are also concerned about what AI will do to the job market. A recent Gallup Poll found that a growing number of workers are worried that technology will make their jobs obsolete. Small businesses employ fewer people than large firms, which makes their workforces especially vulnerable to potential losses.

Balanzat and DiMarino told NBC News they want to use AI to support employees at their businesses, not replace them.

“Machines are expensive,” DiMarino said. “People are priceless.”

World.title: ‘Looksmaxxing’ influencer Clavicular pleads not guilty to Massachusetts rape charges
World.content:
“Looksmaxxing” influencer Clavicular pleaded not guilty in Massachusetts court Thursday to criminal rape charges stemming from an alleged May 2025 incident at this family’s house in Cape Cod.

Clavicular, 20, whose real name is Braden Peters, was charged with rape, drugging someone for sexual intercourse and procuring liquor for someone under 21 years old, according to a criminal complaint filed on Sept. 8 in Orleans District Court in Barnstable County, Massachusetts.

Aleksandra Vasilevna Mendoza, an 18-year-old influencer known online as Alorah or Alorah Ziva, alleged that last May, when she was 17 and in Massachusetts, Peters called her an Uber to his family’s home in Chatham, a beachfront town in Cape Cod.

When Mendoza was at Peters’ home, she alleged, he got her drunk with vodka during a livestream on Twitch and then raped her while she was asleep, the criminal complaint from the Chatham Police Department said. At the time, his mother and grandmother were allegedly in the house.

A representative and Peters’s lawyer declined to comment ahead of the arraignment. Mendoza’s lawyer also declined to comment.

Peters has previously denied any wrongdoing and defended himself in a series of posts on X.

At his Thursday arraignment, a judge set bail for Peters at $10,000 after his defense team filed a memo in Orleans District Court on Wednesday asking for “fair and reasonable bail” in that amount. In it, his attorney argued that Peters is neither a danger to the community nor a flight risk and pointed out that he has no history of felony criminal convictions.

A court clerk confirmed Thursday that Peters paid the $10,000 bail in cash.

The criminal charges follow a civil suit Mendoza filed in Miami last year in which she accused Peters of sexual battery in connection with the alleged May 2025 incident in Cape Cod. In the civil suit, she also alleged he injected her face with a non-FDA-approved fat-dissolving substance during a November livestream in Florida.

A source familiar with the matter confirmed that the criminal charges against Peters stem from Mendoza’s allegations.

Earlier this month, Mendoza refiled her civil lawsuit and dropped the sexual assault allegations against Peters. At the time, her lawyer said it was to avoid interfering with the criminal case in Massachusetts.

The Wednesday memo from Peters’ team also lays out his defense, arguing that Mendoza willingly created social media content with Peters and previously described him to her followers as “so nice.” The memo also says she continued to hang out with Peters and profit from their relationship after the alleged Cape Cod incident in May 2025.

The filing also includes a letter allegedly handwritten by Mendoza, in which she allegedly wrote, “Braden, you have my loyalty 100% ... I admire the man you are,” and added that she wanted to continue working with Peters.

In screenshots of messages between Peters and Mendoza included in the filing, Mendoza appeared to imply she wanted to engage in a romantic relationship with Peters.

By early 2026, Peters’ lawyer alleged, Mendoza’s brand deals were drying up as Peters’ success continued to grow. She then filed the civil suit, the filing said.

When she reported the alleged rape to Chatham police in June 2026, she told officers she had not undergone a sexual assault forensic examination. She told police she told one friend about the alleged assault, then later changed her story and said she never told anyone about it, according to the memo.

This is not Peters’ first run-in with the law.

Peters and two other people were charged in Florida in April with shooting at an alligator. He and another person pleaded no contest to unlawfully discharging a firearm in public and were given six months of probation and ordered to serve 20 hours of community service, according to NBC South Florida.

He was also hospitalized in April in Miami after a suspected overdose, according to his representative.

If you or someone you know has been sexually assaulted, call the National Sexual Assault Hotline at 1-800-656-4673. The hotline, run by the Rape, Abuse, & Incest National Network (RAINN), can put you in contact with your local rape crisis center. You can also access RAINN’s online chat service at rainn.org/get-help.
