World.title: Market sell-off gains steam as concerns about Iran war and high AI spending collide
World.content:
U.S. equity markets sold off sharply Thursday, as fears that Israel and the United States would restart attacks against Iran sent oil prices higher and major tech stocks failed to hold onto recent gains.

The S&P 500 was down 1.4% by midmorning, while the tech-heavy Nasdaq saw declines of 2.2%. The price of international Brent crude climbed more than 2%, while U.S. crude gained more than 1%.

Demand for Treasury bonds also increased — bucking the trend of the last several months — as investors sought out the safe-haven assets as riskier ones like tech stocks sold off. That sent bond yields lower.

The broad sell-off was sparked in part by reporting Wednesday that Israel and the U.S. are preparing for a military operation in Iran after the November midterm elections.

Likely targets include Iran’s energy infrastructure and nuclear sites, according to The New York Times.

U.S. military and diplomatic personnel were also being evacuated from several countries in the Middle East on Wednesday, NBC News reported.

Iranian officials have promised widespread retaliation to any strikes, pointing to critical Middle East data center sites and undersea internet cables as potential targets.

Major tech stocks led the declines in early trading, with Meta and Tesla sliding after both companies reported quarterly earnings Wednesday evening.

Meta, led by Mark Zuckerberg, reported that the expansion of its Muse personal assistant overseas is being hindered by a scarcity of computing power. Annabelle Gordon / Bloomberg via Getty

Meta’s earnings and revenues beat forecasts, but only after excluding billions of dollars in legal penalties the company paid last quarter. It also warned investors that it expects to increase its spending in the coming year to meet demands for computing power.

A separate regulatory filing revealed that Meta intends to spend an additional $825 billion on contracts related to its AI infrastructure buildout.

Tesla, meanwhile, said it was reining in its capital spending plans, disappointing investors who were hoping for a signal of more aggressive expansion.

Elon Musk's Tesla reported that it was scaling up its Cybercab fleet in Austin, Texas. Win McNamee / Getty

The slide in the Nasdaq got additional fuel Thursday morning after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said in an appearance on CNBC that capital to finance the AI investment boom was becoming “scarce” due to higher interest rates and a glut of existing spending commitments.

U.S. markets remain near all-time highs. But signs of flagging returns on the AI investment boom have resulted in more intense gyrations lately.

A major sell off in French government debt has also dragged European stocks lower in recent weeks.

“It’s been another difficult 24 hours for markets, as investors grapple with AI growth concerns, higher oil prices, and ongoing fiscal stress,” wrote Henry Allen, director and macro strategist at Deutsche Bank, in a note to clients Thursday.

A significant market draw-down may also put a further dent in Republicans’ midterm election outlook.

President Donald Trump frequently points to solid stock market gains as evidence that his economic agenda has made Americans richer. A significant market stumble ahead of the Nov. 3 election would undermine a core argument for Trump and the GOP.

World.title: John Anderson, twangy country singer known for ‘Seminole Wind,’ dies at 71
World.content:
John Anderson, the Grammy-nominated country crooner best known for the buoyant “Swingin’” and the plaintive “Seminole Wind,” died this week, according to posts on his official social media pages.

He was 71. No details on his cause of death were provided.

“It is with the heaviest of hearts that we share the passing of our beloved husband, father, grandfather, and best friend,” Anderson’s family wrote on his verified Facebook and Instagram accounts.

“To the world, he was a gifted country music singer whose voice and songs touched countless lives. To us, he was so much more. He was the heart of our family, the one who made us laugh, loved us fiercely, and made every ordinary moment feel special,” Anderson’s family added in part.

In a music career spanning nearly 50 years, Anderson released more than 20 studio albums, landed dozens of singles on the Billboard country music charts, and earned three Grammy Award nominations, including best country vocal performance in 1982.

In early 2024, Anderson was elected into the Country Music Hall of Fame. In remarks at a news conference, he said he was nearly at a loss for words over the “chance to be amongst this kind of greatness.”

“I’m trying to get a grasp ot the reality of this happening to me,” Anderson said, according to a Variety report. “I want to thank all the fans who supported us through the last nearly 50 years. ... They ask just what this means and … this is an institution that preserves greatness.”

John David Anderson was born in Apopka, Florida on Dec. 13, 1954. He moved to Nashville after graduating high school and picked up odd jobs while attempting to break into the music business. He signed with Warner Bros. Records in the late ‘70s after catching attention for a string of local club appearances.

In the early 1980s, Anderson released two back-to-back self-titled studio albums featuring early hits like “Your Lying Blue Eyes” and “She Just Started Liking Cheatin’ Songs.” He hit the mainstream with his fourth studio album, “Wild & Blue” (1982), anchored by the high-wattage single “Swingin.”

Anderson’s commercial fortunes went up and down across the ‘80s, but he rebounded in the early ‘90s thanks in part to the album “Seminole Wind.” The title track, a swampy and melancholy lament about environmental destruction, became one of his signature tunes.

“Ever since the days of old / Men would search for wealth untold / They’d dig for silver and for gold / And leave the empty holes,” Anderson sang.

Anderson was a less visible presence in recent years, though he continued recording and released his final studio album, “Years,” in April 2020. The cover art featured a photo of Anderson gazed off into the distance in a black cowboy hat and white beard.

In a statement, Country Music Hall of Fame and Museum CEO Kyle Young praised Anderson as a “one-of-a-kind song stylist who proved that fresh innovations were best born from time-honored traditions.”

“Whether he borrowed inspiration from Lefty Frizzell’s vocal bends or the Florida swamp land, he brought dynamic distinction and creative soul to a world that needed to hear his voice,” Young said.

In social media posts, country music luminaries like Tim McGraw, Reba McEntire, Blake Shelton and Luke Combs mourned Anderson, too.

“I was talking with John Sunday night at the HOF ceremony,” McGraw wrote on Instagram, using the initials for the Hall of Fame. “He was in such good spirits. We talked, we laughed, we sang his songs that I loved so much together, just goofing off.

“I am completely heartbroken by his passing,” McGraw added. “There will never be a stylist in music, any music, that was so defining as his. It’s just devastating.”

World.title: High-ranking Virginia state Democrat charged in public corruption case
World.content:
NORFOLK, Va. — Federal authorities on Thursday charged a prominent Virginia Democrat with racketeering and a money laundering conspiracy as part of an alleged public corruption case involving a cannabis business she co-owns.

Virginia state Sen. L. Louise Lucas, a frequent critic of President Donald Trump who is one of the most powerful Democrats in the state, surrendered to authorities Thursday. She was also charged with conspiracy to distribute marijuana. A half dozen others, including Lucas’ daughters, were also in custody and charged in the alleged scheme.

The investigation into the 82-year-old Lucas predates the Trump administration, NBC News previously reported. But the Justice Department’s move, just 12 days before a midterm election, is unusual, as federal authorities have typically avoided taking overt investigative steps against political figures so close to an election. Lucas is not up for re-election this year but has ties to prominent Democrats who are on the ballot.

Lucas said in a statement on social media that she will not be intimidated, or back down.

“Today, the FBI, the Department of Justice, and the full weight of the federal government have been wielded against an 82-year-old great-grandmother,” Lucas wrote. “I grew up under Jim Crow. I’ve seen what happens when people in power try to silence those who stand up to them. I spent my life fighting back and I’m not stopping now.”

Attorney General Todd Blanche and FBI Director Kash Patel traveled to in Norfolk, Virginia for a press conference announcing the charges.

Blanche said that Lucas, who has been a public servant for years, put her own financial interests above the people she was elected to serve.

“The Department of Justice intends to prove that Senator Lucas violated the trust of the people of Portsmouth and Chesapeake, Virginia, and of her state senate colleagues,” he said. “Her first duty should have been looking out for her constituents before herself.”

The Justice Department has brought several controversial cases against Trump’s political targets in his second term. Three weeks before the midterms, federal officials searched the home of Democratic Rep. Ilhan Ohmar of Minnesota in an immigration-related investigation and seized her phone. She has said she will not be silenced.

The Justice Department has typically not brought political cases within 60 days of an election, but the Blanche on Thursday dismissed those concerns. “It’s not even a rule, it’s a practice,” he said. He noted Lucas wasn’t up for reelection.

“The justice manual speaks very clearly about what the Department of Justice can and can’t do, and we cannot bring a charge if our purpose is improper,” Blanche said. But he said the case was correctly brought.

In May, federal agents searched Lucas’ office in Portsmouth, along with a business she co-owns called The Cannabis Outlet, which is located on High Street. U.S. Rep. Suhas Subramanyam, D-Va., said his communications with Lucas were monitored and that the Justice Department had become Trump’s “own personal law firm, with his former personal attorney carrying out vendettas on Trump’s political enemies.”

A reporter with WAVY, an NBC affiliate, also received a notification letter showing that his communications with Lucas’ number had been swept up in the wire.

The indictment alleges that members of the conspiracy “used various business entities” to “disguise the proceeds of illegal marijuana distribution,” and that Lucas “used her political position in the Virginia state senate to insulate” the enterprise “from criminal scrutiny, to further the goal of wealth accumulation.”

In one intercepted phone call in February 2026 with an alleged co-conspirator who has not been indicted, Lucas allegedly said that this was their “last chance at generational wealth,” adding “I’ve gotten too old to not be greedy.”

Lucas has been a proponent of marijuana legalization in Virginia. The state now allows for possession of marijuana for adults over 21, but recreational marijuana sales remain unlawful.

That is set to change; this summer, the governor and state legislators announced an agreement to allow the licensed retail sale of marijuana beginning July 1, 2027.

Lucas’ political career began more than four decades ago, when she was elected to the Portsmouth City Council. She was elected to the Virginia General Assembly in 1991.

The Virginia Senate consists of 40 members who serve four year terms and receive an annual salary of $18,000, a figure set in 1988. Members also receive mileage reimbursement and a per diem during the General Assembly session.

U.S. Attorney for the District of Columbia Jeanine Pirro, the former judge and Fox News host Trump named as the top federal prosecutor in the nation’s capital, attempted and failed to indict six sitting members of Congress over a social media video that Trump disliked. A criminal case against former FBI Director James Comey over an Instagram photo of seashells remains ongoing.

World.title: France’s Emmanuel Macron says ‘illegitimate’ protests will be banned as cities block demonstrations
World.content:
French President Emmanuel Macron said on Thursday that “illegitimate” protests would be banned in the coming days and blamed “seditious” ultra-left groups and vandals for last weekend’s riots and looting.

Speaking after a meeting with intelligence chiefs and senior ministers, Macron said demonstrations organised by groups such as trade unions would be allowed to go ahead but could be diverted along alternative routes to protect businesses.

“Last Saturday we had political and seditious acts by ultra-left groups whose aim is to bring down the Republic,” Macron said.

His comments came as authorities across France prepared for fresh protests following some of the country’s worst urban unrest in years.

Authorities in multiple cities had already banned protests planned across the country on Thursday.

The turmoil in Paris and other French cities has prompted a strong security response. Night curfews have been implemented in some areas of the French capital, as well as in other cities where calm has been restored.

Demonstrations planned Thursday in Paris, Lyon, Lille and Grenoble were banned, a move seen by some as an infringement on French people’s right to protest.

But high school and university student groups say they will continue to mobilize, even though the autumn school break started this week.

The Paris police prefecture said the ban was necessary given the risk of street violence that erupted over the weekend, when groups of masked youth clashed with police forces, looted shops and torched cars.

The ban in Paris will last until 8 p.m. local time and apply to areas including the Elysée presidential palace, both houses of parliament, and the city’s main train stations. Areas in downtown Paris which were severely hit by the looting are also covered.

World.title: I’ve tested nearly all of Garmin’s watches — these are my top picks if you’re looking to upgrade or buy one for the first time
World.content:
Garmin makes a lot of different watches. While brands like Apple, Google and Samsung have two or three smartwatches to choose from, Garmin has dozens, which can make it hard to know which one is right for you.

I test out smartwatches, fitness trackers and smart rings regularly: that includes all of Garmin’s latest watches. Below are my top recommendations for anyone looking to make the switch or upgrade an older model.

Want more from NBC Selected? 

The best Garmin watches in 2026

Because Garmin makes so many different watches, it probably makes one that is just right for you. Below are my top recommendations. Every option on this list is a sample I requested from the brand for testing purposes for this story.

Best overall

The Garmin Vivoactive 6 has a subtle and understated look, but still contains many of the brand's best features. Courtesy Harry Rabinowitz

The Garmin Vivoactive 6 hits just the right balance of features and price that makes it the easiest option to recommend, especially for someone trying out the brand for the first time.

It’s a generalist smartwatch: it has many of the brand’s best features without specializing too heavily in one activity (like the Forerunner series). It has in-depth metrics for health, sleep and fitness activity, with staple Garmin features like body battery, workout recovery times, Garmin pace pro and Garmin coach (with running and strength training plans).

I love its workout animations — the watch will play short videos of a silhouette performing certain exercises during HIIT, cardio, strength, yoga or move alert activity. Animated move alerts, in particular, make taking breaks at my desk a lot more fun.

The upgrade: Garmin Venu 4

The budget alternative: Garmin Forerunner 165

Best for runners

I tested the 42-millimeter Garmin Forerunner 570, which fit my wrist much better than the 47-millimeter version.

Anyone who loves to run should look at the Garmin Forerunner series — the watches are made with runners in mind. If you’re already deep into your running journey, the Forerunner 570 is my go-to recommendation: It has more than enough tools for runners and racers and comes in two sizes, so you can get the best fit for your wrist (unlike the Forerunner 70 and Forerunner 970).

The most important features in my expert opinion are training readiness, training status and HRV (heart rate variability) status, which work in tandem to help optimize your training and recovery. Training Readiness combines multiple metrics to give you a top-level score about how beneficial your training will be. In practice, it helps me decide whether today is a rest day, an easy day or a day to push myself.

It has advanced running metrics like power, cadence, stride length and ground contact time, as well as multi-band GPS for the most accurate, consistent distance and time stats possible. It also connects to GPS usually within five seconds.

The upgrade: Garmin Forerunner 970

The budget alternative: Garmin Forerunner 70

Best for battery life

The MIP display is easy to read during the day, especially in direct sunlight Courtesy Harry Rabinowitz

If you don’t even want to think about charging your Garmin, look for a solar-powered model like this Garmin Instinct 3 solar. It’s a rugged, outdoor-focused fitness watch with many of Garmin’s notable fitness and health features, but with potentially unlimited battery life. That’s because the Instinct 3 has a solar panel built into the screen — get enough sunlight and the watch largely charges itself.

Part of this long battery life stems from the screen: it’s a monochrome memory-in-pixel (MIP) display, common on outdoor watches, but not common on many smartwatches. It is easy to see in light conditions, but nearly impossible to see in the dark — press the “Light” button, and the screen will light up for a few seconds.

If an MIP screen sounds like a dealbreaker, you can also get the Instinct 3 AMOLED, which has a more typical bright, colorful smartwatch screen and still gets up to 24 days of battery life.

The Garmin Enduro 3 and Garmin Fenix 8 (Solar) both get even better battery life than the Instinct 3 (and have solar MIP displays with color), but both cost over twice as much.

The upgrade: Garmin Enduro 3

The budget alternative: n/a

Best premium

The Garmin Fenix 8 has a durable titanium case and a sapphire crystal screen I didn’t worry about scratching. Courtesy Harry Rabinowitz

Garmin’s premium, do-it-all watch is the Fenix 8. It has a bevy of features only found in the brand’s high-end watches: things like a dive rating (up to 40 meters), offline maps, navigation and music, a built-in speaker and microphone for calls and music, a built-in flashlight and the list goes on. It’s also likely the most durable — it has a titanium case and sapphire crystal screen, two of the most durable materials you can put in a watch.

Outside of premium hardware (and software), I’d recommend the Fenix 8 if you are interested in diving, hiking and trail running: features like dive modes, ascent planning and stellar battery life make it well-suited to these activities.

All of that comes at a price: literally. The 47 millimeters AMOLED version that I tested (and linked above) costs $1,099. It’s also surprisingly heavy at 73 grams, heavier than every other watch on this list.

The upgrade: Garmin Fenix 8 Pro (AMOLED)

The budget alternative: Garmin Epix Pro (Gen 2), Garmin Forerunner 970

Best for style

The Garmin Venu 4 is one of the brand’s sleekest looking smartwatches.

Most of the Garmin watches I’ve mentioned so far look very fitness-forward. The Garmin Venu series is subtle and classy by comparison, and is a great option for anyone who wants Garmin’s best features but in a package that’s easier to match to any occasion. It has a stainless steel bezel that looks great, and comes in two sizes, including a petite 41-millimeter option. It also has built-in microphones, speakers and a flashlight, one I use all the time in dark spaces.

The Venu 4 also has many of Garmin’s premium training and health features, including health status, lifestyle logging, Garmin fitness coach, training readiness, training status and HRV (heart rate variability) status. It’s a little pricey, but a great all-around option for most people not needing the five-buttons control, fitness look of the Garmin Forerunner series.

The upgrade: n/a

The budget alternative: Garmin Vivoactive 6

Best for Apple Watch converts

If you love everything about your Apple Watch but are considering trying out Garmin, I recommend the Venu X1. It’s Garmin’s most Apple-like watch, with a huge, bright square screen and a very thin case size (eight millimeters). But it has most of the same features as other pricey Garmins, meaning runners, racers, hikers and bikers won’t feel like they are “missing out” getting this model instead of a Forerunner or Fenix.

The Venu X1 does have less battery life than most other Garmin watches — up to eight days in gesture mode and only two in always-on mode.

The upgrade: n/a

The budget alternative: n/a

How I test Garmin watches

I typically wear two watches at the same time (one on each wrist) and compare data between the two. (I don’t typically wear four, as pictured above.) Courtesy Harry Rabinowitz

I am a runner and cyclist, and use smartwatches and fitness trackers to track and monitor live stats like heart rate, pace and time as well as recovery metrics over time. I tend to spend hours tinkering with device settings, exploring what a product offers out of the box, and what I can fine-tune to match my preferences.

I test Garmin watches for at least a week, using as many features as possible, usually comparing them (and the data) to another watch (on my other wrist) or smart ring. I’ve tested nearly a dozen Garmin watches over the years.

I request Garmin watches from the brand — it sends me devices to test out as needed. I send each one back to the brand once I am done testing.

How to shop for a Garmin watch

Even after you pick out which type of Garmin watch you want, there are still a few key factors you should keep in mind.

Size

Many Garmin watches come in multiple size options: the Garmin Fenix 8, for example, comes in 43, 47 and 51 millimeter options. I have smaller wrists (about six inches in circumference), and have tested many smartwatches, so I know that I prefer my smartwatch to be between 42 and 45 millimeters. I err on the larger end if the watch can only be controlled via the touchscreen, and not buttons along the sides.

What size is right for you depends on your wrist circumference, but also personal preference. My advice: visit a store like REI or Fleet Feet in person; most have multiple Garmin watches you can try on, in my experience.

Key sport

If you love one activity in particular: think running, diving or hiking, you should probably stick to a Garmin watch built around that activity. For divers: it’s the Garmin Descent or Garmin Fenix 8. For runners: it’s any of the Garmin Forerunner watches. For hikers and trail runners, there are a few options across the Forerunner, Instinct and Fenix lineup, depending on your exact needs. If you are more of a fitness generalist, the Garmin Vivoactive and Garmin Venu are the best options.

Screen type

Most newer Garmin watches come with a bright, colorful AMOLED display, the kind of screen you see in the Apple Watch, Samsung Galaxy Watch, Google Pixel Watch and most Fitbits. But some Garmin watches, particularly those focused on battery life, solar charging and the outdoors, have a memory-in-pixel (MIP) display.

A MIP display is always on but barely uses any energy to power, so it typically allows for a watch with far greater battery life than one with an AMOLED display. MIP displays are easy to read in sunny conditions but become hard or nearly impossible to see at night or in darkness (unless you hit the “light” button to briefly activate the watch backlight).

I recommend an AMOLED display for most people — if you want an MIP display, you probably already knew it before reading this article.

Why trust NBC Selected?

Harry Rabinowitz is a former reporter at NBC Selected who covered technology and fitness including stories on fitness trackers, wireless earbuds and cameras. He tested new and popular Garmin watches regularly, using them to track stats for his health, sleep and exercise, and leveraged his experience using fitness trackers, smartwatches and smart rings to pick the best Garmin watches.

Catch up on NBC Selected’s in-depth coverage of tech and tools, wellness and more, and

World.title: What experts say the Six Flags death investigation will focus on
World.content:
Ride inspection experts expect the investigation into the death of a man who fell from a Georgia roller coaster this month to examine if maintenance issues, design flaws or human error led to the incident at Six Flags Over Georgia.

The Goliath has been closed since 42-year-old Hassan Kariem died after witnesses say he was ejected from the ride.

John F. King, Georgia's Insurance and Safety Fire Commissioner, who is leading the investigation, said investigators will not "cut corners, rush to conclusions, or leave questions unanswered without making every effort to resolve them."

"Our team has been on the ground working day and night to ensure that every relevant detail receives the attention it deserves," he said in a statement last week.

A spokesperson for the park said in a statement to CBS News that "our thoughts remain with the family and loved ones affected by the tragic incident in Georgia."

"Nothing is more important to Six Flags than the safety of our guests and team members, and we remain focused on supporting ongoing investigations alongside state authorities and the ride manufacturer," the spokesperson said.

A March inspection of the Goliath roller coaster found no violations or deficiencies, King said. The inspection report did include a note indicating that staff "need to replace bushings" — a piece of the puzzle inspectors are sure to home in on, experts said.

Bushings are parts designed to reduce friction and absorb shock in various mechanical assemblies.

Maintenance issues or a design flaw?

Six Flags has opened five Goliath roller coasters at parks across North America in the last 25 years. The coaster, which opened in 2006 in Georgia, can reach speeds of up to 70 miles per hour on towering tracks that rise 200 feet. It was designed by Bolliger & Mabillard, a Swiss-based roller coaster manufacturer.

For Kariem to have been ejected from the ride, ride operators and roller coaster engineers suggested either a mechanical malfunction, operator error — for instance, failing to properly check and secure the restraint — or a combination of both, could have played a part. Rides and their restraints are supposed to be inspected by park maintenance each morning, they said.

The train of the Goliath roller coaster is seen on the track where it was evacuated at Six Flags over Georgia on Oct. 14, 2026. Elijah Nouvelage / Getty Images

The park spokesperson said, "Safety is our ethos and is at the heart of everything we do at Six Flags."

"Every ride undergoes documented safety inspections before opening each day, supported by comprehensive maintenance programs designed to meet or exceed industry safety guidelines," the spokesperson said. "Our ride operators complete a comprehensive, multi-stage training program that includes classroom instruction, hands-on training and supervised, on-the-job experience with additional instruction and evaluation provided whenever necessary."

When riders board the Goliath, they are buckled into the ride's 36 seats using a padded clamshell lap bar, a U-shaped restraint that is typically locked in place over a rider's thighs and waist. Ride operators check restraints to make sure they're locked before the ride begins.

Daniel, a self-described "big roller coaster nerd" who also operates a Goliath at another park, said the coaster is designed so staff can use a control panel with various buttons and a screen to operate the ride.

Daniel, who asked to use his middle name because he is still employed, said it was likely that ride operators used two orange buttons on the control panel to open and close the car restraints. When the sensors detect that every single restraint is closed, two green mushroom-shaped buttons at the bottom start blinking. That means that operators can press on them to dispatch the ride, he said.

Goliath inspection records obtained by CBS News, dating back over a decade, show a smattering of 20 quickly resolved violations between 2016 and 2021, and none since.

However, Troy Richardson, an engineer with experience building and inspecting roller coasters, said the March inspection's note about bushings could be significant.

Bushings are used to keep mechanical pieces in restraints, chassis joints and wheel bogies, positioned correctly amid the repeated friction and bumps of a roller coaster ride.

Even a small defect in a bushing can be a major problem, said Richardson, the founder and CEO of MIT Experts, which provides forensic consulting in amusement park litigation.

"A bushing, if it's slightly off a little bit, now the pin won't go into the hole or it's a little bit loose in the hole," he said.

Richardson added that the manufacturer of the roller coaster most likely laid out a maintenance and replacement schedule for each part in an operation manual. A key question investigators will ask, Richardson said, will be if staff adhered to those instructions.

A person with knowledge of the park's operations said the bushings identified in the March inspection were located on the ride's bogie assemblies, which connect the vehicle to the track, and unrelated to the restraint system. They were changed as recommended, the person said.

Another expert, Kathryn Woodcock, editor-in-chief of the Journal of Themed Experience and Attractions Studies, said investigators will want to know "what exactly is not the way it is expected to be."

"If two parts disconnected (e.g., a latch came undone), it is a different thing than if one part broke (e.g., a crack failed catastrophically)," Woodcock said.

Woodcock described the tricky process behind determining when to replace parts.

"It is not automatically better to replace a part too early," Woodcock, a professor at Toronto Metropolitan University, wrote in an email.

She said the likelihood of failure in roller coaster parts often falls along a "'bathtub curve,' where failure is most common at the start of use due to possible manufacturing defects, and then if it does not fail then, the failure likelihood is very low for a length of time — which depends on its material and shape and loading — when failure likelihood increases again."

"In charge of some very important systems"

Six Flags operates nearly three dozen parks across North America, with more than 47 million guests and 95,000 employees in 2025, according to SEC filings.

At Six Flags Magic Mountain in California, the death of 22-year-old Christopher Hawley after he rode the X2 roller coaster in 2022 prompted questions about ride maintenance and inspection, said Timothy Loranger, an attorney who represented Hawley's family.

File photo of the X2 roller coaster at Six Flags Magic Mountain in Valencia, California. AP Photo/Jae C. Hong

"What I did see in having talked to people who maintained the rides, I did not come away from those conversations feeling confident that they were competent in their jobs, I felt like they didn't have appropriate training," Loranger said. "They were in charge of some very important systems and maybe didn't really even understand what they were doing."

Six Flags Magic Mountain settled the wrongful death lawsuit with Hawley's family. The park shuttered X2 permanently in September, after lawsuits alleging riders suffered brain injuries piled up. (The Doan Law Firm, which tracks published claims of theme park-related fatalities, lists two previous deaths on Goliaths in its database: a 2002 brain aneurysm at Six Flags Magic Mountain in California and a 2006 death listed as a likely heart attack on Six Flags Over Georgia's Goliath.)

Loranger said he wouldn't be surprised if the same challenges he saw at Magic Mountain arose at Six Flags Over Georgia.

File photo of roller coaster riders on the Goliath at Six Flags Magic Mountain in California in 2015. David Bohrer/Los Angeles Times via Getty Images

Ride operators at Six Flags Over Georgia spoke to CBS News about the training and management they received while being tasked with ensuring the safety of thrill-seekers.

Jacobi Edwards, 18, who was a ride operations lead at Six Flags Over Georgia for several months last spring, described it as "a very well-run place," saying he's proud of his work there. But he chose to work on other roller coasters, in part because of Goliath's popularity.

"They have a clock to beat as that is the most famous ride in the park, so they do definitely feel rushed," said Edwards, who was 17 when he worked at the park.

He said when he was on the clock, he prioritized guest safety over trying to get "more cycles in."

Richardson, the MIT engineer, said park supervisors need to trust park staff as "ambassadors … that are trying to keep people safe and be your frontline."

"I don't care if there's 100 people in the line, we don't want somebody to die, you know? And they need to have that ability to come in and say, 'Hey, I have the authority to shut this down if I don't think it's safe,'" Richardson said.

Richard Pretlow, park president of Six Flags Over Georgia, said in a statement after the incident, "our team members receive extensive training to safely operate and maintain our rides."

But Harper Henderson,18, a former employee who started her job at Six Flags Over Georgia when she was 15, said the pressure to keep lines for the Goliath moving was paralleled by the rush to get new employees trained to operate the coaster.

Like Edwards, Henderson said she was promoted to trainer at 17 years old — after six weeks as a ride operator.

"Whenever we got a new employee, I would walk them through the operating procedures for all the rides and then watch them as they pretend they're operating the ride, or pretend to help with the restraints or something," she said. "And I would do that over and over again until I thought they were ready for the test and then I would send them to take the test."

She described it as a process that "could be done in about an hour." Henderson said ride operators needed at least an hour to review all the training.

CBS News reviewed operator tests for two Six Flags Over Georgia rides: Georgia Scorcher and the Log Jamboree. The questions, on a Microsoft Forms sheet, asked about the mechanics of each ride and its safety procedures. For example, in the Georgia Scorcher quiz, operators are asked, "What does it mean when the DISPATCH buttons flash on the main operator?"

Henderson said the rides were often so busy she had to rush the training.

"We would just give them the test answers," Henderson said, adding that new operators would then be ready to work in "15 minutes."

Henderson said she wasn't comfortable with the process. She said she resigned in July 2025.

"The fact that you could just skip, that was not great," she said. "And it was because the managers really pushed to have the minimum amount of people to open every ride."

World.title: Toledo man describes days-long chemical leak: "Looked like a movie"
World.content:
Hundreds of people in Toledo, Ohio, remain evacuated from their homes as officials work to resolve a fiery chemical leak that began Tuesday.

Residents within a mile of an MC Tank facility were order to evacuate on Tuesday, and everyone within a 3-mile radius was told to shelter in place. On Wednesday, the shelter-in-place was lifted and evacuations were reduced to half a mile. They were reduced further, to a quarter-mile, by Thursday morning. But a chemical plume remains.

City officials have been allowing the chemicals to vent from the 5,500-gallon tank, instead of trying to send in crews to stop the leak. Toledo Mayor Wade Kapszukiewicz said Wednesday that the potential for an explosion made it too dangerous for first responders, including hazardous material teams, to approach the tank. One first responder has sustained injuries, Kapszukiewicz said.

The city and MC Tank Transport Inc. said the substance involved in the leak is glycidyl methacrylate, an industrial chemical that is used in plastics, paints and coatings. State officials said the leak happened due to an error as the chemical was being transferred.

Residents have reported symptoms including burning in the eyes, lungs and sinuses, bad headaches and nausea. One area hospital is treating 35 patients. Resident Travis Williams said he "woke up choking" from overwhelming fumes.

"I've never had these feelings, the burnings, itchy skin, irritated eyes," Williams said. "I am definitely worried about the long-term effect of this."

A dense fog has also descended over Toledo. Officials say the fog was indistinguishable from the chemical plume. The conditions are also affecting visibility. Williams said the scene outside his home "looked like a movie."

"I couldn't even see as far as my car to the curb," Williams said.

Officials are asking residents to ventilate their homes by opening windows and doors. Residents are also being encouraged to wash their hands thoroughly and watch for coughing and eye irritation in people and pets. The Environmental Protection Agency is monitoring air quality.

In May, an industrial tank containing another methacrylate compound ruptured in Orange County, California. That incident displaced thousands until a crack formed in the overheating tank, relieving the pressure and ending the risk of explosion.

World.title: Memphis fails to pass 1-year data center moratorium, opts for shorter-term ban
World.content:
In a heated city council meeting on Tuesday, leaders in Memphis, Tennessee, failed to pass a moratorium that would have paused data center development for a year in the city, which has become a hotspot for the facilities driven by Elon Musk's SpaceXAI.

Instead, city council members passed a substitute ordinance — which some said they received on short notice and did not have time to review — that would halt construction of data centers for 135 days.

Residents and activists have pushed back against data center development in the region for years, starting with the construction of SpaceXAI's Colossus 1 data center in 2024. The company has also built two other data centers and has two under construction in Memphis and the surrounding region, including across the state border in Southaven, Mississippi.

Also in Southaven, a plant powering the company's data centers is using methane gas turbines, which prompted a lawsuit from the NAACP and other organizations over alleged pollution.

SpaceXAI did not reply to a request for comment. The Trump administration moved to dismiss the case, but earlier Tuesday, a Mississippi federal judge blocked that bid.

Supporters of data centers argue they are needed to support the growth of artificial intelligence technology. Advocates also say they will create much-needed jobs, although experts counter many of those jobs are in the construction industry and therefore temporary.

The moratorium would have paused the construction of new data centers for a year, allowing the city to adopt permanent zoning and development regulations as well as establish disclosure requirements for data center applicants. It also would have provided the opportunity to study impacts on air quality, electrical infrastructure, water protection and noise. The moratorium would not have halted existing data center operations.

The language of the ordinance that was passed Tuesday states that it is intended to complement Memphis Mayor Paul Young's executive order to establish a 90-day period to study the impacts of data center development.

Many attendees in the chambers appeared shocked and confused at the proposal for the new ordinance. A few members of the crowd remained in the chambers following the vote where they sang, chanted and vocalized their frustrations.

FILE -- Construction on a SpaceXAI data center on Riverport Road in Memphis, Tennessee, on April 25, 2025. Photo by Brandon Dill/The Washington Post via Getty Images

The city council's move comes after a postponement of the vote earlier this month spurred protests in the chambers and resulted in an early end to an Oct. 6 meeting.

Community members' opposition to data center development in Memphis is reflective of the broader attitude across America in recent months. According to a recent Pew Research Center survey, over half of Americans say they're not comfortable with a new data center operating in their area — a sentiment that's spilling over into city council meetings and town halls across the country.

Ahead of the vote, KeShaun Pearson, the executive director of the Memphis Community Against Pollution, said that community members were concerned about what they feel has been a lack of transparency from local government officials and data centers' environmental impact.

"It's as if the people who have been elected to protect us and to stand up to corporations and be that representative have just completely abdicated that responsibility, and left us to fend for ourselves," he said.

Pearson and his brother, Tennessee Rep. Justin Pearson, were among a handful of people barred from city council meetings following the protests at city hall earlier this month.

A federal judge lifted the ban and the two were present during the vote. Pearson and the group have sued the city council over the ban.

World.title: Feds charge powerful Virginia Democrat in alleged drug scheme
World.content:
Norfolk, Virginia — L. Louise Lucas, a powerful Virginia state senator and vocal Trump critic who played a central role in the state's redistricting effort last year, was taken into federal custody Thursday and charged in connection with an alleged bribery and racketeering scheme, the Justice Department said.

According to a 45-page indictment filed in the Eastern District of Virginia, Lucas and six other co-defendants are charged with conspiring to distribute and possess marijuana, conspiring to launder money, laundering money and committing bribery by distributing large quantities of illegal marijuana under the auspices of her legal medical cannabis business.

A federal grand jury returned the indictment last week. Lucas, 82, surrendered to law enforcement on Thursday morning. She faces five of the eight charges included in the indictment and is set to make her initial appearance before a federal magistrate judge Thursday afternoon.

Lucas vowed to fight the charges in a statement on X.

"Today, the FBI, the Department of Justice, and the full weight of the federal government have been wielded against an 82-year-old great-grandmother," she said. "I grew up under Jim Crow. I've seen what happens when people in power try to silence those who stand up to them. I spent my life fighting back, and I'm not stopping now."

At a press conference to discuss the charges in Norfolk, Virginia, Attorney General Todd Blanche dismissed concerns about bringing the charges so close to the midterm elections, noting that Lucas is not on the ballot. He said there was "nothing improper" about the timing of the indictment.

The case comes nearly six months after federal law enforcement searched Lucas' office and a shop called The Cannabis Outlet that she co-owns in Portsmouth, Virginia. One source familiar with the investigation told CBS News at the time of the search that the investigation started during the Biden administration.

The charges

Virginia State Sen. L. Louise Lucas at the Virginia State Capitol in Richmond on Feb. 18, 2026. Kendall Warner/The Virginian-Pilot/Getty Images

Federal prosecutors in the Eastern District of Virginia alleged that since at least 2019, Lucas has been the leader of the scheme and used her political influence in Virginia to enact legislation and regulations to financially benefit herself and co-defendants, as well as insulate the alleged criminal enterprise she was running from state law enforcement.

Lucas allegedly directed the enterprise to buy and sell over 100 kilograms of illegal marijuana. She was indicted alongside her daughters, Lisa Lucas-Burke and Theresa Lucas-Lamb, and grandson, Ryan Eichelberger, in addition to other co-defendants.

Blanche said that Lucas and her co-defendants allegedly engaged in a "large-scale RICO drug trafficking and money laundering conspiracy."

Prosecutors will prove that Lucas "violated the trust of the people of Portsmouth and Chesapeake, Virginia, and of her state Senate colleagues," Blanche said.

"Through her elected office, Sen. Lucas has been a public servant of the people of Virginia. Her first duty should have been looking out for her constituents before herself," the attorney general said. "But the charges listed in the indictment reflect the alleged behavior of a public servant who put her own financial interests before the people she was elected to serve. Whether you are a Democrat or a Republican, an elected official or an everyday citizen, nobody is above the law."

Blanche said the investigation that led to the charges began "many years ago" and was not started by the Trump administration.

FBI Director Kash Patel also spoke at the press conference and said Lucas "has many things to answer for." He characterized her actions as "truly the epitome of hypocrisy for a public official."

As a result of the alleged scheme, Lucas accumulated nearly $5 million in "ill-gotten gains," according to the FBI director.

Medical marijuana can be sold by licensed dispensaries in Virginia and people can possess a certain amount for personal use. The state is set to launch regulated retail marijuana sales next year after the Virginia legislature legalized the sale of recreational cannabis in July.

Lucas sponsored a legalization bill in the state Senate in 2021 and has supported other measures decriminalizing marijuana, according to the National Organization for the Reform of Marijuana Laws.

Prosecutors claimed that in 2023 and 2024, Lucas was issued violation notices from the state's Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services related to The Cannabis Outlet for selling cannabis products that did not comply with state law.

According to the indictment, Lucas allegedly told an unindicted co-conspirator that she wanted a recreational license in the state to create "generational wealth" for her and her family, adding "this is my last chance."

In a phone call with a Virginia state lawmaker in March, Lucas allegedly said she needed the recreational industry to get off the ground, because "when I did it, it was obviously illegal." The indictment also alleges that Lucas was warned by a senior law enforcement official in multiple meetings that selling marijuana was illegal.

Prosecutors unveiled the indictment just weeks before the November elections. Lucas is not up for reelection, but her daughter, Lucas-Burke, is running for the Portsmouth City Council. As a general practice, the Justice Department has historically avoided overt law enforcement or prosecutorial activities involving political figures within 60 days of an election.

Blanche said the unwritten so-called "60-day rule" is not part of the Justice Manual, which lays out internal department policies and procedures. He defended the decision to charge Lucas and her daughter.

"We don't do political paybacks," he said.

Lucas was a key figure in pushing for a new congressional map through Virginia's Legislature that had added four Democratic-leaning seats. The map was approved in a ballot referendum in April but in May the Virginia Supreme Court tossed out the new map, dealing a blow to state Democrats. The U.S. Supreme Court then rejected an effort by Virginia Democrats to revive the new House lines.

Lucas was first elected to the Virginia General Assembly in 1991 and is currently the Senate president pro tempore. As she helped lead the Democratic redistricting plan earlier this year, Lucas used social media to taunt Republicans, President Trump and even the Democratic U.S. senators from her state. She was reelected in 2023 to a four-year term and is not up for reelection until 2027.

"You all started it and we f***ing finished it," she posted on social media after the measure passed, referring to Mr. Trump's push to redraw Texas' congressional map that kicked off the redistricting battle between the two parties.

World.title: Greetings from the Brazil-Argentina border, where waterfalls are flowing at near-record rates
World.content:
Greetings from the Brazil-Argentina border, where waterfalls are flowing at near-record rates

Carrie Kahn/NPR

IGUAZÚ NATIONAL PARK, Argentina — Few times in my life have I felt the enormity and power of nature. Standing at the edge of Iguazú Falls, on the Brazil-Argentina border, was one of them.

Iguazú isn't just one imposing fall, but a complex of cascades spanning more than a mile across both countries. A rain-soaked October in Brazil has sent near-record volumes of water surging over its towering cliffs. Scientists link the relentless rains to this year's Super El Niño, causing extreme weather events across the globe.

But what a spectacular force of nature for the lower-than-average number of tourists who braved the deluge this month. The roar of the rushing Iguazú river under your feet penetrates your body; your eyes strain to keep up as the rusty swells disappear over the steep precipice.



One day during my recent visit, officials registered nearly 12 million liters (more than 3 million gallons) of water per second tumbling over the falls. That's 10 times the normal flow. As the Iguazú river's red, muddy waters raced furiously toward the falls' edge, they lapped the bottom of the narrow metal catwalks that usually hover a few feet above the falls during normal-rainfall years.



Officials closed the spectacular walkways as the river level kept rising. When asked why access was shut off, the national park's director simply said, "It just keeps raining."



That's an understatement. I'm still drying out.

World.title: 5 simple ways to relieve the aches and pains of sitting at a desk all day
World.content:
5 simple ways to relieve the aches and pains of sitting at a desk all day

Olga Pankova/Getty Images/Moment RF

Back pain, eye strain, sluggishness, shoulder aches, restlessness.

If you sit in front of a computer for long periods of time, whether it's for work or leisure, you've probably experienced one of these symptoms.

But there are ways to relieve some of this discomfort — and even combat some of the health risks that may come with prolonged sitting. That includes walking breaks, ergonomic solutions and quick, simple stretches.

Here's a roundup of tips that have been previously featured on Life Kit.

If you feel tired and sluggish … go for a five-minute walk (every half hour)

Antonio_Diaz/Getty Images/iStockphoto

We know that a sedentary lifestyle isn't great for human health. Studies have shown it can lead to fatigue, weight gain and back and joint pain — and it's been linked to chronic diseases like obesity, heart disease and cancer. Yet adults in the United States spend an average of 9.5 hours sitting per day, involved in activities tied to computers, laptops and phones.

Sponsor Message

But there may be a way to mitigate its harms. In 2023, researchers at Columbia University Medical Center set out to find the least amount of movement you need to counteract the dangers of prolonged sitting. And they found that walking for five minutes every 30 minutes was the most effective strategy .

In 2023, our colleagues at NPR's Body Electric tested out this five-minute walking exercise on our NPR listeners. Over 20,000 participants joined the challenge — and reported higher productivity and lower fatigue .

Want to give this walking challenge a try? Get instructions from Body Electric — and use this worksheet to keep track of your walking breaks .

If your back aches from slouching over your desk … rotate your spine

Beck Harlan/NPR

Anyone who works at a desk knows how easy it can be to slip into a slouch. If we're not careful, that mid-back rounding can creep into all of our sitting time and create pain by putting stress on the middle section of our spine.

This movement above seeks to relieve that stress and encourage flexibility by mimicking the natural movements of the spine — side bending, bending backward and rotating, says Vinh Pham, a physical therapist. The idea is to get the body comfortable with these motions so that when you encounter them in real life, they're not painful.

Sponsor Message

To do this modified movement, which Pham calls the 3D T-spine rotation, stand up and drop your right foot behind the left, about a foot apart. Starting with the right arm straight up and the left arm behind you, as if you're shaking the hand of the person behind you, simultaneously drop your arms — still in a straight position — and twist toward your right foot. Move them back to their original position and hold for two seconds. Repeat the movement ten times before switching legs and doing the same exercise on the other side.

For more pain-relieving stretches, read this story.

If your eyes hurt from staring at a screen … stretch your eye muscles

When you stare at a screen for long periods of time, your eyes have to work hard. They must first turn inward to look at a close subject, then adjust the focus for short vision and hold that position.

Digital eye strain, as eye doctors call it, can cause eye fatigue, headaches or blurry vision. Try the exercise below to relieve that strain.

LA Johnson/NPR

If you feel fidgety and restless … change your position (and don't worry too much about the "right" posture)

ljubaphoto/Getty Images/E+

Fidgeting is a sign you need to break out of a stagnant posture, says Katy Bowman , a biomechanist and author of Rethink Your Position and Movement Matters. Even a position that feels comfortable at first can begin causing back pain, headaches or stiffness if you hold it long enough .

So listen to your body and mix things up. Alternate between sitting, standing, reclining and moving. That might mean opting to stand in the back of a conference room during a big staff meeting, taking a call while going on a walk or reading a report with your feet propped up in the break room.

The goal is to put yourself in configurations that contort your body in different ways. They should be "adaptive and dynamic" and easy to "change in and out of," says Leada Malek , a physical therapist and author of the book Science of Stretch.

Sponsor Message

Don't worry too much about what is "good" and "bad" posture. Both Malek and Bowman agree on a common phrase among physical therapists: "Your best posture is your next posture."

If sitting at your desk makes you feel uncomfortable … adjust your workspace

LA Johnson/NPR

Your monitor screen should be at eye level so you're not craning your head down to see. And, your keyboard and mouse should be low enough so you're not shrugging your shoulders and lifting up your arms like a praying mantis to type and click.

Meg Honan, a professional ergonomist, says this common "head down and arms up" position sets you up to feel "achy, sore and tired." To combat this uncomfortable and oftentimes painful position, try repositioning your tech. Bring your laptop or desktop monitor screen up to eye level with a stack of books or some other platform.

Place your keyboard and mouse at a lower height where you don't have to shrug your shoulders to use them. If your keyboard is attached to your laptop, consider connecting an external keyboard and mouse so you can have the computer screen at your eye level and lower your arms. External mouses don't just help lower our arms, but they also prevent the constant strain of using a trackpad.

For more ergonomic tips, read our story .

This story includes reporting from Ruth Tam, Sylvie Douglis, Frank Festa, Andee Tagle, Manoush Zomorodi and Margaret Cirino. This story was edited by Meghan Keane. The visual editor is Beck Harlan. We'd love to hear from you. Leave us a voicemail at 202-216-9823, or email us at LifeKit@npr.org.
