World.title: Trump merchandise stores are closing: 'He has peaked'
World.content:
Trump merchandise stores are closing: 'He has peaked'

toggle caption i Frank Langfitt/NPR

BENSALEM, Pa. – When the Trump merchandise store here announced it was closing earlier this year, Wes Alker, a Trump superfan and retired auto mechanic, came by for some nostalgia and the going-out-of-business deals. They included everything from "Trump Won" caps for $9.99 to Trump pool floats for $19.99.

Trump stores first emerged during the 2016 campaign. But with the president now in his second and final term, store owners say there isn't as much to fire up the consumer fan base and sales have softened.

At least four stores have closed this year. The MAGA Mall , a big online retailer and wholesaler, reports sales of MAGA gear are down 30% compared to a presidential election year when Trump is on the ballot.

toggle caption i Frank Langfitt/NPR

"He's no longer a viable business model for entrepreneurs because he has peaked," said Alker, who wore a gray T-shirt with a photo of former President Joe Biden and former Vice-President Kamala Harris which read, "Dumb and Dumber."

Sponsor Message

Trump's lame duck status isn't the only drag on demand. When the Bensalem store closed – it still maintains an online presence – Trump's average approval rating had already fallen from 50 % when he took office to 44 %.

Nine months later, when Bill Hays shut down his Trump super store outside of Knoxville, Tennessee, the president's approval rating had fallen five more points.

toggle caption i Frank Langfitt/NPR

Hays said unpopular policies – such as DOGE's massive government staff cuts – have had an impact. He noticed that instead of immediately putting on their new Trump gear, more buyers asked for bags.

"People were not wearing their colors, so to speak, like they did before the (2024) election," said Hays, 80.

toggle caption i Frank Langfitt/NPR

When Hays opened his store in April 2024, business boomed. One day, he said, there was a line of 80 people out the door and sales hit $200,000 a month. By the time it closed in September, sales had fallen to just $20,000 a month.

"After the inauguration, I think a lot of people felt that their job was done," said Hays. "They didn't have to promote MAGA or Trump."

Hays still has a Trump store in the Tennessee tourist town of Gatlinburg. He's waiting to see how Christmas sales go before deciding its future.

Trump stores are a phenomenon. Other charismatic presidents such as Ronald Reagan and Barack Obama developed ardent followings, but didn't inspire brick-and-mortar merch outlets in red and blue states. Hays says Trump created such demand because he's a salesman - and he tells people what they want to hear.

Sponsor Message

toggle caption i Frank Langfitt/NPR

Ron Solomon, president of the MAGA Mall, says there are about 20 stores that specialize in Trump merchandise still in operation.

In Myrtle Beach, Rick Kligman sells items out of two stores, but he's trying to get rid of older material, stuffing $40 worth of merchandise into a grab bag that he sells for $9.99. He's concerned about the mid-terms and thinks a Democratic sweep of the House and Senate could turn off the more casual Trump consumer.

"I don't want to be sitting holding thousands and thousands of dollars of Trump merchandise and absolutely no possibility of selling it," said Kligman, 69.

Given term limits and Trump's age, retailers are diversifying beyond the Trump brand and embracing more patriotic products, including hats that say "We the People."

Solomon says this is a natural progression.

Eventually, Trump will leave the national stage. Unless a family member picks up the mantle, Solomon says the Trump merchandise business "will fade away."



Research by NPR's Susie Cummings.

World.title: A GOP congressman voted to cut Medicaid. It covers 62% of his district. Can he win?
World.content:
A GOP congressman voted to cut Medicaid. It covers 62% of his district. Can he win?

toggle caption i Jae C. Hong/AP

Ulises Hernandez, of Bakersfield, Calif., has had health coverage through Medicaid for as long as he can remember.

But he had never waited as long for care as he did in September after a dental crown slipped down his throat during a procedure. He spent eight hours in an emergency room waiting for care and more than two days without food.

This story was produced in partnership with KFF Health News.

Sitting in his wheelchair to protest looming federal Medicaid cuts outside Republican U.S. Rep. David Valadao's Bakersfield office, Hernandez described his wait as a foreshadowing of what's ahead.

"I couldn't eat, I couldn't drink, I couldn't do anything, and I was in pain," said Hernandez, who had been discharged from the hospital a few days before. "I'm livid."

Hernandez, 41, said Valadao "should be ashamed of himself" for voting for the Republicans' One Big Beautiful Bill Act. The law is expected to reduce Medicaid spending by more than $900 billion through 2034, with provisions such as stricter Medicaid eligibility rules and reducing federal money to states.

Sponsor Message

Hernandez plans to vote for challenger Randy Villegas in hopes that this Central Valley toss-up district, where roughly 6 in 10 of constituents are enrolled in Medicaid, can help give Democrats control of Congress.

toggle caption i Mario Tama/Getty Images

Villegas, a political science professor, has embraced the progressive rallying cry for "Medicare for All" and called out Valadao for a vote "that is going to rip away healthcare from Valley families," since many working-age adults may not satisfy new work requirements and twice-a-year eligibility checks that, by political design, start after the midterm elections.

Valadao defends his vote on the GOP bill. During a televised Oct. 6 debate, he said "there are no actual cuts" to Medicaid.

toggle caption i Jackie Fortiér/KFF Health News



An estimated 60,000 more residents of his district could be without coverage by 2034 due to the tax and spending bill and the expiration of enhanced premium tax credits for Affordable Care Act insurance plans, according to the left-leaning Center for American Progress think tank.

Researchers estimate that those new rules will push more than 2 million Californians statewide off their coverage and that the state stands to lose about $30 billion a year, more than any other state.

Fertile Ground, High Unemployment

Bakersfield is an oil town, and it wears that identity proudly. Pump jacks nod in the distance. Streets run wide. The Kern River's bed lies dry, its water siphoned to feed the agricultural fields.

Sponsor Message

Sitting partially in the southernmost portion of the contested congressional district, this city produces much from the land, but unemployment is high.

Democrats have outnumbered Republicans in voter registrations by double-digit percentage points in Valadao's district since he was first elected to the U.S. House in 2012, yet he has won six of his seven congressional elections.

toggle caption i Mario Tama/Getty Images

Valadao has survived by focusing on local issues such as water infrastructure and distancing himself from the Trump administration, said Jeffrey Cummins, a political science professor at California State University-Fresno. Valadao is the last remaining Republican House incumbent who voted to impeach Trump after the Jan. 6, 2021, riot at the U.S. Capitol who is running for reelection to Congress.

"This is an area where, even when we see the registration advantage for Democrats, that they are moderate Democrats who tend to be concerned with agricultural issues, and Valadao in the past has successfully appeased those voters," Cummins said.

But California's congressional map was redrawn last year as part of a national mid-decade redistricting fight, and Valadao's Central Valley seat is considered more favorable for Democrats than before. Cummins said a different mix of voters, coupled with anger toward incumbents, could flip the seat.

"Valadao knows that he's on notice," Cummins said.

toggle caption i Jackie Fortiér/KFF Health News



Nationwide, healthcare costs remain a top affordability concern for voters, and they trust Democrats over Republicans by a 2-to-1 margin on the issue, according to a September KFF poll. Valadao lost in 2018, when Democrats targeted his votes to repeal the ACA, as well as his alliance with Trump.

On Nov. 3, he faces Villegas, a populist backed by Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) who favors a single-payer universal healthcare system.

"The system that we have now, we pay twice as much as other countries across the world, despite the fact that we have worse healthcare outcomes," Villegas said during the debate.

Sponsor Message

At campaign event, no mention of healthcare

On Sept. 30, Valadao held a $1,000-a-ticket fundraiser. It was hosted by House Speaker Mike Johnson, who is campaigning across 22 states in six weeks as Republicans try to hold the chamber.

Afterward, press were allowed at an invitation-only reelection event in Bakersfield, held in an office building just outside of the new district Valadao hopes to represent. Arches of red, white, and blue star-shaped balloons framed the small stage.

toggle caption i Mario Tama/Getty Images

Neither lawmaker mentioned Medicaid or the rising cost of healthcare when they spoke to the audience.

After brief speeches, Valadao repeatedly refused to answer KFF Health News' questions about his vote for the One Big Beautiful Bill Act and its impact on his constituents' Medicaid coverage, saying, "I think you are distorting the truth."

Of the half dozen attendees KFF Health News approached among roughly 50 in the room, none lived in Valadao's district.

They came anyway. Retired nurse Charlotte Brandt lives in the neighboring Republican-held district but follows Valadao's votes closely. She called him "a hero for the Central Valley," citing his work on water, oil, and agriculture, which she said sustain Kern County as the "breadbasket of the world."

toggle caption i Mario Tama/Getty Images

Her daughter, Allison Brandt Oliver, who also lives in Republican Vince Fong's district, said she favored the stricter Medicaid eligibility rules Republicans put into place, saying her concern is whether spending is going to U.S. citizens who contribute to the economy.

A few days later during the televised debate, Valadao said he was among the negotiators who secured community engagement provisions in the law, which will require certain adults on Medicaid to prove they're working or completing other activities such as job training or volunteering.

"It's not an actual cut," Valadao said. "We need people to actually put in and make a fair effort to try to cover their expenses and be a part of their community. This is not an unreasonable ask."

Sponsor Message

$32 million in campaign ads for one swing district

In a sign of how vital this district is, Republicans and Democrats have each booked more than $16 million in ads here through Election Day, according to data compiled by AdImpact.

"When you start getting over $10 million of spending total in the district, I would say that that's pretty high," Cummins said.

Some of the ads are reaching voters in unexpected ways.

Outside a local library, Seslie Maese, a stay-at-home mom from Bakersfield, said her 7-year-old, who often watches Lego videos on YouTube, runs to her whenever a certain ad plays.

"David Valadago is going on vacation again, Mom," he'll tell her, mispronouncing the congressman's name. Her son doesn't realize the ad, paid for by a Democratic political action committee, means that as a criticism.

Maese is undecided. Even though she's a registered Republican, she said what she has heard about Valadao doesn't sound positive, such as that he went back on his pledge not to cut Medicaid for vulnerable populations by voting for the federal tax-and-spending law.

For Maese, a politician who says one thing and does another is a deal-breaker.

"He just hasn't come through with anything he said," she said, "especially since he cut off a lot of Medicaid."

This story comes from NPR's health reporting partnership with KFF Health News, a national newsroom that produces in-depth journalism about health issues and is one of the core operating programs at KFF — the independent source for health policy research, polling, and journalism.

World.title: Trump's redistricting gave Republicans a head start, now it goes to the voters
World.content:
Trump's redistricting gave Republicans a head start, now it goes to the voters

Voters across much of the South are casting ballots ahead of next month's midterm elections in congressional districts that were redrawn following calls from President Trump. He said it would help the GOP hold the House, where they currently outnumber Democrats 218 to 214.

In state legislatures over the last year, Republicans tilted about eight more seats their way than Democrats did in response. (That's an estimate, shown on the bar graph below.)

Loading...

But it's the voters who will decide whether it works.

Here's the catch: Republicans redrew districts partly on how people voted in the presidential election in 2024. Now the political mood has changed and many who voted for President Trump two years ago could be voting for Democrats, or not voting, in the midterms. The Republicans could lose many of the districts they targeted.

Usually, states redistrict early in each decade after the census. But Trump called on legislatures to do it now. It set off a chain reaction of political crises across the country that threw legislatures into the national spotlight.

Sponsor Message

Texas Republicans issued arrest warrants for Democratic legislators who'd left the state. The Louisiana governor suspended a primary after thousands of votes were already cast so the lines could be redrawn. In Missouri, the state supreme court found the Republican secretary of state in contempt for sticking with a GOP map that was not legally in effect.

In California and Virginia, Democrats won approval in statewide votes for redistricting in response to the Republicans in other states – only to have the courts toss out Virginia's plan. And when the Supreme Court weakened the Voting Rights Act this spring, it fueled rushed legislative sessions to draw maps that often ended up weakening the voting power of minority communities.

In a few places, Republicans rejected Trump's call to redistrict, including dramatic votes in the Indiana and South Carolina legislatures. But overall, Trump prompted a cycle of mid-decade redistricting unlike any since the 1960s, when courts set the current rules.

Here's where states redistricted - or didn't.

World.title: How long does it take to save up for a starter home? Twice as long as it did in 2019
World.content:
How long does it take to save up for a starter home? Twice as long as it did in 2019

toggle caption i Justin Sullivan/Getty Images

Mortgage rates topping 7% is the latest sign of how hard it has gotten to buy a first house, with aspiring owners already facing sky-high prices. A new analysis out Thursday shines a light on yet another growing obstacle: the amount needed to close a home loan.

"Over the last seven years, the time to save up that down payment and closing costs has doubled," said Mike Calhoun, president of the Center for Responsible Lending, a research nonprofit that promotes economic opportunity. The report was released by the center's Julian Bond Institute.

Since 2019, the last time the center made the same calculation, home prices have shot up, inflation spiked and has remained stubbornly high, and the rising cost of food, gas, healthcare and more has strained family budgets. Closing costs on a home loan have also ticked up, driven in part by rising homeowners insurance.

Sponsor Message

Amid all this, renters' incomes have not kept pace, and personal savings rates have dropped.

Today, the center calculates that for a median-income renter household, it would take a "staggering 16 years" to save up a down payment and closing costs for a starter home. That's twice as long as in 2019. And it would take even more time — 21 years — for a median-income Black renter household.

That kind of time frame upends a main reason that many look to buy in the first place. As the analysis notes, "young children at the time the family starts saving may have left the household — for higher education or the workforce — before the family will have saved enough to purchase their first home."

The report also narrows its calculations to middle-income households — making roughly $50,000 to $120,000 — whose members are more likely to be viable homeowners. For them, the savings time has also doubled, to 12 years.

For front-line workers, such as police officers, firefighters, EMTs, nurses and teachers, the researchers find that "the years to save has at least doubled and now ranges from 10 to 13 years."

As stark as those numbers are, Calhoun said they're likely an undercount.

The center's calculations are for a 3.5% down payment, since that's what the Federal Housing Administration requires for first-time buyers. The median first-time buyer actually puts down about 10%. The report also assumes families are really "stretching their savings," he said, even though many can't save at all, are forced to eat into savings or take on debt.

Sponsor Message

The divide in the housing economy has widened

The Center for Responsible Lending's report highlights a sharp divide in the housing economy, exacerbated when the COVID-19 pandemic triggered a spike in inflation, mortgage rates and home prices.

"If you look at the last seven years, they have been extraordinarily good to homeowners," Calhoun said. Those who bought when prices were far lower have accumulated enormous equity as home values have shot up. Some were also able to lower their monthly payments by refinancing, as mortgage rates hit historic lows of around 2% or 3% before they spiked.

Many homeowners with low rates have decided they can't afford to move and see their mortgage payments double. That has meant fewer older adults downsizing and fewer overall putting their homes on the market, intensifying a national housing shortage.

Meanwhile, rising rents have consumed an increasing share of family incomes, according to a recent report by the Harvard Joint Center for Housing Studies. "From 2001 to 2024, renter incomes rose by 9 percent in real terms while rents rose by 30 percent," it says. This has left a quarter of renters paying more than half their income on rent and utilities.

Despite a recent softening in rental markets, a record number of renters are still considered cost burdened. Lower-income households are also hit harder by inflation, since basic goods and services make up a larger portion of their budgets.

The center calculates a starter home cost of $335,574, which is 80% of the median sales price of existing homes. And the center finds that it takes less time to save a down payment and closing costs for that in some major metropolitan areas than others — from 11 years in Houston to 24 in Los Angeles.

The report also notes that housing costs have outstripped incomes pretty much everywhere and that "the problem is even more acute in the fastest-growing rural areas than in urban areas." A recent analysis by center-left think tank Third Way found that housing construction has been unable to keep up with rural growth, creating severe pressure on affordability.

Sponsor Message

Many buyers rely on help from family

The widening housing wealth gap leaves a more privileged share of Americans who are able to buy a home. "Cash purchases are way up," Calhoun said. For younger buyers, "the overwhelming way people come up with the money is from assistance from family, the 'bank of mom and dad' and friends."

Far fewer buyers get help from down payment assistance programs, even though there are thousands of them. "The programs often run out of money," Calhoun said. "A lot of these are very small, idiosyncratic."

He'd like to see more assistance programs "to reach a broader array of people who don't have intergenerational wealth."

The center's report also calls for zoning and other reforms to boost the supply of smaller, cheaper starter homes, including duplexes, townhomes and manufactured housing. A sweeping new law passed by Congress this year aims to promote that, but the onus is on states and cities to follow up, and creating new supply will take time.

Despite all this, a related survey from the center finds that millennials and Gen Zers aspire to homeownership at the same rate as earlier generations — a "testament to the resilience of the American dream," according to Thursday's report.

It's the main way "most families generate wealth that they can pass on to the next generation," said report co-author David Silberman. "I think the case for homeownership remains really strong, despite all the trends we're pointing to in the challenges of getting there."

World.title: See how Big Tech is transforming Spain's landscape
World.content:
See how Big Tech is transforming Spain's landscape

Loading...

ZARAGOZA, Spain — Aragon's rugged plains stretch out under a clear blue sky, the buildings visible as "a few tiny cubes sprawled like a throw of dice" across the terrain — as George Orwell wrote in Homage to Catalonia, of his time here during the Spanish Civil War in the 1930s. Today, excavators eat the earth, carving huge chunks of the landscape in the race to build the behemoths of the AI boom.

This drought-stricken region of northeast Spain has become the focus of American companies searching for locations to place their energy- and water-intensive data centers. In Aragon, Amazon Web Services promises to spend almost $40 billion to build multiple vast complexes — one alone as large as 600 American football fields. Microsoft and the asset management firm Blackstone are among those following suit, signing agreements to build data centers that will transform this region and the livelihoods of its inhabitants.

toggle caption i Michael Robinson Chávez/for NPR

Even as other countries enact regulations to curb the expansion of data centers (and Spain's national government weighs new restrictions), Aragon's regional government is welcoming the companies with open arms. Touting themselves as the "Virginia of southern Europe" after the U.S. state with the largest concentration of data centers, they are taking the bet that hosting data centers will bring jobs and prepare the region for the economic shifts they believe AI will bring.

Sponsor Message

"This is a new economy that is evolving, and it's very difficult to foresee how many activities are going to be coming around it," said Eva Valle, the economic counsellor for the regional government. "But they are coming."

toggle caption i Michael Robinson Chávez/for NPR

toggle caption i Michael Robinson Chávez/for NPR

toggle caption i Michael Robinson Chávez/for NPR

The companies were drawn to the region with promises of large tax breaks and fast-tracked planning permissions that give these data centers a special status usually reserved for the general interest of the local population. This order gives them the power to expropriate land, strips local mayors of veto powers, and restricts the time the public has to object to 23 working days. (For the recent Amazon Web Services development, the regional government opened the window to oppose the project over the Christmas period. Opponents of the project believe they did this to try to push it through at a time when people would be paying less attention, though the government denies this.)

toggle caption i Michael Robinson Chávez/for NPR

The rapid approval process for these large and hyperscale facilities has left many in Aragon feeling excluded from decisions that will profoundly impact their region and lives.

"It's going to be like living beside a prison"

toggle caption i Michael Robinson Chávez/for NPR

The first time Silvia Baselga and her family learned of the data center soon to tower over their home was when they noticed the survey markers poking out of the ground on the other side of their garden wall. "When we saw this, we went to the city hall and said, 'OK, we want information. This is really close to our house.'" But the local council told them they had no information. Only when the planning documents were later made public did they learn that the outer perimeter of the data center is to be built within 300 feet of their home in the hilltop village of Botorrita. The plans showed that the complex will be larger than the village itself.

toggle caption i Michael Robinson Chávez/for NPR

Baselga's parents retired here for the tranquility of a life spent in a tight-knit village community. Their home looks out over fields and gently rolling hills. To try to block the noise the data center will emit, Baselga believes the company will build a 20-foot-high wall, as happened in a nearby village. "We're going to open the window and see nothing," she said. Friends regularly visit at night to gaze at the stars in this rural setting. Baselga said the center's 24-hour security lights will block out the night sky. "It's going to be like living beside a prison."

Sponsor Message

Centers like these are set to be built across Aragon — 27 in total, according to official documents — some by Spanish and other firms, but most by American companies, taking up about 7 square miles of land. At least one is built partly on ground originally classified as protected for natural ecosystems. The companies promise employment. Amazon Web Services told NPR it will create 6,200 permanent jobs once these centers are built. But many residents fear they will also deliver an environmental crisis.

Economic development "at the cost of the environment"

toggle caption i Michael Robinson Chávez/for NPR

The data centers will consume many times the current electricity needs of the region and require large amounts of water to cool their servers in one of Spain's driest regions, one that's been repeatedly blighted by drought.

Julio Enfedaque drives across the parched land his family has farmed for generations. This year it barely rained for four months, and the government cut the amount of water available for irrigation by two-thirds. "Even if they say the data centers won't take the water that we need for agriculture, I am sure it's going to become very complicated to farm like my ancestors used to." Enfedaque has advised his nephews to find different careers and leave the land.

toggle caption i Michael Robinson Chávez/for NPR

Amazon Web Services says its data centers will draw water only after temperatures hit 86 degrees Fahrenheit and that they are investing millions of dollars to help fix leaking water pipes and working with farmers to use AI technology to make their water use more efficient. "We're trying to not only use as less [sic] water as possible, but also to help those communities where we operate have the best infrastructure," David Blázquez, Amazon's head of public policy for Spain and Portugal, told NPR.

But the company remains opaque about how much water each center will use. Blázquez said it's "a company policy not to publish water usage per site." Regional figures show Amazon's three existing data centers, which are much smaller than what is planned, used 68 million liters — 48% more than the company had originally told regional officials they would need.

Sponsor Message

Endangering valuable habitat for rare and migratory birds

toggle caption i Michael Robinson Chávez/for NPR

Perhaps an even bigger problem is the energy these centers need to run. Unlike many data centers in the U.S., which are powered by natural gas, companies in Aragon say they will rely mainly on renewable sources (though they also have diesel generators on site). Blázquez says Amazon Web Services has secured "a hundred renewable projects in Spain," including 17 in Aragon.

While that energy is carbon-free, ecologists and biologists warn that additional wind projects could have their own devastating consequences for the environment.

The region is full of hunting grounds for vultures and other birds of prey and an important stop for migrating birds.

toggle caption i Michael Robinson Chávez/for NPR

toggle caption i Michael Robinson Chávez/for NPR

"The vultures look for the thermal air currents to lift them. But they run straight into the windmills — for them it's like flying through knives," explained José Antonio Pinzolas, an ornithologist.

Aragon's own environmental agency has warned that wind farms in this area pose a high risk of collision to the endangered red kite and other protected raptors, and has documented an increase in bird and bat deaths in recent years as the renewable sector expands.

"I've collected ospreys, golden eagles, kestrels by the dozen, black vultures," said Juan Ballesteros, a nature protection officer for the local government.

toggle caption i Michael Robinson Chávez/for NPR

toggle caption i Michael Robinson Chávez/for NPR

Ballesteros used to love his job for its access to wildlife. Now, he said, he spends his days placing the corpses of birds killed by turbine blades into body bags. Ballesteros met NPR as he arrived to collect the body of a young Eurasian black vulture that lay dead on the ground, its wings splayed in the dirt at the foot of a wind turbine.

Blázquez told NPR, of the damage to this important habitat that the expansion of wind and solar farms causes, that Amazon Web Services "definitely shares those concerns." He said they work with renewable energy companies that comply with environmental legislation. But Pinzolas said the growing number of bird deaths shows the current protections in place are not working.

Sponsor Message

Environmental groups say the overall impact of wind turbines on birds isn't being properly assessed.

Several groups have crowdfunded together to mount a legal action to try to stop Amazon Web Services' expansion in Aragon. The court case challenges the Aragon government's fast-tracked approvals of the plans. "We have concerns about water consumption, about energy consumption, the impact on some other industries and on the environment," said Luis García,, an activist with Ecologistas En Accion, one of the organizations involved in the case. He said the economic benefits of data centers are not great enough to justify the "huge damage they do to the environment."

Locals fight to preserve nature for future generations

toggle caption i Michael Robinson Chávez/for NPR

One recent weekend in the region's capital, Zaragoza, an avenue filled with demonstrators protesting against a new data center to be built at the edge of a forest by the city. Residents fear the heat and noise of the complex will destroy a tranquil space that is a haven during the hot summer months.

toggle caption i Michael Robinson Chávez/for NPR

"This is a worthy fight as all the worlds invades us, to save this pine forests, to save the environment, against this voracious capitalism that thinks only of economic interests and not of people," said Marian Rams, a local resident with white hair dyed in hues of pink, green and blue. "They want to swap nature for data centers."

toggle caption i Michael Robinson Chávez/for NPR

Nearby, a little girl no older than 5 chanted along with the demonstrators. Her mother, Ana Domezian, walked alongside her with her second child, a baby, nestled in a carrier against her chest. "If we don't fight now for what we have," she asked, "what are we going to leave to them in the future?"

World.title: Minister giving Stelco owner 15 days to reverse layoffs before taking case to court
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Industry Minister Mélanie Joly is giving the American parent company of Hamilton-based Stelco 15 days to reverse layoffs before turning to the courts.

In a "demand letter" sent to Ohio-based Cleveland-Cliffs on Thursday, Joly says the company is violating its commitments under the Investment Canada Act.

"In the event Cliffs fails to comply with this demand, the Minister may, pursuant to section 40 of the Act, make an application to a superior court," the letter, obtained by Radio-Canada, reads.

Joly indicates that if the government proceeds with legal action, it would be asking the courts to issue monetary penalties against Cleveland-Cliffs and potentially direct the company to divest from Stelco.

"I remain prepared to sit down with Cleveland-Cliffs to find a solution. But our bottom line is clear: protect Canadian jobs, defend our steel industry and ensure that commitments made to Canada are respected," Joly said in a statement.

Industry Minister Mélanie Joly answers questions from reporters in Ottawa on Oct. 14. (Justin Tang/The Canadian Press)

Cleveland-Cliffs said late last month that it plans to lay off as many as 500 workers as it idles certain steel production at Stelco, a move the federal government says violates "binding commitments" made when it bought the company in 2024.

The federal government has said the company's purchase of Stelco included promises to employ "at least the same number of unionized employees and the vast majority of non-unionized employees" as there were in 2024 through 2029.

The company said the planned layoffs are in order to "ensure the survival" of the company, as U.S. tariffs on steel squeeze its sales. But Joly has dismissed that reasoning.

"Let me be clear: no act of god or change in market conditions can relieve Cleveland-Cliffs of the commitments it made to Canada. Those commitments are not optional," she said in her statement.

CBC News has reached out to Cleveland-Cliffs for comment.

Joly previously issued an ultimatum to the company to share a plan to avoid the layoffs or risk legal action. But the company rebuffed the government's claim that it is in violation of its 2024 agreement.

An animation GIF shows an industrial worker walking near Stelco Hamilton Works; signage outside the plant; and a bird's-eye view of the steelmaker with the Lake Ontario and the Toronto skyline in the distance, on Oct. 9 (Evan Mitsui/CBC)

"Your representation that Stelco's planned layoffs cause it to breach its undertakings is false," Paul Simon, president and general counsel at Stelco Inc., wrote in a letter to Joly earlier this month.

Despite the company insisting the layoffs are required to ensure its survival, Cleveland-Cliffs said just days ago that Stelco's third quarter this year was its "strongest" since it acquired the Hamilton plant.

"Third quarter was Stelco's strongest ... since we acquired the company two years ago. The Canadian hot-rolled market has improved substantially," Cleveland-Cliffs CEO Lourenco Goncalves said in a statement on Monday.

If the federal government proceeds to take Cleveland-Cliffs to court, it won't be the first time Stelco has been at the centre of a legal battle. In 2009, Industry Canada sued Stelco's previous owner, U.S. Steel, over job protection. The matter was settled out of court in 2011.

World.title: Carney announces trade and defence partnership with Turkey
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Prime Minister Mark Carney's political and economic tightrope act began Thursday as he and Turkish President Recep Erdogan announced a strategic partnership aimed at expanding trade and defence co-operation.

It is the latest step in the warming of relations between the two nations and an important moment in the prime minister's plan to co-operate more closely with other middle-power countries.

Carney praised Turkey as an "exceptional" partner.

"No country builds strength alone," he said in a joint statement at the sprawling presidential palace compound.

"The most resilient countries bring together complementary strengths with trusted partners. Our goal isn’t self-sufficiency. It is collective resilience. That’s why Canada is building deeper partnerships with reliable partners that create new opportunities for Canadians."

There are four pillars to the new partnership — trade and investment, defence and security, energy, and people-to-people ties.

Next month, negotiators will sit down in Ankara for the first round of free trade talks. Also, the partnership includes a new agreement on defence industry co-operation that will better connect Canadian and Turkish companies.

Minister of Energy and Natural Resources Tim Hodgson, seen here in Ottawa on July 16, is joining Carney for talks with Turkish officials. (Justin Tang/The Canadian Press)

The partnership will also pave the way for investments in the energy and critical minerals sectors. The two countries will also finalize an air transport agreement, increasing passenger flights between the two countries.

The bilateral visit, a first for Canadian prime minister, comes as human rights groups raise the alarm over Turkey's sweeping crackdown last month on dissent and civil society groups, including the dismantling of 2SLGBTQ+ and HIV-advocacy organizations.

"The prime minister has been very clear. We need to engage with the world as it is, not the way we wish it to be," Energy Minister Tim Hodgson said ahead of the trip. He will be joining Carney for talks with Turkish officials.

People run from the police during a march in support of transgender people and their rights during the 2SLGBTQ+ Pride week, in Istanbul, Turkey, on June 21. (Dilara Acikgoz/The Associated Press)

"Where we have differences of opinion, we discuss those in private."

Carney is looking to diversify Canada's trade to make the country less dependent on the United States. Much of the effort has thus far gone into deepening ties with Europe and nations in the Indo-Pacific.

Turkey, a member of NATO with a growing defence industrial sector, is seen as a key ally on the trade and military production fronts, says Thomas Juneau of the University of Ottawa, an expert in the Middle East.

"What the Carney government appears to be making as a choice is not to restrict diversification efforts only to democracies, only to countries that have positive human rights records," said Juneau.

Turkey has become increasingly authoritarian under Erdogan, who has been president since 2014.

"This is morally a difficult dilemma on the Canadian side, but the calculus appears on the part of the government that if Canada were to choose to diversify only with democracies the ceiling for success would be low."

Immediately after landing in Ankara on Thursday, visited Anitkabir, the Mausoleum of Mustafa Kemal Atatürk, who was the founder and first president of the Republic of Turkey.

The structure and its 750,000 square-metre grounds are beautifully maintained, divided into the Peace Park with tens of thousands of plants and trees including Canadian maples, and the Monument Block. Carney laid a wreath at the monument.

Carney pays his respects after laying a wreath during a ceremony at the Anıtkabir, the Mausoleum of Mustafa Kemal Ataturk, in Ankara. (Adrian Wyld/The Canadian Press)

Turkey aims to expand its energy capacity significantly in the coming decades, planning to add roughly 20 gigawatts of nuclear power by 2050.

To that end, Ottawa and Ankara are reportedly planning to set up a working group to study the feasibility of a bid by Canada's Candu nuclear team in order to build Turkey's planned second or third nuclear power plant.

Asked ahead of the trip to Ankara, Hodgson said he wasn't in a position to scoop the prime minister and told reporters to stay tuned.

Sevag Belian, the executive director of the Armenian National Committee of Canada, says any nuclear deal with Turkey deserves close scrutiny.

He pointed to the previous falling out between the two countries which resulted in Canada imposing a de facto arms embargo, which was mostly lifted in 2024. The lifting of those measures was the price Erdogen demanded of the Trudeau government for getting behind Sweden's membership in NATO.

The fallout started in 2020 when Turkish authorities applied for an exemption related to importation of Wescam target acquisition gear used in Turkey's Bayraktar drones.

"We know from the disclosed documents that they had said that they will be using the few cameras that they got through the exemption for reconnaissance activities related to NATO operations in the north of Syria," said Belian.

"But then we know that those cameras were actually diverted illegally to Azerbaijan and used during the war in Nagorno.

"We have established through parliamentary investigation that the Turkish side clearly lied."

World.title: First Nations artists pull art from University of Calgary after event inviting debate on residential schools
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Two First Nations artists have pulled their work from the University of Calgary’s gallery in a protest over a controversial event on campus last month.

The day before the National Day for Truth and Reconciliation, a group set up a table on the University of Calgary campus, inviting students to debate whether residential schools were an act of genocide.

The event led to a demonstration and calls for the university to take action.

The event was put on by Canadian Students for Free Speech, a group launched this summer that advocates for open debate on campuses, with University of Calgary professor emeritus Tom Flanagan and Rebel News reporter Drea Humphrey there to invite debate.

Flanagan described it as a “Charlie Kirk format” debate, referencing the late American conservative political activist.

During the event, one student was caught on camera dumping water on Flanagan. Calgary police say that person was brought in for questioning, but was not charged.

Artists take a stand

The artists, seth cardinal dodginghorse (who only uses lowercase letters in their name) and their mother, Glenna Cardinal, collaborate as an artist duo called tīná gúyáńí, translating to Deer Road in Tsuut'ina.

Individually and together, the duo had seven pieces at the university’s Nickle Galleries.

They spoke at an artists’ talk on campus on Oct. 1, before they had learned about the Sept. 29 event.

“To have people use the topic of residential schools and use it as a way to debate — like we have family that went missing in these schools,” cardinal dodginghorse said.

“To have people debate that any type of genocide took place and occurred from these schools —it's being wilfully ignorant.”

In 2022, the House of Commons backed a motion recognizing Canada’s residential schools as genocide.

After learning of the event on campus, cardinal dodginghorse said the “weight of what had taken place both hit us,” and after a discussion, the two decided to remove their art.

In its place, they left a letter to the school and sage for smudging.

On the left, a silkscreen piece called Xigogu (yesterday) by the artist duo tīná gúyáńí. On the right, sage and a letter to the University of Calgary that the artists left after removing their artwork. (seth cardinal dodginghorse/Facebook)

“I didn't feel safe. I didn't feel our work was safe at the university, and I felt like we had to go get it and bring it home,” said Cardinal, who is also a U of C alumnus.

Response from the gallery was positive, cardinal dodginghorse said, as was response online, including from other artists.

In their letter to the school, the pair expressed their support for a demand that student protesters have made: to remove Flanagan's professor emeritus title.

“Someone like that shouldn't be celebrated in a school that is meant to inspire and also meant to educate others,” cardinal dodginghorse said.

Flanagan responds

In an interview with CBC News, Flanagan says discussions during the event were “calm and respectful on both sides” for about the first hour and a half.

“And then the mob showed up,” he said.

He’s filed a complaint with the university against two students: one who Flanagan says was shouting obscenities, and the one who threw the water. He says their actions went against the U of C’s free speech policy by disrupting the event.

As for the timing of the event, Flanagan says it was not his decision, but it’s not one he disagrees with.

“I personally don't think that you should refrain from holding a legitimate discussion because it's the day before, the day after or whatever. I think it's a good time to try and attract attention to your discussion,” he said.

Universities cannot become places where ideas are shielded from scrutiny. University of Calgary statement

Flanagan said the suggestion of removing his professor emeritus title is “an outrageous demand.”

“It's an academic rank and it's part of the contract with the professors’ union. So the university can’t unilaterally remove that rank from me,” he said.

“I would imagine that the teachers’ union would come to my defence, and so the university would be provoking a legal battle with the union. So I don’t expect anything to happen there.”

In a statement on its website, the Democracy Fund, the registered charity that runs Canadian Students for Free Speech, defended the event.

“Universities exist for the purpose of testing contested ideas through argument and evidence. Whether residential schools meet the legal definition of genocide is a serious historical and legal question on which reasonable Canadians disagree, and it is precisely the kind of question a university should welcome,” the online statement said.

What the university is saying

In a statement, the University of Calgary said it stands with the Indigenous community and is committed to truth and reconciliation.

The university does not endorse the views expressed by the organizers of the Sept. 29 event, the statement said, but is bound by regulation to permit free expression.

“As a university, we have a responsibility to permit lawful assembly and expression, including when the ideas being expressed are unwelcome, upsetting or objectionable to members of our community,” the statement said.

“Universities cannot become places where ideas are shielded from scrutiny. Engaging with challenging ideas and perspectives is fundamental to the role of a public university.”

The university says it will be reviewing its policies in light of recent events to ensure everyone on campus engages respectfully.

Métis artist keeping her work in U of C gallery

Holly Anghel was one of the students who approached the booth on campus to speak with the presenters.

The fourth-year U of C student and Métis artist was familiar with Flanagan's writings. She went up to say she thought the booth was an attempt to “rage-bait” students.

She recorded the interaction and shared it online. She says she is happy that she spoke from the heart, but was caught off guard by the conversation.

“I feel like maybe I was a bit too polite, actually,” she said. “I feel like maybe I could have been a bit harsher with what I was trying to say, but I think actually that was what they were looking for.”

One of two pieces artist Holly Anghel has in the Nickle Galleries: a beadwork piece called Dad's Garden. (Submitted by Holly Anghel)

She attended a protest on campus the week following the event.

Her artwork is also in Nickle Galleries. She considered pulling it, but ultimately decided against it.

“Because I think that the continued presence of my art in the space is vital for sending a message that I'm here at the university. I'm a student here,” she said.

“No matter what, we cannot and will not be pushed out or silenced.”

A national 24-hour Indian Residential School Crisis Line is available at 1-866-925-4419 for emotional and crisis referral services for survivors and those affected.

World.title: Alberta's referendum count still not complete, results to be delayed
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The final ballots for Alberta's remaining referendum questions have still not been counted, and Elections Alberta has no estimate for completion.

In a statement issued shortly after 1:30 a.m. MT on Thursday, officials with the Elections Alberta media team said its teams had not yet completed counting all of the ballots.

"Our teams continue to work around the clock and we are not estimating a time for completion for Oct. 22, 2026," agency officials wrote. "We knew hand counting the referendum was going to be a monumental task."

'Just hasn’t been possible'

In an interview on Wednesday evening, as the deadline for the final count approached, officials with Elections Alberta confirmed that the agency had called in additional staff to help get the work completed overnight but that it wasn't enough.

"Despite the efforts of more than 47,000 election workers, it just hasn't been possible," officials said. "We'll continue to count ballots until the job is done."

Elections Alberta had previously said it had a 48-hour deadline from the closing of the polls on Monday to complete the count and publish the results in order to meet the parameters set under Alberta's referendum regulations.

However, in their statement on Thursday, election officials said that the legislation was "silent" on a deadline for a vote containing more than seven questions.

"Note the legislation is silent after 7+ questions ... it's 12 hrs for 1 to 2; 24 hours for 3 to 4; 36 hours for 5 to 6," the statement reads.

Alberta's referendum regulations dictate that a count must be completed "48 hours after the close of voting on referendum voting day for a referendum in which 7 or more questions are put to the electors."

WATCH | Problems, delays plague polling work: Missing furniture, staffing issues delayed results: Elections Alberta | Duration 1:21 Results for Alberta’s 10 referendum questions are still trickling in as Elections Alberta continues to hand count ballots from the Oct. 19 vote. The agency told CBC Radio that logistics and staffing issues kept polls open later, delaying the results.

Elections Alberta had a strategy set to tackle the historic referendum, first counting the ballots for Question 10 — which explored the possibility of Alberta separation — before moving on to the nine remaining questions that ask Albertans to weigh in on a series of questions about constitutional issues and immigration policies.

As of Thursday morning, 97 per cent of polling stations were reporting across Alberta.

Complete voter turnout won't be known until all votes have been counted, but Elections Alberta was expecting record turnout.

World.title: Ron Duguay, hockey star who made impact on and off ice, dead at 69
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Ron Duguay, who starred for his hometown Sudbury Wolves and became an immediate sensation on and off the ice in the Big Apple with the New York Rangers, has died. He was 69.

Shay Thomas, Duguay's daughter, said in post shared with her two siblings and Duguay's partner that the 12-year NHL player died Thursday "after a hard fought battle with cancer."

"Our hearts are broken. We love you forever Dad," said Thomas, who added that a celebration of life would be announced at a future date.

Sarah Palin, the former Alaska governor and 2008 vice-presidential candidate who was Duguay's girlfriend for at least the past four years, posted a bedside picture on social media on Oct. 18 holding his hand. "Prayers for Ron Duguay so appreciated," she said.

Duguay told the New York Post in February that he had had Stage 4 cancer for about a year at that time, which had originated in the colon. Duguay's daughters Shay and Amber from his first marriage had started a GoFundMe to help their father fund treatment, which involved travelling to California from his Florida home.

Duguay appears with Mark Carney, then the Bank of England governor, at Trafalgar Square, London, for a 'Canada 150' celebration, on July 1, 2017. Janice Charette, then Canada's high commissioner to Britain, is also shown. (Matt Dunham/The Associated Press)

The Wolves held a Ron Duguay Appreciation Night on Sept. 30 to help with his health-care expenses. Wayne Gretzky, in a video message for the event, said he was pulling for the man who was his Canada Cup teammate in 1981 as well as with the Los Angeles Kings later that decade. Gretzky called Duguay a "great person, great family guy."

In a career that also saw him play with legends Phil Esposito, Steve Yzerman and Mario Lemieux, Duguay notched 274 goals and 346 assists for 620 points in 860 NHL games over a dozen seasons. The totals were impressive enough, but in an era when hockey players often didn't make an impression beyond the game's hardcore fans, he was an exception, his smooth skating and helmet-less long, curly locks providing an indelible image in the sport in the late 1970s and early '80s.

Off-ice sensation

Duguay was featured in a cover story in Andy Warhol's Interview magazine, was regularly admitted beyond the velvet rope at Manhattan's legendary Studio 54 nightclub, where Liza Minnelli introduced herself and later connected him with Cher, who he would date for a time.

He was signed by Elite Models for promotional appearances, appeared in a hilarious and now-cringey chorus-line style ad with three Rangers teammates to promote Vidal Sassoon jeans, and partnered with Esposito and teammate Ron Greschner in a Manhattan bar called Sticks.

Duguay, then with the New York Rangers, poses for a portrait on the streets on Manhattan in March 1980. (Bruce Bennett Studios/Getty Images)

Duguay, in large part, backed up the hype off the ice with his play. Drafted 13th overall by the Rangers in 1977, he made the jump to the NHL without playing a single game in the minor leagues. The six-foot-two, 210-pound player would earn the respect of his NHL foes as a two-way player.

"When he's on, he's a dominant force," Craig Ramsay of the Buffalo Sabres said in a 1980 feature for the Toronto Star. "You can't believe how much ice he covers killing penalties, and he's always a scoring threat on the power play."

Duguay, born to parents Fern and Anita on July 6, 1957, grew up in northern Ontario, delivering newspapers for the Sudbury Star and gaining strength while playing minor hockey as a teenager as his father was an avid weightlifter.

He would average 33 goals and 90 points with the Wolves over four seasons in Sudbury, eventually becoming team captain, in what was then called the Ontario Hockey Association (OHA). He represented Canada at the first official world junior hockey championship in 1977, where the team won silver.

Duguay had been mandated to wear a helmet like all OHA players, but chose not to wear one in the NHL. After having his head shaved in an initiation ritual as a rookie, he grew his hair back.

Duguay and Robin Bobo are seen together on Sept. 9, 1983, a few months before their marriage. (Mary Schroeder/Imagn Images/USA Today Network/Reuters)

New York had missed the playoffs in the previous two seasons but made the postseason in his rookie year as he successfully switched from centre to right wing. In his second season, talented Swedes Anders Hedberg and Ulf Nilsson joined the team after playing for Winnipeg in the World Hockey Association, and the Rangers would make the Stanley Cup final before falling to the Montreal Canadiens. Duguay earned nine points in 18 playoff games during that run.

They were heady days for the Rangers. The team also featured Don Murdoch, the talented forward who was once suspended for half the season after beinag caught with five grams of cocaine at the U.S.-Canada border.

Duguay admitted decades later in a podcast that he palled off-ice with Murdoch and sometimes made it to practice without having had any sleep.

"We would do things to keep us awake," he joked.

Canada Cup appearance

After a 40-goal season with the Rangers in 1980-81, Duguay was invited to camp for the 1981 Canada Cup tournament and impressed coach Scotty Bowman and the staff enough to land a spot. Duguay would appear in all seven games as Canada lost to the Soviet Union in the final, and he remembered it decades later in an interview with the Saint-John Telegraph Journal as likely his proudest achievement as a pro player.

Things soured in the 1982-83 NHL season with the Rangers, when he notched just 19 goals. The famed coach Herb Brooks questioned his commitment on the ice and Sonny Werblin, chair of Madison Square Garden, called him a "big, big disappointment."

Duguay, left, plays for the Los Angeles Kings in 1988-89, toward the end of his NHL career. (Mike Powell/Allsport/Getty Images)

Duguay admitted to a reporter days after being traded to then-lowly Detroit in June 1983 that he was depressed about the move, but he would recover to record 80 and 89 points in his first two seasons with the Red Wings, the highest totals of his NHL career.

In December 1983, the New York Daily News reported on his marriage to American model Robin Bobo, writing that Duguay was "finally taking the plunge after being a free agent with such beauties as Cheryl Tiegs etc. etc."

Beginning with a trade to the Penguins late in the 1985-86 season, Duguay would have relatively short stints with Pittsburgh, the Rangers again and in Los Angeles. By the 1990s, he was playing in Germany and in the minor leagues in San Diego.

Duguay's first marriage eventually ended, and in 1994 he would welcome a son, Noah, with his second wife, the model Kim Alexis.

Duguay and Sarah Palin appear together during a campaign event on July 9, 2022, in Anchorage, when she was in the middle of an unsuccessful run for a U.S. Congress seat. (Justin Sullivan/Getty Images)

Duguay stayed busy in retirement. He appeared on an episode of Beverly Hills 90210, coached the Jacksonville Barracudas in the minor leagues for four seasons, spent time as a commentator for the Rangers on the Madison Square Garden network and participated in the first season of CBC's Battle of the Blades with Olympian Barbara Underhill.

Duguay told the Eddie Matta Show podcast in 2021 that he had been single for about seven years, but reports of the Duguay-Palin relationship emerged the following year. She would initially describe him as a "buddy," but he would be by her side as she launched an unsuccessful bid for Congress and was embroiled in a defamation lawsuit with the New York Times.

World.title: Man extorted sister in $7M phone theft from Bell, police say
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Ottawa police say they've arrested and charged a 45-year-old man following an investigation into the alleged theft of thousands of mobile phones worth $7 million.

On Thursday, police said the man threatened, harassed and extorted his sister, who was a Bell Canada employee. She has since died, police said.

The man's sister obtained the phones from the company "through fraudulent means" and the man then sold them, according to police.

Police allege the thefts took place between June 2022 and September 2025, and that the losses in this case exceed $7 million.

Police said Bell initiated the complaint that led to the investigation.

The man has been charged with theft over $5,000, fraud over $5,000, uttering threats of death or bodily harm, extortion and other charges.

World.title: Canadians caught up in Trump voter fraud crackdown as U.S. accuses Canada of election interference
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Robert Harold Corbett was sure he was an American citizen until federal agents showed up at his door with an arrest warrant earlier this month.

Corbett was born in Canada, but raised in the United States, he told reporters outside a federal courthouse in Raleigh, N.C.

"I did not find out I was adopted until I was 51 years old," said Corbett, who has been charged with one count of falsely claiming citizenship to vote and one count of voting by an alien. The U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ) says he voted in six elections since 1998.

Corbett is among at least 11 Canadians who have been caught up in a crackdown on non-citizen voting by U.S. President Donald Trump's administration ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm elections.

Wednesday, the U.S. Embassy in Ottawa drew a direct connection between those prosecutions and what it described as Canadian interference in American politics.

In a statement, the embassy accused Canadian politicians of openly attempting to influence the U.S. election through trade policy, political campaigning and public remarks. It also singled out Canadians for illegally voting, claiming Canada has the second-highest number of its citizens facing fraudulent or illegal voting charges of any country.

"All Canadians should refrain from attempting to participate in or influence U.S. elections in any way. Americans decide America's elections," said the statement, which comes amid heightened tensions between the U.S. and Canada over tariffs and trade.

WATCH | U.S. ambassador to Canada accuses Canadian politicans of interference: Canada 'absolutely not' interfering in U.S. midterms, Joly says | Duration closed caption 1:19 Asked about the United States Ambassador to Canada Pete Hoekstra's comments about watching for Canadian interference in the U.S. midterm elections, Minister of Industry Mélanie Joly says 'we never do that and we never accept that also being done to us in Canada.' She says her recent visits to the U.S. were 'to attract investments' by American companies and she will continue to do so.

Since late last year, federal prosecutors have charged dozens of non-citizens, many of them longtime U.S. permanent residents, with illegally voting in federal elections. But several of those accused say they didn't know they were breaking the law, with some saying they didn't even know they were registered to vote.

Investigations have consistently found that illegal voting by non-citizens is highly uncommon, said David Becker, executive director of the nonpartisan Center for Election Innovation and Research.

"This is likely an attempt to sow doubt about the elections in advance of an election in which the president and his administration might fear the voters might reject them," Becker said.

A Reuters investigation published in September found that software glitches and clerical errors across a dozen states could have added more than 30,000 self-declared non-citizens to voter rolls since 2000.

Becker said the DOJ has an "election crimes manual" that cautions prosecutors against taking enforcement actions close to elections because of the potential to influence voters.

"There's no reason these arrests couldn't have been made on Nov. 4 or some time after," he said.

Aaron Cohen, a Florida criminal defence lawyer who represents several non-citizens facing voting-related charges, said some of the confusion among his clients stems from election officials failing to properly verify eligibility when registering voters.

"I feel strongly that it's a policy decision for whatever policy outcomes are that the current administration is seeking," Cohen said of the U.S. efforts to prosecute non-citizens for voter fraud.

Lawyers who spoke with CBC News said U.S. voter registration systems can sometimes catch non-citizens up in errors, and one of them says he has seen an uptick in non-citizens being questioned last month.

Handcuffs, prison time

The DOJ's news release including information about Corbett's arrest features images of people handcuffed with their arms being held by police officers and faces blurred.

A video posted by the department on social media platform X on Tuesday features a COPS-style montage of masked officers and a man in pyjamas being led down a brightly lit hallway, advertising the arrests of 28 people in California for non-citizen voting. Two Canadians were among them.

Corbett told WRAL, a North Carolina NBC affiliate broadcaster, that he spent the night in a crowded and dirty jail cell with "people peeing on the floor." He said he was certain he was a dual citizen of Canada and the U.S.

Paige Adamson, a Canadian citizen who has lived in Point Roberts, Wash., as a U.S. permanent resident for 14 years, was accused by U.S. border agents of illegally voting and questioned for several hours in September, CBC previously reported.

Adamson, who was heading back to the States after a birthday dinner in British Columbia, was told t he Department of Homeland Security (DHS) believes she falsely claimed she was a U.S. citizen in order to vote in Washington state.

The department also alleged Adamson voted in Washington state's 2018 general election and cited those allegations as grounds for removing Adamson from the U.S. Adamson said she has no memory of ever voting in the U.S.

A North Carolina Election Integrity Team sign in Spanish, seen Oct. 25, 2024, in Durham, N.C., warns non-citizens not to vote and that doing so could lead to deportation — a notice that advocacy groups say could intimidate legitimate voters who speak Spanish. (Jonathan Drake/Reuters)

The consequences for the accusations can be serious. The Trump administration has sought to deport non-citizens convicted of voting illegally, and in June, another North Carolina-based Canadian, Denis Bouchard, was sentenced to two months in federal prison.

Others have successfully challenged their charges. In August, a federal judge in Florida acquitted Gaynell Jeffries, a Canadian citizen accused of illegally voting, after she argued that an election official had mistakenly told her permanent residents were eligible to cast ballots.

Broader implications for democracy

Frédérick Gagnon, a political science professor at the Université du Québec à Montréal and the head of the university's Observatory on the U.S., said the prosecutions in the U.S. are unfolding under a climate of fear and uncertainty for immigrants.

"People are worried about profiling. They're worried of getting arrested, and we can see that ICE wants to operate so quickly that sometimes they're proceeding with arrests that aren't justified," Gagnon said.

LISTEN | Political scientist Lucan Way says the U.S. has crossed the line into 'competitive authoritarianism': The Current 16:14 Is the U.S. sliding into competitive authoritarianism? Ever since U.S. President Donald Trump took office for the second time, he's been criticized for eroding democracy and the rule of law. Now, political scientist Lucan Way, argues that the United States has definitively crossed the line into a system of what he calls competitive authoritarianism. Lucan Way, a Distinguished Professor of Democracy in the Department of Political Science at the University of Toronto, explains what that looks like, and whether it can be reversed.

He said Trump's repeated allegations of widespread voter fraud also serve a political purpose by mobilizing his supporters.

Both Becker and Gagnon see no indication Canadians in particular are being singled out.

"They're looking at anybody they can possibly find because they are desperate to make the lie of widespread non-citizen voting look a little better," Becker said.

World.title: 'Looksmaxxing' streamer Clavicular pleads not guilty to rape charge
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

WARNING: This article contains details of abuse and may affect those who have experienced​ ​​​sexual violence or know someone affected by it.

The "looksmaxxing" livestreamer Braden Peters, better known by his stage name Clavicular, pleaded not guilty Thursday to charges that he raped a 17-year-old girl at his family's Massachusetts home.

A social media personality known for promoting extreme devotion to male beauty, Peters, 20, is accused of giving the girl alcohol until she was drunk and then sexually assaulting her when she visited him in Chatham, on Cape Cod, in May 2025.

Peters has denied the allegations through his lawyers, saying the sexual encounter was consensual.

Peters arrived at the courthouse in Orleans, Mass., wearing a dark suit, walking a barking dog on a leash. He spoke only to the dog as he entered the courthouse and ignored reporters' questions. Peters maintained a neutral facial expression during the brief arraignment.

He has agreed to a $10,000 US bail, surrendered his passport and will not contact or post about the woman who has accused him of assault.

He and his lawyers didn't comment as he left the courthouse.

The case is the latest legal challenge for Peters, who has a million followers on Instagram, and whose hours-long livestreams feature him rating people's looks and talking about methods of becoming better looking that include surgery and drug use.

Earlier this year, he was charged with misdemeanor battery in Florida after police said he provoked a fight between two women and then posted a video of it online. That charge was later dropped.

In a separate Florida case this year, he was sentenced to probation after pleading no contest to a charge that he fired a gun in public.

Peters appears for his arraignment in Orleans District Court. (Merrily Cassidy-Pool/Getty Images)

The woman who accused Peters of rape told police he had been paying her to appear in his "looksmaxxing" videos. She said that during her visit to a Peters family home, he gave her two or three shots of vodka, then livestreamed himself kissing her while she was drunk. She told police that when she woke up the next morning, Peters was raping her.

The woman also described the alleged events in a lawsuit she filed in Florida in April. In that lawsuit, she also accused Peters of injecting her with a fat-dissolving substance during a livestream without her consent.

Peters' attorneys called the lawsuit a "publicity grab."

The Associated Press generally does not name people who say they were victims of sexual assault unless they consent to being identified publicly.

World.title: Marc-Olivier Fortin: The PQ is already remaking Quebec. Killing oath to the King is only the start
World.content:
In 1891, Quebec Lieutenant-Governor Auguste-Réal Angers dismissed Premier Honoré Mercier over the Baie des Chaleurs Railway bribery scandal. One-hundred and thirty-five years later, the province’s current Lieutenant-Governor, Manon Jeannotte, silently watched the newly elected government’s cabinet swearing-in on television from her office across the street, her aide-de-camp by her side. For the first time in Quebec’s, the Lieutenant-Governor was not attending the cabinet swearing in. The empty chair said more than any speech could.

From her desk, she signed each order of appointment as the ministers took their oaths. Her signature is still required while her presence is not. Premier St-Pierre Plamondon had asked her a few days ago to stay away. She obliged. Tradition was shattered.

Slowly but surely, St-Pierre Plamondon is hollowing out the Crown without separation or changing a single law. The Crown is fading away not by a referendum, but through lack of use.

The Parti Québécois leader has been testing the limits of the institution since he was first elected in 2022. Section 128 of the Constitution Act 1867 requires members of the National Assembly to swear allegiance to the monarch. St-Pierre Plamondon made a political showdown out of this protocol at his swearing-in back then. He and his two fellow MNAs refused to swear an oath to King Charles III and were barred from taking their seats. But they held their ground. Facing popular and political pressure, the CAQ government passed Bill 4 making the oath to the King optional. Only the oath towards the people of Quebec is mandatory. The three PQ MNAs could took their seats.

Now, not only is PQ swearing allegiance solely to the people of Quebec, so is every other party, including the Liberals. One Liberal MNA put it simply: they are federalists, not monarchists. Eric Duhaime’s Conservatives are set to do the same. Federalist or not, no party will go back to swearing allegiance to the King. That ship has sailed.

What’s remarkable is that this is no longer solely a PQ project. The party moved the line of what is acceptable, and every other party followed, legitimizing a practice that is constitutionally dubious but broadly embraced.

Lawyer Lawrence David argues that Bill 4 is unconstitutional and that MNAs sitting in the National Assembly without swearing the oath are doing so unlawfully. Despite that, it is business as usual in Quebec politics. Lawful or not, MNAs have been sworn in, the cabinet has been sworn in, and the new government can start to get to work. The Assembly is expected to sit at the end of November. The new premier will be hard at work to build the winning conditions for a referendum.

Lieutenant-Governor Jeannotte will also not be welcome at the opening of the legislative session, breaking another tradition. The premier has sought a legal opinion on redirecting her budget to the fight against homelessness, which could leave the Lieutenant-Governor herself officeless.

Some might say it is unfortunate that it happened to the first Indigenous Lieutenant-Governor. St-Pierre Plamondon is not defying her as a person. He is defying her because of what she represents: an institution he calls humiliating. This is not about Manon Jeannotte. It’s about the chair she sits in.

St-Pierre Plamondon says he will even challenge her in her last stronghold: royal assent, constitutionally required for legislation to become. Many say it remains out of his reach. But St-Pierre Plamondon has never given an inch to the institution, and he is unlikely to start now. In the final week of the campaign, he vowed to abolish the office, separation or not.

In 1933, Irish President Éamon de Valera abolished the oath to the King. He then did exactly what St-Pierre Plamondon is doing now: reducing the governor general to a shadow. Sixteen years later, Ireland became a republic. Could it be St-Pierre Plamondon’s inspiration?

The question now becomes how long the institution can survive when everyone around it acts like it does not exist. In 1891, the Lieutenant-Governor put an end to a premier. In 2026, it might be a premier who puts an end to the Lieutenant-Governor.

National Post
