World.title: 4 white rhinos from France and Germany find a home in Guadalajara
World.content:
Four white rhinoceroses arrived in Guadalajara from Europe on Wednesday in an effort to preserve genetic diversity as successful breeding leaves European zoos running short of space.

The three females and one male traveled aboard an Air France cargo flight from Paris after more than a year of preparation.

Their destination, the Guadalajara Zoo — possibly one of the “happiest” zoos in Latin America — already features rhinos in its safari attraction, and other Mexican facilities also keep rhinos: Africam Safari in Puebla houses black rhinos, while the León Zoo in Guanajuato state has a white rhino named Yuri.

The new arrivals are Salma, 5, and Moana, 9, from Serengeti Park Hodenhagen in Germany; Lewa, 4, from Safari de Peaugres in France; and Wami, a 15-year-old male from the Paris Zoo.

Their relocation is part of conservation and captive breeding programs coordinated by the European Association of Zoos and Aquaria.

Wami’s genetic lineage is particularly valuable in the Americas because it’s not represented there, said Alexis Lécu, the Paris Zoo’s scientific director.

Meanwhile, Europe’s captive breeding program has “less and less space” as rhino reproduction programs succeed, Lécu told the newspaper La Jornada.

European association members hold 326 white rhinos across 83 parks, with five to 10 births annually across the continent, La Jornada reported.

An estimated 15,752 white rhinos were in the wild at the end of 2024, down 25% from more than 21,000 in 2023, according to the International Rhino Foundation’s 2026 report. Poaching remains the major threat — which is why captive-breeding programs are viewed as vital.

Wami — who was born at the Beauval Zoo in Saint-Aignan, France, on Oct. 16, 2011 (belated happy birthday!) — has already had his sperm used for assisted reproduction in European parks. The same is expected to occur in North America.

Getting the rhinos aboard was no small undertaking.

The transfer required more than a year of preparation, including months spent familiarizing the rhinos with their transport crates so they could enter calmly, Guadalajara Zoo officials said.

It reportedly took more than an hour to get Wami, who weighs 2.4 tonnes (about 5,300 pounds), into his container for the 12-hour flight that arrived early Wednesday morning.

Visitors will have to wait to meet the hefty newcomers.

The rhinos, which can live for 35 to 40 years in captivity, will undergo quarantine, examinations and an adjustment period. The newspaper El Heraldo de México reported they would spend 40 days in dedicated accommodations while adapting.

The zoo will announce their public debut after assessing their progress.

The Guadalajara Zoo occupies about 124 acres of developed grounds, according to its website. It houses more than 7,000 animals representing 300 species, the zoo’s general director, Luis Soto Rendón, said on Imagen Radio last week.

He called the quartet’s arrival “the culmination of an extraordinary effort.”

With reports from El Heraldo de México, La Jornada, El Informador and Guadalajara Secreta

World.title: El Jalapeño: Ministry of Agriculture reassures nation no Mexican agave will escape fermentation
World.content:
All stories in El Jalapeño are satire and not real news. Check out the original article here.

MEXICO CITY — Following exhaustive botanical reviews, federal agriculture officials confirmed Tuesday that every last specimen of native Mexican agave will eventually be accounted for, fermented, distilled or otherwise converted into an intoxicating spirit, reassuring a watchful public that no succulent will be left behind to pursue a pointless career as mere flora.

According to a sweeping directive released by the Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Development (SADER), Mexican researchers have successfully mapped more than a dozen distinct traditional beverages — including tequila, mezcal, pulque, bacanora, raicilla, tutsi and tepe — but warned that allowing any of the country’s 159 endemic species to complete their natural life cycle without encountering a copper alembic would constitute a historic administrative failure.

“We have documented agaves that resemble artichokes, agaves that resemble octopuses and specimens that grow 33-foot flower stalks at a rate of four inches a day,” said lead research coordinator Dr. Mateo Escalante, standing beside an experimental fermentation vat containing a rare Agave parviflora. “Yet, despite these incredible evolutionary adaptations, our mandate is absolute: no agave shall evade the barrel.”

The report noted that while pre-Hispanic societies historically utilized the agave plant for structural fibers, construction materials and sewing needles, modern bureaucratic planning has successfully streamlined the plant’s destiny toward liquid form. Officials acknowledged that while smaller varieties may yield little more than a thimble of artisanal spirit per harvest, diligent planning ensures that even roadside succulents will find their way into a clay copita.

Addressing historical anomalies, such as Sonora’s 1915 prohibition on bacanora designed to prevent moral perversion, SADER officials emphasized that government policy has fully pivoted. Rather than restricting regional output, the current administration actively monitors the nation’s flora to guarantee that every municipality exercises its legal right to produce a smoky, high-proof distillate from whatever happens to be growing in the dirt.

“Our ancestors spent thousands of years discovering that Agave tequilana flowers in seven years while Agave deserti takes 55,” Escalante added. “Our duty to future generations is to ensure that no matter how long a plant takes to mature, a distillation schedule is waiting for it the moment it ripens.”

World.title: Over 2,500 arrested for fuel theft since October 2024: Wednesday’s mañanera recapped
World.content:
Sheinbaum’s mañanera in 60 seconds

⛽ Mexico targets fuel theft with thousands of arrests: Deputy Energy Minister for Hydrocarbons Juan José Vidal Amaro reported that federal security forces have arrested 2,539 people for huachicol (fuel theft) offenses since October 2024. Authorities have seized 5,572 vehicles and 173.7 million liters of fuel, and 2,224 companies have been shut down for selling fuel without the required permits. He also said that 180 companies have been removed from the registry of approved fuel importers over alleged involvement in fuel smuggling.

Deputy Energy Minister for Hydrocarbons Juan José Vidal Amaro reported that federal security forces have arrested 2,539 people for huachicol (fuel theft) offenses since October 2024. Authorities have seized 5,572 vehicles and 173.7 million liters of fuel, and 2,224 companies have been shut down for selling fuel without the required permits. He also said that 180 companies have been removed from the registry of approved fuel importers over alleged involvement in fuel smuggling. 🔥🇺🇸 Sheinbaum: No commitment to buy more U.S. natural gas: Asked whether buying more U.S. gas would undermine energy sovereignty, the president said Mexico hasn’t entered into any “agreement” or made any “commitment” to do so. She acknowledged that the idea is “something that the United States has put on the table” as Trump seeks to reduce the U.S. trade deficit with Mexico. However, Sheinbaum said that Mexico’s objective is to produce more gas domestically, including to supply new combined-cycle power plants.

Asked whether buying more U.S. gas would undermine energy sovereignty, the president said Mexico hasn’t entered into any “agreement” or made any “commitment” to do so. She acknowledged that the idea is “something that the United States has put on the table” as Trump seeks to reduce the U.S. trade deficit with Mexico. However, Sheinbaum said that Mexico’s objective is to produce more gas domestically, including to supply new combined-cycle power plants. ✈️ Sheinbaum praises Ambassador Johnson despite disagreements: The president said U.S. Ambassador Ronald Johnson “has helped us on many issues,” including by providing assistance to Mexico to get U.S. restrictions on new flights from Mexico City airports AICM and AIFA lifted. She acknowledged her government has disagreed with some of his public remarks, including his comments on corruption in Mexico, but stressed that Mexico wants “the best possible relationship with the United States.”

Why today’s mañanera matters

At President Sheinbaum’s Wednesday morning press conference, Energy Ministry officials provided an update on the government’s fight against fuel theft (known colloquially as huachicol or huachicoleo) and a fuel smuggle/tax evasion scheme known as huachicol fiscal. Both crimes have cost the federal government and state oil company Pemex huge amounts of money in lost revenue.

Today’s mañanera was also significant as the president told reporters that Mexico has not made any commitment to purchase more natural gas from the United States, as U.S. President Donald Trump has reportedly urged it to do.

Mexico is already heavily reliant on the United States for its natural gas supplies.

On Wednesday morning, Sheinbaum also offered praise for U.S. Ambassador to Mexico Ron Johnson, highlighting that he assisted Mexico in its efforts to have U.S. restrictions lifted on new flights to the U.S. from the Mexico City International Airport and the Felipe Ángeles International Airport.

More than 2,500 huachicol-related arrests since Sheinbaum took office

Juan José Vidal Amaro, deputy energy minister for hydrocarbons, reported that federal security forces have arrested 2,539 people for huachicol offenses since the government took office in October 2024.

He said that authorities have seized 5,572 vehicles used to transport fuel as well as 173.7 million liters of fuel.

Vidal said that the data provides evidence of the progress that has been made in combating “illegal activities in the fuel market.”

Earlier in the press conference, he reported that 2,224 companies have been shut down for selling fuel without holding the applicable permits. Vidal also said that 2,032 gas stations have been fined for not having adequate “volumetric controls” on their gas pumps.

In addition, the deputy minister said that 180 companies have been removed from the government’s registry of approved fuel importers due to their alleged involvement in fuel smuggling.

Sheinbaum says Mexico hasn’t agreed to purchase more natural gas from the US

A reporter raised the possibility of Mexico purchasing more natural gas from the United States in order to reduce the U.S. deficit in the bilateral trade relationship. “Wouldn’t this be a backward step for Mexico in the quest for energy sovereignty?” she asked the president.

Sheinbaum responded that Mexico hasn’t entered into any “agreement” or made any “commitment” to purchase more gas from the United States.

Her remarks came almost two weeks after the Financial Times reported that she and U.S. President Donald Trump had “discussed the prospect of Mexico increasing purchases of U.S. natural gas, on which it already depends for about three-quarters of its demand.”

Sheinbaum acknowledged that the possibility of Mexico buying more U.S. gas is “something that the United States has put on the table” as the Trump administration seeks to reduce the U.S. trade deficit with Mexico.

“It’s not that they’re particularly interested in selling more gas,” she said, explaining that what Trump is interested in is reducing the United States’ trade deficit with Mexico, which increased more than 20% year over year in the first eight months of 2026 to reach almost US $156 billion.

Sheinbaum said that her government has told its U.S. counterpart that its objective is to produce more gas in Mexico, in part to ensure sufficient supplies for new combined-cycle power plants.

“If for any reason we can’t produce the gas [needed for new power plants] in Mexico, we’ll have to get the natural gas from somewhere. But the objective is to produce it in the country,” she said.

The government is open to using fracking to boost natural gas production in Mexico, but no clear timeline has emerged for when new projects could begin.

Environment Minister Alicia Bárcena told Congress earlier this month that, “the conditions for proceeding with hydraulic fracturing operations currently do not exist, nor is there any authorization from the president.”

Sheinbaum: Ambassador Johnson ‘has helped us on many issues’

A reporter asked the president about her recent description of U.S. Ambassador Johnson as “a good ally of Mexico” shortly after she called on him to respect Mexico’s laws in light of the United States cooperation with the state of Querétaro on an “international police training academy” project that hadn’t been authorized by the federal government.

Sheinbaum responded that Johnson, ambassador to Mexico since May 2025, “has helped us on many issues.”

She said that Johnson helped her government “a lot” on the issue of “air transport” after the United States last year revoked approval for existing and planned flights to the U.S. from the Mexico City International Airport and the Felipe Ángeles International Airport (AIFA).

The U.S. Department of Transportation last week lifted restrictions on new flights to the U.S. from AICM and AIFA, allowing Mexican airlines to launch new routes to U.S. airports. The lifting of the restrictions — which were imposed due to aviation disputes between Mexico and the U.S. — will allow U.S.-bound passenger flights to depart from AIFA for the first time.

Sheinbaum said that Johnson worked with Mexican and U.S. officials on the “whole process” related to Mexico’s efforts to have the U.S. restrictions lifted.

“We have to say it, and finally the [U.S.] sanction was lifted,” she said.

“[Johnson] helped on this issue,” Sheinbaum said.

“There are other issues on which the ambassador helped us,” she added.

Sheinbaum acknowledged that her government has disagreed with some of Johnson’s public remarks, including those he made about corruption in Mexico during an address in Sinaloa in April. She said that she and the Ministry of Foreign Affairs have expressed their disagreement to the ambassador.

“But there are issues on which he has helped us,” Sheinbaum reiterated.

“… We don’t have any problem in saying it. What do we want? The best possible relationship with the United States, always with respect for our sovereignty and respect for our compatriots in the United States,” she said.

World.title: MND Local Puerto Vallarta: Hurricanes keep coming, golf course disruption, free drinking water fountains
World.content:
It is feeling a little bit like “Groundhog Day” in Puerto Vallarta as we closely watch the trajectory of Hurricane Trudy, the fourth hurricane to come our way in recent weeks. If we are lucky, the storm will follow the path that Polo, Rachel and Simón took and skirt the coast without making landfall. While the storms’ impacts have been relatively moderate in Vallarta, they have caused flooding on the Baja California peninsula and El Niño-linked erosion damage in Southern California, and our hearts go out to communities affected.

Major headlines this month include the ordered demolition of a controversial condo complex in San Pancho, Nayarit; infrastructure issues and the tragic loss of five lives due to recent storms; the rollout of a new program to bring free drinking water fountains to schools, sports, civic and tourist areas throughout the city; and devastating tree culling at the Marina Golf Course.

Recent storms cause beach erosion, flooding and five deaths

Puerto Vallarta is recovering from four back-to-back hurricanes that skirted the city’s southern coast and Banderas Bay. The first hurricane, Polo, rolled in on Sept. 23, followed by Rachel, then Simón and Trudy. The storms brought major tidal surges and pounding waves to Vallarta’s beaches, filling the Malecón with rocks and sand, eroding beaches and leaving just rocks behind.

Impressive photos and videos show waves hitting the Malecón seawall and bouncing many feet into the air. Communities of Yelapa and Boca de Tomatlán were evacuated as a preventative measure as Hurricane Simón approached. Heavy rainfall also caused sewer system backups in the Versailles neighborhood and street flooding in many parts of town. Authorities also closed local beaches, but tragically, one young woman was swept away and is presumed drowned at Playa de Oro during Hurricane Polo. Four people, including two children, were killed when rushing water swept away their home in La Cuesta in the municipality of Talpa de Allende.

Profepa orders demolition of San Pancho beachfront condo

On Oct. 7, the Federal Attorney’s Office for Environmental Protection (Profepa) ordered the demolition of two towers of the Punta Paraíso condo complex in San Pancho, Nayarit. The towers sit directly on the beach in this coastal community and have been the subject of protests by residents for over a decade due to the buildings’ environmental impacts and encroachment into the protected Federal Maritime Terrestrial Zone.

Hurricanes Rachel and Simón pounded the beachfront towers, severely damaging their foundations, causing the towers to lean and necessitating the evacuation of residents.

The developer, Pacific Lifestyle Properties, was also ordered to pay a 96,220-peso (US $5,216) fine for building in the federal zone. Score one for Mother Nature and zero for illegal development.

Seapal rolls out free drinking fountains in public schools, sports fields and tourist spots

Remember to bring your refillable water bottles on your next trip to Puerto Vallarta because visitors and residents alike will soon have access to free, purified drinking water in various locations throughout the city.

This summer, Puerto Vallarta’s municipal water utility, Seapal, launched a program to bring purified drinking water fountains to public schools, civic, sports and tourist spots around Vallarta. The program aims to improve public health, increase access to safe, free drinking water, and reduce plastic pollution.

New fountains have already been installed in several schools and the Emiliano Zapata Municipal Market, and several more are planned for the Unidad Deportiva Agustín Flores Contreras sports complex, Centro Cultural y Módulo Deportivo La Lija, Seapal Vallarta’s central offices, Unidad Municipal Administrativa (UMA), and on the Malecón.

Marina Golf Course culls trees in major remodel, angering residents

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Marina Vallarta Club De Golf (@marinavallartaclubdegolf)

The Marina Golf Course has been systematically cutting down dozens of large, mature trees over the past several weeks, angering residents and displacing wildlife. Golf course administrators claim the culling of trees is part of a comprehensive remodeling project and that they plan to plant more trees than are being removed.

In the meantime, however, residents must wait decades for new trees to grow to the size of the old ones and face the constant sound of chainsaws and the sadness of watching trees being felled for many more days.

The trees being removed are mostly a nonnative species of ficus, but they provide habitat for native birds such as white ibises, great kiskadees, golden-cheeked woodpeckers, chachalacas and more.

The course has been closed most of the summer and fall during the remodeling project. Rest assured, visitors to Vallarta coming to the course this year will see a drastically different landscape.

They say the only constant is change. Let us just hope the next changes coming to Vallarta are less destructive and more positive, like the free drinking water program. But hurricane season is not over yet, so we will just have to wait and see.

Debbie Slobe is a writer and communications strategist based in Puerto Vallarta, Jalisco. She blogs at Mexpatmama.com and is a senior program director at Resource Media. Find her on Instagram and Facebook.

World.title: Beloved Ballet Folklórico announces US tour in celebration of 75th anniversary
World.content:
Amalia Hernández’s Ballet Folklórico de México will celebrate its 75th anniversary with a tour to 24 cities in the United States, beginning Jan. 30 in Northridge, California, and concluding March 23 in Austin, Texas.

The Ballet Folklórico de México was established in 1952 by dancer and choreographer Amalia Hernández. The group revolutionized Mexican dance and laid the foundation for traditional choreographies and costumes to gain prestige in Mexico and abroad.

The company will travel with more than 50 members and present a repertoire of dances from various regions of Mexico, featuring live music, colorful garments and routines that blend folk traditions with theatrical staging.

“Our 75th anniversary is a celebration not only of Ballet Folklórico de México, but of the people, communities, traditions and artists who have kept Mexico’s cultural heritage alive,” Ballet Folklórico de México General Manager Salvador Lopez, who is also Hernández’s grandson, said in a statement.

“It is an honor to bring Amalia Hernández’s artistic legacy to audiences across the United States and to introduce new generations to the beauty and diversity of Mexico,” he added.

Where will the ballet perform?

In California, the company will perform in Northridge, Modesto, Santa Barbara, Los Angeles, Chico, Davis, Berkeley, San Luis Obispo and Costa Mesa; in Arizona, in Tucson and Mesa; and in Texas, in El Paso, Lubbock, Richardson, San Antonio and Austin.

The tour will also reach Las Vegas, Nevada; Carmel, Indiana; East Lansing, Michigan; Milwaukee, Wisconsin; Minneapolis, Minnesota; Chicago, Illinois; Santa Fe, New Mexico; and Denver, Colorado.

Tickets are available through the official channels of the participating venues and, depending on the city, through platforms such as Ticketmaster.

In addition to its international tours, the Ballet Folklórico de México maintains a residency at the Palacio de Bellas Artes in Mexico City, where it has held regular performances since 1959.

With reports from El Universal

World.title: Jamaica Politics Explained, Who Holds Power in 2026
World.content:
JAMAICA · POLITICS

Key Facts — The country Jamaica is an English-speaking Caribbean island democracy with a two-party system, a British monarch as head of state and a 63-seat elected House of Representatives.

— Who governs Prime Minister Andrew Holness leads the Jamaica Labour Party (JLP), which won a third straight term on 3 September 2025 with 35 of 63 seats.

— The opposition The People’s National Party (PNP), led by Mark Golding, holds 28 seats. The two parties split the 2025 vote 50.54% to 49.16%.

— Turnout Only about 40% of the 2,077,800 registered voters cast a ballot in September 2025, so neither party has a wide public mandate.

— Security Deputy Prime Minister Horace Chang runs national security as of October 2026, with Dr Kevin Blake as police commissioner.

— Still open The plan to replace the monarch with a Jamaican president has stalled in Parliament as of August 2026, and no new vote date is set.

Jamaica politics is a contest between two parties, and Prime Minister Andrew Holness’s Jamaica Labour Party has governed since 2016. For US readers, the same few people control the island’s security cooperation with Washington, its tourism economy and its deportation arrangements.

The waterfront in downtown Kingston, the capital of Jamaica. File photo, 2007. (Photo: Tillon Aniel, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

Jamaica Politics in Brief, a Two-Party Contest

The Jamaica Labour Party (JLP) traces its roots to Sir Alexander Bustamante. The People’s National Party (PNP) was launched in 1938 with Norman Manley as its first president.

On 3 September 2025 the JLP won its third consecutive general election, taking 35 of 63 seats, down from 49 in 2020. The Jamaica Observer reports that the PNP won 28 seats and 401,398 votes (49.16%), against 412,705 votes (50.54%) for the JLP.

Turnout was 39.96% of 2,077,800 registered voters, up from 37.85% in 2020, according to a Jamaica Observer editorial of 21 September 2026. Fewer than four in ten voters took part, and the Observer said the win came ‘not with a blank cheque’.

At a JLP executive meeting in late September 2026, Holness told members the party should not seek office only to hold power. He pointed to the PNP’s 18½ years in government and the economic damage he said followed.

Jamaica politics is shaped by hurricane recovery and a weak economy. The Observer’s September 2026 review noted a 4.1% year-on-year fall in output in early 2026.

This guide is part of the Rio Times coverage of Jamaica. It builds on our Jamaica explainer and the analysis of Jamaica’s place in Latin America.

The Monarch, the Governor-General and the Prime Minister

Jamaica’s head of state is the King, the British monarch, who is represented on the island by the Governor-General. Sir Patrick Allen holds that post.

The Jamaica Information Service named him as host of the national honours ceremony on 19 October 2026. The role is largely ceremonial.

Real power sits with the Prime Minister, who leads the party with a majority in the House of Representatives.

Andrew Holness leads the JLP and has been Prime Minister since 2016. The Jamaica Observer’s October 2026 Cabinet review says he also holds the defence portfolio.

His wife, Juliet Holness, is Speaker of the House, the official who chairs its debates. She was still in the post in September 2026.

Prime Minister Andrew Holness greets US Secretary of State Rex Tillerson in Kingston. File photo, February 2018. (Photo: US Department of State, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons)

The Cabinet and Its Key Ministers

Jamaica’s Cabinet had 19 members as of October 2026, according to the Jamaica Observer. Ministers sit in either chamber, and the January 2026 protocol list shows Johnson Smith, Hill and Morris Dixon in the Senate.

The ministers who matter most, with portfolios as listed by the Jamaica Observer in September and October 2026, are these:

Dr Horace Chang, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of National Security and Peace, who met the US defence secretary in Panama on 12 August 2026.

Fayval Williams, Minister of Finance and the Public Service, who succeeded Nigel Clarke and runs the national budget.

Senator Kamina Johnson Smith, Minister of Foreign Affairs and Foreign Trade, who leads Jamaica’s diplomacy.

Edmund Bartlett, Tourism Minister, whose sector earned about US$3.8 billion from 3.7 million visitors in 2025.

Dr Christopher Tufton, Minister of Health and Wellness, who faces pressure over hospital care and the grievances of doctors and nurses.

Delroy Chuck, Justice Minister, who leads the republic debate.

Daryl Vaz, whose portfolio covers science, energy, telecommunications and transport, including the island’s power-company licence.

Dr Andrew Wheatley, a minister without portfolio in the Office of the Prime Minister, responsible for science, technology and special projects.

Parliament, the Senate and the Opposition

Parliament has two chambers. The House of Representatives has 63 elected members, and the Senate has 21 appointed members, according to the Constitution of Jamaica.

Thirteen senators are named on the Prime Minister’s advice and eight on the advice of the Leader of the Opposition. That gives the governing party a clear Senate majority.

Mark Golding has led the PNP since 7 November 2020 and is Leader of the Opposition. An Observer columnist argued after the 2025 defeat that he should have resigned, but he was still in place in September 2026.

Dr Dayton Campbell, the PNP’s general secretary and MP for Westmoreland Eastern, spoke at the party’s 88th annual conference in September 2026. It was the first public session the party had held outside Kingston.

The Opposition has pressed the Government on hurricane recovery, the case against Minister Wheatley and the arrangement for third-country deportees.

Police, Army and the New US Security Deal

Two forces carry the security load. The Jamaica Constabulary Force (JCF) is the national police, and Dr Kevin Blake was its commissioner as of October 2026.

Security shapes Jamaica politics. The Jamaica Defence Force (JDF) is the army, coast guard and air wing, and it works alongside the police.

The Observer reported on 27 September 2026 that murders fell to 673 in 2025, a 31-year low, and were down 22% in 2026.

After gunmen killed a police officer in Sligoville on 16 October 2026, Holness told the commissioner to intensify operations.

On 20 August 2026 Washington and Kingston announced a Status of Forces Agreement for US troops visiting Jamaica. It covers training, joint operations and disaster response.

Chang and US Secretary of War Pete Hegseth had met in Panama on 12 August. Jamaica joined more than 120 partner nations with similar US accords.

A Jamaica Constabulary Force patrol truck at a junction in Kingston. File photo, February 2025. (Photo: Jason Lawrence, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

Courts, Watchdogs and the Final Appeal

Chief Justice Bryan Sykes heads the judiciary and has argued in 2026 for judge-alone trials and more mediation. Justice Marva McDonald-Bishop has been President of the Court of Appeal since 2024, the first woman in that post.

The highest court for Jamaican cases is still the Privy Council in London. The Opposition wants the Caribbean Court of Justice (CCJ), a regional appeals court, to replace it.

The question is covered in our report on the final court debate.

The Integrity Commission is the independent body that examines public officials’ wealth declarations. In June 2026 it recommended four criminal charges against Wheatley, including illicit enrichment of more than J$164 million (about US$1.0 million).

Wheatley is challenging that report in the Supreme Court, and a judge has barred any prosecution until the case is decided. A hearing is set for 12 November 2026, and he has been convicted of nothing.

Parishes, Mayors and Local Power

Local Jamaica politics has no state governors. It has 14 parishes, and local councils called municipal corporations run local services.

Voters elect councillors, and the mayor comes from the party with the council majority. Portmore is the only town that elects its mayor directly, though the Government plans to make it the 15th parish.

Desmond McKenzie, the local government minister, oversees the councils. Andrew Swaby was Mayor of Kingston in September 2026.

In Clarendon the council is split 11-11 after a November 2024 by-election. The Gleaner reported on 9 October 2026 that the PNP caucus plans a no-confidence motion against Mayor Joel Williams.

The Half Way Tree clock tower, a landmark of the Kingston and St Andrew area. File photo. (Photo: Raw9345, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

Rising Figures and the Republic Debate

The Observer’s October 2026 review called Matthew Samuda, the water and environment minister, a politician to watch. It also praised Delano Seiveright, a junior minister in the ministry led by Aubyn Hill.

Floyd Green, the minister of agriculture, fisheries and mining, was called an asset to the Cabinet in the same review.

The republic plan would replace the monarch with a Jamaican president. Justice Minister Chuck says the Constitution (Amendment) (Republic) Bill of 2024 has not moved for over a year.

Golding prefers to pass the CCJ switch and the republic plan together, followed by a referendum. Chuck summed up the state of play in August 2026 with the words ‘We are nowhere’.

What It Means for US Readers

Washington now deals with a government that signed a troop-status deal in August 2026. On 13 October 2026 Jamaica received a first group of 22 third-country nationals from the United States, mostly from Latin America.

Jamaica politics remains a stable two-party democracy in which power changes by ballot. Investors and travellers should watch hurricane rebuilding, the Wheatley case and the security deal.

For the wider picture, read Jamaica Geopolitics Explained 2026 and Jamaica and Its Neighbours in the Caribbean. The guide to who runs Jamaica’s economy covers the business side.

What Is Not Known

No date for the next general election has been announced. Nobody has said when the republic bill will return to the House.

The Supreme Court has yet to decide Wheatley’s challenge.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who is the Prime Minister of Jamaica in 2026?

Andrew Holness, leader of the Jamaica Labour Party, is Prime Minister as of October 2026. Jamaica politics has been led by him since 2016.

Who leads the opposition in Jamaica?

Mark Golding, president of the People’s National Party, is Leader of the Opposition. His party holds 28 of the 63 House seats.

Who is Jamaica’s head of state?

The British monarch is head of state, represented by Governor-General Sir Patrick Allen. The Prime Minister holds the day-to-day power.

How many seats does each party have in Jamaica?

After the 3 September 2025 election the JLP holds 35 seats and the PNP 28 in the 63-seat House. In 2020 the JLP had won 49.

Does Jamaica have governors?

No, Jamaica has no state governors. It has 14 parishes run by municipal corporations and mayors, plus a Governor-General who represents the monarch.

Will Jamaica become a republic?

The republic bill was before Parliament as of August 2026 but has stalled. The Opposition wants the Caribbean Court of Justice and a referendum added.

World.title: Cameroon Politics Explained, Who Holds Power in 2026
World.content:
CAMEROON · POLITICS

Key Facts — The country Cameroon is a Central African country of 10 regions, led since 6 November 1982 by President Paul Biya, who is 93.

— Who holds power Biya names the prime minister, ministers and generals, and his RDPC party holds 152 of 180 Assembly seats, according to the 2020 results.

— Why now The Constitutional Council declared Biya winner of the October 2025 vote with 53.66%, and the runner-up, Issa Tchiroma Bakary, rejects the result from exile.

— The new post A constitutional change of 4 April 2026 restored the post of vice president, but as of October 2026 nobody holds the job.

— Security The army fights separatists in two English-speaking regions and Boko Haram in the Far North, and the US warns against travel there.

— What it means for you The State Department rates Cameroon at Level 2 overall, as of May 2026, and a disorderly handover would test investors and aid.

Cameroon politics in October 2026 rests on one man, President Paul Biya, 93, who has ruled since 1982. For US readers it matters because a disorderly handover next to Nigeria and Chad would hit security, aid and investment.

This guide names who holds each major office as of October 2026, and what is still undecided.

President Paul Biya and first lady Chantal Biya with US President Barack Obama and Michelle Obama in an official White House photograph. File photo. (Photo: Lawrence Jackson, Official White House Photo, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons)

Ask Open the full Ask Rio Times →

Cameroon Politics at a Glance, One Ruler and a Waiting Game

Cameroon politics is built around a republic of 10 regions in which the president holds almost every lever of power. Paul Biya, 93, has held the office since 6 November 1982.

The Constitutional Council, the court that certifies elections, declared Biya the winner of the 12 October 2025 vote on 27 October 2025. It gave him 53.66% of the ballots, according to Hespress.

The runner-up, Issa Tchiroma Bakary, received 35.19% and rejects the result.

Cabral Libii finished third with 3.41%, and Bello Bouba Maïgari fourth with 2.45%. Hermine Patricia Tomaïno Ndam Njoya took 1.66%, on a turnout of 46.31%.

Almost every senior post is filled by presidential decree, so Cameroon politics is mostly the story of one man and his circle. The open questions are his health, his successor and the new government.

The President and His Circle at Etoudi

Biya governs from the Etoudi presidential palace in Yaoundé, the capital. He names the prime minister, the ministers and the generals.

Joseph Dion Ngute is prime minister. In September 2026 he met religious and traditional leaders from the English-speaking regions in Yaoundé, according to Benin Web TV.

On 31 December 2025 Biya said a new government would be formed in the coming days. By 6 October 2026 none had been named, Al Jazeera reported.

Dion Ngute was still listed as prime minister in late August 2026, Benin Web TV reported.

Biya spent more than ten weeks abroad this summer and returned to Yaoundé on 20 August 2026, the presidency’s website says. On 2 August 2026 government spokesman René Emmanuel Sadi said the president was alive and that there was no vacancy of power.

Who Else Matters in the Cabinet

Louis Paul Motaze is finance minister, and Alamine Ousmane Mey is economy minister.

On 13 October 2026 Mey signed a loan agreement of 139.2 billion CFA francs (about US$238 million) in Bangkok. It funds the Douala-Bafoussam road, Investir au Cameroun reported.

Motaze put the cost of holding pump prices steady at 57 billion CFA francs (about US$98 million) for September 2026. Ministers hold power only as far as the president lets them.

Government office buildings in Yaoundé that Wikimedia Commons lists as the Prime Minister’s offices. (Photo: Frederic Papy, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

The Succession Question and the Empty Vice Presidency

Parliament approved a constitutional change on 4 April 2026 that restores the post of vice president. The holder is appointed by the president and would be first in the line of succession.

As of October 2026 no vice president has been named, Al Jazeera reported on 17 October 2026. The amendment sets no deadline.

Koaci reported on 7 October 2026, citing Africa Intelligence, that networks around possible successors each hope to control the handover through the new post. The report adds that part of the elite sees Franck Biya, the president’s eldest son, as the most reassuring choice for stability.

For the legal detail, see the Rio Times guide to Cameroon succession rules. Our news report on Cabral Libii’s warning covers the debate.

Biya has led Cameroon since 1982. Here he meets US President Ronald Reagan in the Oval Office. File photo from the 1980s. (Photo: White House Photographic Office, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons)

The Ruling Party and Parliament

The Cameroon People’s Democratic Movement, known as the RDPC, is Biya’s party and dominates Cameroon politics in parliament.

In the 2020 vote it won 152 of the 180 seats in the National Assembly, according to the Inter-Parliamentary Union.

The Assembly’s mandate was extended to 20 December 2026, the same source says. The next elections must fall between 29 January and 19 April 2027.

On 17 March 2026 deputies elected Théodore Datouo, 65, an RDPC member from the West region, as speaker. He took 133 of 147 votes and succeeded Cavaye Yéguié Djibril, who had held the post for 34 years, according to Afrik.

The Senate has 100 members, of whom 70 are elected indirectly and 30 are appointed by the president. Aboubakary Abdoulaye, 64, the traditional ruler of Rey-Bouba, was elected Senate president on 17 March 2026 with every vote cast, Afrik reported.

Opposition Parties and Their Leaders

Issa Tchiroma Bakary leads the Front for the National Salvation of Cameroon (FSNC) and rejects the result of the 2025 vote. He took refuge in Nigeria and then in Banjul, The Gambia, in November 2025.

Cameroon Tribune noted on 14 October 2026 that his legal actions abroad have gained little.

Cabral Libii leads the Cameroonian Party for National Reconciliation (PCRN), which won 5 seats in the Assembly in 2020. Bello Bouba Maïgari’s National Union for Democracy and Progress (UNDP) won 7 seats, the most of any opposition party.

The Social Democratic Front (SDF), once the main opposition force in Cameroon politics, won 5 seats in 2020. Its national president, Joshua Osih, said on 23 July 2026 that the party would accept no further delay to legislative and municipal elections, allAfrica reported.

The Cameroon Renaissance Movement (MRC) is the party of Maurice Kamto, a former presidential candidate.

A party convention on 17 October 2026 elected Tiriane Balbine Noah as president. Willy Mengue still contests the result, Journal du Cameroun reported on 19 October.

The Army, the Police and the Intelligence Service

General René Claude Meka, 87, was kept as chief of the defence staff in August 2026, Koaci reported. His new deputy, General Hippolyte Ebaka, 73, replaced General Hector Marie Tchemo.

Biya signed those decrees on 3 August 2026 while abroad, Daba Finance reported. Raymond Beko’o Abongo, promoted to brigadier general, kept command of the Presidential Guard.

Brigadier General Elie Romance Mezui Zo’o was named to lead the Rapid Intervention Brigade, which is used in counter-insurgency operations.

Maxime Eko Eko, the former head of the external intelligence service (DGRE), is on trial for complicity in torture. The Yaoundé military tribunal is hearing the 2023 killing of radio journalist Martínez Zogo, Afrik reported on 1 September 2026.

The armed forces face two threats. The US State Department describes separatist violence in the North-West and South-West regions and Boko Haram attacks in the Far North.

Courts, Governors and the Regions

The Constitutional Council has been working since February 2018, according to Cameroun Actuel. Its first president, Clément Atangana, died in Paris on 4 October 2026 at the age of 84, Journal du Cameroun reported.

On 16 October 2026 Biya named Rémy Nama, a senior magistrate who served as a special assignment officer at the presidency, to replace him. The council is the court that certifies elections.

Cameroon politics also plays out in the regions.

Each of the 10 regions has a governor. In the North-West, Governor Adolphe Lele Lafrique said security measures were in place for the school reopening on 7 September 2026, Benin Web TV reported.

Separatist groups imposed a one-week lockdown there from that day, and attendance in one district’s secondary schools reached only 47.23%. The conflict in the English-speaking regions has lasted since 2017.

Hills of the Boyo area in Cameroon’s North-West region, where armed separatists have fought the state since 2017. (Photo: Alangi Derick, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

What It Means for US Readers

The US State Department rates Cameroon at Level 2, “exercise increased caution,” in an advisory issued on 15 May 2026.

It tells Americans not to travel to the Southwest, Northwest and Far North regions. The same warning covers a 20-kilometre strip along the borders with Chad, Nigeria and the Central African Republic.

For investors and aid groups, the main risk in Cameroon politics is a disorderly handover at the top. Readers who want the economic picture can turn to the Rio Times guide on who runs Cameroon’s economy.

The wider picture sits on the Rio Times Cameroon page.

The country’s regional role is covered in Cameroon’s role in Africa. Our news report on Cabral Libii’s warning covers the succession debate.

What Is Not Known

No date has been given for a new government, and the cabinet promised for 31 December 2025 has not appeared. Nor is there a date for Biya to name a vice president.

Nobody can say who would take over if the president could no longer serve before a vice president is named.

Seat counts for the next Assembly cannot be foreseen, because the vote has no fixed date inside the legal window. Whether Tchiroma can return and compete is also open.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who is the president of Cameroon in 2026?

In Cameroon politics, Paul Biya, 93, has been president since 6 November 1982. The Constitutional Council declared him winner of the 12 October 2025 election with 53.66% of the vote.

Who is the prime minister of Cameroon?

Joseph Dion Ngute, who was still listed as prime minister in September 2026.

How is Cameroon politics shaped by the vice presidency?

In Cameroon politics, a change approved on 4 April 2026 restored an appointed vice president. As of October 2026 the post is empty.

Which parties hold seats in the National Assembly?

The RDPC holds 152 of 180 seats, according to the 2020 results from the Inter-Parliamentary Union. The UNDP has 7, the PCRN and SDF 5 each, and the UDC 4.

Is it safe for Americans to travel to Cameroon?

The State Department rates Cameroon at Level 2 overall, as of May 2026. It tells Americans not to travel to the Southwest, Northwest and Far North regions.

Who is the opposition leader in Cameroon?

In Cameroon politics, Issa Tchiroma Bakary placed second in the 2025 election with 35.19% and lives in exile in The Gambia. Cabral Libii, who finished third, leads the PCRN.

Sources: Hespress, Cameroon presidential results (Constitutional Council, 27 October 2025), 2025-10-27; Inter-Parliamentary Union, Cameroon National Assembly, 2026-10-22; Inter-Parliamentary Union, Cameroon National Assembly election 2020, 2026-10-22; Inter-Parliamentary Union, Cameroon Senate, 2026-10-22; US Department of State, Cameroon travel advisory, 2026-05-15; Presidency of the Republic of Cameroon, 2026-10-22; Afrik, Parliament leadership change, 2026-03-18; Koaci, army chiefs, 2026-08-05; Cameroun Actuel, Constitutional Council appointments, 2026-10-16; Journal du Cameroun, death of Clement Atangana, 2026-10-04; Cameroon Tribune, Issa Tchiroma Bakary, 2026-10-14; Benin Web TV, back-to-school lockdown, 2026-09-09; Al Jazeera, Cameroonians await government reshuffle after Biya’s return, 2026-10-17; Investir au Cameroun, 2026-10-22; Journal du Cameroun, MRC and Constitutional Council headlines, 2026-10-22; Koaci, succession debate, 2026-10-07; Daba Finance, military decrees, 2026-08-11; Afrik, Eko Eko trial, 2026-09-01; allAfrica, Joshua Osih press conference, 2026-07-23; allAfrica, Sadi interview, 2026-08-03; Benin Web TV, new government not announced, 2026-08-26.

World.title: Who Runs Belize’s Economy, the Key Players in 2026
World.content:
BELIZE · ECONOMY

Key Facts — The country Belize is an English-speaking nation of 418,982 people (mid-2026 estimate) on the Caribbean coast of Central America, with a currency fixed at two Belize dollars to one US dollar.

— The size Output was BZ$1.388 billion (about US$694 million) in April to June 2026, up 1.4% on a year earlier. Consumer prices were 4.4% higher in August 2026.

— What earns the money Domestic exports were BZ$390 million (about US$195 million) in 2025. Sugar supplied 29%, bananas 23%, marine products 12% and citrus 8%.

— The state’s reach The government and the Social Security Board are majority owners of the phone company BTL, and the state bought the Macal River hydro plants and a one-third stake in Belize Electricity in 2025.

— The banks Four domestic banks held BZ$5.68 billion (about US$2.84 billion) in assets in March 2026. Atlantic Bank and Belize Bank hold about 82% of that.

— Who decides Prime Minister John Briceño leads the government and Kareem Michael governs the Central Bank of Belize, both as of October 2026.

— Still open Sugar and citrus earnings are falling, public debt stood at 66.4% of output in August 2026, and the state’s telecom and power moves face public pushback.

The Belize economy is small enough that a few state bodies, four banks and some foreign-owned firms decide most of it.

For Americans who holiday, retire or invest there, the same names set interest rates, power bills and the price of a hotel room.

Harvest Caye Cruise Port in southern Belize, one of the country’s two cruise ports. File photo, 2022. (Photo: Lucas EDVK, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

The Belize Economy in Numbers

Belize is a country of 418,982 people, according to the Statistical Institute of Belize (SIB), the government’s statistics office, in its mid-2026 estimate. Its economy produced BZ$1.388 billion (about US$694 million) of goods and services in April to June 2026, SIB said on 30 September 2026.

That was 1.4% more than a year earlier, and unemployment stood at 1.9% in April 2026, SIB said. Consumer prices rose 4.4% in the year to August 2026, with transport costs leading the climb.

The Belize dollar has been fixed at two to one US dollar since May 1976, the Central Bank of Belize (CBB) says. Halve any Belize dollar price and you have the US dollar price.

The fixed rate works because the central bank holds enough dollars to back it. At the end of July 2026 its reserves covered 4.0 months of merchandise imports, against a benchmark of 3.0 months, the CBB reported.

Imports are the weak spot. Gross imports rose 15.1% to BZ$1.96 billion (about US$982 million) in January to July 2026, the CBB said.

Domestic exports fell 17.9% to BZ$207.7 million (about US$104 million) over the same seven months.

Public sector debt was BZ$4.65 billion (about US$2.33 billion) at the end of July 2026, or 65.3% of output. Of that, BZ$2.96 billion (about US$1.48 billion) is owed abroad, and the central government accounts for about nine-tenths of the foreign part.

The Government and the Central Bank

Belize is a parliamentary democracy, and power over the Belize economy sits with one office. Prime Minister John Briceño leads the governing People’s United Party (PUP), and his government sets the budget.

On 15 October 2026 Briceño spoke to a Caribbean ministerial meeting at the World Bank and IMF annual meetings, the Press Office said. He said fuel had risen 27.7% since the Hormuz crisis.

Public debt reached 66.4% of output in August 2026, he added.

The Central Bank of Belize is the second pillar. Governor Kareem Michael heads it, according to the bank’s website in October 2026, and also serves as Registrar of Credit Unions.

The bank defends the dollar peg, supervises the banks and keeps the national reserves. The law requires external assets of at least 40% of notes, coins and deposits, and it held 65.1% at the end of July 2026.

The government also borrows from regional lenders.

The Caribbean Development Bank paid out the most in January to July 2026, BZ$19.1 million (about US$9.6 million). The World Bank, the Inter-American Development Bank and the Kuwait Fund followed.

Those loans fund road, school and water projects. Read the Rio Times report on Belize’s talks with lenders for the latest on the government’s borrowing.

Sugar and Its Foreign Owner

Farm exports still pay for much of what the Belize economy imports. In 2025 domestic exports earned BZ$390 million (about US$195 million), down 16% from BZ$464 million (about US$232 million) in 2024, according to SIB.

Sugar was the largest line at BZ$113.7 million (about US$56.8 million), or 29% of the total. Bananas earned BZ$91.0 million (about US$45.5 million), marine products BZ$46.4 million (about US$23.2 million) and citrus BZ$30.4 million (about US$15.2 million).

Sugar is run by Belize Sugar Industries (BSI), which runs the country’s two mills. BSI is part of ASR Group, which says on its website that it is owned by Florida Crystals Corporation.

The 2025/26 cane crop came to 1,504,325 long tons, down 0.5%, but sugar output rose 2.4% to 133,618 long tons, the CBB reported. Sugar earnings fell 35.5% to BZ$56.6 million (about US$28.3 million) in January to July 2026 because world prices dropped.

Old steam-engine machinery at the Serpon sugar mill site, a relic of Belize’s long sugar history. File photo, 2026. (Photo: Nosferattus, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons)

Bananas, Citrus and the Sea

Bananas are organised through the Banana Growers’ Association.

Output slipped 3.3% to 51,653 metric tons in January to July 2026, the CBB said. Export earnings still rose 5.1% to BZ$63.4 million (about US$31.7 million) on better prices.

Citrus is in trouble. Deliveries fell 43.0% in the 2025/26 season, which the CBB blamed on higher costs, fewer plantings and citrus greening, a tree disease.

The Sea and the Ranch

Marine exports are smaller but growing. Lobster tail earned BZ$23.6 million (about US$11.8 million) in 2025, and conch earned BZ$14.5 million (about US$7.2 million), SIB data show.

Cattle sales abroad reached BZ$16.3 million (about US$8.1 million) in 2025, up from BZ$11.9 million (about US$6.0 million) a year earlier.

Banana plants with green fruit on Ambergris Caye, Belize. File photo, 2015. (Photo: Asdfjrjjj, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

The Four Banks and Who Holds the Money

Belize has four domestic banks, and the CBB publishes their books every quarter. At 31 March 2026 they held BZ$5.68 billion (about US$2.84 billion) in assets and BZ$4.89 billion (about US$2.44 billion) in deposits.

Atlantic Bank is the largest, with assets of BZ$2.41 billion (about US$1.21 billion) and 12 branches. Belize Bank follows at BZ$2.26 billion (about US$1.13 billion) with 11 branches.

Heritage Bank holds BZ$782 million (about US$391 million) in assets and has 13 branches. National Bank of Belize holds BZ$229 million (about US$114 million) and has 3.

Belize Bank is the most profitable. Its return on average equity was 28.7% in the CBB’s March 2026 table, against 8.6% at Atlantic Bank.

Belize Bank grew in 2021, when Scotiabank sold its Belize business. The buyer was Caribbean Investment Holdings Limited, the holding company that owns Belize Bank, Breaking Belize News reported.

The average rate on new deposits was 1.86% in July 2026, while the average rate on new loans was 8.77%, the CBB said. That gap of 6.91 points is the banks’ main income.

Lending is tilting toward business and building. Private-sector credit rose 4.2% to BZ$2.99 billion (about US$1.50 billion) in the first seven months of 2026, while personal loans fell.

Power, Phones and the State Companies

The state has pulled back into the Belize economy since 2025. In October 2025 the government agreed to buy three Macal River hydro plants from Fortis Inc. of Canada.

The deal also took Fortis’s 33.3% stake in Belize Electricity Limited (BEL), the national grid company.

The price was about BZ$256 million (about US$128 million), Lexpert reported, with US$110 million for the plants and US$18 million for the BEL shares. The plants, Mollejon, Chalillo and Vaca, supply over a third of the electricity Belizeans use each year, the government said.

The government then offered half of Hydro Belize Limited to the public at BZ$29 a share. Applications topped 4.45 million shares for the 4 million on offer.

The sale raised BZ$129.1 million (about US$64.6 million), Prime Minister Briceño said in March 2026.

About 2,000 Belizeans took part, along with institutions. The Social Security Board (SSB) manages workers’ pensions and bought extra shares worth BZ$5.7 million (about US$2.9 million).

Breaking Belize News reported in July 2026 that the SSB proposed a further BZ$20 million (about US$10 million) purchase. The board runs contributions for about 190,000 workers and pensioners.

Telecoms is the other state-owned giant. Belize Telemedia Limited (BTL) reported a record net profit of BZ$36.9 million (about US$18.5 million) for the year to 31 March 2026.

Shareholders approved a dividend of BZ$0.37 (about US$0.19) a share on 17 September 2026. Cash stood at BZ$62.8 million (about US$31.4 million) and long-term debt fell to BZ$15.6 million (about US$7.8 million).

Cabinet said the government, the SSB and the people of Belize are BTL’s majority owners. On 13 August 2026 it refused to back BTL’s proposed purchase of the rival Smart network, also known as Speednet.

The National Trade Union Congress of Belize opposed the deal. BTL’s chairman confirmed in August 2026 that the Public Utilities Commission, the regulator, has ruled BTL a dominant provider, which brings extra rules.

BTL’s chief executive is Ivan Tesucum, as of September 2026.

Tourism and the Cruise Business

Tourism is the other big source of foreign currency. Stay-over visitors numbered 332,038 in January to July 2026, down 0.8% on a year earlier, with 282,555 arriving by air, the CBB said.

Cruise passengers did better. Disembarkations rose 9.9% to 589,413 and ship calls rose to 217 in the same seven months.

Two ports share the traffic. Fort Street Cruise Port in Belize City took 147 calls, down from 159, the CBB said.

Harvest Caye Cruise Port in southern Belize took 70 calls, the most it has recorded for the first seven months of a year.

The banks lean on this trade too. Lending to tourism businesses grew by BZ$8.8 million (about US$4.4 million) in the first seven months of 2026, the CBB said.

Air links matter as much as ports, and the Rio Times has covered the first direct flight from Europe that Belize has signed for.

The Swing Bridge in Belize City, the country’s largest city. File photo, 2015. (Photo: Haakon S. Krohn, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

Drinks, Retail and the Private Groups

Outside farming and finance, a few private firms are household names. BOW Beverages sells Belikin beer, Coca-Cola soft drinks, Heineken, Guinness and Red Stripe, its own website lists.

Shops and distribution led new bank lending, with BZ$30.0 million (about US$15.0 million) added in the first seven months of 2026, the CBB said. Imports of food, drink and tobacco rose 5.4%.

Foreign owners such as Florida Crystals control sugar, and the state controls power and phones. The other large private groups behind the shops, hotels and importers sit outside the central bank’s published data.

For more on the country’s politics and place in the region, see the Rio Times guide Belize explained and its report on Belize geopolitics.

What It Means for US Readers

For Americans, the peg is the main comfort. A Belize dollar is always worth 50 US cents, so local prices convert simply and do not swing against the dollar.

The cost is that Belize cannot cheapen its currency in a bad year. When tourism slows or fuel costs jump, the adjustment lands on government budgets, jobs and imports.

Visitors meet the fuel bill in transport. Transport prices rose 6.3% in January to July 2026, and restaurants and accommodation rose 3.0%, the CBB said.

Anyone weighing the Belize economy as an investment should watch the same few names. The government’s borrowing, the two big banks and the cruise lines decide how much money moves.

Read the Rio Times report on Belize’s slower growth for the latest figures, or the Belize hub for more coverage.

What Is Not Known

The final split of Hydro Belize shares between small investors, the SSB and the government has not been published. The full board of Hydro Belize had not been put in place in March 2026, the Prime Minister said.

Who owns the largest private groups is not disclosed in official statistics or central bank reports. The final cost of the hydro purchase to taxpayers, once share-sale proceeds and plant revenue are counted, has not been set out in full.

Whether BTL will try another acquisition after the Cabinet’s refusal is open. The company’s chairman has said BTL accepts the decision and the regulator’s dominance ruling.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who runs the Belize economy?

The government, led by Prime Minister John Briceño, sets the budget. The Central Bank of Belize, under Governor Kareem Michael, runs the dollar peg and supervises the banks.

What is the Belize economy based on?

The Belize economy rests on tourism, farming exports and services. In 2025 sugar, bananas, marine products and citrus made up about 72% of domestic exports, according to the Statistical Institute of Belize.

Who owns Belize Telemedia Limited?

Cabinet said in August 2026 that the government, the Social Security Board and the people of Belize are the majority owners of BTL. The company reported a record net profit of BZ$36.9 million (about US$18.5 million) for the year to March 2026.

Which are the biggest banks in Belize?

Atlantic Bank (assets BZ$2.41 billion, or about US$1.21 billion) and Belize Bank (BZ$2.26 billion, or about US$1.13 billion) lead. Heritage Bank and National Bank of Belize are smaller, according to the Central Bank’s March 2026 data.

Is the Belize dollar tied to the US dollar?

Yes. The Belize dollar has been fixed at two to one US dollar since May 1976, the Central Bank says, so US visitors can halve any local price.

Who owns Belize’s sugar industry?

Belize Sugar Industries is part of ASR Group, which says Florida Crystals Corporation owns it. Cane farmers supply the mills, and sugar earned BZ$113.7 million (about US$56.8 million) in 2025.

Sources: Statistical Institute of Belize, September 2026 release (GDP Q2 2026, CPI, trade), 30 September 2026; Statistical Institute of Belize, External Trade Bulletin December 2025 (2025 domestic exports), December 2025; Central Bank of Belize, Monthly Economic Highlights July 2026, 24 September 2026; Central Bank of Belize, Quarterly Financial Information of Domestic Banks, March 2026, 31 March 2026; Central Bank of Belize, home page (governor, exchange rate), 22 October 2026; Government of Belize Press Office, release on the Fortis hydro and BEL purchase, 16 October 2025; Government of Belize Press Office, Hydro Belize share offer, 17 December 2025; Breaking Belize News, Hydro Belize share offer oversubscribed, 10 March 2026; Breaking Belize News, Cabinet rejects the Speednet acquisition, 13 August 2026; Breaking Belize News, BTL record profit, 18 September 2026; Government of Belize Press Office, Prime Minister Briceño at the World Bank-IMF annual meetings, 15 October 2026; Breaking Belize News, Social Security Board and Hydro Belize, 17 July 2026; Lexpert, Fortis sells Belize hydro assets and BEL stake, 22 July 2026; Breaking Belize News, BTL accepts defeat on Smart takeover, 14 August 2026; ASR Group, About us, October 2026; BOW Beverages, products, October 2026; Central Bank of Belize, Office of the Governor, 22 October 2026.

World.title: Reports Name 2 CIA Officers Killed in Mexico
World.content:
MEXICO · SECURITY

Key Facts — Who Two Americans, named in reports as Richard Leiter Johnston III and John Dudley Black, died in Chihuahua on 19 April.

— What Mexican prosecutors and US media say both worked for the CIA, the US foreign intelligence agency.

— Why now Mexico’s federal prosecutors are pursuing a treason case against Chihuahua’s former attorney general over the operation.

— Still open Neither the CIA nor the US government has publicly confirmed the two men’s employer.

— Power Index Mexico ranks 2nd of 14 in Mexico ranks 2nd of 14 in The Rio Times Latin America Power Index , with 71.4 points (October 2026 edition).

Two Americans who died in a Mexican drug-lab operation in April have now been named in reports as CIA officers.

Two Americans killed in a vehicle crash after an April anti-drug operation in northern Mexico have been named in reports as CIA officers. The Washington Post and the Associated Press, citing sources, first identified the two men as working for the US foreign intelligence agency.

Mexican officials have since pointed the same way, which makes this a test of how far US agents may work alongside Mexican state police. Mexico’s federal government says foreign security agencies must work through federal channels, not directly with state police.

Latin America Power Index · October 2026 edition Mexico ranks 2nd of 14 with 71.4 points. Strongest pillar: economic relationships (90); weakest: state capacity & security (46). Alignment group: Hedging. Watch21 homicides per 100,000; organised crime at 7.7 of 10. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

What Happened on 19 April

A vehicle returning from an operation against clandestine drug laboratories near El Pinal, in Morelos municipality, left the road in the Sierra Tarahumara mountains of Chihuahua state. It overturned and caught fire at about 1:50 a.m. local time on Sunday, 19 April, which was 3:50 a.m. US Eastern time.

Four people died: the two Americans, Pedro Román Oseguera Cervantes, director of Chihuahua’s State Investigation Agency, and his escort, Manuel Genaro Méndez Montes. The crash happened on a road between Morelos and Guachochi.

The Copper Canyon in Chihuahua’s Sierra Tarahumara. File photo; it does not show the crash site. Photo: Comisión Mexicana de Filmaciones, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

Free download · Expat checklist Get the free checklist as PDF Moving to Mexico 2026: the step-by-step checklist. This guide condensed into 2 printable pages with tick boxes and the key official links. Email address Get the PDF Free. We send a confirmation link first, and the same address then receives The Rio Times Brief, our daily briefing. Unsubscribe with one click at any time; see our privacy policy. Your checklist is ready. Download the PDF checklist

How the CIA Link Emerged

On the day of the crash, Chihuahua officials described the Americans as embassy liaisons and instructors. Chihuahua’s special prosecutor said on 27 April that four US agents had gone undercover, according to Proceso.

Reports then named the dead as Johnston, reportedly aged 35 or 36, and Black, reportedly aged 43 or 44. Press accounts describe Johnston as a former US Army officer and Black as a former Marine who served in Afghanistan, which the CIA and the Pentagon have not confirmed.

President Claudia Sheinbaum said on 27 May that four Americans had taken part and two had died. She said the other two, who lacked Mexican accreditation, were asked to leave the country, according to El Universal.

The Legal Fight in Mexico

On 17 October, Attorney General Ernestina Godoy described the foreigners as presumably attached to the CIA, according to Infobae. Her office accuses Chihuahua’s former attorney general, César Jáuregui Moreno, of letting them take part without federal authorisation.

State officers detained Jáuregui on Saturday, 17 October, and federal agents executed a warrant the next day. A federal judge ordered him held in pretrial detention at the Altiplano prison on 21 October, according to La Jornada, and he is presumed innocent.

Our report on the treason case against Jáuregui and our earlier story on his arrest cover the proceedings, and the Mexico hub has the latest news.

Accident, Not Attack

An expert examination confirmed that the four deaths were accidental, El Diario de Chihuahua reported on 26 May. No report says the Americans were targeted.

Initial accounts blamed a difficult dirt road and poor visibility. Reports differ on how many drug laboratories were found, from one to six.

What It Means for US Readers

The case puts rare public attention on US intelligence officers working inside Mexico during President Donald Trump’s second term. It also raises scrutiny of security cooperation that Washington relies on against fentanyl production.

Mexico’s insistence on federal approval may slow joint operations that start with state police. The dispute is likely to shape how the two governments set the rules for future security cooperation.

What Is Not Known

The CIA and the US government have not publicly confirmed the two men’s employer, and their exact status in Mexico has not been made public. Ages and some biographical details differ between reports.

Who authorised the Americans’ role is under investigation, and no court has ruled on the treason accusation. The two Americans who left Mexico have not been named.

Frequently Asked Questions

Were the two Americans confirmed as CIA officers?

The Washington Post and AP, citing sources, identified them as CIA officers, and Mexico’s attorney general described the foreigners as presumably attached to the agency. The CIA and the US government have not publicly confirmed it.

What is César Jáuregui accused of?

Federal prosecutors accuse the former Chihuahua attorney general of letting foreign agents take part in the operation without federal authorisation. A federal judge ordered him held in pretrial detention on 21 October, and he is presumed innocent.

Was the crash an attack or an accident?

An expert examination confirmed accidental deaths, according to El Diario de Chihuahua. No report says the Americans were targeted.

What happened to the other two Americans?

President Claudia Sheinbaum said on 27 May that two other Americans involved were asked to leave Mexico. Their names have not been made public.

Sources: Proceso; Infobae; El Universal; El Financiero; La Jornada; El Diario de Chihuahua; PBS NewsHour (AP) (all accessed 22 October 2026).

World.title: Venezuela Opposition Calls Election Protests
World.content:
VENEZUELA · POLITICS

Key Facts — Who Opposition leader María Corina Machado and her party, Vente Venezuela, called protests across Venezuela for Thursday, 22 October.

— What Demonstrators want a 2027 presidential election date, Machado’s safe return and the release of political prisoners.

— When The main Caracas rally starts at 4:00 p.m. Venezuela time, which is 4:00 p.m. US Eastern (20:00 UTC).

— Where Organisers announced events in every state; the Caracas rally is at Plaza Venezuela, in front of Torre Polar.

— Prediction markets Polymarket prices the 31 December option of its “Venezuela presidential election scheduled by…?” market at 8.5% (22 October 2026, 11:06 a.m. ET).

— Power Index Venezuela ranks 13th of 14 in Venezuela ranks 13th of 14 in The Rio Times Latin America Power Index , with 27.0 points (October 2026 edition).

Venezuela’s opposition has called a nationwide day of protest today to demand a date for the next presidential election.

Venezuela’s opposition has called protests in every state for Thursday, 22 October, to demand a date for a presidential election in 2027. The main rally in Caracas is due to start at 4:00 p.m. local time, which is also 4:00 p.m. US Eastern time.

The call comes from María Corina Machado, the opposition leader and 2025 Nobel Peace Prize winner, who is outside the country. For Americans, the protests test how quickly the country run by acting president Delcy Rodríguez moves towards a vote after the US operation that captured Nicolás Maduro in January.

Latin America Power Index · October 2026 edition Venezuela ranks 13th of 14 with 27.0 points. Strongest pillar: military means (81); weakest: economic relationships (0). Alignment group: Closer to Beijing. Some pillar data are incomplete for Venezuela; see the index notes. WatchSovereign in selective default; inflation of 252%; public debt at 309% of GDP. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

What Is Planned on Thursday

Vente Venezuela, the party Machado founded, announced the mobilisation earlier this week. Machado then urged Venezuelans to take part, according to Europa Press and Infobae on 21 October.

Organisers say the events will be peaceful and will take place in all Venezuelan states. In Caracas, the main gathering is at Plaza Venezuela, in front of the Torre Polar office tower, at 4:00 p.m.

Plaza Venezuela in Caracas, where the main rally is planned. File photo. Photo: George Miquilena, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

Carlos Fernández, a Vente Venezuela leader, said at a press conference that mothers, teachers and young people would join. He added that the Unitary Platform, the main opposition alliance, and parties outside it would also take part.

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on Venezuela Transformation Email address Follow Free. One email a day at most, and only when there is news. This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

What the Opposition Demands

The organisers list three demands: Machado’s safe return to Venezuela, a formal electoral timetable for a presidential vote in 2027, and the freedom of political prisoners. Their slogan is “La fecha de la elección es la fecha de la liberación”, or “The election date is the date of liberation”.

Machado backs 24 July 2027 as the election date, the anniversary of the birth of independence hero Simón Bolívar. US Senator Bernie Moreno proposed that date in September, according to Voz.us.

Where Machado Is and Why It Matters

Machado has been reported in Panama and has not announced when she will return. Her communications coordinator, Claudia Macero, returned to Venezuela on 27 September, according to eldiario.com, but said she did not know when Machado would follow.

Supporters say Machado has made seven failed attempts to return this year, according to Voz.us. They say a boat trip was cancelled because of engine damage and that Caribbean islands refused landing permission for a flight, which no independent source has confirmed.

Our earlier report on her stance on amnesty and the 24 July vote covers the political background, and the Venezuela hub collects the latest news.

A Rival March the Same Day

El Nacional reports that the governing side has called its own march for 22 October. Diosdado Cabello, a senior chavista leader, announced it as a women’s march for breast-cancer awareness, with no time or route given.

Two events in one city on the same day raise the risk of clashes, but no source reports any plan by the authorities to restrict the opposition rally. Nothing in our reporting shows how the government will respond.

What Prediction Markets Say

On Polymarket, the “Venezuela presidential election scheduled by…?” market prices the 31 December 2026 option at 8.5%, with US$644,439 traded (22 October 2026, 11:06 a.m. ET). Read literally, traders see little chance that the question resolves yes by year-end.

Why we show this: prediction markets turn real-money bets into a live probability that moves within minutes of the news, which is why investors, campaigns and newsrooms in the United States now follow them closely. We show them next to polls and official results, never instead of them.

What It Means for US Readers

Washington has a stake in how Venezuela’s transition ends, from oil exports to migration. A clear election date would give US investors and policymakers a timetable they can plan around.

A large, peaceful turnout would strengthen the opposition’s case for a 2027 vote. Violence or arrests would more likely harden positions on both sides.

What Is Not Known

No turnout figure exists yet, because the rally has not started as this article is published. Nothing is known about arrests, injuries or any police response.

The government has not announced an election timetable, and the 2027 date remains an opposition demand. Machado’s return date and route are also unknown.

Frequently Asked Questions

What does Venezuela’s opposition want from the protests?

It wants an election date for a 2027 presidential vote, Machado’s safe return and the release of political prisoners. The organisers presented these as the core demands of the mobilisation.

When and where is the main Caracas protest?

It starts at 4:00 p.m. Venezuela time on Thursday, 22 October, at Plaza Venezuela in front of Torre Polar. That is 4:00 p.m. US Eastern time and 20:00 UTC.

Where is María Corina Machado?

Reports place her in Panama, and she has not announced a return date. Supporters say several attempts to return this year failed.

Who is Delcy Rodríguez?

She is Venezuela’s acting president after US forces captured Nicolás Maduro in January. The opposition wants her government to set a date for a presidential election.

Sources: Caretas; El Nacional; Infobae; Europa Press; eldiario.com; Voz.us; Polymarket (all accessed 22 October 2026).
