We cannot do what we do without your support. By Aleks Szczerbiak Political scandals generate intense media attention and public outrage but rarely produce dramatic shifts in party support that they once did. They are now more likely to affect electoral outcomes indirectly by demobilising softer, less committed voters and influencing turnout, particularly among supporters of the government disappointed by its apparent underperformance and broken election promises. The hospital scandal Two high-profile political scandals dominated the Polish news agenda for much of this summer. The first centred on irregularities at Warsaw’s Southern Hospital (Szpital Południowy) and involved a young and relatively inexperienced doctor, Dawid Kacprzyk. In spite of his lack of a specialist qualification, Kacprzyk coordinated the hospital’s emergency department and reportedly earned a staggering 1.6 million złoty (€366,000) in the previous year alone. He also served as a Warsaw district councilor for the liberal-centrist Civic Coalition (KO) grouping, Poland’s main governing party led by Prime Minister Donald Tusk. Public outrage intensified following reports that the hospital had operated a dedicated “VIP path” or special lounge where ruling-party-linked politicians and their families were allowed faster access and medical examinations without the usual queues faced by ordinary patients. Further claims emerged, including a whistleblower surgeon alleging that supervisory failures contributed to patient deaths and of improper private business activity in the hospital morgue. Poland’s health minister has unveiled a set of reforms intended to “rebuild trust” in public hospitals following a series of reports about exorbitant pay for some doctors and that politically connected patients could skip queues and use a "VIP lounge" https://t.co/pidAHxohc4 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 8, 2026 For its part, KO insisted that the scandal was the personal misconduct of one former party member rather than a general problem affecting the entire healthcare system. They noted that Kacprzyk quickly resigned his council seat and hospital role, and that party-aligned Warsaw mayor Rafał Trzaskowski had dismissed the hospital board and two of his deputy mayors overseeing the city’s health services. KO argued that no specific names of preferential VIP patients had been publicly confirmed, any irregularities were being fully investigated by prosecutors and independent bodies, and political and legal accountability would follow if ethical breaches or crimes were proven. The government also pledged systemic reforms including measures to curb excessive pay for doctors. Nonetheless, the scandal struck a deep chord with the Polish public, triggering massive negative media and political fallout that aligned perfectly with the right-wing opposition’s narrative painting KO as part of a “Warsaw elite” that enjoys special privileges at the expense of ordinary citizens. The cryptocurrency scandal The second major summer scandal centred on allegations of financial impropriety and political entanglement involving Zondacrypto, once Poland’s largest crypto trading platform, that claimed over a million users but earlier this year collapsed abruptly after thousands of retail investors were unable to access their funds. However, what began as a major financial scandal escalated into political warfare, providing the government with powerful ammunition to attack the right-wing Law and Justice (PiS), Poland’s ruling party between 2015 and 2023 and currently the main opposition grouping, party-aligned President Karol Nawrocki, and the broader conservative political eco-system over payments and donations made by the crypto firm. Prosecutors are investigating possible criminal offences relating to financing by Zondacrypto, a collapsed crypto firm, of organisations and individuals linked to the right-wing opposition, including the Polish version of US conservative conference CPAC https://t.co/swceV864nA — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 26, 2026 For example, Zondacrypto sponsored the 2025 Polish edition of the Conservative Political Action Committee (CPAC) conference attended by the then-presidential candidate Nawrocki, advertised heavily with conservative media outlets such as the TV Republika television network, and made donations to foundations linked to high-ranking PiS figures such as former justice minister Zbigniew Ziobro. The government also tried to entangle Nawrocki, who repeatedly vetoed its cryptocurrency regulation laws, into the scandal, arguing that he was protecting the shady interests of the industry and its political beneficiaries at the expense of ordinary Poles (the Tusk administration lacks the three-fifths parliamentary majority required to overturn a presidential veto). For their part, PiS and the broader Polish right dismissed the government’s accusations as a smear campaign and sought to shift blame for the scandal onto the Tusk administration for inadequate oversight to protect investors. Figures on the right, including those connected to foundations that received money, framed these dealings as legitimate sponsorships common across the media and other organisations. The president of the Polish Olympic Committee has been detained as part of a criminal investigation into Zondacrypto, a crypto firm that collapsed earlier this year and was a major sponsor of Poland's Olympic team https://t.co/QPG7ejAImD — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 27, 2026 PiS rejected claims that the party or associated groups received funds from the firm and defended Nawrocki’s vetoes as necessary against flawed legislation. Nonetheless, opinion polls found that most respondents linked the scandal to PiS and the right-wing opposition, providing the government with numerous attack lines to force them onto the defensive. The diminishing impact of scandals It is worth recalling how an earlier era of post-communist politics scandals possessed much greater transformative, system-altering capacity and could act as catalysts for the restructuring of the electoral landscape. For example, at the beginning of the 2000s, the so-called “Rywin scandal” was widely seen as a decisive factor in the near-destruction as a political force of the previously powerful, and then-governing, communist-successor Democratic Left Alliance (SLD). The scandal erupted in late 2002 when film producer Lew Rywin allegedly solicited a large bribe from the Agora media group, publisher of the influential liberal-left Gazeta Wyborcza newspaper, in exchange for media legislation changes while claiming to act on behalf of a “group holding power” (grupa trzymająca władzę) linked to the ruling party. A high-profile parliamentary investigative commission, sustained media focus, and a series of follow-on scandals and accumulation of allegations of deep-seated influence peddling by post-communist networks created a powerful narrative of systemic bribery and corruption, completely discrediting the SLD as a competent governing force. Having won a substantial victory in the 2001 parliamentary election, securing 41% of the votes, its support collapsed to only 11% at the next 2005 poll. This helped clear the way for the rise of the KO (originally Civic Platform)-PiS duopoly that has structured the Polish party system ever since, thereby establishing a precedent that scandals were electorally fatal transgressions. The contrast with the recent hospital and cryptocurrency scandals is instructive and illustrates a broader transformation in the relationship between political misconduct and electoral politics in Poland. Whereas in the more fluid party system of the early post-communist period a cluster of major scandals or single-event shocks could rapidly destroy dominant parties and restructure competition, now – although they still generate intense, high-octane political and media outrage – such controversies appear to slide off the main political actors with remarkably little immediate consequence. Indeed, neither of these recent scandals produced the dramatic shift in headline polling numbers that some observers, drawing on historical precedent, might have anticipated given the intensity of the media coverage. Scandal-neutralising structural shifts This change stems from three interlocking shifts in the structural dynamics of Poland’s political system. Taken together, they have substantially diminished the capacity of scandals to move headline poll numbers and trigger the kind of large-scale systemic realignments seen in an earlier era of post-communist politics. Firstly, the sheer velocity of modern political communication prevents single-issue-based scandals from sustaining public focus. In the early 2000s, a major corruption scandal could dominate the news headlines for months through concentrated media attention. The Rywin scandal unfolded through prolonged televised parliamentary commission hearings, keeping the story alive and allowing public outrage to build into a sustained narrative that slowly drained the ruling party’s legitimacy. Today, digital algorithms and the 24-hour news cycle ensure that a major story, whether about healthcare management or cryptocurrency, moves at a breathtaking pace and is overtaken rapidly as public attention moves onto the next domestic controversy, international development, or strategic counter-narrative. Seven people have been charged in relation to alleged corruption in the issuing of Polish visas to foreign nationals The scandal has engulfed the government since last week, but officials say the opposition is exaggerating the scale and nature of the case https://t.co/iHnIShb1pQ — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 15, 2023 This hyper-accelerated news cycle means that even a high-profile case that generates intense short-term media coverage does not remain the dominant story for long enough to produce cumulative, system-level damage by limiting the time window in which a scandal can convert temporary disapproval into lasting shifts in voting intentions. Scandals thereby become a form of ambient “background noise” in Polish public life rather than a singular focal point for popular outrage. Secondly, and perhaps most formidably, the protective shield of deep polarisation and socio-political division renders large segments of the electorate relatively impervious to allegations against “their” side. After 2005, the Polish party system crystallised around a durable “post-transition” socio-economic divide reinforced by cultural and geopolitical fault lines. In this deeply fractured and highly polarised landscape, with large segments of the electorate embedded within hostile camps, when a scandal like the hospital crisis or cryptocurrency controversy breaks, voters interpret allegations levelled against “their” party through a tribal filter as a politically motivated hit job or the work of hostile media. So even severe scandals are shaped by, and largely confirm, existing political loyalties and rarely trigger cross-camp voter defections. This is a sharp contrast with the early 2000s, when the party system was still fluid and electoral volatility high. Our essential guide to Poland's parliamentary elections, which will take place one year from now. How does voting work? What do polls suggest the outcome will be? Which issues may animate the campaign? And what role will President Nawrocki play? https://t.co/fmdoFpBaxz — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 15, 2026 Thirdly, the parties themselves have become far more professional at message discipline and crisis management. Today’s parties are centralised media machines staffed by sophisticated public relations strategists who view a scandal not as a moral crisis but a communication problem requiring aggressive damage containment. Rather than allowing a controversy to fester, they immediately launch counterattacks, accusing their opponents of far greater historical or concurrent corruption, and ruthlessly enforce internal party discipline and message conformity. They also deploy well-rehearsed crisis management playbooks including: personnel sanctions; framing the problem as local or individual responsibility, or residual rather than systemic failure; ordering visible audits, investigations, or reforms to demonstrate “taking action”; and co-ordinated messaging that seeks to close the story quickly and shift the focus back onto the other side’s weaknesses or broader policy issues. Differential mobilisation, not voter persuasion Yet while polarisation and professional crisis management allow parties to survive the immediate news cycle, this does not mean that scandals have become irrelevant. Rather, their effects are more subtle and delayed through the “slow-burn” mechanism of differential turnout by selectively demobilising specific voter segments. Although in a highly polarised polity the most committed hard-core partisans are relatively immune to negative information about “their” side, soft or conditional supporters may become disillusioned, or simply less motivated, when repeated scandals reinforce a narrative of self-interest or incompetence. The net result is a gradual, cumulative, asymmetric demobilisation of one camp that does not fully register in standard inter-election voting intention surveys, which generally show expressed party preferences among those willing to answer but not necessarily the intensity of that preference or the probability that a respondent will actually turn out to vote. In Poland’s deeply polarised political landscape, the next parliamentary election, scheduled for autumn 2027, is unlikely to be determined by persuading voters to cross the ideological divide. Rather differential levels of electoral turnout and mobilisation are likely to be the key, specifically: whichever side’s core base is more motivated to – and peripheral, less ideologically committed “softer” supporters are demotivated from – showing up on polling day. Young Poles are bucking the international trend by turning out at a higher rate than the oldest voters in recent elections. We spoke with experts and young voters to find out more about the growing frustrations that are driving this political engagement https://t.co/y1JpYYmbjb — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 11, 2025 And in a context where the election is likely to be closely fought, and relatively small differences in participation rates could prove decisive, although they may not produce dramatic changes in headline party polling preferences, scandals can still play a significant role. However, we are only likely to see the full impact of any such scandals when voters eventually go to the polls and actual turnout patterns are revealed. Given the general disillusionment with the current government and growing narrative of its underperformance and failure to deliver on its electoral promises, scandals are more likely to contribute to the demobilisation of the governing camp. It is anyway inherently more difficult for incumbent parties to mobilise their disillusioned supporters to turn out and vote than it is for motivated oppositions to rally their base to oust them. Indeed, revealed voter preferences in the summer 2025 presidential election – when Nawrocki won an unexpected victory over Trzaskowski, the ruling party-backed favourite – and more recently the severe setback for KO in the Kraków mayoral by-election, suggest that government supporters are already showing greater reluctance to vote. So, while their effects are routinely neutralised by fast-moving news, tribal shielding and professional spin, scandals still matter in Polish politics, although the battleground has shifted from voter persuasion to differential mobilisation. World.title: Court acquits Polish soldier who accidentally shot Syrian refugee at Belarus border
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! A Polish soldier who accidentally shot a Syrian refugee who had entered Poland over the border from Belarus has been acquitted of negligent use of a weapon. The Syrian man had been seeking 50,000 zloty (€11,500) in compensation from the soldier. The verdict was welcomed by defence minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz, whose ministry had supported the soldier’s legal defence. ❗Podporucznik Wojska Polskiego został dziś uniewinniony przez Wojskowy Sąd Garnizonowy w Warszawie. Nie udowodniono mu żadnych zaniedbań w czasie służby na granicy z Białorusią. W listopadzie 2023 r. przypadkowo postrzelił on migranta. Od początku zapewniliśmy mu pomoc prawną… pic.twitter.com/RS2p2WsQ7Z — Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz (@KosiniakKamysz) October 21, 2026 The incident in question took place in November 2023 in Poland’s northeastern Podlasie province. The soldier, named only as Adam Ł. under Polish privacy law and who holds the rank of second lieutenant, had only recently received his first posting to the border, reports legal news service Prawo.pl. Since 2021, Belarus has been encouraging, assisting and in some cases coercing tens of thousands of migrants, mainly from Asia and Africa, to try to cross into Poland. Among those who make it over the border, most head westwards to Germany, while some have sought to claim international protection in Poland. In response, Poland has posted thousands of soldiers to the border, where they provide support to the border guard and police. Officers have at times faced violence from migrants trying to cross. In one case, in June 2023, a Polish soldier died after being stabbed. Poland has named a Moroccan man, Mohamed Addamrou, as the suspect in the 2024 murder of a Polish soldier, Mateusz Sitek, who was fatally stabbed while trying to stop a group of migrants from forcing their way through the border from Belarus to Poland https://t.co/mw8JuOPwcE — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 10, 2026 A few months after that tragedy, Adam Ł. took part in an operation to apprehend a group of migrants who had crossed from Belarus and were around 2 kilometres from the border. After the soldiers called on the migrants to stop, one of them, a 23-year-old Syrian man, began to flee. As Adam Ł. chased him, the soldier slipped and fell, resulting in his gun, a PM-98 Glauberyt submachine gun, accidentally discharging two rounds. One bullet hit the Syrian man in the back, close to his spine. The soldier immediately began providing him with first aid, before the Syrian was taken to hospital. He was discharged a few weeks later and, in May 2024, was granted asylum in Poland. Initially, when it appeared possible that the Syrian could suffer partial paralysis, military prosecutors considered charging Adam Ł. with negligent use of a weapon resulting in serious injury, a crime carrying a prison sentence of up to eight years. In the end, that was downgraded to a lower charge of negligent use of a weapon causing impairment or a health disorder, which is punishable by up to three years in prison. The defence ministry provided the soldier with legal counsel from a special team set up in 2024 to defend military personnel. They advised him not to plead guilty. Eventually, prosecutors asked only that the court impose an indemnity of 2,000 zloty on Adam Ł., to be paid to the Syrian. The Syrian’s lawyer, meanwhile, sought 50,000 zloty for his client. The president has signed into law new rules removing criminal liability from officers who use firearms while serving on the border. The measures were passed in response to a surge in aggression from some migrants seeking to cross the border from Belarus https://t.co/sBMaoYhoCw — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 16, 2024 In a ruling announced on Wednesday, a military court in Warsaw fully acquitted Adam Ł. Judge Michał Żak said that it remained unclear how the incident unfolded. He also pointed to expert evidence commissioned by the court that found the soldier’s gun could have had defects that caused it to fire when it hit the ground. Those doubts, and a lack of convincing evidence to support the prosecutor’s version of events, meant the charge of negligence could not be proven, found Żak. The verdict can still be appealed. The Syrian’s lawyer said they would wait for the judge’s full written justification before deciding whether to appeal. Kosiniak-Kamysz, meanwhile, welcomed the ruling in a social media post. “From the very beginning, we provided him with legal assistance,” wrote the defence minister. “A soldier who carries out his duties cannot be left alone, even in a difficult situation.” In May this year, another soldier was acquitted over an incident in which he fired shots towards a group of migrants who had illegally crossed the Belarussian border. The judge found that, in fact, the soldier had been fulfilling his obligation to defend the Polish border. A Polish soldier who fired shots towards migrants who had illegally crossed the border from Belarus has been acquitted of abusing his powers and threatening the lives of others The military judge found he had been fulfilling his duty to protect the border https://t.co/ugxq5tkdFV — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 27, 2026 In 2024, Poland’s government introduced a new law making it easier for soldiers and other uniformed officers serving at the border to use firearms. They now no longer face criminal liability for employing their weapons in certain cases. Since then, the government has also further strengthened physical border barriers and banned asylum claims by migrants who cross irregularly from Belarus. That has been followed by a significant drop in attempted crossings by migrants from Belarus: in the first half of this year, only 250 attempts were recorded, down from 15,500 in the same period of 2025 – a 98% drop. Poland also now claims to have a 100% success rate in apprehending those who do manage to cross. World.title: Poland condemns Ukrainian region for honouring figures associated with WWII massacres of Poles
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland has condemned a decision by the Lviv region in Ukraine to declare 2027 a year honouring the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA), which led the massacre of Poles during World War Two, and one of its leaders, Roman Shukhevych. Prime Minister Donald Tusk called the decision “suicidal”, saying that it harms Ukraine by making it harder for the country’s friends to support it. Foreign minister Radosław Sikorski announced that the local official responsible for pushing through the commemorations in Lviv has been banned from entering Poland. Decyzja Lwowskiej Rady Obwodowej, by 2027 rok był rokiem UPA i Szuchewycza, jest nieakceptowalna. Taka decyzja nie buduje wzajemnego zaufania między narodami, lecz wzmacnia podziały. Konieczne jest odcięcie się władz Ukrainy od tego stanowiska. — Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz (@KosiniakKamysz) October 20, 2026 On Tuesday, the Lviv regional council adopted resolutions proclaiming 2027 the year of the UPA, of Shukhevych, and of Oleh Olzhych, a poet and leading figure in the Organisation of Ukrainian Nationalists (OUN). Sviatoslav Sheremeta, chair of the region’s committee on culture, said the decisions will pave the way for “large-scale events” to commemorate the UPA, Shukhevych and Olzhych. “This is our history, our heroes, and we must duly honour their memory,” he added, quoted by local news service Sokal Voice. The OUN was a nationalist organisation that sought Ukrainian independence. The UPA, a partisan formation, emerged in 1942 from a more radical faction of the OUN, with Shukhevych serving as its military commander. While the UPA is still remembered positively by some in Ukraine for its role in fighting against Moscow-imposed Soviet rule, in Poland it is associated with the Volhynia massacres, in which the UPA led the slaughter of around 100,000 Poles, mostly women and children. Poland has previously condemned official commemorations in Ukraine of Shukhevych and other figures associated with the UPA. And the resolutions adopted by the Lviv region on Tuesday likewise prompted a swift response from Warsaw. “Glorifying the UPA and criminal figures is contrary to European values ​​and the strategic and good-neighbourly nature of relations between Poland and Ukraine,” foreign ministry spokesman Maciej Wewiór told news website Wirtualna Polska. “Shukhevych is a criminal stained with the blood of thousands of innocent victims, people who were murdered simply because they were Poles,” he added, also noting that the UPA’s victims included Jews, Czechs, Armenians and Ukrainians themselves. Wewiór warned that, while the Ukrainian and Polish governments have recently made progress towards reconciliation over historical issues, “irresponsible local activists are damaging these relations by honouring people clearly responsible for crimes and collaborating with the Nazis”. The European Parliament has criticised Ukraine's @ZelenskyyUa for naming a military unit after a group that massacred Poles during WWII, calling it an "unprovoked escalation" that is “not in line with European values” and "disregards Polish sensitivities" https://t.co/54rbPSrs9S — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 8, 2026 On Wednesday, Tusk said that such decisions “harm Ukraine” by “making the work of Ukraine’s friends and supporters of closer cooperation very difficult”. By contrast, the “Russians always rub their hands in glee in situations like these”, added Tusk, quoted by Polsat News. Meanwhile, Sikorski announced that he had signed a motion to place Sheremeta, who has led the efforts to commemorate the UPA and Shukhevych in Lviv, on Poland’s “list of undesirable persons”. Wirtualna Polska reports that Sheremeta was previously banned from entry in 2017, under Poland’s former government, for his actions in blocking the exhumation and commemoration of Polish massacre victims buried in Ukraine. Podpisałem wniosek o wpisanie na listę osób niepożądanych w RP radnego obwodu lwowskiego S. Szeremeta, rekonstruktora Galizien Waffen-SS, autora pomysłu ustanowienia 2027 rokiem R.Szuchewycza, dowódcy UPA, który wydawał rozkazy wysiedlania i mordowania Polaków.… — Radosław Sikorski 🇵🇱🇪🇺 (@sikorskiradek) October 21, 2026 Poland’s state Institute of National Remembrance (IPN) also condemned the resolutions. It called Shukhevych “an architect of the genocide in Volhynia” as well as the “co-founder of collaborationist units operating alongside Germany”. It quoted an order issued by Shukhevych in which he wrote: “Cut them down to the last man. Burn villages inhabited exclusively by Poles; in mixed villages, eliminate only the Polish population.” However, the IPN noted that Olzhych – whom Lviv is also honouring next year – was the head of a group that condemned the crimes committed by the more radical faction of the OUN. The Lviv Regional Council has designated 2027 in the Lviv region as the Year of Roman Shukhevych, an architect of the genocide in Volhynia, the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA), and Oleh Olzhych, a leader of the OUN-M. Among those being commemorated, Roman Shukhevych stands out as… pic.twitter.com/Bge2muwjHz — Institute of National Remembrance (@ipngovpl_eng) October 21, 2026 Polish leaders have previously warned that the honouring of the UPA and figures associated with it would harm Ukraine’s chances of joining the European Union. Poland, like all other member states, can veto accession. However, there have also been recent signs of progress on issues of historical memory. Last year, in a diplomatic breakthrough, Ukraine lifted a ban on exhuming the remains of Volhynia massacre victims on its territory. But this year, President Volodymyr Zelensky triggered a diplomatic crisis when he approved the naming of a Ukrainian military unit after the “heroes of the UPA”. Since then, tensions have calmed, with Zelensky setting out a five-point plan that includes approving more exhumations. This month, the head of the IPN and its Ukrainian counterpart held their first meeting since 2018. World.title: Parliament approves liberalisation of Poland’s abortion laws
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. The government’s majority in parliament has approved two bills that would liberalise Poland’s strict abortion laws. One would reverse the 2020 constitutional court ruling introducing a near-total ban on abortion; the other would decriminalise providing help to women in obtaining unlawful abortions. However, it appears likely that both measures will be vetoed by President Karol Nawrocki, who is aligned with the right-wing opposition. His chief of staff reiterated on Tuesday that Nawrocki “supports the protection of life from conception to natural death”. Mamy to! Sejm przyjął dwa projekty: dekryminalizujący pomocnictwo w aborcji i przywracający aborcyjny kompromis. To niezbędne minimum i pierwszy krok. Jesteśmy to winni kobietom. pic.twitter.com/1yLyfuFCQC — Aleksandra LEO (@AleksandraLeo) October 20, 2026 When Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s ruling coalition, which ranges from left to centre right, took power in December 2023 from the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government, it pledged to soften abortion laws. However, since then, it has failed to do so, largely due to disputes between more conservative and liberal elements within the coalition. But now, a year ahead of parliamentary elections, that has changed, with the more powerful lower-house Sejm pushing through two abortion bills on Tuesday. One would once again allow abortions to be carried out in cases where a severe foetal abnormality is diagnosed. That would reverse a ruling by the Constitutional Tribunal (TK) in 2020 outlawing such abortions, which the TK found contravened various constitutional principles, including the right to life. That judgement, which went into force in January 2021, means that abortion is currently only allowed in two cases: when a pregnancy results from a crime (such as rape or incest) or when it threatens the mother’s life or health. In Europe, only Malta has a stricter abortion law. The ruling was issued when the TK was stacked with PiS-appointed judges – including three who had been illegitimately appointed – and regarded as being under the control of the then-ruling party. It prompted the largest protests Poland has witnessed since the communist era. In the Sejm vote on Tuesday, 233 MPs were in favour of the new bill, with 203 opposed. Support came from parties in Tusk’s coalition, as well as the small left-wing Together (Razem). Tusk’s centrist Civic Coalition (KO) and The Left (Lewica), one of its coalition partners, have previously expressed support for an even greater liberalisation of the law, allowing abortion on demand up to the 12th week of pregnancy. However, all of their MPs voted in favour of the compromise option on the table. Meanwhile, five MPs from the centre-right Polish People’s Party (PSL), the most conservative element of the coalition, joined with the right-wing and far-right opposition in voting against the bill. In a separate vote, the Sejm also approved a bill that would decriminalise the act of helping a woman obtain an unlawful abortion. Currently, that is an offence that carries a prison sentence of up to three years. A previous attempt to pass such a bill was defeated in 2024, after most PSL MPs joined with the opposition to block it. That prompted Tusk to declare that abortion reform would be impossible during the current parliamentary term. However, on Tuesday, 217 MPs voted in favour and 213 against, meaning the bill was approved. A total of 27 MPs failed to attend the vote, including 10 from PiS, among them party leader Jarosław Kaczyński. If they had participated, the bill would likely have been rejected. All MPs from KO, The Left and Razem voted in favour of the bill, as did almost all from the centrist Poland 2050. However, 14 PSL MPs joined with the opposition in voting against it, including PSL’s leader, deputy prime minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz. Both the bills approved by the Sejm now pass to the upper-house Senate, which can propose amendments but not block the passage of legislation. Tusk’s coalition has an even larger majority in the Senate than the Sejm. Once final versions of the bills are approved by parliament, they pass to the president, who can sign them into law, veto them, or ask the TK to assess whether they comply with the constitution. Given that Nawrocki is aligned with the right-wing opposition, has vetoed a record number of government bills, and has declared his opposition to abortion, it appears very unlikely that he will sign either bill into law. President Nawrocki joined thousands of people on the National March of Life, Poland’s largest annual anti-abortion event, which is held under the patronage of the Catholic church https://t.co/8BQEVUoMZn — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) April 20, 2026 Speaking to broadcaster Polsat on Tuesday evening after the Sejm votes, the president’s chief of staff, Zbigniew Bogucki, said that Nawrocki would wait to see what the legislation looked like by the time it reached him. However, Bogucki noted that, “during his campaign, the president said he supported the protection of life from conception to natural death”. Bogucki also pointed to the fact that the TK, even before PiS was in power, had been “very clear” on “protection of life”. He also suggested that abortion was now suddenly back on the table because Tusk wants to “rehash ideological issues in order to cover up his incompetence in matters he should actually be dealing with”. .@BoguckiZbigniew o stanowisku prezydenta ws. aborcji ⬇️ 🗨️ Pan prezydent w tej kampanii mówił, że jest za ochroną życia od poczęcia do naturalnej śmierci@GoscWydarzen 🎙️ @mtejchmanhttps://t.co/ZJ4gKAPywM — PolsatNews.pl (@PolsatNewsPL) October 20, 2026 A further complication is the fact that the TK is currently in crisis. The government does not recognise any of its rulings (including the 2020 abortion ruling) due to the continued presence of judges illegitimately appointed under PiS. Meanwhile, Nawrocki and the court’s chief justice, Bogdan Święczkowski, have refused to accept five new TK judges appointed by the Sejm this year. Opinion polling has consistently shown that a majority of Poles want to liberalise the abortion law. World.title: Polish leaders condemn Hegseth’s “scandalous” remarks downplaying role of US allies in Afghanistan

Leading figures from Poland’s ruling coalition have hit back at US Secretary of Defence Pete Hegseth over his recent remarks downplaying the contribution of America’s allies during the war in Afghanistan. The speaker of parliament, Włodzimierz Czarzasty, called the comments “scandalous”, while Prime Minister Donald Tusk read out a message sent to him by a Polish army medic who was serving in Afghanistan when the last of 44 Polish soldiers who died there was declared dead. 💬 Premier @donaldtusk ⤵️ Chciałbym, żeby te słowa dotarły do naszych sojuszników, żeby już nigdy więcej nikt nie lekceważył wysiłku naszych żołnierzy. pic.twitter.com/gGJkh4Gnft — Kancelaria Premiera (@PremierRP) October 20, 2026 The controversy stemmed from a speech the US defence secretary gave to US military cadets in Tennessee on Saturday. Hegseth referred to his time serving as a US Army officer in Afghanistan, where he recalled that the International Security Assistance Force (ISAF) headquarters had flags from over 50 countries. “Except,” Hegseth said, “there were maybe five [countries] that contributed. It was actually closer to one or two that actually, by the end, were involved in kinetic operations. In fact, the patch ‘ISAF’ – we joked that it meant ‘I Saw Americans Fighting.'” The comments earned quick reproach from Polish foreign minister Radosław Sikorski, who aimed a message at Hegseth on social media, saying: “Tell that to the families of 44 Polish soldiers who died securing the tough Ghazni province.” Tell that, Mr @SecWar, to the families of 44 Polish soldiers who died securing the tough Ghazni province. https://t.co/vm4TM0sMJO — Radosław Sikorski 🇵🇱🇪🇺 (@sikorskiradek) October 18, 2026 On Tuesday, the remarks earned even stronger reproach from Czarzasty, who is the speaker of the Sejm, the more powerful lower house of parliament, and the leader of The Left (Lewica), one of the groups that forms Poland’s ruling coalition. At a press conference, Czarzasty said that Hegseth’s “scandalous” comments are “harmful to the families of Polish soldiers and to Polish national pride”. He also criticised President Karol Nawrocki – an opponent of the government and conservative ally of Donald Trump – for not condemning Hegseth’s remarks. It is “an insult to Polish soldiers” that Nawrocki, who serves as commander-in-chief, “is unable to stand up for their dignity and the dignity of those who died”, declared Czarzasty. To skandaliczne, że prezydent Polski boi się potępić polityków amerykańskich za brak szacunku do polskich żołnierzy, którzy zginęli w Afganistanie. pic.twitter.com/uyv54yDvrI — Włodzimierz Czarzasty 📚📖 (@wlodekczarzasty) October 20, 2026 Later on Tuesday, Tusk read out to his cabinet a text message he said he had received from a former military medic, whom he did not name. “Please stand up for soldiers, I beg you,” wrote the medic. “During my tour in Afghanistan, we confirmed the death of the last Polish casualty, a platoon sergeant whose wife was pregnant in Poland at the time.” “I received a medal from the Americans for helping them, for treating Americans. I didn’t have to do that. We treated them with our own Polish medicines,” they added. Tusk then added his own remarks, stating: “I would like these words to reach our allies. So that no one will ever again downplay the efforts of our soldiers. Wherever our allies, including our closest ally, the Americans, have needed our participation, Polish soldiers stood shoulder to shoulder with them.” Tusk also referenced Nawrocki’s silence on the matter. “Frankly, I was also counting on the president speaking out on this matter. But it seems I miscalculated.” Tusk is the first European head of government to directly criticise Hegseth’s remarks, although a spokesperson for British Prime Minister Andy Burnham did say on Monday that it was “wrong to diminish the role” of British personnel, 457 of whom died in Afghanistan. Of the 3,621 coalition deaths during the war in Afghanistan, around two thirds were Americans (2,461). The rest came from 31 different countries, with Poland’s 44 fatalities the seventh most of any nation. Hegseth’s remarks are not the first time that the Trump administration has caused anger in Poland by downplaying allies’ role in Afghanistan. In January, Trump himself suggested that other countries had “stayed a little back, a little off the front lines”. That prompted General Roman Polko, who commanded Poland’s GROM special forces unit in Iraq and Afghanistan, to call the US president “a coward who has never been on the front lines”. The former commander of Poland's special forces in Iraq and Afghanistan has condemned Donald Trump for questioning the contribution of America's allies "This is the cynicism of a coward who hasn’t been on the front lines himself," said General @PolkoRoman https://t.co/kElkAO5qX4 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) January 23, 2026 The Polish government has also clashed with the US on other issues. In January, Tusk joined other European leaders in calling for Greenland’s sovereignty to be respected, following Trump’s calls for the island to be brought under US control. The following month, Tusk declared that Poland would not be a “vassal” of the US and suggested that Nawrocki wanted Poland to be too subservient to Washington. Czarzasty has twice this year clashed with the US ambassador over critical remarks he made towards Trump. However, at the same time, the Polish government has sought to maintain positive relations with Washington, given the United States’ role as Poland’s most important security partner. In June, Poland formally requested that the US establish a new permanent military base on its territory. Hegseth himself has praised Poland, calling it a “model ally” last year. The US State Department this month also announced that it was pushing for Poland to be allowed to join the G20 “as soon as possible”, pointing to its “growing leadership position in the international arena”. World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! We cannot do what we do without your support. A member of Poland’s military reserve force has been detained for alleged espionage. On Monday afternoon, following media reports of the arrest, a spokesman for the military police confirmed that they had detained a 31-year-old man of Polish and Ukrainian citizenship, who holds the rank of senior private reserve. The suspect, who had at the time been undertaking a course at the Military Medical Academy (WAM) in Łódź, is being held on suspicion of declaring readiness to act for the benefit of a foreign intelligence service against Poland. That crime is punishable by up to eight years in prison. W dniu 16 października 2026 r. żołnierze z Oddziału Żandarmerii Wojskowej w Łodzi, zgodnie z postanowieniem Prokuratora Działu do Spraw Wojskowych Prokuratury Rejonowej Łódź-Polesie w Łodzi, dokonali zatrzymania mężczyzny w wieku 31 lat, obywatelstwa polskiego i ukraińskiego, w… pic.twitter.com/MLpqzfT4iO — Żandarmeria Wojskowa (@Zandarmeria) October 19, 2026 The Polish authorities have not revealed which foreign intelligence service the suspect – who has been placed in detention for three months – is believed to be associated with. Speaking later to reporters, deputy defence minister Cezary Tomczyk said that the man had “clearly shown himself to be someone who is conducting reconnaissance of certain types of military installations belonging to the Polish armed forces”. He also revealed that the suspect had recently obtained Polish citizenship. While the authorities have not released further information, Rzeczpospolita, a leading newspaper, reported earlier on Monday that the suspect, whom it named as Vasiliy, had been found in possession of several different phones, documents, and a large amount of money and gold. Poland has recently seen a number of high-profile cases of individuals charged – and in some cases convicted – of spying on behalf of Russia and Belarus. Poland’s security services recently revealed that the number of espionage cases they launched last year was more than double the figure for 2024. Over those two years combined, there were more investigations than in the previous three decades. This month, a former Polish soldier was sentenced to five and a half years for spying on behalf of Russia. The tasks assigned to him included reconnaissance of Rzeszów-Jasionka airport as part of a possible plan to assassinate Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky while he travelled through Poland. A Polish man has been sentenced to five and a half years in prison for spying on behalf of Russia. He was tasked with reconnaissance of Rzeszów-Jasionka airport as part of a possible plan to assassinate @ZelenskyyUa while he travelled through Poland https://t.co/WCmhyHG1Kp — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 8, 2026 In July, a Russian married couple who had been studying in Poland were jailed for spying on behalf of Moscow and involvement in a plot to send a parcel bomb. In April, prosecutors charged a soldier from Poland’s Territorial Defence Force (WOT) with seeking to spy on behalf of Russia. The following month, three Polish citizens were charged with working on behalf of Russian intelligence to spread disinformation and conduct reconnaissance of NATO troops. In December last year, a Russian national was charged with running an espionage and sabotage network in Poland on behalf of Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB). The agents he oversaw were mainly Ukrainians and Belarusians, as have been many others convicted of conducting Russian hybrid activities in Poland. Poland has detained and expelled 15 Russians and Belarusians who tried to take part in youth world karate championships that were taking place in the Polish city of Bielsko-Biała. “Eleven Belarusian citizens and four Russians entered the country on tourist visas, which was inconsistent with the declared purpose of their stay in Poland,” said border guard spokesman Szymon Mościcki. After being detained, they received orders to leave the country within eight days, which is “the shortest possible deadline”, he added, quoted by broadcaster TVP. Piętnastu obywateli Rosji i Białorusi zostało zatrzymanych przez Straż Graniczną. Przyjechali do Polski na wizach turystycznych, choć prawdopodobnie zamierzali wziąć udział w mistrzostwach świata w karate. Otrzymali decyzje nakazujące opuszczenie kraju.https://t.co/czcjQKZ2kw — tvp.info 🇵🇱 (@tvp_info) October 19, 2026 The announcement came one day after the karate world championships in the cadet, junior and U-21 categories had finished in Bielsko-Biała. In early October, Russia’s TASS news agency had reported that some of the country’s junior karatekas, as competitors are known, had planned to compete in the tournament. The World Karate Federation (WKF) allows Russian and Belarusian athletes to compete under a neutral banner. However, Poland has a strict policy of not allowing Russian and Belarusian athletes to compete in tournaments on its territory. This year, it banned them from taking part in a World Cup ski jumping event. It was also removed as host of two European junior weightlifting championships for banning Russian and Belarusian athletes. On 15 October, the day after the championships in Bielsko-Biała had started, TASS reported that none of the Russian athletes had been allowed to register by the Polish organisers. Paweł Połtorzecki, president of the Polish Karate Union (PUK), confirmed that, despite PUK warning them not to come, Russian and Belarusian athletes had sought to take part, prompting the organisers to ask the border guard to conduct an inspection. “The first sign was the appearance of a Russian at the refereeing course,” he revealed, quoted by TVP. “That’s when the first detention occurred.” Gazeta Wyborcza, a leading Polish daily, reports that the Russian karatekas had obtained tourist visas from other countries in the European Schengen area, of which Poland is part. Poland itself does not issue tourist visas to Russians. Meanwhile, Poland has become the primary target in Europe for sabotage operations carried out by operatives working on behalf of Russia, including arson attacks and an attempt to derail a train. Russia has also repeatedly violated Polish airspace with drones, missiles and, most recently, a helicopter. In response to Russia’s aggressive actions, Poland has successively shut down all Russian consulates on its territory. Moscow responded by likewise closing all Polish consulates that it previously hosted. In January, Russia warned its citizens against travelling to Poland due to “Russophobia”. World.title: Prague’s Indian Community to Celebrate Navratri With Music and Dance
World.content:
The Indian community in Prague will gather for an evening of traditional music, dancing and food on Saturday, October 24, as Navratri 2026 returns to Top Hotel Prague.

Organized by Bharatiya Gujarati Samaj, the event will celebrate the cultural traditions of Gujarat, a state in western India known for its distinctive music, colourful clothing and energetic folk dances.

The programme will start at 5 pm and is open to people interested in Indian culture and traditions.



The celebration will feature Garba and Dandiya Raas, two traditional dances closely associated with Navratri festivities in Gujarat.

Visitors will also have an opportunity to enjoy Indian food, see traditional clothing and learn more about Gujarati culture.

Garba will be one of the main attractions of the event. The traditional Gujarati folk dance is performed in circles, with participants moving rhythmically to music and following a series of coordinated steps. The dance is closely associated with Navratri, a Hindu festival celebrated over nine nights in honour of the goddess Durga and the feminine divine.

Dandiya Raas is another traditional dance associated with the festival. Participants dance in pairs or groups while striking decorated wooden sticks together in time with the music. The movements, rhythms and colourful outfits make it one of the most recognisable features of Gujarati Navratri celebrations.

Beyond the dancing, the event will offer visitors an opportunity to explore different aspects of Gujarati culture, including traditional clothing and Indian food.

Traditional clothing is also an important part of the festivities. Women often wear colourful chaniya cholis, while men may dress in traditional kediyu outfits. Embroidery, decorative patterns and bright colours are common features of clothing worn for Garba and Dandiya Raas.

Tickets and further information are available on the Bharatiya Gujarati Samaj website.

World.title: Czech Constitutional Court Rules Sex Workers Must Pay Taxes
World.content:
The Czech Constitutional Court has ruled that income from voluntary sex work is subject to taxation, placing it on the same footing as earnings from other self-employed professions.

The decision clarifies that collecting taxes from sex workers does not amount to state approval of the activity.

The case concerned a woman who was ordered to pay more than CZK 900,000 in back taxes for income earned from paid sexual services in 2013 and 2014.



She challenged the assessment in court, but lower courts upheld the decision of the Czech Financial Administration. She subsequently appealed to the Constitutional Court, Novinky reported.

The woman argued that taxing prostitution effectively turned the state into a pimp, pointing to the distinction in Czech law between providing sexual services voluntarily for payment and acting as an intermediary in such activities.

While the former is not a criminal offense, procuring or facilitating prostitution in certain circumstances can be punishable under the Criminal Code.

The Constitutional Court rejected her argument, ruling that taxation serves a different purpose. According to the judges, the state is not profiting from another person’s labor but ensuring that taxpayers contribute fairly to public finances.

The court added that taxation should not be interpreted as moral approval of sex work or as official state recognition of the activity.

Under the ruling, income from prostitution falls into the category of earnings from independent professions.

The same broad category includes income earned by entertainers, coaches, athletes and models, as well as people who publish sexually explicit material on subscription platforms such as OnlyFans.

The court warned that exempting income from sex work would undermine the fair distribution of the tax burden and discriminate against other taxpayers.

The ruling does not legalize every activity associated with prostitution. Instead, it establishes that income earned through voluntary sex work must be declared and taxed under the same general principles that apply to other forms of self-employment.

World.title: Prague’s First Film Screening Took Place 130 Years Ago
World.content:
Prague’s first public film screening took place on October 18, 1896, at the Hotel U Černého koně on Na Příkopě Street.

Organized by the French branch of Thomas Edison’s company, the presentation introduced audiences to moving pictures, a technology that would soon transform entertainment across Bohemia.

The screening marked another milestone in a period of rapid technological change that had begun five years earlier.

In 1891, Prague hosted the Jubilee Provincial Exhibition, celebrating a century of industrial progress. The event helped reshape the city, leaving behind landmarks including the Industrial Palace, Petřín Lookout Tower and mirror maze.



The Hotel That Brought New Technology to Prague

The Hotel U Černého koně, or At the Black Horse, was among Prague’s most luxurious establishments in the late 19th century. Its owners, brothers Jindřich and Karel Cífka, were quick to recognize the commercial potential of new inventions.

Later in 1896, the hotel introduced another technological novelty, the X-ray machine. The device had been developed by German physicist Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen, who announced his discovery in December 1895.

Initially presented as an attraction, the machine soon acquired medical significance. In January 1897, physician Rudolf Jedlička used it to examine a patient suspected of having swallowed a foreign object. The image revealed a nail lodged in the man’s stomach.

Edison and the Lumière Brothers Compete for Audiences

The first film screening was organized by Adolf Oppenheimer, an optician and mechanic who operated a cinematograph supplied by Edison’s French company.

According to a contemporary invitation reproduced by Czech Radio, screenings took place daily, beginning at 4 p.m. and continuing hourly until 8 p.m. Additional shows were held on Sundays and public holidays. Admission cost 40 kreutzers, with discounts for schools.

Competition arrived almost immediately. Just five days after the Edison presentation, the Lumière brothers’ cinematograph was shown at the Hotel U Saského dvora on Hybernská Street.

Both companies promoted their technology as the genuine article. Their s emphasized the quality of their moving pictures and their international reputations, reflecting the intense competition surrounding the new medium.

Czech filmmakers soon began producing their own material. In June 1898, Národní listy reported on a cinematograph pavilion at the Prague Exhibition Grounds where two young architects presented original films, including scenes from everyday life in Prague.

Viktor Ponrepo Opens a Permanent Cinema

For several years, traveling cinematographs brought films to audiences around the country. A permanent venue eventually followed.

In September 1907, Dismas Šlambor, better known as Viktor Ponrepo, opened what is widely regarded as the first permanent cinema in the Czech lands. It was located in the U Modré štiky building on Karlova Street.

Originally a magician and illusionist, Ponrepo had become interested in image-recording technology after encountering Edison’s phonograph at the 1891 exhibition. He later toured the country with a traveling cinema before establishing his Prague venue.

Ponrepo became famous for greeting audiences with a bow before every screening. He eventually filmed the gesture and projected it before his shows, turning it into his personal signature.

By then, moving pictures had evolved from a technological curiosity into a new form of mass entertainment, with Prague among the cities embracing the change.

World.title: Meet Paulo Dias, the Expat Behind Prague’s Pintz Beer App
World.content:
Finding a good beer in Prague is rarely a difficult task. Finding the right pub, knowing what a pint costs and deciding where to go next is a different question.

For Paulo Dias, that challenge became the idea behind Pintz, a web app built to help people navigate Prague’s rich beer scene.

Originally from Portugal, Paulo has spent almost 15 years living abroad, moving between Slovakia and the UK before eventually taking a job in the Czech Republic.



He first arrived in the Czech Republic in 2021, spending several months in Opava before moving to Prague in February 2022. Even after the move, he was cautious about settling in. “When I moved to Prague, I wasn’t buying many things for my apartment, because if I moved again, I’d have to pack everything,” Paulo recalls.

That changed once his new job became more stable. By the end of the year, he was already thinking about staying.

I think the quality of life in Prague is quite amazing. It’s one of the best, if not the best, of the cities I know. I feel good here, I feel at home. That’s why I decided to stay.”

Prague’s pub culture

Prague’s pub culture became one of the ways Paulo built a social life after moving to the city. He started with local pubs in Žižkov.

“I started to make friends there, and then I thought it was a good opportunity for me to become more social.”

What struck him was how different the culture was from Portugal. He describes drinking there as more centered around wine, home gatherings, watching football with friends or celebrating birthdays, rather than regularly meeting at pubs during the week.

“I know people who meet every Monday. It’s impossible in Portugal, this mindset. People just stay at home or go for a coffee after dinner. There’s no culture like going to a pub.”

In Prague, meeting for a beer could instead become part of an ordinary weekday. That was something Paulo gradually came to appreciate about his new home.

“I don’t need to wait for the weekend to have my social life active.”

From sneaker prices to Pintz

The idea for Pintz grew out of a sneaker-price platform “The Real Sneaker Index” Paulo had been working on in his spare time. The two projects are quite different, but the first gave him a way of thinking about how prices could be collected and compared.

The connection to beer came almost as an afterthought. Paulo was already spending time in Prague’s pubs, and the idea eventually brought his side project closer to something he was experiencing himself.

“I was thinking, maybe I could apply the same idea to something more connected to everyday life. And then I thought, why not use it to track beer prices?”

What started as a price tracker gradually expanded into a way of exploring pubs. Users can now add information about individual places, from terraces and beer gardens to the beers they serve, while ratings give people a way to share their own experiences. “It’s not only about finding the cheapest beer. It started that way, but it’s really about quality.”

Pintz is now present in the US, Mexico, Atlantic Islands and across many countries in Europe.

Building it alone with AI

Paulo has been building Pintz alongside his Lead AI Platforms job, developing the platform himself with the help of AI. He works on it in the evenings, at weekends and whenever he can find the time.

“I’m not a coder, I’m not a developer, but I know what I want to do.”

AI has allowed him to take those ideas further without having to build every part of the platform from scratch himself. He sets up processes, monitors how they work and keeps adding and improving features as the project develops.

The speed at which he can turn an idea into something functional has been one of the biggest surprises for him.

“What impressed me the most is the capability of building anything with AI, especially digital products.”

What’s next for Pintz?

For now, his focus is on getting more people to use Pintz and bringing more pubs, breweries and beer brands onto the platform. He is also looking at sponsorships and other ways of turning the project into a sustainable business.

At the same time, he is conscious of how easily monetisation could get in the way of the experience he is trying to create. He does not want users to feel like they are constantly being sold something while using the app.

“I don’t want this to become an advertising app that people are annoyed to use.”

World.title: Prague Light Park at Žluté Lázně Takes Visitors Back to the 14th Century
World.content:
Prague’s Žluté lázně has opened a new edition of the Story of Lights, a seasonal light park inspired by the city’s medieval history.

Running from October 16, 2026, to January 31, 2027, the event features illuminated sculptures, interactive installations and, from November, evening boat trips on the Vltava River.



The park takes visitors back to 14th-century Prague during the reign of Charles IV, the Bohemian king and Holy Roman Emperor whose rule helped shape the city’s development.

Thousands of LED lights illuminate the grounds after dark, forming a route through displays inspired by the architecture, symbols and history of medieval Prague.

Among the installations are illuminated representations of Charles Bridge, Gothic towers, church arches, royal crowns and coronation regalia. The displays reinterpret historical motifs using modern lighting technology.

Some installations are interactive, with the organizers targeting families with children as well as adults looking for an evening activity outdoors.

The historical theme focuses on a period when Prague underwent major urban development.

Charles IV initiated the construction of Charles Bridge, founded the New Town in 1348 and helped establish Prague as an important political, cultural and religious centre in medieval Europe.

From November 6, visitors will also be able to combine their visit with an illuminated boat trip along the Vltava. The evening cruises are scheduled for Fridays, Saturdays, Sundays and public holidays.

World.title: Prague Expands Tram Network With Five Projects Underway
World.content:
Prague is expanding its tram network, with five projects now under construction across the capital.

Two new projects began in October 2026, extending the network from Malovanka to Strahov and from Libuš to Nové Dvory.

Work is also progressing on the tram line across Wenceslas Square, where the tracks have been connected between Vinohradská Street and the junction of Jindřišská and Vodičkova streets.



The projects aim to improve public transport connections to developing residential areas and strengthen links with other transport services, including the future Metro Line D.

New tram line to connect Malovanka with Strahov

Construction of the new tram line from Malovanka to Strahov began on October 5, following preparatory work. The tracks will run along Vaníčkova Street, starting at Bělohorská Street and continuing toward Strahov Stadium.

The Malovanka stop will also be modified and moved to a position before the intersection, allowing it to serve trams heading toward Strahov.

The existing Stadion Strahov stop, currently used for passengers to disembark, will be renamed Strahov.

Tram extension to Nové Dvory will complement Metro Line D

Construction of the second new line, extending the tram network from Modřany through Libuš to Nové Dvory, began on October 7, 2026.

The extension will introduce two stops, Přírodní and Nové Dvory. At Nové Dvory, the line will end in a loop using Durychova, Libušská and Chýnovská streets.

The new connection is being developed alongside plans for Metro Line D and the wider expansion of the surrounding residential area. It will provide a direct tram connection to central Prague, including the Palackého náměstí area, with a future connection toward Smíchov also planned.

The extension will change operations on tram line 17. Once the project is completed, the temporary dead-end terminus in Libuš will be removed, allowing single-ended trams to return to longer routes. A second tram line is also planned for the new tracks after Metro Line D opens.

Hodkovičky gains a new tram stop

The new Hodkovičky stop, located between Belárie and Černý kůň, is another addition to Prague’s tram infrastructure in the south of the city.

The stop is intended to improve access to public transport for residents of the growing residential developments nearby. Further housing construction is also expected in Nové Dvory, where the planned tram extension will provide additional transport capacity.

Tram tracks connected across Wenceslas Square

Work on restoring tram services across Wenceslas Square is also progressing. In early autumn, construction crews connected the tracks running from Vinohradská Street, past the National Museum, across the square and toward the junction of Jindřišská and Vodičkova streets.

The track infrastructure in this section is complete. Remaining work includes finishing the surrounding surfaces and installing overhead power lines.

Once these works are finished, the new line will restore tram services across Wenceslas Square, strengthening public transport connections in central Prague.

World.title: Prague Christmas Markets 2026 Start in November – Dates and Locations
World.content:
Prague’s Christmas markets will return in November 2026, with the first stalls opening at Náměstí Míru on November 20.

The main markets in Old Town Square and Wenceslas Square will follow on November 28, bringing traditional Czech food, handmade decorations and a program of seasonal performances to the city center.

Náměstí Republiky follows on November 25, and Tylovo náměstí opens on November 26.



The main markets at Old Town Square and Wenceslas Square begin on November 28 and continue until January 6, 2027. The other markets close on Christmas Eve, December 24.

Here are the opening dates and hours for the main locations.

– náměstí Míru — November 20 to December 24, 10 a.m. to 7 p.m.

– náměstí Republiky — November 25 to December 24, 10 a.m. to 8 p.m.

– Tylovo náměsti — November 26 to December 24, 10 a.m. to 7 p.m.

– Old Town Square — November 28 to January 6, 2027, 10 a.m. to 10 p.m.

– Wenceslas Square — November 28 to January 6, 2027, 10 a.m. to 10 p.m.

Smaller Christmas Markets Across Prague

Several markets open before the main city-center venues and offer alternatives for visitors who want to explore different neighborhoods.

Further options include the market at Anděl and Lesser Town Christmas on Kampa Island.

náměstí Jiřího z Poděbrad will host farmers’ markets during Advent, with a design market joining them every Sunday during the season. These events offer opportunities to browse locally made products and find gifts beyond the usual Christmas-market stalls.

World.title: Modeselektor to Open Spectaculare Festival at Prague’s ROXY
World.content:
Berlin electronic duo Modeselektor will open the 14th edition of Spectaculare on 3 March 2027, bringing their live show to ROXY alongside new music from their latest album, MDSLKTR

Gernot Bronsert and Sebastian Szary will perform a set combining techno, electro, hip-hop and bass music, accompanied by visual projections and lighting.

The concert comes shortly after the release of MDSLKTR, an album that revisits the sound and influences that have shaped the duo’s nearly three-decade career.



The record follows Classics Vol. 01, a project that revisited material from their early albums Hello Mom! and Happy Birthday! and drew on years of studio recordings and unfinished ideas.

With MDSLKTR, Modeselektor return to the sounds that first defined their music, drawing on Berlin rave culture, techno, electro, IDM and hip-hop while continuing to move between genres.

Since emerging from Berlin’s underground electronic scene, the duo have built an international following through their studio albums, live performances and collaborations with artists including Radiohead frontman Thom Yorke, Tommy Cash, Flohio and Blixa Bargeld.

They also formed Moderat with producer Apparat and run the independent record label Monkeytown Records.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Festival Spectaculare (@spectaculare_music)

Berlin-based multi-instrumentalist Philipp Johann Thimm will open the evening. A longtime collaborator of Apparat, Thimm has worked across electronic and acoustic music as well as audiovisual projects. His work on Apparat’s album *LP5* contributed to a Grammy-nominated project, while his solo work explores the meeting point between electronic composition and live instrumentation.

World.title: Budapest’s Buda Castle could ban Airbnb rentals completely from 2028
World.content:
Budapest’s District I council has proposed a complete ban on short-term accommodation rentals in the Buda Castle district from 2028, following a local survey in which two-thirds of respondents from the historic neighbourhood backed the measure. Stricter rules, substantial fines and new powers to temporarily close accommodation providers are also on the table.

Airbnb-style short-term rentals could disappear entirely from Budapest’s Buda Castle district from 1 January 2028 under new proposals put forward by the District I Municipality. The plans are part of a wider effort to protect the residential character of the historic area and the peace and quiet of its residents.

The municipality announced on its official Facebook page that a draft regulation had been prepared based on residents’ feedback. The proposal has now been opened for public consultation.

A survey conducted in September attracted 4,503 district residents. Of those who responded, 58.6% supported a complete ban on short-term rentals across the district, while support for the measure reached 66% among respondents living in Buda Castle itself.

What would change for Airbnb hosts in Budapest?

The proposed regulation would introduce different rules for Buda Castle and the rest of District I.

Buda Castle: Short-term accommodation rentals could be completely prohibited from 1 January 2028.

Short-term accommodation rentals could be completely prohibited from 1 January 2028. The rest of District I: Existing accommodation providers operating in apartment buildings would need the building community’s consent to continue their activities from 2028.

Existing accommodation providers operating in apartment buildings would need the building community’s consent to continue their activities from 2028. Stricter enforcement: Authorities would carry out tighter checks, with substantial fines and temporary closures possible for violations.

The plans are not yet final. The municipality is inviting residents and other interested parties to submit comments and suggestions over a 15-day consultation period. Feedback can be sent to airbnb@budavar.hu, and the local council is expected to decide on the final regulation in November.

Don’t miss this: New EU housing rules could pave the way for tighter Airbnb restrictions in Budapest

Existing rentals would have a transition period

Owners of short-term accommodation properties in Buda Castle would not necessarily have to stop operating immediately if the proposal is adopted. Under the draft rules published on the municipality’s website, accommodation providers already registered by 31 December 2026 in the protected World Heritage area could continue operating until the end of 2027.

This would give owners a one-year transition period to prepare for the proposed ban, the municipality said.

District I says the main objective is to protect Buda Castle’s role as a place to live and safeguard the long-term interests of people who call the area home.

Photo: Anadolu/İlkin Eskipehlivan

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official Telegram channel!

Fines of up to HUF 2 million and temporary closures proposed

The draft regulation would also introduce tougher penalties for accommodation providers that fail to comply with the rules.

The district clerk would be responsible for checking compliance. In the event of a violation, the authority could impose a fine and order the accommodation to close temporarily for 45 days.

The proposed fines would be charged for each inspection:

HUF 200,000 (approximately EUR 546): For private individuals and sole traders.

For private individuals and sole traders. HUF 2 million (approximately EUR 5,464): For legal entities and other organisations.

The measures are still proposals, and their final form will depend on the outcome of the public consultation and the council’s decision, expected in November.

World.title: Budapest braces for major traffic chaos on 23 October: Roads closed, metro changes and tram disruptions
World.content:
Budapest is preparing for significant traffic restrictions on 22 and 23 October as Hungary marks the 70th anniversary of the 1956 Revolution. Road closures, commemorations, torchlight marches and visiting high-level delegations will disrupt traffic across the city centre, with several public transport services running on altered routes.

Residents, commuters and visitors to Budapest should plan their journeys carefully on Thursday and Friday, as major roads and sections of the Danube embankments will close for events marking Hungary’s national holiday.

According to the Budapest Transport Centre (BKK), the restrictions will affect both motorists and public transport passengers, particularly around the city centre, the Buda embankment, Kossuth Lajos Square and Andrássy Avenue.

The BKK recommends using the metro network and trams 4 and 6 for journeys through central Budapest. Metro line M2 and tram 2 will run more frequently than usual to accommodate passengers.

Real-time updates and planned changes are available on the BKK’s official national holiday transport information page.

Thursday, 22 October: Torchlight procession to disrupt Buda traffic

The Műegyetem Embankment will be closed from approximately 8 am to 8 pm on Thursday. A commemorative ceremony and wreath-laying event will take place near the Budapest University of Technology and Economics between 2 pm and 4 pm, followed by a traditional torchlight procession starting at 4 pm.

The march will travel along the Műegyetem Embankment, Szent Gellért Square, Szent Gellért Embankment, Döbrentei Square, Várkert Embankment, Ybl Miklós Square, Lánchíd Street, Clark Ádám Square, Fő Street, Jégverem Street, Bem Embankment, Csalogány Street, Nagy Imre Square and Fő Street before reaching Bem József Square.

The procession will cause temporary disruptions to several bus and tram services, particularly between 4 pm and 6.30 pm.

Friday, 23 October: Major closures around Parliament and Heroes’ Square

Anyone planning to visit central Budapest on 22 or 23 October should allow extra time for their journey and check their route before setting off.
