World.title: British influencer living in Estonia: My first sauna was a shock
World.content:
Shauna Soitu moved to Estonia two years ago, loves the country's nature, culture and outlook on life. Although learning Estonian's special characters proved quite a headache, she is determined to master the language.

Shauna Soitu, originally from the United Kingdom, moved to Estonia two years ago. Love brought her here.

"We met on vacation in Mexico. We were staying at the same hotel and we met in the swimming pool. The odds of us meeting were so small. I'm so grateful because now I live in Estonia and I have an amazing life here," Soitu told ETV's "Ringvaade."

Estonia was not entirely unfamiliar to her. For example, she knew that companies such as Skype and Bolt originated here. She had also visited Estonia a few times before moving.

"I fell in love with, not just Tallinn, but the countryside as well. We were going on hikes in the bogs. The peacefulness and the safety; everything I felt here, I just loved it. When we decided England or Estonia, I was like, 'Let's give Estonia a try.'"

Today, Soitu's observations about Estonia and Estonians have attracted tens of thousands of followers on social media. Her decision to start making videos about life in Estonia came about by chance when she wanted to share what she had learned in an Estonian language class on TikTok.

"I'd just learned fully how to introduce myself, say where I was from. I was so proud of myself! 'Oh my God, I need to tell everyone!' I was telling all my friends at work, too, like so excited. And I said I need to record this and send it to my mom and dad, like 'I can speak Estonian.' So I recorded it and said I'm just going to post this on TikTok as well. I didn't look at my phone for a while and it had just blown up on TikTok, which surprised me. So I decided to start documenting my journey," she said.

While the English enjoy making small talk even with strangers, Soitu has found that Estonians are rather different.

"The first time I went to work in Estonia and I was trying to talk to someone in the kitchen, they were so confused. They were like, 'Why is this girl talking to me? Why is she asking me what I've got for lunch? Why does she care?' I was a little taken back by that, but I'm used to it now. Now, I'm a little more reserved and protective of my time and energy, which I think is good," she said. "Also, I love being outdoors and I love the sauna. So I'd say I've been Estonianized."

Soitu still vividly remembers her first sauna experience. She was visiting the parents of her husband, Kert, in Rapla at the time. What stood out most was the traditional practice of vihtlemine or striking the skin with a bundle of leafy branches.

"I was like, 'what the hell is going on?!' I was blown away and I'd never had a sauna like it. But it was a cool experience," she said with a laugh.

A couple of months ago, Shauna and Kert held a big wedding celebration. That, too, came with plenty of surprises for Shauna and the other English guests. One particularly memorable experience was the traditional Estonian custom of "bride kidnapping," in which the groom must complete challenges to win back his bride.

"My husband was challenged to do some things. He had to change a doll's diaper and sing a song to get me back. The English [guests ] were just like, what is going on. It was crazy! But they loved it. I'm just getting such good feedback from everyone that came to Tallinn. They want to come back, they want to see more of Estonia. And they said it was the best wedding ever!"

There are still some things Soitu has not quite gotten used to, however, such as how much pork Estonians eat. She has yet to develop a taste for blood sausage, either.

"Maybe this year I will like it. I don't know? Apparently, it grows on you over time," Soitu said with a smile.

At home, Shauna and Kert speak a mixture of Estonian and English. Shauna believes it is important to learn at least some basic Estonian as a sign of respect.

"I want to have children and raise them here. They're going to speak Estonian. How silly that the mom doesn't understand her children. I'm definitely going to be putting full effort into being fluent in Estonian."

World.title: Education ministry to temporarily restrict access to Moodle platform
World.content:
The Ministry of Education and Research is implementing additional security measures starting Thursday in response to critical software vulnerabilities to ensure the security of the Moodle learning platform and the data processed within it.

The Moodle learning platform will be temporarily shut down starting Thursday until the necessary security updates have been installed and their effectiveness verified.

The ministry emphasized that ensuring the security of the learning platform and the data it contains is its top priority.

"The temporary shutdown of Moodle is a preventive measure aimed at avoiding potential data leaks, damage to the learning platform and resulting prolonged disruptions," the Ministry of Education and Research added.

The ministry said it understands that the temporary shutdown may cause inconvenience to users and is working with technical partners to implement the necessary security updates as quickly as possible.

Normal operations will resume once the necessary security updates have been installed and their effectiveness verified. A separate announcement will be made when Moodle reopens.

On Wednesday, the National Archives also announced that several of its online services had been temporarily shut down or restricted to users with Estonian IP addresses as a precautionary measure.

"Critical security vulnerabilities have been discovered in the widely used PHP web software. We are installing security patches and will restore services as soon as possible."

Moodle is an open-source Learning Management System (LMS) designed to create customizable online classrooms where educators can organize course content, host interactive assignments, run tests, and facilitate discussions. In Estonia's digital education ecosystem, Moodle serves as a core e-learning platform used extensively across vocational schools, general education institutions, and major universities such as the University of Tartu and TalTech.

World.title: Shorter-range HIMARS missiles arrive in Estonia
World.content:
Defense Minister Martin Herem confirmed to ERR that missiles with a range of 70 kilometers for the HIMARS rocket artillery system have arrived in Estonia.

Estonia has been waiting for some time for U.S.-supplied ammunition for its HIMARS multiple launch rocket systems.

Estonia ordered both ATACMS missiles with a range of up to 300 kilometers and GMLRS rockets with a range of approximately 70 kilometers.

However, the United States suspended ammunition deliveries in the spring due to the war in Iraq.

While deliveries of long-range ammunition remain on hold, the 70-kilometer-range rockets have arrived, Herem told Vikerraadio.

"Everything that was originally included in our contract is now in Estonia. The launchers for the Korean system (K239 Chunmoo) will arrive next year, while the ammunition will hopefully arrive next year as well, but more likely in early 2028," Herem said.

"In addition, we are expecting various types of ammunition both this year and next year with ranges well beyond 50 kilometers, approaching 100 kilometers. These include artillery ammunition as well as loitering munitions, which are large, winged drones," the defense minister added.

The Estonian Defense Forces (EDF) has six HIMARS (M142 High Mobility Artillery Rocket System) multiple launch rocket systems. In April, the Estonian Center for Defense Investments and U.S. defense contractor Lockheed Martin signed a contract to purchase three additional HIMARS launchers, which are expected to arrive in Estonia in 2027.

A HIMARS interchangeable rocket pod can carry either six GMLRS rockets with a range of 15 to 92 kilometers, two guided PrSM (Precision Strike Missile) missiles with a range of 60 to 499 kilometers or one guided ATACMS (Army Tactical Missile System) missile with a range of up to 300 kilometers.

World.title: Prime minister: We'll definitely work better with the Social Democrats under Vseviov
World.content:
Prime Minister and Reform Party Chairman Kristen Michal said his party would certainly have better cooperation with the Social Democratic Party if it were led by Jonatan Vseviov.

Jonatan Vseviov, the longtime secretary general of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and a security expert who has announced he is joining the Social Democrats, criticized the current government and Prime Minister Kristen Michal's leadership at a press conference Thursday, saying they lacked sharpness of mind, intellectual breadth and the courage to assert themselves.

Michal responded to Vseviov's criticism in broader terms.

"I think it's very good that Jonatan has entered politics. When I think about people who want to have a say and contribute, it's very good that they enter politics. It would be rather peculiar if people just wrote poetry and kept it in a drawer — not that there's anything wrong with that. Writing poetry and keeping it in a drawer is fine, too. But if you actually want to engage in politics, you have to do it in politics. So I certainly welcome Jonatan's arrival," Michal said at the government's press conference.

"And I'll add something on a personal note. I understand that he may have been given a few Social Democratic talking points. I think we'll certainly have better cooperation with the Social Democrats led by Jonatan Vseviov. I really do. So I'm genuinely pleased. I understand it might not seem logical for me to be happy about a political rival, but I actually am," Michal said.

SDE head Lauri Läänemets said at the Social Democratic Party's press conference that he would remain the party's leader. Michal's reference to the Social Democrats being led by Vseviov can therefore be interpreted as a jab at the party's current chairman.

"Second, I want to thank him for his work on foreign policy. We've done a great many things together. Some really impressive things. We've shared all the highs and lows of Estonian foreign policy and I want to thank him for that. We've carried that responsibility together," he added.

"And third, I understand that there's one recurring point in the Social Democrats' talking points, which I also noticed during Monday's confidence vote. They say Estonia's economy is on the wrong track. I heard something similar from that press conference, that Estonia's economy is supposedly heading for catastrophe or something along those lines. Well, it isn't. This year, Estonia's economy is growing twice as fast as the European Union average. I think that should be written in the corner at every press conference and we should say: Friends, let's start with that. I'm not just talking about the economy in general — Estonians' incomes have increased, precisely because of what we did with income tax reform: We eliminated the tax hump created by the progressive income tax system introduced by the Social Democrats, the Center Party and Isamaa," Michal said.

Michal added that the Reform Party and the Social Democrats would not find common ground on economic issues, but said cooperation was possible on foreign and security policy.

Both Lauri Läänemets and Vseviov said Estonia needs to do more to assert itself on the international stage and in various discussions concerning security. In their view, the country's current leadership has failed to achieve this.

"After all, we've all worked on foreign policy together. Jonatan, myself, Margus [Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna — ed.] and everyone else, including the presidents. If I look at the issues that matter to us, first of all, Russian assets have been permanently frozen since the end of last year. From our perspective, that's a very good result. Previously, we had to vote on extending the freeze every three or six months. Should our voice be heard? I think it has been. When it comes to the shadow fleet, we took the lead. I even remember criticism at home and I remember going to parliament where I think it was either EKRE or the Center Party trying to argue that we shouldn't be bothering these honest ships sailing to and from Russia. Why were we harassing them? They said the whole thing was suspicious and some even claimed we were about to trigger World War III. But then [French President] Emmanuel Macron came up to me and said they were doing the same thing and they also detained a ship that we had already detained. Then the Americans came along and said, 'Good, let's get to work.' I don't know, is that good or not? I think it is. I'm personally satisfied and I think it was the right thing to do," Michal said.

"Then there are Russian fighters. This is something we're all working on, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs is working on, Jonatan has worked hard on it, Margus has worked on it, I've worked on it and I think many others have as well. The result is that European countries are seriously discussing, at the European Council summit I'm attending, how to put an end to Russians vacationing in Europe — the very same people who are killing women and children. We want to stop issuing them visas. Finland has joined us, Petteri Orpo [the Finnish prime minister — ed.] has made such a proposal and many other countries have come on board. I think the countries where Russians go on vacation are clearly moving in that direction as well," Michal said.

"I'm not sure how you would measure that. I also read an article by Lauri Läänemets, again featuring Social Democratic talking points, in which he said Kaja Kallas used to exchange messages with Macron. But here's a candid admission: I exchange messages with Macron more often than I do with Lauri Läänemets. It's actually quite funny," Michal added.

World.title: Gallery: Tallinn hosts 11 Ukrainian artists' work from international residency
World.content:
Three Tallinn locations are showing work by 11 Ukrainian photographers and visual artists, capping a recent international art residency held in Estonia, Finland and Germany.

The four-and-a-half-month "Waves of Creativity" project supported Ukrainian artists whose lives and work have been affected by Russia's war against Ukraine, including two who have spent time on the front.

Residencies took place in Saaremaa, Estonia, Joutsa, Finland and Stuttgart, Germany earlier this year.

The project's final exhibition opened in Tallinn on October 15, with displays at the Vabamu Museum of Occupations and Freedom, Okapi Gallery and the open-air Baltic Station Art Street.

The Tallinn show brings together documentary photography, experimental photo art, video and installations. While not all the works depict war directly, many explore personal experience, memory, home, everyday life, changing surroundings and people's relationships with the world around them.

Three ways to encounter the work

The three participating locations offer three different ways to encounter the work.

Okapi Gallery presents work developed during the residency in a traditional gallery setting, while a pop-up exhibition at Vabamu connects the artists' personal experiences with broader historical and social themes.

An outdoor display along the Art Street at Tallinn's Balti jaam, meanwhile, brings contemporary Ukrainian photography into public space, reaching audiences who may not typically visit galleries.

Curated by Temuri Hvingija and co-curator Andrii Mur, participating artists include Mykyta Bezus, Oxana Chorna, Iryna Klachek, Olia Koval, Herman Krieger, Ievgeniia Kupchan, Valentyn Kuzan, Oleh Pereverziev, Alina Prisich, Olesia Saienko and Elena Subach.

The exhibition runs at Okapi Gallery through November 20 and will remain on display at Baltic Station Art Street through March 30. 2027.

World.title: President's economic adviser: Politics has been emotionally draining
World.content:
In an interview with ERR, Maris Lauri reflects on the Reform Party's electoral prospects, the challenges of coalition government and the importance of avoiding costly election promises.

What led you to decide to leave politics? Was it perhaps because you didn't see much of a future for the Reform Party in the upcoming Riigikogu elections?

The president's offer was very appealing and I've been in politics for 12 years. The past few years have been somewhat emotionally exhausting. And I felt this was an opportunity to do something similar to what I'd done professionally earlier in my life, without moving too far away from politics and Estonian affairs.

It certainly wasn't because I thought I wouldn't have any prospects or opportunities if I ran in the Riigikogu elections. That was definitely not on my mind.

But what prospects do you see for the Reform Party to succeed in the upcoming Riigikogu elections?

There's always an opportunity to achieve a good result. There are still quite a few months until the elections. And as we've seen over the past decade, things can sometimes change very quickly.

We've had a very strong team and plenty of good ideas. I'm deeply convinced that Estonia needs a center-right liberal party in politics. There are plenty of voters who want that and it's simply necessary. The entire political spectrum needs to be represented — nature abhors a vacuum.

On the one hand, it's understandable that people have been disappointed and perhaps even angry about things that have happened. But things can always be changed and improved and lessons can certainly be learned.

Are you referring to the confusion over taxes or the "tax festival" as it was called at one point? Various taxes were proposed — tax increases, which were then scrapped, followed by announcements that taxes would be cut. Is that what you had in mind?

No, I'm talking about a broader range of issues. There have been various crises and these have been global crises, not just ones affecting Estonia. They've made people more sensitive and frustrated, not just in Estonia but across society in other parts of the world as well.

In situations like these, perhaps the best decisions haven't always been made or there hasn't been enough explanation of why certain decisions were taken.

It's also true that we've had governments made up of different coalitions, with partners holding opposing views. Coalition governments always involve finding compromises and quite often those compromises have reflected the positions of our partners much more than those of the Reform Party.

But the biggest party always ends up taking the blame, as unfortunately often happens in life.

So perhaps there hasn't been enough explanation of why certain decisions were made and the best choices haven't always been made or things haven't always turned out for the best in difficult circumstances.

Even now, in recent weeks, we've seen quite a lot of blame directed at the former coalition partner, the Social Democratic Party, when explaining the situation. The argument seems to be that the Social Democrats prevented the government from governing properly and making the right decisions that reflect the Reform Party's principles. You just said things should be explained better. Is that what you consider a better explanation?

I haven't heard any direct accusations against one party or another. It's perfectly natural for political parties to have different views of the world and that's why they debate these issues. They debate them in the Riigikogu, among themselves and certainly in public as well. That's simply inevitable.

We can't expect people with different political views to agree on everything.

There isn't even 100 percent agreement within any single party. People still debate, discuss and ultimately choose what they feel is the best option at that moment and what they can agree on. And if they can't reach an agreement, then that's how it is.

There are undoubtedly situations where coalition partners have such opposing positions that they simply can't reach an agreement on certain issues.

I think that's happened in every government. One partner doesn't like a particular issue or proposed solution, so no agreement can be reached and no solution emerges.

What would you consider the achievement closest to your heart from your time in politics?

There have been various achievements and it's difficult to immediately single out one or another.

One important change has certainly been marriage equality, which was already being debated more than 12 years ago when we were discussing the Registered Partnership Act. That issue also stirred a lot of strong emotions. Now that marriage equality has been adopted, the whole issue has settled down.

Another little project of mine at the Riigikogu is the Foresight Center, a think tank that provides an opportunity to discuss and analyze Estonia's development prospects.

I spearheaded the legislation and the ideas behind how such a center should operate and what requirements it should meet. So I hope the Foresight Center will continue doing valuable work for Estonian society for many years to come.

Now that you're leaving politics, what's your final piece of economic advice for the Reform Party?

I think it's important that when a party goes into an election, it focuses not on handing out lots of money or giving people gifts, but on taking steps and pursuing policies that genuinely make life better in Estonia.

People generally understand and appreciate that.

The idea that handing out money will win votes... It won't. At some point, it leads to disappointment.

It's worth relying on people who share your worldview rather than those who are simply looking for the biggest promises and the most money.

I recall that the Reform Party itself was involved in handing out money quite generously in the social welfare sector not long ago. There was the €20 increase in the single-parent benefit.

Having a right-wing worldview doesn't mean you don't spend money on social issues or that you approach them coldly.

A liberal worldview values individual freedom, but it also values responsibility — responsibility for the consequences of one's own actions, as well as responsibility toward people who are economically disadvantaged or in a worse position due to circumstances beyond their control.

So helping vulnerable people is a perfectly normal and logical part of a liberal worldview.

But what kind of economic advice do you think the president needs and how can you be useful to her?

The specific responsibilities will certainly become clearer over time and we'll sit down and discuss them in more detail.

But the president has various meetings to attend and when she's spoken about her role as being, so to speak, the mortar between the bricks, that also means she needs to be able to understand economic issues and explain them to people.

That's certainly where I can help — by helping her understand these issues, articulate her views and, more broadly, explain to the public why certain decisions are made, which policies are good and which may be less effective and what the strengths and weaknesses of different approaches are. That will certainly be part of my role.

World.title: Foreign ministry top official to run for prime minister in 2027 election
World.content:
The top official at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Jonatan Vseviov, has said he will resign on Thursday to run in next spring's national election for the opposition Social Democratic Party (SDE). He will be the party's prime ministerial candidate.

Vseviov is currently in his second term as the ministry's secretary general and is Estonia's former ambassador to Washington. Previously, he was secretary general at the Ministry of Defense.

Vseviov will submit his resignation on Thursday and will leave his post on November 1.

"I have devoted my entire life so far to protecting and developing Estonia as a diplomat and civil servant. I have had the honor of leading dedicated teams with whom we have shaped Estonia's foreign and defense policy and implemented many of the decisions that have brought us to where we are today," Vseviov said.

"Today, however, I see that protecting Estonia and moving it forward requires more than what I can do as a civil servant. That is why I have decided to leave the civil service, join the Social Democrats and run in the upcoming elections," he said.

SDE Chairman Lauri Läänemets said Estonia's security and its position in the international arena require strong leadership.

Jonatan Vseviov Source: Siim Lõvi / ERR

"Jonatan Vseviov knows Estonia's security and foreign policy inside out and has extensive international experience. He has shaped Estonia's defense policy, led the Ministry of Defense, represented Estonia as ambassador in Washington and headed the Ministry of Foreign Affairs," Läänemets said.

Vseviov took office as secretary general of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs in February 2021. Before that, he had served as Estonia's ambassador to the United States since August 2018.

From 2008 to 2018, Vseviov worked at the Ministry of Defense, eventually becoming its secretary general.

Before being appointed secretary general in January 2016, Vseviov served as deputy secretary general for defense planning, acting deputy secretary general for defense policy and director of the policy planning department.

Vseviov graduated from the University of Tartu with a degree in political science and earned a master's degree with honors in security studies from Georgetown University.

From 1999 to 2005, Vseviov was a member of the Reform Party.

Vseviov to run for prime minister

Läänemets said the party reached an agreement with Vseviov in the summer. The deal included Vseviov becoming the SDE's candidate for prime minister. At the time, the media was linking the secretary general to a possible presidential bid.

Läänemets said at a press conference on Thursday morning that he will propose at a board meeting on November 1 that Vseviov stand as the party's prime ministerial candidate.

Läänemets told ERR the process began around a year ago, when he started thinking about how the party could achieve the best possible result in the 2027 Riigikogu elections.

Asked whether the agreement also included the position of candidate for prime minister, Läänemets said it did.

Jonatan Vseviov and Lauri Läänemets at the press conference. Source: Siim Lõvi / ERR

"The idea didn't start with me saying, 'Come into politics.' As secretary general, he attended government meetings when I was a minister, and you could see common ground developing from there. Ultimately, it was a process of growing closer on both sides."

Läänemets added that security determines a great deal in Estonia today and that, given Vseviov's experience and knowledge, he would make a very good next prime minister of Estonia.

"We came to the conclusion that we cannot move forward the way [Reform Prime Minister Kristen] Michal is doing things now. Or the way [Isamaa Chairman Urmas] Reinsalu would do them. And I'm not even going to talk about [Center's Mihhail] Kõlvart. Can anyone imagine Kõlvart negotiating with Russia on behalf of Ukraine?" the chairman said.

Vseviov said: "I will now first seek a mandate from the Social Democratic Party — specifically from the Social Democratic Party, because I see in this team the potential to be a responsible and forward-looking force at Estonia's helm. And if the party grants me that mandate, I will seek a mandate from the Estonian people."

Läänemets said he will continue as leader of the party and will also run in the elections.

'We are capable of more and deserve better'

Both men said Estonia must be able to assert itself more on the international stage and participate in various discussions concerning security.

"We must understand that the surest guarantee of our freedom is that it is also valuable to other like-minded countries. Our freedom must be valuable to others, and then others will value our freedom. For our freedom to be valuable to others, we need courage, sharpness of mind, intellectual reach and political reach as well, to bring Estonia back into Europe's political core. In doing so, we must understand that those who remain silent go unnoticed, so we must not remain silent. But those who rant are not listened to, so we must not rant either," Vseviov said.

"I feel that today we are desperately lacking both intellectual reach and the courage to assert ourselves," he added.

Vseviov said Estonia needs radical progress to survive, and that the Reform Party no longer offers this.

"If I believed that Estonia's current political leadership was up to the task, I would continue working as a civil servant and would not be standing here before you today. I am absolutely convinced that with the current leadership, we are incapable of sailing through this storm, and I believe that the team beside me and behind me is the team that today offers Estonia intelligent but also forward-looking policies," he said.

"Some want to tell us that we should be satisfied that the economy is no longer shrinking and that the war has not yet reached Estonia. My message is that we are capable of more and deserve better," he said.

Läänemets was more specific in his criticism of the government, saying that it should have responded immediately to the arson attack on defense industry company Milrem's production facility and made greater efforts to secure a seat at the table in discussions concerning Ukraine's security.

"As for Ukraine and the negotiations or conditions being imposed on Ukraine, the president of Finland and the Norwegian head of state are holding meetings, the Americans are going there, and I ask whether Estonia has even tried to have a say in this at the level of its national leadership, to get involved. Certain things are beyond the reach of civil servants; there are limits to what officials can do. But when such agreements are being made in one place or another and we are not invited, does that mean we should not at least try to have a say? We could start listing examples, both close to home and farther afield, where Kristen Michal simply takes the opportunity to do nothing," Läänemets said.

Vseviov said his decision to enter politics has absolutely nothing to do with the fact that he was nominated as a presidential candidate.

Minister: Not a surprise to me

Margus Tsahkna. Source: Ken Mürk/ERR

Minister of Foreign Affairs Margus Tsahkna (Eesti 200) said Vseviov's move did not come as a surprise to him.

"For several years, I have encouraged senior civil servants to enter politics. And I am glad that some of them are doing so. Because there is a big difference between developing policies as a civil servant and literally putting your own skin in the game. Taking a mandate and assuming responsibility as a politician. So in that sense, it was not a surprise to me. Jonatan Vseviov informed me yesterday that he would be running in the elections with the Social Democrats," Tsahkna told ERR.

The minister did not want to comment on Vseviov joining the SDE, adding it is up to him to explain his ideological choices.

Tsahkna said he had not forced Vseviov to resign.

"But I didn't try to keep him either. We discussed it, and it was his own suggestion that these things are incompatible if you have decided to enter politics and are moving into the active campaign phase while simultaneously serving as secretary general. Although, yes, there is no legal requirement whatsoever for a person to leave their position. But it was his own wish, and as of November 1, Jonatan Vseviov will no longer be secretary general of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs," he said.

Tsahkna said there are no criteria for the next secretary general to come from within the ministry.

"But clearly, this person must not only understand foreign policy theoretically and be an expert, but also know how foreign and security policy is handled in Estonia and who is involved. It is certainly difficult to separate defense policy from foreign policy, because today they are very closely intertwined. So this person must be capable of working with everyone: the Riigikogu, the president, coordinating our own ministry, the Ministry of Defense, and also think tanks. And communicating with international partners. That is also extremely important," the minister said.

This story was updated to add comments from Margus Tsahkna, Jonatan Vseviov and Lauri Läänemets.

World.title: Estonia receives €32 million from EU for drone surveillance
World.content:
Estonia will be able to significantly boost its drone surveillance, as the European Union has allocated over €30 million for the cause, Minister of Interior Igor Taro (Eesti 200) said on Thursday.

"Last week, we learned that Estonia will receive €32 million from the European Union to strengthen drone surveillance along the eastern border. [This has been] a very pressing issue for us," Taro said at the government's weekly press conference on Thursday.

"To put the figures into perspective, we have allocated €4 million for other infrastructure along the eastern border next year, while drone defense will receive €32 million," Taro added, explaining the significance of the amount.

No migration crisis

The interior minister also discussed migration pressure originating from Belarus, highlighting how much it has increased this year.

"While a total of 39 people were apprehended in Estonia last year for illegally transiting through the country after crossing the Latvia-Belarus border, that number had already reached 406 as of October 20 this year," he said.

Although this places considerable pressure on the Police and Border Guard Board (PPA), there is still no reason to speak of a migration crisis, Taro assured.

Interior Minister Igor Taro (Eesti 200) speaking at Wednesday lunchtime's government press conference, following the overnight drone incursions into Estonian airspace. Source: Jürgen Randma/Government Office

"Our emergency plans are designed for entirely different magnitudes. We are nowhere near that point, and even if the emergency plan were activated, there would still be a substantial reserve of capacity, meaning that resources are available and nobody would be overwhelmed as a result," he said.

According to figures provided by Taro, nearly 50 patrols are involved in managing migration-related matters in Estonia every day.

"Our police officers have worked more than 8,000 hours of overtime, and as of today, we have returned 134 people apprehended for illegal transit to Latvia, with more awaiting return shortly," he said.

The interior minister said the number of attempted illegal border crossings at the Latvia-Belarus border is now clearly declining, having fallen from 340 prevented attempts to 122 over three weeks.

"But the threat has not disappeared, and our preparedness must remain high. More of these people may still come toward Estonia. But the main conclusion is that Estonia is managing this situation," he stressed.

World.title: Iraq, UAE discuss options to de-escalate regional tensions
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraqi Foreign Minister Fuad Hussein and UAE’s Foreign Minister Abdullah bin Zayed Al Nahyan discussed on Wednesday options to de-escalate tensions in the region.

During a phone conversation, the two sides discussed bilateral relations between the two countries, reaffirming the depth of the bonds that bind them together as well as a shared commitment to strengthening and expanding these ties, according to a statement released by the Iraqi Foreign Ministry.

The discussion addressed the outcomes of the 52nd session of the Organization of Islamic Cooperation’s (OIC) Council of Foreign Ministers, which took place in Baghdad on October 17–18. Both parties emphasized the importance of leveraging these achievements to enhance communication, foster unity, and encourage collaborative Islamic initiatives.

Along with regional developments, the discussion included approaches to foster a peaceful understanding that helps reduce tensions and improve security and stability in the region.

Hussein said on Sunday that Baghdad is attempting to arrange a meeting between Iran and the Gulf States as part of diplomatic efforts to reduce tensions and advance regional stability.

There are ongoing discussions between Iraq, the Gulf countries, and Iran aimed at bringing their viewpoints closer together, according to Hussein.

“We are trying to organize a meeting in Baghdad between Iran and the Gulf States,” Hussein said, without specifying a date or the degree of representation expected.

The proposal comes amid regional tensions that severely impacted maritime shipping and security in the Arabian Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz.

World.title: Iraq’s Fly Erbil gets Air Operator Certificate
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraq-based airline Fly Erbil announced on Thursday that it had obtained an Air Operator Certificate (AOC) by the Iraqi Civil Aviation Authority (ICAA)—a milestone the company says paves the way for a new phase of development and the expansion of its flight network.

The airline said in a statement that obtaining the license is a result of years of diligent work by its management and employees in different divisions.

Fly Erbil reaffirmed its commitment to safety and security requirements, as well as the regulations of the aviation sector.

The company mentioned that the step supports the development of air transport in both Iraqi Kurdistan and throughout Iraq.

The airline plans to broaden its flight network by adding more Iraqi cities and introducing new destinations both regionally and globally. Additionally, it aims to enhance its services to comply with international standards and meet travelers’ expectations.

The Iraqi Kurdish airline based at Erbil International Airport emphasized that obtaining this certification marks the beginning of a new phase in its journey.

World.title: Iraq signs seawater deal with ExxonMobil
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – The Iraqi Ministry of Oil announced on Wednesday that the state-run Basra Oil Company (BOC) and US-based ExxonMobil signed a memorandum of understanding for the second phase of an Iraq seawater supply project.

On the sidelines of a ceremony held to sign the agreement, Iraqi Oil Minister Basim Khudair said that the second phase of the seawater project is designed to support oil fields and maintain reservoir pressure.

With a capacity of up to 2.5 million barrels per day, this initiative complements a separate project currently being carried out by France-based TotalEnergies, which has a capacity of five million barrels per day.

The project is part of the Iraqi government’s approach to attract foreign firms to develop the country’s oil industry, ensure the sustainability of operations, and increase production rates, according to Khudair.

The development highlights Iraq’s appealing investment climate for implementing promising projects.

Khudair confirmed on Saturday that US firms are showing increasing interest in entering the Iraqi market and developing the country’s oil resources and petroleum industry.

The oil minister clarified that the Iraqi government supports US corporations’ involvement in the Iraqi market, citing their significant expertise in the oil sector, as well as their ability to transfer knowledge to Iraqi staff.

Several American companies are operating in Iraq, including oil services and consulting firms such as Halliburton, Schlumberger, Baker Hughes, and KBR, according to Khudair. He indicated that the ministry reached agreements with Chevron, ExxonMobil, and ConocoPhillips.

World.title: Iraq plans to purchase 10 large oil tankers
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraq is moving toward the acquisition of supertankers to bolster its capacity for transporting and marketing crude oil globally—a strategic step intended to reduce transportation costs and enhance financial returns from crude exports.

The Iraqi Ministry of Oil is considering the purchase of 10 oil tankers as part of its efforts to develop its export infrastructure and expand options for delivering shipments to global markets.

The step is part of the government’s efforts to strengthen the role of the Iraqi Oil Tankers Company (IOTC) and leverage the ownership of maritime transport assets, which would provide greater flexibility in marketing crude oil and managing shipments.

The plan is considered crucial given Iraq’s desire to improve the terms of its oil sales and reduce the discounts associated with certain existing marketing and transportation arrangements.

In a televised statement, Iraqi Oil Minister Basim Khudair revealed that the ministry is considering the purchase of 10 supertankers, with an estimated total cost of $2 billion, according to Attaqa News.

According to Khudair, the projected fleet will have a total capacity of 10 million barrels since each tanker has a capacity of around one million barrels.

Owning these tankers would increase export earnings; estimates indicate that Iraq might save between 30 percent and 40 percent on the losses it presently suffers from price reductions.

The Ministry of Oil has more alternatives than only direct procurement; it is also considering proposals from specialist companies to establish joint ventures for the supply of oil tankers.

According to Khudair, one of the suggestions is specialized businesses funding the acquisition of tankers in exchange for a portion of the revenues made from the vessels’ operations, with the price paid over a period of three or four years.

Direct procurement is still a possibility, and the Iraqi government has said that it supports this approach.

World.title: Iraq’s Diwaniyah refinery undergoes major $800 million expansion project
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – An oil refinery expansion project in Iraq is making tangible progress, as part of the country’s efforts to reduce its reliance on imported fuel and increase the value of its crude oil.

The Al-Barham Group (ABG) is carrying out an $800 million expansion project at the Diwaniyah refinery in Iraq.

This project is one of several refinery expansion initiatives that Iraq is pursuing, including those in al-Amarah, Muthanna, Kirkuk, and Qayyarah.

The refinery manager projected in September 2025 that monthly revenues would reach approximately $35 million once the expansion is complete.

The Diwaniyah refinery expansion is progressing steadily toward the operational phase. An atmospheric distillation unit with a capacity of 70,000 barrels per day will bring the refinery’s total production capacity to 90,000 barrels per day—more than four times its current capacity—according to the British magazine Middle East Economic Digest (MEED).

The Iraqi government signed the expansion deal in February 2025. The Prime Minister’s Office (PMO) declared that the contractor will start moving equipment on-site within days after securing the required finance.

In July 2025, work officially commenced at the site, with the Ministry of Oil establishing a five-year timeline for the project’s completion.

In addition to the main distillation unit, the project includes a liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) processing unit with a capacity of 180 tons per day, a naphtha hydro-treating unit with a capacity of 18,000 barrels per day, a gasoline upgrading unit with a capacity of 10,000 barrels per day, a naphtha isomerization unit with a capacity of 8,000 barrels per day, and a loading terminal with a capacity of 90,000 barrels per day.

The project also includes a power generation plant, a nitrogen plant, a water pumping and purification station, an industrial wastewater treatment plant, and 24 storage tanks for crude oil and petroleum products.

Beside high-quality gasoline, the refinery will produce naphtha, kerosene, red diesel, fuel oil, and LPG, supporting Iraq’s objective of achieving self-sufficiency in petroleum products.

World.title: Iraq’s customs revenues hit record high in September
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraq’s General Authority of Customs has announced a revenue increase of over $72 million in September 2026 compared to the same month in 2025.

The authority said in a statement that total customs revenues rose from $222.8 million in September 2025 to $294.8 million in September 2026—a growth rate of approximately 32.34 percent.

The rise reflects the importance of developing the customs operational system and enhancing the efficiency of revenue collection in accordance with applicable laws and regulations, according to the state-run Iraqi News Agency (INA).

The authority indicated that it is implementing a plan to enhance institutional performance, improve customs operational procedures, and increase the efficiency of revenue collection.

The measures are designed to protect public funds, strengthen the state’s financial resources, support financial reform, and promote the growth of non-oil revenues.

In January, head of the authority’s valuation department, Ahmed al-Akeedi, said that the deployment of the ASYCUDA system and the new customs tariff will improve earnings.

Al-Akeedi said that Iraqi customs revenues reached $1.9 billion in 2025, an unprecedented milestone in Iraqi customs history and an exceptional achievement.

Revenues are predicted to grow by at least four to six times with the application of the ASYCUDA system and complete compliance with customs rates, perhaps exceeding $7.63 billion by the end of 2026, according to al-Akeedi.

World.title: Iraq shuts Sheeb border crossing with Iran for security reasons
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraq has closed the al-Sheeb border crossing with Iran to all passengers, vehicles, and commercial transit until further notice.

An Iraqi border crossings official told Reuters that the sudden shutdown on Wednesday was implemented to review existing security procedures and install advanced detection equipment.

Officials mentioned that current security protocols at the busy Maysan province crossing were weak and inadequate to effectively halt the smuggling of prohibited materials.

Iranian security official Valiollah Hayati has advised passengers and cargo trucks to divert to the Shalamcheh crossing in Khuzestan province.

No official date has been announced for the resumption of operations. Local reports suggest the Iraqi government is currently evaluating security at other checkpoints and may gradually close additional borders with Iran in the coming days.

Iran’s Interior Ministry is currently in talks with Iraqi provincial authorities to coordinate a timeline for reopening the border.

In mid-September, Iraq announced the resumption of trade through its border crossings with Iran, following a brief closure due to security concerns.

Iraq closed several border crossings with Iran following a drone attack targeting a pipeline in Saudi Arabia, which Riyadh and Baghdad said originated from Iraqi territory.

Iraqi authorities had discovered drone launchers near the Iraqi-Iranian border in the remote al-Tayeb area in the ​​southern province of Maysan.

World.title: Five things to know about Chinese AI startup DeepSeek
World.content:
Beijing – The United States Department of Homeland Security ordered government agencies on Monday to stop using artificial intelligence tools from DeepSeek, citing concerns over data being transferred to China.

Here are five things to know about the Chinese AI startup following the new restrictions:

– ‘Sputnik moment’ –

Founded by Liang Wenfeng in the eastern Chinese tech hub Hangzhou, DeepSeek started life in 2023 as a side project of Liang’s data-driven hedge fund that had access to a cache of powerful AI processors made by US chip giant Nvidia.

It gained global attention in January 2025 with the release of its R1 deep-reasoning large language model, which sparked a US tech share sell-off.

Industry insiders were stunned by R1’s high performance — at a level similar to ChatGPT and other leading US chatbots — and DeepSeek’s claims to have developed it at a fraction of the cost.

Venture capitalist Marc Andreessen described it as a “Sputnik moment”, referencing the 1957 launch of Earth’s first artificial satellite by the Soviet Union that stunned the Western world.

– Censorship concerns –

Like other Chinese chatbots, DeepSeek’s AI tools eschew topics usually censored in the world’s second-largest economy, such as the 1989 Tiananmen crackdown.

That and data privacy concerns have led DeepSeek AI to be banned or restricted on government-issued devices in several countries, including the United States, Australia and South Korea.

On Monday, the US went further by banning civilian government agencies from using products developed by DeepSeek and third-party tools created using DeepSeek.

China’s foreign ministry said it opposed that move and accused the US of “overstretching” the concept of national security.

DeepSeek’s low cost and ease of deployment have made it a popular choice in developing countries, analysts say.

The company holds around four percent of global market share for chatbots, according to web traffic analysis company Similarweb. ChatGPT dominates at 68 percent.

– Open source –

DeepSeek’s systems are open-source, meaning their inner workings are public, allowing programmers to customise parts of the software to suit their needs.

That is the same for other major Chinese AI players, including tech giant Alibaba, in contrast to the “closed” models sold by OpenAI and other Western rivals.

The Chinese government has trumpeted its lead in open-source AI technology, which it says can accelerate innovation.

“Chinese AI models are leading the way in the open-source innovation ecosystem,” National People’s Congress spokesman Lou Qinjian told policymakers in April.

– Startup boost –

The success of DeepSeek has galvanised China’s AI scene, despite hurdles posed by rivalry with the United States and fears of a global market bubble.

Shares in two leading Chinese AI startups, Zhipu AI and MiniMax, soared on their market debuts in Hong Kong this year, and it has been a similar story for Chinese chipmakers such as MetaX.

In June, investors valued DeepSeek at more than $50 billion in the company’s first funding round, according to the Wall Street Journal.

Shi Yaqiong and her team at Beijing-based Jinqiu Capital told AFP there has been a “clear surge” in enthusiasm around Chinese AI — and competition among investors — since the DeepSeek shock.

– Chip smuggling reports –

DeepSeek’s rise has not been without controversy.

Reports, including in technology outlet The Information, say DeepSeek has been skirting a US ban on the export of top-end chips to China to train its new V4 model.

The Information said in December, citing six people with knowledge of the matter, that DeepSeek developed V4 using thousands of chips dismantled in third countries and smuggled to China.

DeepSeek did not respond to AFP’s request for comment at the time. Nvidia did not respond to a request for comment but told The Information that they had not seen any evidence of this and that “such smuggling seems farfetched”.

In April, DeepSeek said it had used both Nvidia and Huawei’s domestically-produced Ascend chips for its new model.

Huawei, at the forefront of Chinese efforts to reduce reliance on US semiconductor technology, said in a statement that the full range of its Ascend products support DeepSeek’s V4 series.

Washington says DeepSeek’s latest model is about eight months behind the top offerings from US companies.

World.title: Natco’s generic SMA drug approved; ‘clinical trial’ labels trigger Kerala row
World.content:
NEW DELHI: Days after a controversy erupted in Kerala over Natco Pharmaâs generic drug for spinal muscular atrophy (SMA), regulatory clarifications suggest the row stemmed from labels on bottles supplied free of cost.

The words âPhysician Sample/Clinical Trialâ raised fears among parents that their children were being given medicines meant for clinical trials rather than an authorised drug for routine treatment.

In response to queries from TOI, Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO) officials said Natcoâs risdiplam powder for oral solution (0.75 mg/ml) had been approved by the Telangana State Food and Drug Administration under the applicable regulations.

The bulk drug had received CDSCO approval on April 7, 2025.

The officials said bioequivalence studies were not required for the oral solution under the regulatorâs draft guidance and that additional clinical trials were not necessary before patients could be switched to the generic formulation.

Natco said it emerged as the lowest bidder in Keralaâs tender and supplies one free bottle for every three purchased under its Patient Assistance Programme, bringing the effective cost to around â¹8,500 per bottle against â¹1.5 lakh earlier for Rocheâs drug.





The company acknowledged that the free bottles carry the label âPhysician Sample/Clinical trials onlyâ, but said they were supplied as samples under the rate contract and not for clinical trials.

It said its generic risdiplam, priced at an MRP of â¹15,900 against â¹6 lakh for Rocheâs product, had met regulatory requirements.

The issue became a political controversy after Leader of the Opposition Pinarayi Vijayan said parents of children with SMA had flagged the labels on medicines distributed through SAT Hospital in Thiruvananthapuram.

He alleged violations of the Drugs and Cosmetics Rules and procurement norms and demanded an inquiry.

SAT Hospital authorities have maintained that the medicine distributed was the approved generic formulation, not an experimental drug.

Risdiplam is used to treat SMA, a rare genetic disorder that causes progressive muscle weakness. Kerala had been supplying Rocheâs branded medicine free to eligible children at a negotiated price.

The shift to Natcoâs generic version could substantially reduce treatment costs and potentially allow the state to extend support to more patients.

The controversy comes amid opposition from parents and the Cure SMA Foundation of India to Keralaâs decision to replace Rocheâs medicine with Natcoâs generic version. Parents have sought assurances about the safety and efficacy of switching children who have improved on the existing treatment.

While the regulatory clarification addresses the generic drugâs approval status, the episode raises a separate question: whether labelling that combines âPhysician Sampleâ and âClinical Trialâ can cause confusion when medicines are supplied for patient use.

World.title: Indian diaspora could pay price for West’s immigration backlash, warns Sushant Sareen
World.content:
US President Donald Trump has blamed immigration for the recent unrest in France and urged President Emmanuel Macron to close the countryâs borders, reigniting a wider debate over migration, integration and the future of Western societies.

But the backlash could also hurt Indians who have built successful lives abroad through legal migration, strategic affairs expert Sushant Sareen has warned.

âThe law breakers don't care anyways but it's the guys who follow the law who will also get crushed,â Sareen said in an interview on Faultline, hosted by Ananya Dasgupta.

Trump has described Franceâs unrest as a consequence of immigration and warned that Europe risks decline unless it tightens its borders.

Macron, however, has rejected attempts by foreign leaders to blame migrants for the violence, pointing to the exploitation of Franceâs domestic tensions for political gain.

Why Indians could pay the price

Sareen said the Indian diaspora had established a reputation for success in countries such as the US, Canada, Australia and New Zealand.

âThe Indian diaspora wherever it went it made a success of itself,â he said.

However, he argued that this reputation could come under pressure as anti-immigration sentiment grows.





Referring to Canada, Sareen alleged that criminal activity involving some members of the Indian community, including people he linked to Khalistani networks, had damaged the image of the wider diaspora.

His concern is that Indians unconnected with such activities could also face the consequences of a broader backlash against migrants.

Is the West paying for its own mistakes?

Sareen sees the immigration debate as part of a wider crisis facing Western societies.

He argued that governments had failed to manage integration and address tensions around migration, leaving established political and social models under strain.

âMulticulturalism has collapsed,â he said, describing what he sees as the failure of the Western approach to managing cultural diversity.

Yet Western economies continue to need migrant workers, particularly as populations age and employers face labour shortages.

Sareen said governments must rethink their immigration systems, including how long migrants can stay and what rights they should have.

For Indians hoping to study, work or settle abroad, tougher visa rules could complicate future plans. Those already settled overseas could also face uncertainty if immigration becomes a proxy for wider anxieties about jobs, identity and cultural change.

Join conversation Commentsâ Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

The contradiction is that Western countries need foreign talent even as political pressure to restrict immigration grows.

For India, the stakes extend beyond visa policies. If the West responds to its immigration crisis by treating migrant communities as a single group, law-abiding Indians who have contributed to their host countries could find themselves paying the price.

Watch

Faultline

with Ananya Dasgupta and Sushant Sareen as they discuss the France crisis, the Westâs immigration trap, the growing backlash and why Indians could pay the price.

World.title: Dark side of glow-ups: The ugly truth of India's beauty trends and what you need to be aware of
World.content:
The NMC guidelines do not aim to stop people from seeking treatment. Instead, they aim to ensure that patients make informed medical decisions guided by clinical expertise rather than an algorithm-driven sales pitch.

Dermatology vs cosmetology

The NMC rulebook: What changes on your feed

Shift in strategy: Before vs after the guidelines

Education vs covert marketing

Performance marketing, DMs, and tele-consult safeguards

When aesthetics go wrong: The clinical and human cost

How patients can assess practitioners in the post-hype era

Verify core medical qualifications:

Evaluate the consultation:

Review case examples privately:

Demand clinical assessment and safety protocols:

Putting clinical care ahead of the sales pitch

Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

Scroll through Instagram on any given Tuesday, and you are bound to hit the "Glow Up" algorithm. With the dramatic "before-and-after" transitions, an influencer gushing over their new "glass skin" chemical peels, and local clinics promising a "100% guaranteed acne cure," cosmetic medicine has officially crossed over into pop culture.It feels less like an invasive clinical procedure and more like buying a new pair of sneakers. One click, instant gratification.In India's hyper-visual, social-media-obsessed culture, looking "filtered" in real life has created a massive boom for cosmetic clinics. But behind the glossy aesthetic lies a wild-west market where non-clinical salon technicians, short-course certificate holders, and non-core medical practitioners are offering everything from laser hair removal to dermal fillers.The reels make the procedures seem cheap and accessible, but the noise creates a great deal of confusion for potential customers and raises risk of botched procedures.To halt this commercial noise and protect patients from predatory marketing, the National Medical Commission (NMC), India's apex regulator for medical practice, has introduced a strict ethical framework.The goal? Drawing a hard line between legitimate clinical care and commercial hype.The biggest source of consumer confusion is the assumption that a "dermatologist" and a "cosmetologist" are the same thing. They aren't.Confusing the two can leave you with severe skin damage.A dermatologist completes a rigorous eight-and-a-half-year medical training pathway, comprising a Bachelor of Medicine and Bachelor of Surgery (MBBS) degree followed by a three-year Doctor of Medicine (MD) or Diplomate of National Board (DNB) in Dermatology, Venereology, and Leprosy.It also includes comprehensive hands-on training in clinical pathology, complex skin diseases, dermatosurgery, and laser medicine. Similarly, a plastic surgeon undergoes specialized post-doctoral surgical training (MCh or DNB) in reconstructive and aesthetic surgery.On the flip side, "cosmetology" is not a recognized medical specialty or postgraduate qualification under the National Medical Commission (NMC) framework.In practice, the term often describes salon estheticians, technicians, or non-core operators who hold short 3- to 6-month diploma certificates from private, unaccredited institutes.Under the regulatory mandates of the NMC's ethics, non-core practitioners, non-clinical operators, and salon technicians are strictly prohibited from procedures such as laser resurfacing, deep chemical peels, hair transplants, or injectable dermal fillers.As Dr Tanvi Gupta Arora, dermatology consultant at CK Birla Hospital says, "Earlier, there was no term like 'cosmetology' in medical residency. Aesthetic procedures were an integrated part of our clinical curriculum under Dermatosurgery, complete with hands-on surgical training under senior guides.âShe adds, âThe challenge in India is that regulations were historically lax. Non-clinical entities like salon technicians and short-course diploma holders started performing deep chemical peels, aggressive lasers, and recommending fillers without clinical supervision."If your favorite clinic's social media page suddenly looks a lot quieter, blame (or thank) the NMC rules.Now, doctors cannot post promotional "before-and-after" grid shots, transition reels, or retouched result photos on public feeds. Clinical photos are strictly restricted to anonymized, scientific, or educational use. They set clear boundaries on how practitioners can advertise their services, use social media and engage with influencers.Influencer barter crackdown: Free Botox, fillers, or hair transplants given to social media influencers in exchange for "spontaneous" glowing reviews are now outright banned. Doctors cannot solicit or feature patient video testimonials or star-rating screenshots.Killing Superlatives & Guarantees: Phrases like "Best Dermatologist in Delhi," "No. 1 Plastic Surgeon," or "100% Glass Skin Guarantee" are illegal. Doctors are also prohibited from claiming non-existent qualifications (like US-style "Board Certified Plastic Surgeon" titles, which do not exist in India).AI & Pay-Per-Lead Bans: AI-generated "synthetic" patient cases, face filters, or synthetic doctor voices are prohibited without explicit disclaimers. Furthermore, clinics cannot pay marketing agencies "per-patient" commissions.As Dr Vivek Gupta, plastic & cosmetic surgery consultant at Madhukar Rainbow Childrenâs Hospital, Delhi views it, âIn a field where social media creates unrealistic expectations, decisions must be guided by clinical suitability rather than promotional claims. Restrictions on promotional photographs and testimonials mean we must adapt our communication strategies.âHe also says how he has upgraded the advertising guidelines for his own clinic. âOur clinic now focuses on expert-led public health education rather than promoting individual outcomes," he says.The daily operational shift across Indian aesthetic clinics is stark.In the earlier, largely unregulated aesthetic medicine market described in the draft, clinics relied on visuals that showcased dramatic transformations and could create the impression that similar results were achievable for everyone.Under the NMC-compliant approach, clinics shift towards educational content, such as anatomical diagrams, procedure explainers and skin-science reels.Rather than promoting individual treatment outcomes, these formats help explain medical conditions, how procedures work and what patients should understand before considering treatment.Dr. Vivek Gupta acknowledges that while digital platforms remain an important source of information for people exploring aesthetic options, restricting promotional material presents a distinct communication challenge."Restrictions on testimonials, promotional photographs, and advertising can make it harder to communicate treatment outcomes and recovery experiences," he says.However, he maintains that "the solution lies in adapting communication strategies rather than compromising ethical standards. Clearer guidance on distinguishing medical education from commercial promotion would help practitioners remain informative while complying with professional regulations."He explains that his practice uses digital platforms to discuss common cosmetic concerns, treatment options, recovery expectations, and potential risks, such as acne scars or skin aging, while strictly avoiding exaggerated claims or guaranteed results."The objective is to build credibility through scientifically accurate information and responsible communication rather than promotional testimonials," he explains.This strategic overhaul also extends to how doctors manage public interaction on digital platforms. Dr. Tanvi Gupta Arora notes that sponsored endorsements and flashing contact numbers over educational reels are now firmly off-limits."Under the guidelines, we cannot do sponsored product endorsements or flash clinic phone numbers over educational videos," she points out, "If I post an educational reel about acne, I turn off comments to prevent direct social media prescribing. We redirect inquiries through proper clinical consultations or telemedicine."In her experience, this levels the playing field for doctors who built their practice on "clinical labor rather than massive ad budgets."In an era where skincare trends go viral overnight on reels and shorts, the distinction between public health awareness and disguised product placement has grown dangerously blurry.The NMCâs crackdown directly addresses this hidden marketplace by prohibiting barter deals where influencers trade shoutouts for free treatments.Dr Vivek Gupta highlights that the true test of educational content lies in its intent and presentation."The distinction lies in the information's purpose and presentation. Public health education helps people understand cosmetic concerns, treatment options, preventive measures, and potential risks," he explains, "Covert marketing uses educational content to promote a particular procedure or commercial interest. Every communication should prioritise scientific accuracy, balanced information, and patient welfare rather than encouraging people to purchase a specific service or product. "When asked about using non-medical influencers, Dr Gupta reveals he has never relied on them for endorsements."Aesthetic treatments require individual assessment, and their suitability, risks, and outcomes vary from person to person. Influencers can help raise awareness about skincare, but personal experiences should never be mistaken for medical evidence," he says, adding that credibility in this field "should ultimately come from clinical expertise and responsible patient care."Instead of chasing influencer viral loops, his clinic prioritizes expert-led educational content, media interactions, and public awareness initiatives.He asserts, "Trust is also established during consultations, where patients receive realistic expectations, understand potential risks and learn about alternatives. This approach places greater emphasis on clinical credibility than online popularity. In aesthetic care, sustainable trust comes from transparent communication, professional competence and a consistent commitment to patient welfare."The regulatory overhaul doesn't just stop at Instagram reels; it reshapes the entire digital sales funnel used by modern cosmetic chains.Historically, aesthetic marketing relied heavily on aggressive performance marketing campaigns. Clickbait s proclaiming "Get glass skin in 3 days" or "call now for 50% off hair transplants" were explicitly designed to exploit appearance-related insecurities, feeding directly into pay-per-lead models.Under the new guidelines, performance marketing must be stripped of high-pressure sales tactics, artificial urgency, and guaranteed outcome claims.Dr Vivek Gupta emphasizes that digital visibility must remain factual and consistent with medical ethics requirements."Campaigns should avoid guaranteed outcomes, misleading claims, patient testimonials used for promotion, and messaging that exploits appearance-related insecurities," he states, adding that marketing agencies must understand these boundaries.This shift has also forced a total overhaul of digital triage and initial online consultations. In the past, prospective patients could drop a comment under a video or send a direct message (DM) detailing their skin issues, receiving direct prescriptions or treatment quotes from social media managers.Dr Gupta stresses the vital difference between general inquiries and actual consultations, noting, "Digital messages can provide basic information, but individual treatment recommendations require an appropriate clinical assessment."For tele-consultations, safeguards such as identity verification, informed consent, confidentiality, and proper documentation are essential."Photographs shared online may not provide sufficient information to determine treatment suitability. Where physical examination or a detailed assessment is necessary, patients should be advised to attend an in-person consultation," he warns, concluding that "convenience must never override clinical judgement, privacy or patient safety."When cosmetic procedures are marketed like fast-fashion beauty products, patients pay a heavy price with their physical and financial well-being.Both dermatologists and plastic surgeons frequently find themselves functioning as corrective specialists, tasked with repairing severe damage caused by non-core practitioners or aggressive "assembly-line" cosmetic chains.For instance, in a September 30 order, the Bengaluru urban district consumer disputes redressal commission held a clinic liable for deficiency in service and unfair trade practice after a woman suffered second-degree facial burns during laser hair removal in April.The commission directed the clinic to refund the Rs 1,100 procedure fee with interest, pay Rs 1 lakh in damages and Rs 10,000 in litigation costs, giving it 45 days to comply.Dr Tanvi Gupta Arora highlights how these botched cases unfold in daily practice, pointing out that aggressive commercial chains routinely lure vulnerable patients into spending massive sums on guaranteed outcomes."Some of these cosmetology chains, what they are doing is they are running these s that 'we will just cure your pigmentation, you will be 100% free of your pigmentation.' And people, they fall into the trap and go and spend thousands or lakhs with no result," Dr Tanvi explains.When these uncalibrated procedures fail, patients are thrown back into the market with damaged skin and exhausted finances.Dr Tanvi notes that treating these complications requires extensive time and care before even touching the patient's original cosmetic concern."Sometimes the damages are irreversible. You had so much damage that you now cannot treat it," she shares, adding: "So you have to further do more procedures. Like sometimes these patients come to me with even worse pigmentation. First I have to spend two to three months correcting that issue, the skin has become thin or it has become burnt, and then we talk about the pigmentation correction."The experts map out certain points that a patient could look for to assess the authenticity of the clinic or expert.Patients should look for recognised postgraduate qualifications, such as an MD or DNB in dermatology or an MCh or DNB in Plastic Surgery, and verify registration details with the state medical council or NMC register.Dr Vivek Gupta stresses the importance of qualifications and competence: "Plastic surgeons and dermatologists have different areas of expertise, and the procedures offered must align with their respective training and applicable scope of practice. Non-core practitioners must not misrepresent their qualifications or undertake procedures beyond their competence. Patients should be able to verify credentials and understand who is performing a procedure. "Consultations should offer factual information about diagnosis, risks, alternatives and realistic outcomes, without guarantees or pressure to proceed.Dr Vivek Gupta explains: "Trust is established during consultations, where patients receive realistic expectations, understand potential risks and learn about alternatives. This approach places greater emphasis on clinical credibility than online popularity.âHe also cautions against relying on online reviews to judge clinical capability: "Instead of promotional testimonials, patients should focus on recognised qualifications, relevant experience, consultation quality, and transparent discussions about risks, alternatives, and recovery."Instead of public promotional posts, patients can ask to see clinical case records during a consultation to understand the likely scope and outcomes of a procedure.Dr Tanvi Gupta Arora says: "Before and after photos should not be on your social media. You can put it on your website, or if somebody comes to your clinic, then any day they can come to your clinic and then you can show them the before and after pictures or whatever particular procedure they are looking for."Patients should ensure that clinics conduct appropriate assessments, use approved devices and injectables, and have emergency procedures to manage adverse reactions. Digital messages and photographs may not be sufficient to determine whether a procedure is suitable.Dr Vivek Gupta emphasises: "Digital messages can provide basic information, but individual treatment recommendations require an appropriate clinical assessment... Photographs shared online may not provide sufficient information to determine treatment suitability. Where physical examination or a detailed assessment is necessary, patients should be advised to attend an in-person consultation. Convenience must never override clinical judgement, privacy or patient safety. "The NMC guidelines aim to curb predatory marketing, banning influencer barter culture, and restricting invasive procedures strictly to qualified specialists.For clinics and marketing agencies, this transition demands a total overhaul of digital strategy, swapping sensationalism, clickbait, and artificial transformation grids for transparent, expert-led public education.For patients, the rules offer much-needed protection in a market that has grown dangerously confusing. A cosmetic procedure is not an off-the-rack beauty buy; it is a medical intervention carried out on living human tissue. Ultimately, the new regulatory landscape encourages consumers to value what truly matters when choosing a doctor: prioritizing clinical expertise, authentic qualifications, and patient safety over an algorithm-driven sales pitch.
