For years, Russian and Chechen authorities have repeated the same explanation: Chechnya has no laboratory capable of identifying human remains, and Russia lacks the necessary specialists. In reality, Russia began building the infrastructure for identifying the dead, particularly soldiers, as early as 1995. American military personnel helped their counterparts in the Russian Defence Ministry master modern techniques and supplied equipment for DNA analysis.

The United States was a pioneer in this field. American anthropologists, forensic pathologists and criminal investigators played a crucial role in investigating crimes committed by military dictatorships in Latin America. FBI experts helped establish what became the world’s most advanced system for exhuming and identifying remains from mass graves in the former Yugoslavia. Mukomolov repeatedly cited the experience of Bosnia and Herzegovina as an international benchmark and urged the authorities to apply the same approach in Chechnya.

Russia itself drew on American expertise in 2008, immediately after the five-day war in Georgia. More than 100 Russian forensic specialists were deployed to South Ossetia, accompanied by a mobile laboratory. Russian authorities announced to the world that between 1,500 and 2,000 civilians had been killed in South Ossetia during the five-day war and attempted to accuse the Georgian authorities of genocide. In reality, the number of South Ossetian victims was ten times lower: 162 people. There was no need to deploy so many forensic specialists other than for propaganda purposes.

Two months before the war in Georgia, in June 2008, one of the largest burial sites in Chechnya was discovered in Grozny’s Leninsky district, near a Christian cemetery. It contained around 800 bodies. In July, another site containing several hundred bodies was found near the village of Goryacheistochnenskaya. But Viktor Ledenev, head of the Investigative Committee in Chechnya, refused to conduct exhumations, citing a shortage of specialists and inadequate infrastructure.

Even Nurdi Nukhazhiev, the former human rights ombudsman under the head of Chechnya, publicly identified what he saw as the real reason behind this policy of concealment:“It is precisely the Defence Ministry that is doing everything possible to obstruct the creation of an interagency commission to identify abducted and missing persons, as well as the establishment of a laboratory in the Chechen Republic to identify exhumed bodies…”

Freedom in Exchange for Danger

The official objective of the Second Chechen War was to combat terrorism. The authorities persistently referred to the campaign as a “counterterrorism operation,” rather than a war. This was largely a legal manoeuvre. Declaring martial law would have required the approval of a parliament that was still independent at the time and compliance with international obligations, above all the Geneva Conventions.

But in September 1999, public concern centred above all on security. Political scientists would later describe the social contract offered to citizens by the new prime minister, Vladimir Putin, as “freedom in exchange for security.” The public readily accepted it.

Initially, the West sharply criticised Russia’s methods. But those methods only drove more recruits into the militants’ ranks. The unrestrained brutality of the military and security services became one of the factors behind the emergence of shahidkas — women, often the widows and sisters of those killed, who were turned into “human bombs” after relatively rudimentary psychological and ideological conditioning.

After the September 11, 2001, terrorist attacks, Vladimir Putin was the first foreign leader to call US President George W. Bush to offer his condolences. Putin stressed that Russia had already spent two years defending the civilised world against Islamist terrorism in Chechnya. Western attitudes began to shift. Basayev, Khattab, Umarov and the Caucasus Emirate they led were placed on US terrorist lists. The West definitively abandoned the idea of an international tribunal for Chechnya.

When Putin opened Russian airspace to NATO aircraft and raised no objections to US military bases in Central Asia, the Second Chechen War came to be regarded as one front in the global war on terror.

In reality, the West and Russia shared a record of war crimes in this conflict. When confronted with accusations of human rights abuses in Chechnya, Russia pointed to Guantánamo Bay, Abu Ghraib, secret CIA prisons in Europe, and civilian casualties in Afghanistan and Iraq.

But a comparison of how the United States and Russia protected their citizens from terrorist attacks suggests that counterterrorism was never a priority for the Russian authorities. After September 11, the United States overhauled its security system. In the quarter-century since, no terrorist organisation has come close to repeating Osama bin Laden’s “success.” In Russia, by contrast, terrorist attacks became a recurring feature of life: the 2002 Moscow theatre siege, the 2004 attacks in Ingushetia and the Beslan school hostage-taking, the 2005 assault on Nalchik, and countless bombings targeting cars, buildings, hospitals, markets, aircraft and metro stations.

The authorities exploited every attack to concentrate presidential power and strengthen the security services. But the goal was not to fight terrorists; it was to suppress political opposition and civic dissent.

It was not until 2013, on the eve of the Sochi Winter Olympics, that the security services managed to stabilise the situation in the Caucasus. International developments played a significant role. When the Islamic State (ISIS), founded by former members of Saddam Hussein’s Iraqi security services, seized parts of Iraq and Syria and declared a caliphate, radicals from around the world, including the North Caucasus, flocked to join it. Russian security services simply opened the border to them.

In March 2024, Islamic State followers stormed the Crocus City Hall concert venue, opened fire and set the building ablaze. The attack killed 151 people and injured more than 600. Foreign intelligence agencies had warned the FSB of an impending terrorist attack. Yet on March 19, three days before the assault, Russia’s leadership publicly dismissed the warnings as “outright blackmail by Western countries” and an attempt to destabilise society. The FSB did nothing to prevent the attack.

Today, in Russia, Ukrainians are branded terrorists, while Islamic State militants are no longer the primary focus.

The terrorist attack took place in a climate of complete public silence. There is nowhere left to ask the authorities what became of the social contract of September 1999, and no one left to ask the question. This is what became of it: the methods of terror honed in Chechnya have become a central instrument of Russian state policy, both at home and abroad.

The practices of filtration — enforced disappearances, secret prisons, torture and extrajudicial executions — became a principal means of “bringing the population into line” after the annexation of Crimea, and later across all the regions of Ukraine occupied by Russian forces in the first months of the war. According to human rights defenders, the practice of so-called “short-term enforced disappearances” has also spread beyond Chechnya to regions across Russia itself.

▇ Replace Chechens with Ukrainians in Anna Politkovskaya’s articles, Novye Aldy and Khatuni with Bucha, Izium or Kherson, and Grozny, Komsomolskoye, Argun and Shali with Mariupol, Bakhmut, Kharkiv or, right now, Kyiv, and her reporting will read as entirely contemporary — and entirely prophetic.

This article was produced in collaboration with the Memory Project, a civic initiative comprising Russian lawyers, human rights defenders and researchers who investigate enforced disappearances and preserve historical memory.

Exchange

World.title: Azerbaijan and Norway hold political consultations
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 22. The next round of political consultations between the Ministries of Foreign Affairs of Azerbaijan and Norway was held in Baku on October 22.

This was reported by the Azerbaijani Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

According to the information, the Azerbaijani delegation was led by Deputy Foreign Minister Fariz Rzayev, while the Norwegian delegation was headed by State Secretary at the Norwegian Ministry of Foreign Affairs Eivind Vad Petersson.

During the consultations, the current state of political relations between Azerbaijan and Norway was reviewed, and the importance of ensuring the continuity of bilateral dialogue was noted.

Opportunities for expanding cooperation in the trade-economic, humanitarian, scientific, and educational spheres were reviewed. Additionally, prospects for cooperation within the framework of strategic energy and transport projects, realized through Azerbaijan’s initiative and participation, were discussed.

Besides, the importance of expanding the legal-treaty framework was emphasized. Attention was also directed toward relations and interaction within international organizations, as well as the mutual support of candidacies. The parties were briefed on the current situation in the region, the efforts toward the normalization of Azerbaijan-Armenia relations, as well as the large-scale restoration, reconstruction, and demining activities being carried out in the liberated territories.

Furthermore, an exchange of views took place regarding other regional and international issues of mutual interest.

World.title: Azerbaijan’s MFA meets National Defense University course attendees (PHOTO)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 22. A meeting was held at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MFA) of Azerbaijan with participants of the National Defense University’s "Academic course on strategic studies and state defense management" on October 22.

This was reported by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

According to the information, during the meeting, Spokesperson for the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Aykhan Hajizada, delivered a presentation on "Azerbaijan's foreign policy priorities" and answered numerous questions from the participants.

Then, the course participants were briefed on the operational processes of the MFA.

A total of 29 representatives are participating in the course, including personnel from the Ministry of Defense and other state institutions, as well as representatives from Türkiye, Pakistan, and Kazakhstan.

World.title: Russia leads Azerbaijan's fruit, vegetable exports with 83.1% in 8 months
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 22. Russia accounted for 83.1% of the value of Azerbaijan’s fruit and vegetable exports in January–August 2026, making it the country’s leading export destination, the Azerbaijani Ministry of Agriculture told Trend in response to a request.

The ministry said Russia, Italy, Germany, Belarus, and Georgia ranked as Azerbaijan’s top five fruit and vegetable export destinations by value during the reporting period.

Azerbaijan exported 540,900 tons of fruit and vegetables worth $637.1 million from January through August 2026.

Shipments to Russia totaled 462,200 tons worth $529.5 million.

Italy ranked second, with exports totaling 2,000 tons worth $27.7 million. Germany followed with 1,200 tons worth $17.4 million, Belarus with 12,700 tons worth $13.9 million, and Georgia with 31,500 tons worth $10 million. These countries accounted for 4.3%, 2.7%, 2.2%, and 1.6% of Azerbaijan’s total fruit and vegetable export value, respectively.

The main products exported to Russia included tomatoes, peaches and nectarines, strawberries, hazelnut kernels, and apples. Shipments included 134,500 tons of tomatoes worth $160.8 million, 61,000 tons of peaches and nectarines worth $85.2 million, and 55,300 tons of strawberries worth $81.5 million.

Exports to Italy consisted entirely of hazelnut kernels, totaling 2,000 tons worth $27.7 million. Hazelnut kernels were also the main product exported to Germany, with shipments reaching 1,100 tons worth $17.2 million.

Tomatoes and potatoes accounted for the largest shares of Azerbaijan’s exports to Belarus by value, while onions and tomatoes dominated shipments to Georgia.

In 2025, Russia, Germany, Türkiye, Ukraine, and Belarus ranked among the top five destinations for Azerbaijan’s fruit and vegetable exports, according to the ministry. Azerbaijan exported 846,000 tons of fruit and vegetables worth $901.5 million that year.

Exports to Russia totaled 704,700 tons worth $696.5 million. Shipments to Germany amounted to 3,900 tons worth $40.8 million, while exports to Türkiye reached 28,400 tons worth $31.3 million. Ukraine received 31,100 tons worth $27.5 million, and Belarus received 19,000 tons worth $22 million. These countries accounted for 77.3%, 4.5%, 3.5%, 3.0%, and 2.4% of the total export value, respectively.

World.title: Hacking attempts surge as websites race to patch PHP issues
World.content:
Millions of hacking attempts have been made since critical vulnerabilities were discovered in a key piece of internet software used by more than two-thirds of websites.

Governments and major websites have rushed to patch two critical issues with PHP, a widely used computing language, after they were reportedly discovered by AI.

Australia's own cyber security agency, the Australian Signals Directorate, is among agencies around the world to issue urgent warnings for websites to implement a new patch.

In some instances, governments have taken websites offline as a precautionary measure.

The emergency shutdowns of banking, airline, rail, tax and government services from Tokyo to Helsinki mark one of the most dramatic tests of the decades-old programming tools that keep the web running, exposing how deeply governments and companies depend on code that few people understand.

AI helped discover the "critical" vulnerability. (ABC News: Scott Preston)

Cloud services firm Cloudfare said since the two vulnerabilities were made public, hacking attempts had surged into the millions.

"In the 10 hours before it was publicly announced, across the network we saw thousands of attempts to exploit it," Cloudflare chief executive Matthew Prince said in a post on X late on Wednesday, US time.

" That jumped to tens of thousands in the 45 minutes post announcement, hundreds of thousands within 2 hours, and millions now. "

The developers of PHP released fixes for vulnerabilities that had lurked in the software for years until they were uncovered using AI, urging users to "update immediately".

"I've not seen anything like this in a long, long time," Microsoft chief executive Satya Nadella said at an event in Germany on Thursday, local time.

He said the incident showed the importance of building software that can be maintained securely as systems grow more complex.

"It was a long day and a long night, I know, for all the IT and security folks."

Government sites exposed to 'critical' PHP flaw The Australian Signals Directorate is among global cyber agencies urging organisations to quickly act to fix flaws in a programming language that hackers are believed to be exploiting.

Several Asian governments ordered cybersecurity inspections related to the PHP vulnerabilities.

China's industry ministry urged organisations and users to inspect systems and upgrade to the latest secure version of PHP.

It also recommended strengthening cybersecurity monitoring and changing accounts, passwords and keys where necessary.

South Korea raised its private-sector cybersecurity alert level and activated emergency response measures, citing concerns over an increased risk of hacking attacks.

ABC/Reuters

World.title: Zelenskyy says fresh Russian strikes show 'no change' in Kremlin position
World.content:
Russia has fired missiles at Ukraine shortly after talks between US envoy Steve Witkoff and President Vladimir Putin.

The move proves the Kremlin's position on the war had not changed, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said.

The Kremlin had said it was willing to restart trilateral talks with Kyiv and Washington next month, though dismissed new ideas brought by Mr Witkoff as lacking substance.

Russia hit a dozen Ukrainian regions overnight, including Kyiv, killing at least two people and wounding 34, Mr Zelenskyy said.

Residential houses, energy sites, a shopping mall and a monastery had been damaged in Kyiv, where Russia has significantly intensified its strikes ahead of winter.

Mr Zelenskyy said the latest strikes began "almost immediately" after US President Donald Trump's envoy Mr Witkoff held hours-long talks with Mr Putin in Saint Petersburg.

The aftermath of one of the Russian missile attacks in central Kyiv. (AP: Efrem Lukatsky)

Russia downs Ukrainian drones, Moscow says

Russia also said it had downed 808 Ukrainian drones fired overnight and that two people were wounded in Moscow.

Mr Witkoff faced widespread criticism for calling Mr Putin a "humanitarian" after Moscow released an elderly US citizen who had been jailed on charges of fighting for Ukraine as a "mercenary".

Mr Trump sought an optimistic tone as his envoy returned from Russia, saying that negotiators were "maybe now the closest we've been" to ending the war.

But in Kyiv and European capitals, hopes for a breakthrough were slim, with many worried the White House was siding with Moscow.

Mr Zelenskyy says only a meeting of leaders can end the deadlock. (Reuters: Alina Smutko)

"Three waves of ballistic missiles have been launched at Kyiv by Russian 'humanitarians' since yesterday evening," Mr Zelenskyy said.

" Almost immediately after another round of talks, Russia launched a pointed attack. This means there has been no real change in its attitude towards everything that is happening. "

He called on allies to keep up "real pressure" on Moscow and for more air defence supplies.

Three-way talks to resume

Moscow invaded Ukraine in February 2022 in what it hoped would be a swift attack to topple Mr Zelenskyy and seize land.

Instead it has become bogged down in Europe's biggest conflict since World War II.

Zelenskyy meets Trump envoys Marco Rubio denies intelligence-sharing has been limited as US envoys meet the Ukrainian president for talks.

Hundreds of thousands have been killed, millions forced from their homes and much of eastern and southern Ukraine destroyed.

Mr Zelenskyy had met with Mr Witkoff in Norway a day before the US-Russia talks in a meeting that came after days of spiralling Washington-Kyiv tensions.

In recent days, Mr Trump has blocked new sanctions on Russia, struck a deal to buy Russian diesel, and called for the Ukrainian leader to be replaced.

Mr Zelenskyy has backed resuming trilateral talks — several rounds of which over the last 18 months have failed to move the sides closer to a deal.

Russia is demanding Ukraine pull out of territory in the eastern Donetsk region that it still controls, and wants sweeping political and military restrictions on the size of its army and Western alliances.

Ukraine rejects the demands as tantamount to capitulation that would leave it exposed to a fresh attack.

The Kremlin said Mr Witkoff had briefed Mr Putin on "some new aspects in the approaches of the Europeans and Kyiv" from the Oslo meeting, but that "there wasn't really much substance in them".

Moscow also said that a summit between Mr Trump, Mr Putin and China's Xi was being prepared in China for next month, with Europeans and Ukraine worrying a deal could be struck over their heads.

AFP

World.title: Shark trapped in South Korean city won't return to sea
World.content:
She has become one of the most popular attractions in South Korea, with more than 1.6 million people flocking to the port city of Busan for a glimpse.

A month ago the 3-metre dusky shark unexpectedly entered the city's canal — one of Asia's busiest ports — and now appears reluctant to leave.

The shark, named Bukangi, has become so popular she is now a mascot for the city and Busan Mayor Chun Jae-soo thanked her for generating publicity he said would otherwise have cost "trillions".

Loading...

There have been three attempts to help her return to the ocean, including a mammoth operation on Wednesday, during which hours were spent guiding her with floating platforms, nets and divers.

A few hours later, the oceans ministry said the shark had swum under one of the nets and back into the canal.

It said Bukangi's condition was stable but authorities were worried the shark had not been feeding regularly and could face health risks from falling water temperatures.

The shark entered the canal in September. (Cha Keun-ho/Yonhap via AP)

South Korean National Institute of Fisheries Science senior researcher Kim Hyun-woo said it was possible the bright lights and noise from vessels had interfered with the shark’s senses and the canal now appeared to be a safe space for it.

Sharks seek sea change as water temperature rises Several shark species are on the move as waters warm along Australia’s east coast. Here's how climate change is affecting the range of three major species.

"The shark has been staying inside the canal for an extended period, so I didn't expect it to head straight out into the open water," he said.

"It would be best to give it about a week to leave on its own."

Officials have opened the outer net and reinforced barriers to prevent the shark from retreating further back into the canal.

Environmentalists believe climate change and warming ocean temperatures may have caused the shark to enter the canal.

Dusky sharks are classified as endangered by the International Union for Conservation of Nature.

Reuters/AP

World.title: Chalmers says investors feel good about Australia despite gloom at home
World.content:
Business investment is booming in Australia despite stubborn inflation and a stagnant economy, according to Treasurer Jim Chalmers, as global investors rush to park their money in what they see as "an island of opportunity and stability" in troubled times.

Speaking to a gathering of investors in Sydney on Friday, the treasurer will boast of the warm reception he received in a string of international visits last week and reveal that business investment is growing more than twice as fast as was previously expected.

The optimism comes in the midst of a difficult period for Mr Chalmers, who has been weighed down by gloomy domestic conditions and backlash to his tax hikes on wealth, which have angered business lobbies and unsettled some Labor MPs.

Though acknowledging what he calls Australia's "fair share of challenges" and revealing that Treasury will forecast higher unemployment and lower growth, Mr Chalmers will frame the investment boom as a bright spot.

"I [have] heard the same message over and over: in a world of ratcheting risk, Australia is more and more reliable," he will tell investors at the Citi A50 Economic Forum, according to an excerpt of his remarks seen by the ABC.

"You wouldn't be here with your $25 trillion of capital if you disagreed."

Investment $50 billion better than expected

Mr Chalmers will reveal Treasury now expects business investment to grow faster than 5 per cent this financial year, doubling the May forecast.

That forecast will be formally updated in December's mid-year budget update, and while acknowledging that "potential surprises" could change this early figure, Mr Chalmers will say it would amount to an extra $50 billion in extra investment.

Earlier this year, Australia's peak business lobby the BCA declared Australia was in the middle of the pack as a global investment destination, more favourable than China, South Korea and France, but less than the United States, the UK and New Zealand.

AI investment boom Australian data centre operators have raised a record $35 billion so far this year. Meanwhile, the RBA governor says central banks globally are monitoring the risk of an AI investment bubble.

Among the BCA's recommendations was for Australia to streamline the application process for foreign investors, something the government was already progressing.

Mr Chalmers will argue it is working, with $278 billion approved so far this year and more than half of all applications now processed within a month by the Foreign Investment Review Board.

Investment in data centres for artificial intelligence has been a big factor. The ABC reported in September that Australian data centre investment had reached $35 billion for the calendar year, more than one-10th of the total $278 billion investment.

Reserve Bank burnishes inflation concern

While this investment will boost Australia's growth figures, it is also one of a handful of factors concerning the Reserve Bank as it grapples with inflation.

The bank raised the cash rate to 4.60 per cent last month, above the previous 2024 peak. Markets believe another rate hike in early November is possible.

RBA Deputy Governor Andrew Hauser sounded pessimistic in public remarks on Wednesday, saying the inflation outlook was "materially worse" than forecast.

RBA warns inflation outlook 'materially worse' As markets put the chance of a rate hike in November at more than 50 per cent, Reserve Bank deputy governor Andrew Hauser warns of a "central banker's nightmare".

The unemployment rate hit a five-year high of 4.7 per cent in September. Mr Hauser said it was "a little weaker" than had been expected but did not suggest that this would deter a rate hike, adding: "I stress the 'little' … we need to see some easing in the economy."

The economic conditions have added to political pressure on the Albanese government, with usually placid backbenchers increasingly willing to bemoan the government's handling of economic conditions in private commentary.

For some, the tax hikes on capital gains and discretionary trusts and the clumsy handling of the issue of credit card surcharges, described by one backbencher as "compounding attacks on small business", have fuelled a sense of mid-term malaise.

Shadow Treasurer Tim Wilson has seized on the prospect of a rate hike, which he attributes to the government's "spending addiction".

"I think a lot of households are looking at it right now and saying, 'We cannot bear any more'… It's quite worrying," he said in an interview on 2GB on Wednesday.

But those within government ranks who are defensive of the treasurer's performance believe that the domestic debate over economic conditions does not give enough recognition of the contribution of wars in Ukraine and the Middle East.

This was a regular feature in Mr Chalmers's international meetings, which included a G20 Finance Ministers' meeting in Bangkok, an APEC Finance Ministers' meeting in Hong Kong, and a bilateral meeting with China's Finance Minister.

The two wars [are] impacting almost every economy in one way or another, posing risks to global growth, pushing up global inflation, and pushing up borrowing costs," he will say on Friday.

"In this sea of uncertainty and risk … Australia's strengths and stability are clear and they are compelling."

World.title: Nationals leader set to attempt switch to lower house
World.content:
Federal Nationals MP Michelle Landry is set to announce her intention to retire from politics on Friday, paving the way for her leader Matt Canavan to switch to the lower house at the next election.

Ms Landry, the Nationals' chief whip, has held the Queensland seat of Capricornia since 2013.

But according to several LNP sources, she has decided to step aside at the next election, which is due in 2028.

Her office said she would make a "significant announcement" on Friday, alongside Senator Canavan.

The Nationals leader holds the number two spot on the LNP senate ticket, behind Liberal James McGrath, but is expected to nominate as the LNP candidate for Capricornia after Ms Landry's statement.

When asked recently if he had any interest in running for the seat, Senator Canavan, who lives in Yeppoon, said he would "do whatever it takes", as the Nationals faced the prospect of a wipe-out from One Nation.

Matt Canavan, Barnaby Joyce and Michelle Landry back in 2020. (Supplied: Chris Lawson)

The minor party, which is surging in the polls, announced it would open a branch in Yeppoon late last year to "help shape the future of One Nation in the region", according to its website.

"We've got a great local member there in Capricornia, Michelle Landry. I'd love to see her continue. I'd love to see all, of, my members continue," he told News24 earlier this month.

"But if I'm required, if it is required to hold one more seat in the lower house somewhere, I will do it.

" This could be my last election. I'm not going to die wondering, I'm just going to leave it all on the field now. "

Some LNP members in Capricornia have told the ABC they are ready for a change.

Senator Canavan took over the Nationals leadership in March and in recent months has become a lead campaigner for rowing to be held in Rockhampton, in Capricornia, in the 2032 Brisbane Olympic and Paralympic games.

Croc-infested river floated as 2032 Games venue The Fitzroy River in Rockhampton could host rowing events for the 2032 Games if LNP politicians get their way.

There is a view within the Nationals that their leader should be in the lower house with the other major party leaders.

LNP sources have told the ABC that ahead of Friday's announcement, there had been a lot of internal discussion about who could replace Senator Canavan on the party's senate ticket.

Support for One Nation has skyrocketed since the 2025 election, with the minor party winning seats in South Australia, Western Australia and its first ever lower house seat in federal parliament.

According to the latest Newspoll, One Nation's primary vote is sitting at 28 per cent, just below Labor on 29 per cent, and well above the Coalition which is languishing on 20 per cent.

Senator Canavan's office has been contacted for comment.

World.title: Snowy 2.0 to cost 12 times more than initial budget with further delays
World.content:
The cost of delivering Australia's biggest renewable energy project has doubled since the last estimate and is now set to become fully operational a year later than expected, according to a major review.

Snowy Hydro has released its much-anticipated cost reassessment for the Snowy 2.0 hydropower project, revealing it could cost up to $25 billion, with first power expected in early 2029 and the project to be fully operational later that year.

While the Commonwealth-owned company has set a target cost of $22 billion, it is allowing for an additional $3 billion to be spent on the project if required.

Snowy 2.0, which started being built seven years ago, had an initial budget of $2 billion and was originally expected to start operating in 2021.

Those figures were revised as part of a "project reset" three years ago, which projected first power would be delivered in late 2027 and Snowy 2.0 would be fully operational a year later, at a cost of $12 billion.

Dennis Barnes was appointed Snowy Hydro CEO in 2023. (ABC News: Isla Evans)

Late last year it was announced that the project's contractor Future Generation Joint Venture (FGJV) would conduct a "line-by-line reassessment", which has now been released three months later than initially expected.

Snowy Hydro CEO Dennis Barnes said he was "incredibly disappointed" with the update.

"We had a project that was stalled and had billions of dollars of claims on the table in 2023," he said.

"I'm pleased we've got progress, progress doubled in the first year after the reset.

"What I'm disappointed about is obviously the resultant costs of the progress we're making."

Dennis Barnes says more people are now working on Snowy 2.0 than what was expected in 2023. (ABC News: Isla Evans)

Mr Barnes said the "design immaturity" that was faced before the 2023 reset had contributed to the latest cost blowouts.

"We've understood that we're going to need a lot more people for a lot longer to deliver this job," he said.

"This job is 80 per cent people costs, we've got 5,000 people on the job now working across multiple work fronts and that's obviously a lot more than we thought in 2023."

The review found 65 per cent of machine tunnelling and 90 per cent of cavern excavation had now been completed and work to build the underground power station was underway.

While Mr Barnes said the project was in its "strongest position yet", he could not rule out further cost blowouts beyond the most recent targets.

"There's never any guarantees with mega projects, we're doing a world first thing in many respects in really complex conditions," he said.

" But the project is hitting its milestones of late, we have a lot of the risks behind us. "

How did Snowy 2.0 get here?

Snowy 2.0 is designed to underpin Australia's electricity security and affordability over coming decades, as the country transitions away from fossil fuels.

Based in the New South Wales Snowy Mountains, it will link two dams through about 27 kilometres of tunnels and include an underground pumped hydro station the size of the Sydney Opera House.

The project will act like a giant battery, pumping water upstream when electricity is cheap and releasing it back downstream to generate power when demand is high.

Snowy 2.0 will store excess power from wind and solar and deliver it to the grid when needed. (Supplied: Snowy Hydro )

It has a total capacity of 2,200 MW and is expected to power three million homes for a week, the equivalent of about 26 million household batteries.

Unlike batteries, pumped hydro offers long-duration storage, meaning it is designed to be a renewable energy insurance policy during days when there is limited sun or wind.

But Snowy 2.0 has been embroiled in controversy since it was announced by former Prime Minister Malcolm Turnbull in 2017, including cost blowouts, missed deadlines, scrutiny over safety issues and contractor disputes.

A major setback came after one of the initial three tunnel boring machines, Florence, got stuck in early 2023 for 11 months after hitting soft ground and creating a sinkhole.

The National Audit Office gave Snowy 2.0 a glowing review in 2022 but the most recent audit, released earlier this year, found "significant deficiencies" in the management of the hydropower project.

The project is billed as critical for the security of the national energy grid as coal-fired power stations continue to close. (ABC South East NSW: Isla Evans)

In a submission to a parliamentary inquiry examining the project's delivery, Snowy Hydro said initial "design immaturity" and the project's "inherent complexity" had been the primary drivers of additional costs.

"Productivity underperformance and cost escalation have also been significant factors," the submission read.

"Others have related to project-specific complexities that have developed during delivery.

" Snowy Hydro has learned and taken action in response to these challenges. "

A submission from Future Generation Joint Venture (FGJV), the group responsible for the project's construction, said "unprecedented geotechnical uncertainty" and "significant geopolitical upheaval" had contributed to cost escalations.

"Unlike metropolitan tunnelling projects, where initial ground investigations are typically well-developed, ground investigations within a national park are necessarily limited," the submission said.

"As a result, conditions only become fully apparent as excavation progresses."

Snowy 2.0 is being built in complex geological and remote conditions. (ABC News: Isla Evans)

Project benefits report released

Along with the cost reassessment, Snowy Hydro has also released an economic study conducted by engineering consultant GHD.

It found the project will contribute $18 billion to Australia's economy during the delivery phase and reduce wholesale electricity costs by more than $7b by 2075.

Mr Barnes said all technologies were needed for the energy transition, including batteries, pumped hydro and gas for firming.

"We issued a report earlier in the year to show what the grid looked like with and without Snowy 2.0 and on those periods, which are pretty common, where we get no wind and we get no sun for days on end, batteries run out of juice, they don't get recharged," he said.

"We actually saw that in January in South Australia, there was a period where the batteries run out of juice and prices went very high.

"So with Snowy 2.0 in the grid, we see that the prices in those periods were $7,000 a MWh lower."

Chris Bowen has previously criticised the former Coalition government's handling of the project prior to Labor taking over. (ABC South East NSW: Isla Evans)

A joint statement from Energy Minister Chris Bowen and Finance Minister Katy Gallagher said abandoning the hydropower project would "undermine grid reliability", scrap 5,000 jobs and lead to higher electricity bills.

"Once completed, Snowy 2.0 will be an incredible national asset, supporting Australia's energy security, price stability and the transition to renewable energy," the statement said.

"The pumped hydro expansion of the Snowy Scheme will provide more than half of the total energy storage the grid needs by 2050, strengthening energy security and putting downwards pressure on energy prices."

World.title: NT government accused of politicising Kumanjayi Little Baby's death
World.content:
Emotions boiled over in Northern Territory parliament today, with the government accused of politicising the tragic death of a five-year-old girl through a parliamentary motion against an opposition member.

Country Liberal Party Child Protection Minister Robyn Cahill began the day by moving a motion condemning her Labor counterpart Chansey Paech over comments he made to the media on Tuesday.

Following the release of a damning report into the NT's Department of Children and Families and its failings relating to Kumanjayi Little Baby, Mr Paech referenced Jefferson Lewis, who has been charged with her murder and is yet to enter a plea or face trial.

Robyn Cahill says Mr Paech's comments cannot be justified by grief, politics or frustration. (ABC News: Pete Garnish)

While speaking on the motion today, Ms Cahill used parliamentary privilege to repeat Mr Paech's comments, which were later aired by Channel 9 and the broadcast shared on the MLA's social media account.

During her speech, Ms Cahill told parliament "a man has been charged over the death of this little girl and that matter is before the courts".

"Every member of this house knows what that means," she said.

" We choose our words carefully because what matters most now is that justice is done for her and seen to be done. "

Ms Cahill said Mr Paech's comments were "offender-focused commentary" and "condemnable".

"There is no justification [Mr Paech] can offer for these comments — not grief, not politics and not frustration with the government," she said.

The report by Greg Shanahan and Karen Webb released on Tuesday found there were extensive failings by the department. (ABC News: Randi Dahnial)

"Kumanjayi Little Baby's family deserve better and so does our community."

Following the release of the report into the child protection system, Mr Paech and some child safety advocacy organisations criticised the government for only scrutinising the department while glossing over failures in other areas, including corrections, the justice system, domestic violence and housing.

They also said the report focused too much on the actions of Kumanjayi Little Baby's mother — a repeated victim of domestic violence.

Paech hits back

During Mr Paech's contribution to the debate, he said the government had politicised Kumanjayi Little Baby's death by moving the motion, which the government used its majority to pass.

A Central Australia-based MLA, Mr Paech said he had also supported the little girl's family throughout their ordeal in Alice Springs.

"I was there when Kumanjayi Little Baby's family needed someone," he said.

" I was there, I helped out with the sorry camps, I helped out with the family, I continue to help out with the family and I am not going to apologise for standing up and calling out the injustices. "

Mr Paech also said "everyone in [the] community" knew the "situation around the tragic loss of life of Kumanjayi Little Baby".

Chansey Paech accused Ms Cahill of "leaking to the media" following reports by News 24 and the NT News yesterday. (ABC News: Dane Hirst)

"To pretend or suggest I have said something that is not already out in the public domain, that my communities are not already talking about, is disrespectful to them," he said.

Mr Paech also accused Ms Cahill of "leaking to the media because that's where the stories" around Kumanjayi Little Baby "are coming from".

During question time, Labor backbencher Dheran Young asked Ms Cahill whether her department was investigating how "confidential information" identifying Mr Lewis as one of five "safe adults" in Kumanjayi Little Baby's life, had been leaked to News 24 and the NT News.

The outlets reported yesterday that a person referenced in the Webb-Shanahan report released on Tuesday as having been nominated by the department as "safe" was Mr Lewis.

In response, Ms Cahill did not address whether there was an investigation, instead saying "any information coming into the public arena that one would not expect" was "of concern".

"We are absolutely focused on not having information in the public arena that shouldn't be," she said.

"I am absolutely confident that nobody would have released information that they know that they shouldn't be releasing."

Ms Cahill said Mr Young should ask the "people who have actually put that information out into the public arena where they got it from".

"That's really the obvious place to start," she said.

World.title: Police investigating death of woman and child in Melbourne's east
World.content:
Detectives are investigating the circumstances around the death of a woman and a child in Melbourne's east tonight.

Victoria Police said they were called to Prospect Street in Box Hill just before 6:20pm, with reports a woman had been found unresponsive outside an apartment block.

An unresponsive child was discovered nearby a short time later.

"The woman and primary school-aged child could not be revived and sadly died at the scene," a police spokesperson said.

At this stage, police are not looking for anyone else in relation to the incident.

Anyone who witnessed the incident or has information has been urged to phone Crime Stoppers on 1800 333 000.

World.content:
NationalWAAUKUS Inside the rescue submarine the Navy hopes it never has to use Hamish Hastie October 23, 2026 — 3:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. There are no windows in the back, the condensation from your breath clinging to the roof drips down your neck, and you have to fold your body in half just to fit, but for a submariner stranded hundreds of metres underwater, boarding the LR5 would feel like getting into the back of a Rolls Royce. The LR5 is operated by the Australian arm of James Fisher Defence and is one of six air dispatchable submarines in the world that can be called on with just 12-hours notice to rescue submariners stranded underwater. JFD’s LR5 rescue submarine. Hamish Hastie For the past few weeks, the LR5 has been running simulated submarine rescue missions at the bottom of the Cockburn Sound and off the coast of Rottnest Island to ensure they’re match fit if the real thing ever happens. WAtoday joined the JFD team alongside senior Royal Australian Navy personnel for one of those simulated missions last week when the LR5 had to locate and connect to a fake submarine hatch known as a target plate 20 metres underwater.



The simulation tests all facets of the rescue chain, from deploying the vessel to locating the submarine, rescuing the crew and bringing them back to the surface where they exit the LR5 straight into hyperbaric chambers. JFD has held the rescue contract with the Navy since 2017, but neither the company nor the Navy would reveal the exact cost – only that it was about $23 million per annum. LR5 operator Nathan Young. Hamish Hastie That cost covers at least two full-scale training simulations each year. RAN Submarine Force commander Commodore Dan Sutherland said the LR5 and its supporting systems was essential to Australia’s submarine operations.



“This submarine and the system that supports it is really important to us. It provides assurance that should the worst happen, and all the design redundancies and features built into our submarines, should they fail or in the event of some unforeseen catastrophe, this is our lifeline,” he said. “This is the hope that we have that we will get home to our loved ones, back to Australia and to where we’ve come from in one piece, safe and sound.” JFD Australia managing director Adrian Capner in the LR5 submarine. Hamish Hastie JFD Australia managing director Adrian Capner said he didn’t believe it was expensive when it came to preserving lives. “There’s a number of different ways you can cut that, but not least of which is how much is a life worth,” he said.



“We’re only going to get one chance in a generation to prove ourselves with this system, and you know it’s going to happen on a day where it’s going to be after a grand final, or in the middle of school holidays, or like most things that happen, you know, seems to be Christmas Day. “So we have to be ready every time, fully booted and spurred.” Our simulation involved bundling into the back of the LR5, a narrow steel tube, no wider than two metres in diameter, and being slowly lowered into the ocean from the Stoker, the privately operated Navy ship transporting the submarine and hyperbaric chamber set up. RAN Submarine Force commander Commodore Dan Sutherland aboard the MV Stoker. Hamish Hastie To locate the target plate, connect, disconnect and head back to the surface took about two hours and by that time this reporter’s lower back muscles were on fire.



In a real scenario, the submarine can pick up between 14 and 16 submariners from a stranded submarine and depending on the depth of the sub and difficulty of connecting with it, could be more than six hours for a round trip. If the stranded submarine was a fully manned Collins Class that would mean days of ferrying back and forth. For the Virginia-class submarines Australia plans to purchase from the US under the AUKUS agreement, a fully manned submarine could mean more than 130 submariners needing rescue, so both JFD and the Navy are contemplating scaling up rescue capacity when the LR5 comes to the end of its life by 2032.

World.title: ‘A five-minute photo op’: Politicians scramble to contain Rivervale anger
World.content:
Exclusive NationalWACrime ‘A five-minute photo op’: Politicians scramble to contain Rivervale anger Hannah Murphy October 23, 2026 — 3:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Politicians have been left scrambling to contain growing frustration in Perth’s inner-east, as Rivervale residents hit with spiralling anti-social behaviour accuse the Cook government of passing the buck while ignoring a community living in fear. Cassie Rowe and Police Minister Reece Whitby met with local businesses to discuss ongoing issues earlier this month. Hannah Murphy Rivervale is a suburb about 10 minutes from the Perth city centre, and locals have recently highlighted ongoing dysfunction and anti-social behaviour they are experiencing due to unchecked and unsupported public housing in the suburb. Local member Cassie Rowe and Minister for Police Reece Whitby toured the suburb last week and spoke to business owners on the Kooyong Road strip, after many raised concerns when a teenager charged a passerby with a machete last month. Rowe is understood to have attended the shopping strip with a state government photographer, but did not notify media of the visit. Cafe owner Richie Harrop was one of the locals Rowe and Whitby met with, and said the visit came after months of the community working to be heard.



“The community of Rivervale is tired of being ignored, patronised and handed generic political responses that tip-toe around the edges, while the problems affecting our neighbourhood continue to escalate,” he said. Somewhere Coffee owner Richie Harrop. Hannah Murphy “We are tired of a five-minute political photo ops that generate a Facebook post but deliver no actual change.” When asked about the purpose of his visit, Whitby told reporters Rowe had approached him with concerns that had been raised with her about the Kooyong shopping strip, and asked him to visit. “I simply went along and I spoke to some of the local business people there and had a conversation with some local people about the issues,” he said.



“I know that things have improved in terms of greater police presence, [and] that had already occurred before I went there. Cassie had communicated her concerns, and police responded with some extra patrols. WA Police Minister Reece Whitby. Michael Philipps “You get those issues from time to time in areas like that.” In a follow-up email sent to business owners on Wednesday after the visit, Rowe said she was working behind the scenes to address their concerns. “I want to be very clear that the absence of a detailed update should not be mistaken for inaction,” she said.



“Anti-social community behaviour can be a challenging and complex matter to address, not exclusive to the Rivervale community, and takes time to manage.” She said she had “multiple meetings” with the City of Belmont, the Department of Communities, WA Police, and Minister for Housing and Works John Carey. Rowe also said she had hosted a public community meeting, and confirmed her discussions with Whitby. Cassie Rowe outside the Rivervale IGA complex earlier this year. Instagram “We need to address the anti-social behaviour whilst recognising that some individuals require significant support to tackle the underlying issues contributing to their circumstances,” Rowe said. However, she also urged locals to “be realistic”.



Related Article Exclusive

Public housing Footage captures teen allegedly charging man with machete at Perth shops “I recognise the frustration felt by residents and businesses who continue to experience these issues. I also believe it is important to be realistic about what can be achieved, the responsibilities of the different agencies involved and the time it can take to work through difficult and often sensitive matters. I am not going to make promises about immediate solutions or commit to deadlines that are outside my control,” Rowe said. Harrop said the email had done little to assuage local’s fears they weren’t being heard. “We’ve heard it all before; ‘it’s complicated’, ‘there are so many layers’ and ‘multiple agencies are involved’. Of course the problems are complicated - nobody suggested otherwise ... we do not expect every problem to be solved overnight, but we do expect a clear plan,” he said. Liberal MLC Phil Twiss also met locals this week, including a Rivervale couple who lodged over 60 complaints about a problematic public housing tenancy in three years.



Related Article Exclusive

Public housing Debra complained about her Rivervale neighbours 60 times in three years. It’s worse than ever Twiss went on to ask a question in parliament on Tuesday, calling on the Minister for Housing and Works John Carey to explain what was being done to help residents. “I refer to reports from business owners along Kooyong Road in Rivervale and Belmont who have experienced an increase in antisocial behaviour, including public intoxication, threatening conduct and individuals allegedly carrying weapons,” he asked. “Is the minister aware of these concerns?” Answering on behalf of Carey, Minister Jackie Jarvis offered this response.



“Complaints related to public housing tenancies must relate to a tenancy matter. Where concerns are identified, appropriate action is taken in accordance with the Residential Tenancies Act 1987,” she said. “The conduct described is a matter for the Western Australia Police Force. The Department of Housing and Works (DHW) works closely with WA Police where criminal matters related to tenancies are identified. “It is important to note that the Department of Housing and Works has no power to investigate matters that occur away from a property.” Harrop said the response is emblematic of an enduring attitude in government. “The involvement of multiple government agencies should not mean that nobody ultimately takes responsibility - if the government can identify the problem, it can develop a plan to address it,” he said.

World.title: Built by hand, cooked by heart: The story behind Freo’s backyard supper club
World.content:
NationalWAItalian Built by hand, cooked by heart: The story behind Freo’s backyard supper club Max Veenhuyzen October 23, 2026 — 3:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. There’s food that’s made by hand, and then there’s Flour & Fire: a private supper club and catering business run by Anna Tamburri and Valerio Fantinelli. Each Flour & Fire dinner is held in a commercial kitchen and homely dining area that the couple built and dug out themselves in the backyard of their suburban family home near Freo (The council are across what’s happening, as are neighbours). Valerio Fantinelli shares his thoughts on a dish with guests. Max Veenhuyzen Guests sit around a table that sits up to a dozen people and dinner is a bespoke set menu showcasing vegetables, fruits and herbs from the couple’s farm in Waroona. Some of these ingredients, such as the radicchio whose bitterness quietly contrasts the richness of roasted wagyu beef, is served fresh. Others such as the vinegars made with white wine, red wine and pomegranate that provide the thrust behind the smoked posca – a tart, aperitivo-style drink that kicks things off – are the result of patience and resourceful thinking many seasons ago.



Even some of the tableware and cutlery that guests will use over dinner (or lunch) are made from timber and other natural materials from the farm. Basically, if something’s on the table, it’s there for a reason. Tamburri and Fantinelli either made it themselves or know the person that did as well as the backstory of said item. This ability to speak to the origin of ingredients has long informed Fantinelli’s approach to cooking. One thing that the Italian-born chef wasn’t so sure about, however, was whether bringing the dinner party back to their place was a good idea. “I never thought people would pay money for dinner at our place,” Fantinelli admitted, whose CV includes stints in his native Abruzzo, Western Australia and even Bali.



Valerio Fantinelli (left), Rosie Fantinelli (second from left), friend and Anna Tamburri (right) in action during a Flour & Fire dinner. Max Veenhuyzen As it turns out, they would. What began in 2018 as a one-off vegan dinner for a group of parents from daughter Rosie’s primary school grew into the current model that sees Flour & Fire host groups on Friday and Saturday nights and, when the weather allows, Sunday lunch. In a neat full circle moment, Rosie and the couple’s son Xavier also help with dinner services, although the core team is Fantinelli in the kitchen and Tamburri running front of house. Guests can choose from two dining options when making a reservation: a traditional, share-style family meal that includes large format cuts of meat, vegetables, bread and other common sightings at nonna and nonno’s house ($180 per person), or a more contemporary degustation menu ($200 per person) that features individual plated portions of the dozen-or-so dishes on that night’s menu. Admittedly, the prices being charged are higher than your local neighbourhood pasta or pizza joint, but so is the calibre of the cooking. Perth isn’t exactly struggling for Italian dining options, yet the food that Fantinelli is serving at his Flour & Fire dinners is unique, personal and very delicious.



The wood-fired oven is a key part of Flour & Fire’s cooking. Max Veenhuyzen I’ve been lucky enough to experience these dinners twice and learned something new about Italian cuisine each time. What’s really turned my head, though, is seeing Fantinelli cleverly connects his past and present. But now, the million dollar – or more accurately, the $180 or $200 per head – question: how does one get in on this Flour & Fire action? Reservations are released seasonally with bookings for summer (December to February) going live from 9am on Monday October 26. If you can lock in a date, the table is all yours, but your party needs to be a minimum of six guests and a maximum of 12.



Crucially, reservations need to be made via email with dates being booked on a first-in, best-served basis. While Fantinelli admits that investing in an online booking system would make things easier, this booking process was chosen on purpose. “I like having that personal touch with guests,” he said. “It feels like you’re coming to my house from the very beginning.” Flour & Fire reservations for December, January and February are available from 9am on Monday, October 26. To make a reservation, send an email to val@flourandfire.com.au

World.content:
SportCricketAustralian cricket Player ratings: From the determined and a hundred to a captain’s shocker Daniel Brettig October 23, 2026 — 1:35am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Gqeberha: How did Australia’s cricketers fare individually in one of the worst defeats of Pat Cummins’ time as captain of the national team? Scott Boland - 9 Stood up with the ball to pluck another five wickets on his return to the side, then performed sterling service after being asked to play the role of nightwatchman in both innings. Continues to make the most of his opportunities in Test cricket with humility and quiet determination to succeed. Australia’s Scott Boland plays a shot on day five. AP Photo/Themba Hadebe Travis Head - 8



Well beaten by Marco Jansen in the first innings, Head responded by compiling his first overseas Test hundred in the second to give the Australians a chance of survival. Still scored at his customary good rate, but also showed considerable steel to absorb 190 balls – in many ways it was the kind of innings he had often been asked to play for a struggling South Australia but less so the Test team. Will keep opening. Travis Head celebrates his century. AP Photo/Themba Hadebe Mitchell Starc - 5 Bowled presentably after struggling on day one with damp footholds and went past 450 wickets in Tests, the most by a left-arm quick. Could have offered a little more with the bat in each innings. Steve Smith - 4



A difficult game for Smith on account of a neck problem that severely restricted him in the first innings and then dropped him to number seven in the order in the second. Will be annoyed at himself for skying a pull shot against Kagiso Rabada with the second new ball. Passed 11,000 Test runs, the third Australian after Allan Border and Ricky Ponting. Alex Carey - 4 Four catches in South Africa’s innings were somewhat overshadowed by a very poor shot to be out second ball amid the first innings collapse. Played better in the second innings but was unable to guide the tail to safety. Marnus Labuschagne - 3 Australia’s selectors have a decision to make after Labuschagne flattered to deceive yet again. Victim of an excellent slips catch in the first innings, he had made it once more into the 30s when he unwisely tried to beat a strong wind and the tallest man on the field Marco Jansen when lofting Simon Harmer down the ground. It can’t keep happening.



Marnus Labuschagne. Getty Images Matt Renshaw - 3 Fell back to earth after his Durban heroics with a pair of low scores under sustained pressure from the Proteas pacemen. Took a blinder of a catch at slip to claim a wicket for Boland. May well find himself back opening in the third Test. Beau Webster - 3 Appears to have run his race as a Test cricketer after a couple of useful years. This is the fourth game in a row in which Webster has not been able to make a significant mark, and he looked decidedly vulnerable outside off stump in both innings. Bowled tidily but without the wicket threat of his opposite number Wiaan Mulder.





Nic Maddinson - 1 Unable to resist Rabada in either innings, and on both occasions out edging new ball deliveries that he would have been better off letting go. Apart from a cavalier 48 in the second innings in Durban, Maddinson has looked off the pace, although it was the toughest of commissions to face Rabada under floodlights on night three. World.title: Australia humiliated by an innings and 31 runs in Gqeberha
World.content:
Australia’s day-four nightmare has come back to haunt them in the second Test, after falling to an innings-and-31-run defeat to South Africa in the final session.

After Travis Head’s century and Scott Boland’s defence initially repelled the Proteas, Australia lost their last wicket with 28.5 overs to play on the final day on Thursday.

South Africa’s Marco Jansen, centre, celebrates with teammates after taking the last wicket of Australia’s Josh Hazlewood. AP Photo/Themba Hadebe

It means the series will head to the third and final Test in Cape Town next Tuesday with the series level at 1-1.

Aided by rain that washed out the morning session, Australia did well to hold on for as long as they did on Thursday with Boland soaking up 166 balls as nightwatchman.

But after Head (117) and Steve Smith fell before tea, Boland was bowled shortly after the break to open the door for the Proteas at St George’s Park.

Australia’s Steve Smith reacts as he walks off the field after his dismissal on day five. AP Photo/Themba Hadebe

And when Kagiso Rabada (4-77) bowled a hard-swinging Mitchell Starc and Josh Hazlewood edged Marco Jansen to slip, the game was over.

Ultimately, Australia have been left to lick their wounds in a match they should never have been in a position to lose.

Pat Cummins’ men had South Africa 6-110 early on the third morning, after Boland’s five-wicket haul ripped through the Proteas on a wet opening two days.

But they allowed Temba Bavuma to lead a South African recovery to 9-425 declared.

And when Australia recorded their lowest first-innings score in almost 10 years on Thursday and were bowled out for 99, they were fighting to save the match.

This Test will go down as one of the Proteas’ great wins given the position they were in, with Bavuma and Marco Jansen the heroes.

For Australia, though, there will be recriminations.

Marnus Labuschagne, Nic Maddinson and Beau Webster are all under pressure to keep their spots, particularly with Cameron Green and Josh Inglis fit again.

Boland and Head briefly looked likely to save their blushes on Thursday, with their 59-run fifth-wicket stand surviving through the first 80 minutes.

But when Head played a Wiaan Mulder delivery that seamed back in at him onto his own stumps, South Africa could sniff victory again.

Smith then inexplicably attempted to pull Rabada (3-73) seven overs later against the new ball, skying him to Matthew Breetzke at mid-wicket.

That shot was one of several questionable ones for Australia over the past two days, with Labuschagne’s into gusty winds on the fourth evening with his side 1-100 equally poor.

Starc was also dismissed swinging hard at a Rabada delivery late as threatening clouds began rolling in, before Hazlewood guided Jansen straight to slip and left Alex Carey (37no) with no more support.

The pair appeared frustrated by their shots, but it is the batters that must accept the blame for Australia’s crushing defeat.

AAP

World.title: ‘Incredibly disappointing’: Snowy 2.0 cost blows out to $25b in biggest setback yet
World.content:
BusinessThe economyRenewables ‘Incredibly disappointing’: Snowy 2.0 cost blows out to $25b in biggest setback yet Nick Toscano October 22, 2026 — 10:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. The cost of the Commonwealth government’s troubled Snowy 2.0 pumped hydro scheme has exploded to potentially $25 billion – more than four times its original estimate – and its completion date has been pushed out to late 2029 as its builders grapple with severe geological challenges and soaring construction pressures. Updated advice released by Snowy Hydro Limited on Thursday night moves the estimated cost of the problem-plagued mega-project from $12 billion to $22.2 billion, with a contingency buffer bringing the potential price tag to $25 billion, marking the most severe setback yet for Australia’s largest renewable energy development. Snowy 2.0 involves digging 27 kilometres of tunnels beneath the Kosciuszko National Park. Alex Ellinghausen Snowy 2.0, a massive 2200-megawatt energy-storage project in the Snowy Mountains of NSW, is designed to act like a giant battery, storing vast amounts of energy by pumping water uphill when electricity is plentiful and then releasing it downhill through turbines when the grid needs a critical boost. Energy planners consider it a project of national significance in Australia’s shift away from ageing coal-fired power stations because of its ability to back up renewables during stretches of low wind and sunlight, with enough storage capacity to power 3 million homes for a week. When the project was first conceived in 2017, then-prime minister Malcolm Turnbull thought it could be built for $2 billion in just four years. But a year later, when the project received final investment approval in 2018, its estimated cost had already risen to nearly $6 billion. This week’s latest revision means the potential cost has quadrupled since construction began.



One of the largest and most challenging engineering projects undertaken in Australia, the project faced a succession of setbacks and delays, bogged down pandemic-related disruption, supply chain pressures and difficult tunnelling conditions deep beneath an alpine national park. The complexity of excavating extensive underground tunnels through unpredictable rock has compounded construction delays and added to costs. Related Article Electricity ‘Potentially catastrophic’: Leaked videos reveal severity of Snowy project’s blunders The latest cost revision, however, arrives at a sensitive time for the Albanese government, which is under pressure from the Coalition and One Nation over the cost of its ambitious renewable energy rollout plans. It also intensifies broader anxieties about Australia’s ability to build enough renewable energy and storage capacity in time to keep power supplies and prices steady as the majority of the nation’s ageing coal-fired power stations reach the end of their operational lives over the coming decade. Dennis Barnes, chief executive of Snowy Hydro, on Thursday acknowledged that the cost increase was “incredibly disappointing”, but insisted the long-term value of Snowy 2.0 to Australia’s energy reliability was stronger than ever.



“The scale of Snowy 2.0’s energy storage is world-leading – more than half of the total energy storage the grid needs by 2050 will come from Snowy 2.0 alone,” he said. “Snowy 2.0’s massive, long-duration storage will be the grid’s insurance policy against multi-day wind and solar droughts, helping to prevent blackouts and control price spikes that would otherwise flow through to household electricity bills,” he said. Related Article Renewables ‘Diabolic’: Massive cost pressures on $12 billion Snowy 2.0 revealed Barnes attributed the bulk of the cost blowout to “design immaturity”, saying underdeveloped planning work when the project was first conceived had obscured the true scale and geotechnical complexity. He said the decision to reset Snowy’s contract with its principal construction contractor, Future Generation Joint Venture, in 2023, had protected the project from the threat of an even larger cost overruns. “Moving from a fixed-price contract, which was never suitable for such scale, uniqueness and complexity, has protected the project from an even greater cost increase,” he said.



Federal Energy Minister Chris Bowen and Finance Minister Katy Gallagher pointed the finger at the previous Coalition government for signing off on underprepared plans. “This revised cost and delivery schedule has been driven by cost pressures in the construction sector and the significant geological challenges of the project, exacerbated by design immaturity when it was first announced by the former government,” they said. “The government remains transparent about the pressures facing this project and securing the best possible outcome for taxpayers, energy consumers and the grid. The former Coalition government left behind a project facing major delays, rising costs and serious delivery risks.” The ministers cited the findings of a new independent economic assessment of Snowy 2.0’s net benefits, which include improving the availability of low-cost renewable energy and limiting wholesale power price spikes by reducing the need to call on expensive gas-fired power generation during peak evening demand periods and ageing, failure-prone coal-fired power plants. “The Coalition itself said Snowy 2.0 was ‘critical to the security and stability’ of the national electricity market and will ‘put downward pressure on wholesale electricity prices’ – those facts have not changed,” they said.



However, opposition energy spokesman Dan Tehan called on Bowen to apologise to taxpayers for the extent to which “costs have blown out under his watch” and said Bowen should resign or be removed as energy minister. “If the CEO of a company oversaw such blowouts, the board would have no choice but to sack him – Anthony Albanese should do the same to Chris Bowen,” he said. Related Article Updated

Energy Tesla and power giants revolt against Australia’s ‘EV charger tax’ As Australia’s energy transition approaches a critical juncture, state and federal governments are relying on Snowy 2.0 to play a major role in the future make-up of the grid. More than half of the remaining coal-fired generators are scheduled to close by 2035 as their owners grapple with rising maintenance costs, declining reliability and competition from cheaper renewables, especially during daylight hours. The Australian Energy Market Operator and major electric companies insist that replacing those plants with wind and solar – backed up by gas-powered generation, large batteries, and pumped hydroelectric systems like Snowy 2.0 – is the cheapest way to maintain grid reliability, rather than forcing the extensions of coal-fired power plants that can break down with no notice and cause huge price rises. There are clear signs that the clean energy transition is having a positive impact on prices. New data from the market operator, to be released on Friday, reveals wholesale electricity costs – what retailers pay generators before selling power to customers – fell 27 per cent year-on-year across eastern Australia in the September quarter, the lowest average for that period since 2021, partly due to a boom in grid-scale batteries smoothing out price spikes by shifting greater volumes of lower-cost renewable energy from the daytime to the evening peaks.



“Electricity use continues to grow, but more solar and storage is changing when energy is produced, drawn from the grid and shifted across the day,” AEMO executive manager of policy Violette Mouchaileh said. World.content:
NationalWAAUKUS Inside the rescue submarine the Navy hopes it never has to use Hamish Hastie October 23, 2026 — 3:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. There are no windows in the back, the condensation from your breath clinging to the roof drips down your neck, and you have to fold your body in half just to fit, but for a submariner stranded hundreds of metres underwater, boarding the LR5 would feel like getting into the back of a Rolls Royce. The LR5 is operated by the Australian arm of James Fisher Defence and is one of six air dispatchable submarines in the world that can be called on with just 12-hours notice to rescue submariners stranded underwater. JFD’s LR5 rescue submarine. Hamish Hastie For the past few weeks, the LR5 has been running simulated submarine rescue missions at the bottom of the Cockburn Sound and off the coast of Rottnest Island to ensure they’re match fit if the real thing ever happens. WAtoday joined the JFD team alongside senior Royal Australian Navy personnel for one of those simulated missions last week when the LR5 had to locate and connect to a fake submarine hatch known as a target plate 20 metres underwater.



The simulation tests all facets of the rescue chain, from deploying the vessel to locating the submarine, rescuing the crew and bringing them back to the surface where they exit the LR5 straight into hyperbaric chambers. JFD has held the rescue contract with the Navy since 2017, but neither the company nor the Navy would reveal the exact cost – only that it was about $23 million per annum. LR5 operator Nathan Young. Hamish Hastie That cost covers at least two full-scale training simulations each year. RAN Submarine Force commander Commodore Dan Sutherland said the LR5 and its supporting systems was essential to Australia’s submarine operations.



“This submarine and the system that supports it is really important to us. It provides assurance that should the worst happen, and all the design redundancies and features built into our submarines, should they fail or in the event of some unforeseen catastrophe, this is our lifeline,” he said. “This is the hope that we have that we will get home to our loved ones, back to Australia and to where we’ve come from in one piece, safe and sound.” JFD Australia managing director Adrian Capner in the LR5 submarine. Hamish Hastie JFD Australia managing director Adrian Capner said he didn’t believe it was expensive when it came to preserving lives. “There’s a number of different ways you can cut that, but not least of which is how much is a life worth,” he said.



“We’re only going to get one chance in a generation to prove ourselves with this system, and you know it’s going to happen on a day where it’s going to be after a grand final, or in the middle of school holidays, or like most things that happen, you know, seems to be Christmas Day. “So we have to be ready every time, fully booted and spurred.” Our simulation involved bundling into the back of the LR5, a narrow steel tube, no wider than two metres in diameter, and being slowly lowered into the ocean from the Stoker, the privately operated Navy ship transporting the submarine and hyperbaric chamber set up. RAN Submarine Force commander Commodore Dan Sutherland aboard the MV Stoker. Hamish Hastie To locate the target plate, connect, disconnect and head back to the surface took about two hours and by that time this reporter’s lower back muscles were on fire.



In a real scenario, the submarine can pick up between 14 and 16 submariners from a stranded submarine and depending on the depth of the sub and difficulty of connecting with it, could be more than six hours for a round trip. If the stranded submarine was a fully manned Collins Class that would mean days of ferrying back and forth. For the Virginia-class submarines Australia plans to purchase from the US under the AUKUS agreement, a fully manned submarine could mean more than 130 submariners needing rescue, so both JFD and the Navy are contemplating scaling up rescue capacity when the LR5 comes to the end of its life by 2032.
