World.title: ‘A five-minute photo op’: Politicians scramble to contain Rivervale anger
World.content:
Exclusive NationalWACrime ‘A five-minute photo op’: Politicians scramble to contain Rivervale anger Hannah Murphy October 23, 2026 — 3:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Politicians have been left scrambling to contain growing frustration in Perth’s inner-east, as Rivervale residents hit with spiralling anti-social behaviour accuse the Cook government of passing the buck while ignoring a community living in fear. Cassie Rowe and Police Minister Reece Whitby met with local businesses to discuss ongoing issues earlier this month. Hannah Murphy Rivervale is a suburb about 10 minutes from the Perth city centre, and locals have recently highlighted ongoing dysfunction and anti-social behaviour they are experiencing due to unchecked and unsupported public housing in the suburb. Local member Cassie Rowe and Minister for Police Reece Whitby toured the suburb last week and spoke to business owners on the Kooyong Road strip, after many raised concerns when a teenager charged a passerby with a machete last month. Rowe is understood to have attended the shopping strip with a state government photographer, but did not notify media of the visit. Cafe owner Richie Harrop was one of the locals Rowe and Whitby met with, and said the visit came after months of the community working to be heard.



“The community of Rivervale is tired of being ignored, patronised and handed generic political responses that tip-toe around the edges, while the problems affecting our neighbourhood continue to escalate,” he said. Somewhere Coffee owner Richie Harrop. Hannah Murphy “We are tired of a five-minute political photo ops that generate a Facebook post but deliver no actual change.” When asked about the purpose of his visit, Whitby told reporters Rowe had approached him with concerns that had been raised with her about the Kooyong shopping strip, and asked him to visit. “I simply went along and I spoke to some of the local business people there and had a conversation with some local people about the issues,” he said.



“I know that things have improved in terms of greater police presence, [and] that had already occurred before I went there. Cassie had communicated her concerns, and police responded with some extra patrols. WA Police Minister Reece Whitby. Michael Philipps “You get those issues from time to time in areas like that.” In a follow-up email sent to business owners on Wednesday after the visit, Rowe said she was working behind the scenes to address their concerns. “I want to be very clear that the absence of a detailed update should not be mistaken for inaction,” she said.



“Anti-social community behaviour can be a challenging and complex matter to address, not exclusive to the Rivervale community, and takes time to manage.” She said she had “multiple meetings” with the City of Belmont, the Department of Communities, WA Police, and Minister for Housing and Works John Carey. Rowe also said she had hosted a public community meeting, and confirmed her discussions with Whitby. Cassie Rowe outside the Rivervale IGA complex earlier this year. Instagram “We need to address the anti-social behaviour whilst recognising that some individuals require significant support to tackle the underlying issues contributing to their circumstances,” Rowe said. However, she also urged locals to “be realistic”.



Related Article Exclusive

Public housing Footage captures teen allegedly charging man with machete at Perth shops “I recognise the frustration felt by residents and businesses who continue to experience these issues. I also believe it is important to be realistic about what can be achieved, the responsibilities of the different agencies involved and the time it can take to work through difficult and often sensitive matters. I am not going to make promises about immediate solutions or commit to deadlines that are outside my control,” Rowe said. Harrop said the email had done little to assuage local’s fears they weren’t being heard. “We’ve heard it all before; ‘it’s complicated’, ‘there are so many layers’ and ‘multiple agencies are involved’. Of course the problems are complicated - nobody suggested otherwise ... we do not expect every problem to be solved overnight, but we do expect a clear plan,” he said. Liberal MLC Phil Twiss also met locals this week, including a Rivervale couple who lodged over 60 complaints about a problematic public housing tenancy in three years.



Related Article Exclusive

Public housing Debra complained about her Rivervale neighbours 60 times in three years. It’s worse than ever Twiss went on to ask a question in parliament on Tuesday, calling on the Minister for Housing and Works John Carey to explain what was being done to help residents. “I refer to reports from business owners along Kooyong Road in Rivervale and Belmont who have experienced an increase in antisocial behaviour, including public intoxication, threatening conduct and individuals allegedly carrying weapons,” he asked. “Is the minister aware of these concerns?” Answering on behalf of Carey, Minister Jackie Jarvis offered this response.



“Complaints related to public housing tenancies must relate to a tenancy matter. Where concerns are identified, appropriate action is taken in accordance with the Residential Tenancies Act 1987,” she said. “The conduct described is a matter for the Western Australia Police Force. The Department of Housing and Works (DHW) works closely with WA Police where criminal matters related to tenancies are identified. “It is important to note that the Department of Housing and Works has no power to investigate matters that occur away from a property.” Harrop said the response is emblematic of an enduring attitude in government. “The involvement of multiple government agencies should not mean that nobody ultimately takes responsibility - if the government can identify the problem, it can develop a plan to address it,” he said.

World.title: Built by hand, cooked by heart: The story behind Freo’s backyard supper club
World.content:
NationalWAItalian Built by hand, cooked by heart: The story behind Freo’s backyard supper club Max Veenhuyzen October 23, 2026 — 3:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. There’s food that’s made by hand, and then there’s Flour & Fire: a private supper club and catering business run by Anna Tamburri and Valerio Fantinelli. Each Flour & Fire dinner is held in a commercial kitchen and homely dining area that the couple built and dug out themselves in the backyard of their suburban family home near Freo (The council are across what’s happening, as are neighbours). Valerio Fantinelli shares his thoughts on a dish with guests. Max Veenhuyzen Guests sit around a table that sits up to a dozen people and dinner is a bespoke set menu showcasing vegetables, fruits and herbs from the couple’s farm in Waroona. Some of these ingredients, such as the radicchio whose bitterness quietly contrasts the richness of roasted wagyu beef, is served fresh. Others such as the vinegars made with white wine, red wine and pomegranate that provide the thrust behind the smoked posca – a tart, aperitivo-style drink that kicks things off – are the result of patience and resourceful thinking many seasons ago.



Even some of the tableware and cutlery that guests will use over dinner (or lunch) are made from timber and other natural materials from the farm. Basically, if something’s on the table, it’s there for a reason. Tamburri and Fantinelli either made it themselves or know the person that did as well as the backstory of said item. This ability to speak to the origin of ingredients has long informed Fantinelli’s approach to cooking. One thing that the Italian-born chef wasn’t so sure about, however, was whether bringing the dinner party back to their place was a good idea. “I never thought people would pay money for dinner at our place,” Fantinelli admitted, whose CV includes stints in his native Abruzzo, Western Australia and even Bali.



Valerio Fantinelli (left), Rosie Fantinelli (second from left), friend and Anna Tamburri (right) in action during a Flour & Fire dinner. Max Veenhuyzen As it turns out, they would. What began in 2018 as a one-off vegan dinner for a group of parents from daughter Rosie’s primary school grew into the current model that sees Flour & Fire host groups on Friday and Saturday nights and, when the weather allows, Sunday lunch. In a neat full circle moment, Rosie and the couple’s son Xavier also help with dinner services, although the core team is Fantinelli in the kitchen and Tamburri running front of house. Guests can choose from two dining options when making a reservation: a traditional, share-style family meal that includes large format cuts of meat, vegetables, bread and other common sightings at nonna and nonno’s house ($180 per person), or a more contemporary degustation menu ($200 per person) that features individual plated portions of the dozen-or-so dishes on that night’s menu. Admittedly, the prices being charged are higher than your local neighbourhood pasta or pizza joint, but so is the calibre of the cooking. Perth isn’t exactly struggling for Italian dining options, yet the food that Fantinelli is serving at his Flour & Fire dinners is unique, personal and very delicious.



The wood-fired oven is a key part of Flour & Fire’s cooking. Max Veenhuyzen I’ve been lucky enough to experience these dinners twice and learned something new about Italian cuisine each time. What’s really turned my head, though, is seeing Fantinelli cleverly connects his past and present. But now, the million dollar – or more accurately, the $180 or $200 per head – question: how does one get in on this Flour & Fire action? Reservations are released seasonally with bookings for summer (December to February) going live from 9am on Monday October 26. If you can lock in a date, the table is all yours, but your party needs to be a minimum of six guests and a maximum of 12.



Crucially, reservations need to be made via email with dates being booked on a first-in, best-served basis. While Fantinelli admits that investing in an online booking system would make things easier, this booking process was chosen on purpose. “I like having that personal touch with guests,” he said. “It feels like you’re coming to my house from the very beginning.” Flour & Fire reservations for December, January and February are available from 9am on Monday, October 26. To make a reservation, send an email to val@flourandfire.com.au

World.content:
SportCricketAustralian cricket Player ratings: From the determined and a hundred to a captain’s shocker Daniel Brettig October 23, 2026 — 1:35am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Gqeberha: How did Australia’s cricketers fare individually in one of the worst defeats of Pat Cummins’ time as captain of the national team? Scott Boland - 9 Stood up with the ball to pluck another five wickets on his return to the side, then performed sterling service after being asked to play the role of nightwatchman in both innings. Continues to make the most of his opportunities in Test cricket with humility and quiet determination to succeed. Australia’s Scott Boland plays a shot on day five. AP Photo/Themba Hadebe Travis Head - 8



Well beaten by Marco Jansen in the first innings, Head responded by compiling his first overseas Test hundred in the second to give the Australians a chance of survival. Still scored at his customary good rate, but also showed considerable steel to absorb 190 balls – in many ways it was the kind of innings he had often been asked to play for a struggling South Australia but less so the Test team. Will keep opening. Travis Head celebrates his century. AP Photo/Themba Hadebe Mitchell Starc - 5 Bowled presentably after struggling on day one with damp footholds and went past 450 wickets in Tests, the most by a left-arm quick. Could have offered a little more with the bat in each innings. Steve Smith - 4



A difficult game for Smith on account of a neck problem that severely restricted him in the first innings and then dropped him to number seven in the order in the second. Will be annoyed at himself for skying a pull shot against Kagiso Rabada with the second new ball. Passed 11,000 Test runs, the third Australian after Allan Border and Ricky Ponting. Alex Carey - 4 Four catches in South Africa’s innings were somewhat overshadowed by a very poor shot to be out second ball amid the first innings collapse. Played better in the second innings but was unable to guide the tail to safety. Marnus Labuschagne - 3 Australia’s selectors have a decision to make after Labuschagne flattered to deceive yet again. Victim of an excellent slips catch in the first innings, he had made it once more into the 30s when he unwisely tried to beat a strong wind and the tallest man on the field Marco Jansen when lofting Simon Harmer down the ground. It can’t keep happening.



Marnus Labuschagne. Getty Images Matt Renshaw - 3 Fell back to earth after his Durban heroics with a pair of low scores under sustained pressure from the Proteas pacemen. Took a blinder of a catch at slip to claim a wicket for Boland. May well find himself back opening in the third Test. Beau Webster - 3 Appears to have run his race as a Test cricketer after a couple of useful years. This is the fourth game in a row in which Webster has not been able to make a significant mark, and he looked decidedly vulnerable outside off stump in both innings. Bowled tidily but without the wicket threat of his opposite number Wiaan Mulder.





Nic Maddinson - 1 Unable to resist Rabada in either innings, and on both occasions out edging new ball deliveries that he would have been better off letting go. Apart from a cavalier 48 in the second innings in Durban, Maddinson has looked off the pace, although it was the toughest of commissions to face Rabada under floodlights on night three. World.title: Australia humiliated by an innings and 31 runs in Gqeberha
World.content:
Australia’s day-four nightmare has come back to haunt them in the second Test, after falling to an innings-and-31-run defeat to South Africa in the final session.

After Travis Head’s century and Scott Boland’s defence initially repelled the Proteas, Australia lost their last wicket with 28.5 overs to play on the final day on Thursday.

South Africa’s Marco Jansen, centre, celebrates with teammates after taking the last wicket of Australia’s Josh Hazlewood. AP Photo/Themba Hadebe

It means the series will head to the third and final Test in Cape Town next Tuesday with the series level at 1-1.

Aided by rain that washed out the morning session, Australia did well to hold on for as long as they did on Thursday with Boland soaking up 166 balls as nightwatchman.

But after Head (117) and Steve Smith fell before tea, Boland was bowled shortly after the break to open the door for the Proteas at St George’s Park.

Australia’s Steve Smith reacts as he walks off the field after his dismissal on day five. AP Photo/Themba Hadebe

And when Kagiso Rabada (4-77) bowled a hard-swinging Mitchell Starc and Josh Hazlewood edged Marco Jansen to slip, the game was over.

Ultimately, Australia have been left to lick their wounds in a match they should never have been in a position to lose.

Pat Cummins’ men had South Africa 6-110 early on the third morning, after Boland’s five-wicket haul ripped through the Proteas on a wet opening two days.

But they allowed Temba Bavuma to lead a South African recovery to 9-425 declared.

And when Australia recorded their lowest first-innings score in almost 10 years on Thursday and were bowled out for 99, they were fighting to save the match.

This Test will go down as one of the Proteas’ great wins given the position they were in, with Bavuma and Marco Jansen the heroes.

For Australia, though, there will be recriminations.

Marnus Labuschagne, Nic Maddinson and Beau Webster are all under pressure to keep their spots, particularly with Cameron Green and Josh Inglis fit again.

Boland and Head briefly looked likely to save their blushes on Thursday, with their 59-run fifth-wicket stand surviving through the first 80 minutes.

But when Head played a Wiaan Mulder delivery that seamed back in at him onto his own stumps, South Africa could sniff victory again.

Smith then inexplicably attempted to pull Rabada (3-73) seven overs later against the new ball, skying him to Matthew Breetzke at mid-wicket.

That shot was one of several questionable ones for Australia over the past two days, with Labuschagne’s into gusty winds on the fourth evening with his side 1-100 equally poor.

Starc was also dismissed swinging hard at a Rabada delivery late as threatening clouds began rolling in, before Hazlewood guided Jansen straight to slip and left Alex Carey (37no) with no more support.

The pair appeared frustrated by their shots, but it is the batters that must accept the blame for Australia’s crushing defeat.

AAP

World.title: ‘Incredibly disappointing’: Snowy 2.0 cost blows out to $25b in biggest setback yet
World.content:
BusinessThe economyRenewables ‘Incredibly disappointing’: Snowy 2.0 cost blows out to $25b in biggest setback yet Nick Toscano October 22, 2026 — 10:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

The cost of the Commonwealth government’s troubled Snowy 2.0 pumped hydro scheme has exploded to potentially $25 billion – more than four times its original estimate – and its completion date has been pushed out to late 2029 as its builders grapple with severe geological challenges and soaring construction pressures. Updated advice released by Snowy Hydro Limited on Thursday night moves the estimated cost of the problem-plagued mega-project from $12 billion to $22.2 billion, with a contingency buffer bringing the potential price tag to $25 billion, marking the most severe setback yet for Australia’s largest renewable energy development. Snowy 2.0 involves digging 27 kilometres of tunnels beneath the Kosciuszko National Park. Alex Ellinghausen Snowy 2.0, a massive 2200-megawatt energy-storage project in the Snowy Mountains of NSW, is designed to act like a giant battery, storing vast amounts of energy by pumping water uphill when electricity is plentiful and then releasing it downhill through turbines when the grid needs a critical boost. Energy planners consider it a project of national significance in Australia’s shift away from ageing coal-fired power stations because of its ability to back up renewables during stretches of low wind and sunlight, with enough storage capacity to power 3 million homes for a week. When the project was first conceived in 2017, then-prime minister Malcolm Turnbull thought it could be built for $2 billion in just four years. But a year later, when the project received final investment approval in 2018, its estimated cost had already risen to nearly $6 billion. This week’s latest revision means the potential cost has quadrupled since construction began.



One of the largest and most challenging engineering projects undertaken in Australia, the project faced a succession of setbacks and delays, bogged down pandemic-related disruption, supply chain pressures and difficult tunnelling conditions deep beneath an alpine national park. The complexity of excavating extensive underground tunnels through unpredictable rock has compounded construction delays and added to costs. Related Article Electricity ‘Potentially catastrophic’: Leaked videos reveal severity of Snowy project’s blunders The latest cost revision, however, arrives at a sensitive time for the Albanese government, which is under pressure from the Coalition and One Nation over the cost of its ambitious renewable energy rollout plans. It also intensifies broader anxieties about Australia’s ability to build enough renewable energy and storage capacity in time to keep power supplies and prices steady as the majority of the nation’s ageing coal-fired power stations reach the end of their operational lives over the coming decade. Dennis Barnes, chief executive of Snowy Hydro, on Thursday acknowledged that the cost increase was “incredibly disappointing”, but insisted the long-term value of Snowy 2.0 to Australia’s energy reliability was stronger than ever.



“The scale of Snowy 2.0’s energy storage is world-leading – more than half of the total energy storage the grid needs by 2050 will come from Snowy 2.0 alone,” he said. “Snowy 2.0’s massive, long-duration storage will be the grid’s insurance policy against multi-day wind and solar droughts, helping to prevent blackouts and control price spikes that would otherwise flow through to household electricity bills,” he said. Related Article Renewables ‘Diabolic’: Massive cost pressures on $12 billion Snowy 2.0 revealed Barnes attributed the bulk of the cost blowout to “design immaturity”, saying underdeveloped planning work when the project was first conceived had obscured the true scale and geotechnical complexity. He said the decision to reset Snowy’s contract with its principal construction contractor, Future Generation Joint Venture, in 2023, had protected the project from the threat of an even larger cost overruns. “Moving from a fixed-price contract, which was never suitable for such scale, uniqueness and complexity, has protected the project from an even greater cost increase,” he said.



Federal Energy Minister Chris Bowen and Finance Minister Katy Gallagher pointed the finger at the previous Coalition government for signing off on underprepared plans. “This revised cost and delivery schedule has been driven by cost pressures in the construction sector and the significant geological challenges of the project, exacerbated by design immaturity when it was first announced by the former government,” they said. “The government remains transparent about the pressures facing this project and securing the best possible outcome for taxpayers, energy consumers and the grid. The former Coalition government left behind a project facing major delays, rising costs and serious delivery risks.” The ministers cited the findings of a new independent economic assessment of Snowy 2.0’s net benefits, which include improving the availability of low-cost renewable energy and limiting wholesale power price spikes by reducing the need to call on expensive gas-fired power generation during peak evening demand periods and ageing, failure-prone coal-fired power plants. “The Coalition itself said Snowy 2.0 was ‘critical to the security and stability’ of the national electricity market and will ‘put downward pressure on wholesale electricity prices’ – those facts have not changed,” they said.



However, opposition energy spokesman Dan Tehan called on Bowen to apologise to taxpayers for the extent to which “costs have blown out under his watch” and said Bowen should resign or be removed as energy minister. “If the CEO of a company oversaw such blowouts, the board would have no choice but to sack him – Anthony Albanese should do the same to Chris Bowen,” he said. Related Article Updated

Energy Tesla and power giants revolt against Australia’s ‘EV charger tax’ As Australia’s energy transition approaches a critical juncture, state and federal governments are relying on Snowy 2.0 to play a major role in the future make-up of the grid. More than half of the remaining coal-fired generators are scheduled to close by 2035 as their owners grapple with rising maintenance costs, declining reliability and competition from cheaper renewables, especially during daylight hours. The Australian Energy Market Operator and major electric companies insist that replacing those plants with wind and solar – backed up by gas-powered generation, large batteries, and pumped hydroelectric systems like Snowy 2.0 – is the cheapest way to maintain grid reliability, rather than forcing the extensions of coal-fired power plants that can break down with no notice and cause huge price rises. There are clear signs that the clean energy transition is having a positive impact on prices. New data from the market operator, to be released on Friday, reveals wholesale electricity costs – what retailers pay generators before selling power to customers – fell 27 per cent year-on-year across eastern Australia in the September quarter, the lowest average for that period since 2021, partly due to a boom in grid-scale batteries smoothing out price spikes by shifting greater volumes of lower-cost renewable energy from the daytime to the evening peaks.



“Electricity use continues to grow, but more solar and storage is changing when energy is produced, drawn from the grid and shifted across the day,” AEMO executive manager of policy Violette Mouchaileh said. World.title: More funding needed for GPs in areas of high deprivation, researchers say
World.content:
More funding is needed for general practices that serve patients with high needs, researchers say.

A study of more than 4700 patients at a Porirua practice found a quarter had been diagnosed with diabetes or prediabetes.

Researchers examined the healthcare provided at the Porirua Union and Community Health Service in Cannons Creek, an area of high socioeconomic deprivation, over a 12-month period between April 2022 and March 2023.

Lead researcher Dr Christine Barthow from the University of Otago, Wellington, said one of the most striking findings was that people with prediabetes, like those with diabetes, often had a number of other long-term health conditions that needed to be managed.

"Prediabetes is often viewed as simply a risk state, but we found that many people already had complex health needs before diabetes was diagnosed," she said.

Compared with people with normal blood sugar levels, those with prediabetes and diabetes used healthcare services more frequently.

People with diabetes had nearly twice as many consultations, three times as many prescriptions, and substantially higher rates of emergency department visits and potentially preventable hospital admissions.

The research was co-led by Porirua Union and Community Health Service GP Dr Bryan Betty.

Betty said government funding for primary healthcare needed to be better targeted to reflect the complexity and intensity of care required in communities with high-needs patients.

"Most of the healthcare for people with type 2 diabetes, prediabetes and multiple long-term conditions is provided through general practice, but these services are under increasing strain," he said.

"The pressure is particularly acute in practices which serve mainly patients with greater clinical complexity or who experience socioeconomic deprivation."

Betty said early diagnosis, consistent monitoring and timely intervention was important for patients with diabetes and those at risk of developing the disease.

Almost 350,000 New Zealanders have diabetes and this number is expected to rise to half a million by 2044.

Dr Christine Barthow from the University of Otago, Wellington. Supplied / University of Otago

Barthow said there were significant inequities in terms of the impact of diabetes on New Zealanders.

"People living in the most socioeconomically deprived areas are 2.7 times more likely to develop diabetes than those in the least deprived areas, and people of Pacific, Indian/South Asian, or Māori descent have a significantly higher incidence than those of European descent," she said.

"Ensuring primary healthcare is properly funded to manage high-needs patients really is vital if we are to improve population health outcomes and reduce inequities."

World.title: 'We've got to do things differently': Goldsmith makes his plea at lively Epsom debate
World.content:
Epsom voters have long been savvy about strategic voting, giving ACT their electorate vote, and National the party vote.

The country's smallest and wealthiest seat was the only one where National won the largest party vote share in its 2020 drubbing.

But the days of a deal over a cup of tea are long gone.

Polling on 11 percent in this week's 1News Verian poll, ACT doesn't need the seat to survive anymore.

Instead, it's National's Paul Goldsmith who's at risk.

The veteran candidate is ranked sixth on the party list. Even that might not be enough to save him.

Goldsmith, who has spent his entire time in Parliament as a list MP ("Not from any lack of desire, on my part," he says) faces a future outside of Parliament on current polling, unless he can loosen his coalition colleague David Seymour's iron grip on the seat.

At the Sommervell Presbyterian Church on Thursday night, the 10th election debate at this location, moderator Tim Watkin acknowledged there was a "real interest, nationally" in the electorate, as Goldsmith set out his claim.

"For 15 years that I've been in Parliament, we've had an ACT MP and National MP based here, and I think it's been a good combination," Goldsmith said.

Goldsmith said "at the start" it made sense not to contest the seat.

"Not from any lack of desire on my part. It's just the way things were."

But now, he's arguing for two ticks blue.

"If we want to keep both an ACT and a National presence in the electorate, we've got to do things differently this time."

The Epsom candidates. RNZ / Giles Dexter

ACT has held the seat since 2005, Seymour since 2014.

He thought Goldsmith was talking down his party's chances, and that National would bring a number of list MPs in.

"Epsom has always had a strategy, but Epsom has never been only a strategy. You do actually have to want the job, and do the job, and be up there representing people day by day, whether you think it's to your electoral advantage or not. There's a difference between public service and politics," he said.

"It belongs, and has always belonged, to the people of Epsom."

The duo were joined by Labour's Camilla Belich, the Greens' Lawrence Xu-Nan, and New Zealand First's Martin Gummer.

The Opportunity Party's candidate Paul Jackson was a late no-show.

"A lost opportunity," remarked one crowd member.

Health, tax, Winston ... and the mob

Perhaps because he was sat on the end, and furthest away from the moderator, Seymour spent some early portions of the two-hour debate frozen out.

Amidst an argument between Goldsmith, Belich, and Xu-Nan on the health system, he joked their parties would not be able to run supermarkets as they would be "arguing about whose job it was to put Toffee Pops on the shelf".

He was able to get going when talking about debt, tax, and interest rates, and his contributions garnered strong support from the crowd, albeit helped by the pink jacket-clad crew of supporters in the front row.

Despite Goldsmith's role as National's justice spokesperson, the controversy around candidates appearing at a gang pad was only occasionally mentioned, and usually as an effort from Goldsmith to change the subject.

"When's she going to talk about the Mongrel Mob?" Goldsmith interjected when Belich spoke of her background in law, and her opposition to changes to unjustified dismissal laws.

Epsom is the country's smallest and wealthiest seat. RNZ / Giles Dexter

A question from the floor about US Vice President JD Vance appeared to floor Goldsmith, until he took advantage of being in the spotlight.

"While I've got the microphone, I do want to ask my neighbour: has she visited a Mongrel Mob pad?"

"No, I haven't," responded Belich. "Have you?"

With Auckland Hospital and Starship both in the electorate, Belich was keen to talk about health.

As the candidates debated whether or not the health system was in crisis, she told them to speak to the frontline.

"I think it is worth listening to them, the people who actually do the work, and when they say it's in crisis actually believe them."

Xu-Nan, holder of the record for the most words spoken in the House last term, also held his own in the church, getting support for criticising comments Winston Peters made to him in the House.

The Green MP also denied Peters' claim that he spoke to him directly about the comments.

"This particular issue has never been discussed, and I'm flabbergasted that he's actually gone out and said we had a conversation. Perhaps he could be lying. Perhaps he could have mistaken me for another MP, which, to be honest, is also highly likely."

Gummer, the only candidate on stage who has not been a member of Parliament, told Xu-Nan that Parliament was a robust place, that much worse things were said in Parliament, and it was time to move on.

But the crowd at times turned against Xu-Nan, none more so than when he started to explain why parties have met with the Mongrel Mob.

After the debate, a constituent named Jane told RNZ she was not sure what the outcome of the vote would be.

"People around here that I know of have their own minds about things. They're not looking to someone to tell them how to vote," she said.

"A lot of them will vote for who they most want to represent them, not for concocting numbers."

Another voter, also named Jane, said she enjoyed the opportunity to see the candidates' characters, and was on the lookout for arrogance and humility.

"It's those offhand, arrogant comments that actually have more of an influence on their personality than their good ideas," she said.

Jane called Seymour "trumped up", and "sort of" felt sorry for Goldsmith and the situation he was in.

World.title: Destiny Church leader Brian Tamaki says he's been denied entry to Australia
World.content:
Destiny Church leader Brian Tamaki says he has been denied entry into Australia over "inflammatory and concerning" statements online.

Tamaki took to social media saying he had flown to Brisbane for a church conference, when he was detained by the border force.

In the video, the religious leader says he was interrogated for 12 hours, before his visa was cancelled.

"It was a whole day spent on Tuesday being interrogated by different border control officers in a tiny cell-like room, shut doors, and it was a very intense time," Tamaki said.

Tamaki said he had been detained in Australia under Section 116 of Australia's Migration Act.

He claimed Australian Border Force documents said his presence in Australia "may risk the good order of the Australian community, or a segment of the Australian community, namely the Sikh and Muslim communities".

The documents also described his social media statements as "inflammatory and concerning", Tamaki claimed.

Tamaki had earlier this week appeared in Manukau District Court, where he denied claims he incited rational disharmony.

In June, he accused India's Prime Minister Narendra Modi of purging Christians in the South Asian nation.

"He [Modi] is currently purging India of all Christians and burning church buildings down," Tamaki had said in a video posted on social media.

"I think we should reciprocate in kind. Let's purge New Zealand of Hindus, Sikhs and Muslims. And, while we're at it, if they're burning churches down, why don't we burn mosques and their temples down? Tit for tat."

Tamaki told media outside court that he had challenged religion, not race.

"They're trying to say it's racial, and I'm saying to them it never has been. I don't dislike or hate anybody," he said.

"In all my 35, 40 years of ministry, it's about acceptance, it's about love, it's hope and faith."

Tamaki denied intentionally picking 31 October for a rally of his Destiny Church supporters in central Auckland to coincide with the city's annual Diwali Festival.

In June, police seized Tamaki's firearms after temporarily suspending his licence. They revoked his licence in August.

He had announced on social media that police had decided he was no longer a "fit and proper person".

A spokesperson from the Australian Department of Home Affairs said they couldn't comment on individual cases, but said the Australian Government was committed to protecting the community from the risk of harm posed by non-citizens who engage in criminal conduct or behaviour of concern.

"The Australian government will continue to act decisively to protect the community from the risk of harm posed by individuals who choose to engage in criminal activity or behaviour of concern, including visa cancellation or refusal where appropriate."

World.title: Firefighters battle bushfire at Christchurch's Bottle Lake
World.content:
Firefighters are responding to a vegetation fire at Bottle Lake in north-east Christchurch.

Fire and Emergency (FENZ) received multiple calls around 8.30pm on Thursday about a fire on the perimeter of Bottle Lake.

FENZ said three fire engines, two water tankers and a rural pump were at the scene, with the first arriving appliance describing the blaze as the size of a bus.

It said the fire may have started on the beach.

The blaze was not close to any structures, FENZ said.

Earlier this year, both Civil Defence and FENZ warned Christchurch City Council that Bottle Lake Forest Park could be problematic in a fire.

FENZ Canterbury district commander Dave Stackhouse told the August meeting people may have trouble escaping.

World.title: Enrolled but not that interested: Three first time voters on why they are or aren't engaged with politics
World.content:
Audio player for " The race to enrol NZ’s youth " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/politics_election-2026/2088411%2Fenrolled-but-not-that-interested-three-first-time-voters-on-why-they-are-or-aren-t-engaged-with-politics

The race to enrol NZ’s youth Checkpoint Download MP3 27m

Over 100,000 young people may miss the chance to vote, with enrolment numbers still drastically low and the deadline to sign up just days away.

With the last chance to register to vote fast approaching this Sunday, still less than 69 percent of 18-24 year olds have signed up to cast their vote.

In many electorates, youth enrolments are even lower, sitting between 50 and 60 percent.

South Auckland's Ōtāhuhu has the lowest numbers of all, with only 50.6 percent of rangatahi enrolled to vote.

The main street of Ōtāhuhu. (File photo) RNZ / Cole Eastham-Farrelly

By contrast, the Banks Peninsula has nearly 94 percent of young voters signed up.

Unlike the sparsely populated area most people know, the Banks Peninsula electorate consists of rural areas like Little River, Akaroa and Mount Herbert, but also includes the suburban edges of Christchurch, like Halswell and Cashmere.

But what exactly is causing the drastic difference, and why are so many young people not enrolling?

Checkpoint brought together three first time voters to find out what is on the minds of rangatahi as voting day fast approaches.

Enrolled, but 'not that interested in politics'

Eighteen-year-old Gordon Shapiro lives in Little River, a tiny rural town on the Banks Peninsula, where he enrolled to vote last month, a few weeks after his 18th birthday.

He's about to graduate from Akaroa Area School, where he's one of less than 130 students from Year 1 to 13.

Gordon Shapiro is one of less than 130 students at Akaroa Area School. (File photo) RNZ / Dan Dalgety

Shapiro said he has never really been interested in politics, and only started engaging in the past year.

With his first chance to vote only weeks away he's not feeling too confident about where his vote will land.

"I feel like it's pretty harsh on us because this year is a pretty interesting one... because what I've seen from looking at all the parties, I reckon it's going to be quite a close one."

Meliame Mafoa is also 18, and about to finish her last year at South Auckland's Ōtāhuhu College, where she is head girl.

Coming from an electorate with the lowest enrolment rate for youth in the country, she's also feeling unsure about who she will cast her vote for.

While her school encouraged her to enrol, Mafoa said she feels like there's a lack of information for young people in her community.

"This group came over and they gave this whole presentation about voting and they even gave us a presentation about how we have the lowest enrolment rates... we were surprised to see that.

"My information either [comes] from a few of my friends who keep up with the news, with the politics, because I'm not interested in politics as well."

She said she wants to access more information about the election, but doesn't always know how.

Toreakore Ford-Takiri, 19, is in her first year of a law degree at Victoria University in Wellington, where she moved from her hometown of Tokoroa.

Tokoroa town centre. (File photo) RNZ / Evie Richardson

She's enrolled in the Māori electorate of Te Tai Hauauru on the West Coast of the North Island which takes in Tokoroa.

It's been two years since she pre-enroled at 17, and now that she's finally able to, she said it's incredibly important to her to vote.

"Being a Pacific Islander, but also being of Māori descent, it's technically in our blood. You know, it's everything around us is political and it may not look like it, but it does impact us quite a lot.

"I want to vote on behalf of my siblings that cannot, and on behalf the mokopuna or the teina that may come after me. So for me, I'm thinking for the future and not just my present."

What issues are young people worried about?

Checkpoint asked all three what they thought the biggest issues currently affecting rangatahi were.

Shapiro said living in a rural community, natural disasters and weather events were becoming a bigger issue.

"It's certainly a major concern for a lot of the people who live here and a lot of the businesses out here, because a lot of the businesses are around the centre area, which is in the low ground, which is where all the water will go."

Little River has been hit by floods multiple times in recent years. (File photo) Nathan Mckinnon/RNZ

As a first year university student living away from home, Ford-Takiri said she worried about the fact the fees free programme had been scrapped.

"I am so privileged to have been received a scholarship... from when I was a school leaver and that goes through three years of my studies, so that's accommodation, taken off of my plate.

"But also the tuition fees just go up... I just see it go up and up each year and I just feel like next year, what is going to happen to our fees? Am I going to be needing to have an extra loan?"

Dreams to give back to the community

With record numbers of young kiwis leaving the country, politicians have been pushing to convince youth to remain in the country this election campaign.

But Mafoa, Ford-Takiri and Shapiro all said they don't need any convincing, and have no plans to leave any time soon.

Shapiro, who aims to join the Defence Force as an army officer after finishing school, said he feels loyal to New Zealand.

"I don't see myself really moving away, at least not just yet. Currently, I think I have a pretty good chance at staying in the country and doing well.

"What my friends usually do is they either go to uni or start traveling, and I feel like I don't really want that big burden of debt initially. So what I want to do is I want to join the military who can pay for my education, teach me skills, let me lead people and help people overseas and in the country, I think it's just a great way to start my adult life."

After Mafoa finishes school at the end of this year, she plans to study to be a doctor. Specifically, a heart surgeon.

She said she wanted to stay and work in New Zealand to give back to her community.

With close to a decade of study in front of her though, she's worried about the cost it will take to get there.

"The tuition fees, the debt that comes with that is very big, and that's what pushes us to think, do we really, really want to go through this path, knowing that after this we have so much money to pay off."

But she said her reasons for pursuing medicine were driving her forward.

"The reason why I want to become a doctor is because of my grandmother. She couldn't go to any healthcare, any hospitals, no clinics because of that barrier with healthcare, because you don't see many of our people there in that department, in that field.

"She didn't feel like she would be understood, she couldn't speak English very well.

"For me... getting into that medical field, I'm representing many, many cultures, many Pacifica families, not only my Tongan culture. Because seeing that familiarity in a place you don't have much knowledge of - I mean, it's healthcare, it's medical stuff, you don't know all these words, you don't know where to go - but seeing that familiar face, it just brings that warmth in you, in you thinking, I'll be understood because I see somebody I know, I see somebody that might understand me."

After she finished her degree, Ford-Takiri hoped to work as a criminal and family lawyer.

She didn't always see herself staying in the country after finishing high school, a few years ago she envisioned herself leaving to earn a higher salary, before bringing her skills back home.

But since beginning study, she said she's realised what an impact she can have on her community.

"Having looked at this current coalition and what's been going on, it just made me realise that I could be here for better things and I'd rather be serving my people from where I am than going away and coming back trying to serve them with knowledge that is so not relevant to them."

'It's just the financial barrier stopping us'

With student loans looming, the cost of living was something all three rangatahi brought up.

Mafoa lives in an eight person household, with five siblings. Her father is the only income for the family.

"Sometimes we need a ration on some things to pay the bills, to pay rent, but then also send money back to the islands, help our family there, because they too are struggling.

"I know that my family has a lot of potential to do great things, me and my siblings, we have a lot of potential, it's just that financial barrier that's really stopping us."

Ford-Takiri said she's worried about the rising cost of petrol and how it's impacting her whānau .

With 10 siblings, her family already have a lot on their plate.

"I also have little brothers who want to pursue rugby league, and for them to pursue rugby league, it's very essential for them to be in clubs and be in rep teams and etcetera, so drive.

"My mum and dad, they drive to Auckland and back, to Rotorua and back."

'A lot of them are there just to show face'

The young people Checkpoint spoke to weren't all that confident that politicians really knew what it felt like to be a young person today.

Ford-Takiri said studying in Wellington meant she often saw politicians out on the street, and at university events, but she said there presence alone didn't feel like enough.

"Usually at our open days there will be like Labour Party, National, Greens and there will always be a few politicians there if not just their leaders. From what I have experienced a lot of them are there just to show face, just to be like yeah I'm in the community but they're not, they're not in the community, they're not participating, they're not taking part in any of the community events.

"They haven't really... talked one-on-one or within a group or participating in an event that youth will be at or that youth will thrive in."

Ford-Takiri threw a "special mention" to the Green Party's Tamatha Paul, who also comes from Tokoroa, something she said was "mind-boggling."

Tamatha Paul. (File photo) RNZ / Mark Papalii

She said it mattered to her that she was able to see herself reflected in those sitting in parliament.

"What matters to me most is seeing people like her in our communities, not only in our universities or workplaces, but at DJing parties or having fun with youth for youth and coming up with bright ideas."

Shapiro said the local candidates for Banks Peninsula had recently come into his school to answer their questions.

"My first initial reaction from meeting them was that most of them, I feel like most of them are from the outskirts of Christchurch... but I feel like it takes a real local to fully grasp things that are needed and what can be fixed."

He said he'd like to see the candidates getting out in the community more often, particularly in between election cycles, to keep young people informed as they reach voting age.

"I feel like they should do a regular thing where they go to a school every, I don't know, half a year or a year just to keep in contact with that younger community."

World.title: Labour candidate Kerrin Leoni clarifies whānau function with gang members
World.content:
A video seen by RNZ shows Labour candidate Kerrin Leoni, wearing her Labour Party jacket, speaking with Mongrel Mob members about enrolling to vote and changing the government.

Labour leader Chris Hipkins has heavily criticised Green and Te Pāti Māori candidates for their recent election campaign visit to a Mongrel Mob pad.

He said it was unacceptable for politicians to "go out and celebrate with gangs", and that it was "really, really ill considered, they made a real error of judgement."

Leoni acknowledged she has whānau in gangs and said she attended a whānau function earlier this month, with some gang members present - but it was not a gang pad.

One of the candidates Hipkins criticised was Te Pāti Māori's Oriini Kaipara, who told a Whakaata Māori debate this week her Tāmaki Makaurau opponent Kerrin Leoni had recently been campaigning with gang members.

Kaipara said Leoni had since deleted a social media post about it.

Leoni denied that during the debate, and sought to clarify the situation in a Facebook post on Thursday evening.

"To be clear, I have not attended a gang pad, at all during this campaign. I said at the debate I have close whānau who are gang members. In early October, I attended a whānau function where some of those present were whānau gang members."

Leoni - a former Auckland councillor - said her whānau supported her political career.

"I will not turn my back on them or pretend they are not my whānau because of their associations. I've always tried to be a role model for my whānau," she wrote.

She said she was disappointed it had become the main focus following the debate, and she wanted to focus on the issues that matter to voters.

RNZ has seen a video of Leoni at a whare with Mongrel Mob members, wearing her Labour jacket, holding a sign depicting her and Hipkins and handing out flyers.

"Some of them you might know, that aren't enrolled to vote, and they can have the power to change this government," she said in the video.

RNZ sought comment from Hipkins and his office referred to his statements earlier in the day.

He said Leoni has been open that she has whānau in gangs.

"I have not asked her for a detailed breakdown of every interaction that she's had with members of her own family, but she did say yesterday that she had not visited a gang pad as part of her election campaigning, and I have absolutely accepted that," he said.

World.title: 'I want a revolutionary': Tauranga councillor seeks new CEO
World.content:
Tauranga City Council has approved a six-figure budget to find a new chief executive, who councillors say will need to lead significant organisational change.

Marty Grenfell resigned suddenly on September 29 after eight years in the role. He left three days later.

The council appointed Gareth Green, who managed the mayor's office, as acting chief executive.

Today, it confirmed he would continue as interim chief executive from Tuesday.

The appointment was made at Wednesday's council meeting, at which the council also set a budget of up to $100,000 (excluding GST) to recruit a permanent replacement.

Tauranga City Council acting chief executive Gareth Green. LDR/Kelly O'Hara

It could be used for executive search fees, advertising, assessment, due diligence, candidate travel, legal and independent remuneration advice and other recruitment and appointment costs.

A subcommittee will oversee the recruitment process, made up of Mayor Mahé Drysdale, Deputy Mayor Jen Scoular, Tauriko councillor Martin Rozeboom and Pāpāmoa councillor Steve Morris.

Tauranga mayor Mahé Drysdale. LDR/Alyse Wright

This committee would recommend a shortlist of candidates for interview. The full council will make the final appointment.

Drysdale told the meeting that finding a new chief executive needed to be treated as a priority and was expected to run until March.

He said Tauranga was grappling with growth, a difficult financial situation and significant reform, while the council also needed to drive change from the Davison review.

The review into January's Mount Maunganui landslide tragedy criticised how the organisation managed risk.

"It's about finding someone that has the ability to implement change within the organisation," Drysdale said.

The council needed a leader who could take staff through that change, improve organisational culture, manage risk and strengthen the council's service to the community.

Local government experience was not vital, but would help, given the complexity of the sector.

Appointing a new chief executive was "probably the most important role that we will do through our term".

Scoular said the council needed an experienced, independent person involved in the recruitment process.

She said transformational leadership would be critical, pointing to major infrastructure delivery, cultural change and what she described as a period of instability and continuing change.

Rozeboom said the successful candidate would need to quickly assess whether the organisation had the expertise and capacity to meet the demands of Tauranga's growth.

Arataki councillor Rick Curach said understanding public service and the relationship between the chief executive and elected members would be critical.

Welcome Bay councillor Hautapu Baker said he did not want "another CEO that's just rewrapped, but the same archetype".

Tauranga City Council Welcome Bay ward councillor Hautapu Baker. LDR/Kelly O'Hara

"I want a revolutionary, I want a disruptor, but I also want someone who can weave people, weave opportunities, weave outcomes together."

Matua Ōtūmoetai councillor Glen Crowther said the council needed to find a "sweet spot" between experience, an understanding of local government and innovative thinking.

Te Papa councillor Rod Taylor said he was looking for someone who could "bring the organisation back together" after years of change.

Te Awanui councillor Hemi Rolleston said the council also needed to consider what would attract strong candidates, given the organisation's highly public challenges.

"It's become an extraordinarily big job and extraordinarily big challenge."

The council needed someone courageous enough to challenge elected members.

"We don't want somebody that's just coming in to execute what this council wants. We want a healthy tension at the table."

The permanent chief executive may be appointed for a term of up to five years.

A report presented to the meeting identified desired capabilities including organisational transformation, risk leadership, major infrastructure delivery, financial management, political acumen, relationship-building with iwi and hapū, and the ability to provide elected members with "free, frank and high-quality advice".

The council plans to appoint an independent executive search partner after a selective closed-tender process. Proposals were received on October 14.

Under the indicative timetable, the position description, candidate brief and selection criteria would be finalised next month before advertising and the executive search begin.

The report indicated the recruitment process was expected to run until about March.

Former Tauranga City Council chief executive Marty Grenfell. LDR/Alyse Wright

Grenfell resigned amid fallout from the Davison report.

Former judge Paul Davison's report criticised the council's risk management over four decades before January's deadly Mauao landslide, which killed six holidaymakers at a council-owned holiday park.

He recommended ways the council could improve, which it has committed to completing.

In a statement today announcing Green's interim appointment, Drysdale said he had the council's "full support and a clear mandate to lead the organisation with the authority of the chief executive".

This included making whatever changes Green considered necessary to "strengthen the organisation and its performance".
