World.title: Australia falls to defeat in final session, South Africa levels series
World.content:
Australia's has fallen to defeat by an innings and 31 runs against South Africa in the second Test at St George's Park in Gqeberha.

Brave innings from Travis Head (121) and night watchman Scott Boland (40) were not enough for Australia, as the Proteas levelled the series at 1-1.

"We were a long way away from our best," Pat Cummins said at the presentation.

"Across the board just not enough of us contributed.

"Ideally we'd be scoring more runs. The pitch was pretty good out there."

The two teams will now head to Newlands in Cape Town for the final Test on Tuesday with the series on the line.

The hosts came into the final day needing just six wickets for victory, but were made to wait to get on the field after the first session was washed out by rain.

The persistent drizzle, interspersed by heavier squalls, may have given Australia hope that they may be able to orchestrate a great escape.

Even once play eventually resumed, every over that Head and Boland successfully negotiated raised hopes even further.

Head's 13th Test century was the first by an Australian batter in a follow-on innings since the 1980s and added to the pressure South Africa must have been feeling, with Anrich Nortje's injury leaving the Proteas a bowler down.

"I thought there was some good fight today," Cummins said.

"Scotty Boland and Trav [Head] both played their roles really well, but it was a fair way to come back from and it wasn't quite enough."

Travis Head scored his 13th Test century. (AP Photo: Themba Hadebe)

Once Head chopped on to Wiaan Mulder just before the second new ball was due, the writing may have been on the wall.

Steve Smith, batting at seven after being hampered by a sore neck on day four, initially looked sprightly, before he top edged a Kagiso Rabada bouncer to Matthew Breetzke when on 3.

Boland's brave, 166-ball vigil came to an end soon after, a brilliant off cutter from Mulder taking the top of his off stump.

Pat Cummins followed in the same way for just 4 to leave South Africa just two wickets from victory.

Still, Australia had hope as clouds gathered and threatened yet more rain to rescue an unlikely draw.

But then Rabada returned, bowling Mitch Starc for 11, before Marco Jansen extracted an edge from Josh Hazlewood for a duck.

Look back on how all the action unfolded in our live blog.

World.title: Schutt banned for two matches after prescription medication failure
World.content:
Australian women's fast bowler Megan Schutt has been banned for two matches for failing to meet guidelines on the use of prescription medication.

Cricket Australia confirmed Schutt's suspension in a release on Thursday afternoon.

"The breach was a failure to adhere to requirements under the Sports Science and Sports Medicine guidelines with regard to prescription medication," Cricket Australia said.



"This relates to a single incidence which occurred while out of competition and was not for performance-enhancing purposes."



The two-match ban applies to all international and domestic cricket.

Schutt starred in the recent three-match ODI series against Bangladesh. She had series figures of 10-71.

She has not played in a three-match T20 international series against New Zealand, which wraps up tonight at North Sydney.

Schutt released a statement acknowledging the breach and accepting the penalty.

"I fully accept the penalty handed down and apologise for failing to meet the standards expected of me," Schutt said in her statement.

"I'm sorry for the attention this has caused and appreciate the support I've received.

"While this occurred out of competition and was not performance related, I understand that I am responsible for following the Sports Science and Sports Medicine Guidelines, which players receive regular education on, and I should have adhered to these guidelines."



Cricket Australia said it would continue to provide "appropriate support" to Schutt and to reinforce standards and responsibilities expected of all involved in the game.

World.title: Aussie Borlase on winning side as Atlanta Dream leads WNBA Finals
World.content:
Angel Reese recorded 21 points and 12 rebounds to help the Atlanta Dream secure a 97-71 home victory over the Golden State Valkyries, giving the Dream a 2-1 lead in the WNBA Finals after Game 3.

Rhyne Howard added 16 points, and Naz Hillmon had 15 for the Dream, who also host Game 4 on Sunday (AEDT).

Australian guard Izzy Borlase played a solid role for the Dream on Wednesday night, local time. She played 26 minutes, finishing with 12 points, including one three-pointer, plus five rebounds, two assists and a block.

Another Australian Opals star, Miela Sowah, sat on the bench for the Valkyries and will remain there throughout the finals due to her restricted status as a development player.

The Dream highlighted one of Borlase's drives to the basket on its social media.

It was the second straight strong game for Reese, who had 30 points and 16 rebounds in Game 2, which the Dream also won for its first-ever victory in the Finals. She now has a double-double in each game of the Finals.

"It feels good when you're in the finals. It's a long season, and you play against everybody and go through and push through, but when you can do it at the highest level, this is what you live for, this is what the off-season is for," Reese said.

"I put the work in for this moment, and I'm just happy I could lead the team to a win. We're feeling good going into Saturday."

With the game tied at 49 in the third quarter, Atlanta scored eight straight, including four by Reese. Golden State got within 59-55 on Tiffany Hayes's lay-up, but could get no closer as Atlanta closed the quarter, scoring 12 of the final 14 points.

With Atlanta up 17 in the fourth quarter, Jordin Canada overthrew Reese on the break, but she saved the ball by throwing it over her head underneath the basket to Howard, who got fouled.

Do you have a story idea about women in sport? Email us abcsport5050@your.abc.net.au

Golden State could never recover. Gabby Williams scored 15 points, and Hayes added 14 for the Valkyries.

"Protect home court," Howard said of the team's focus. "Giving our fans a show. We fought for this arena so we had to protect it. It's big. We went and stole one, but we can't let them come in and do the same thing."

The game was moved from the Dream's home Gateway Center Arena to the NBA's Atlanta Hawks home arena. Wednesday night's game was sold out, with more than 17,000 fans attending, as is Game 4 on Saturday at the same venue.

The game got off to a slow start as Atlanta led 9-1 after the first five minutes. Golden State missed its first eight shots before Aminata Gueye scored the first basket with 4:39 left.

They got within 13-10 before Naz Hillmon hit consecutive 3-pointers and then Reese hit one. The Dream led 23-15 after the opening quarter.

Atlanta built its lead to 37-26 midway through the period. Golden State was able to hang around and only trailed 46-40 at the break as the teams combined to shoot 15-for-31 (48 per cent) from behind the arc.

That was more completed 3-pointers in the first 20 minutes than in either Game 1 or Game 2.

Game 1 and 2 had huge ratings, with the opener on NBC averaging 2.1 million, the most ever for a first game of the Finals. Game 2, which was broadcast on USA Network, averaged 1.33 million viewers.

AP/ABC

World.title: Amid the hunt for World Cup glory one of Tonga's greats is not done yet
World.content:
As Tonga's World Cup campaign prepares to hit fever pitch, Tui Lolohea cannot stop smiling even when the young bulls give him stick.

After a training session in the lead-up to Friday's match against Lebanon it is rising prop Demetric Vaimauga, who is the kind of guy you hear before you see, that gees Lolohea up.

"Awwww yeah, it's Mr I Ain't Done Yet!" Vaimauga crows as he grabs Lolohea by the shoulders.

That's what they called Lolohea in an Instagram post after he came off the bench for an injured Latu Fainu to set up a try in Tonga's 30-12 win over England last week and he's been copping it ever since.

It was a cameo Lolohea, at 31 and with Tonga enjoying more depth and talent in the halves than ever before, thought would never come.

But once it did it added to an already sterling legacy in the red jersey, tacking an extra chapter on a story that, against all odds, is still being written.

Lolohea has already played for Tonga more times than any other player in history and against the Cedars he'll extend his own record with his 23rd cap.

Along with Jason Taumalolo, Lolohea is the only player to have appeared in each of Tonga's five wins over Tier 1 nations, making them the only two constant faces in every image of Tonga's greatest days.

Loading Instagram content

Lolohea has been wearing these colours when those days were still just a dream. When he debuted for Tonga back in 2015, Fainu, the man he replaced last week and will partner in the halves on Friday, was only nine years old.

Vaimauga himself had just turned 11 and as the giant youngster runs away cackling, Lolohea fires back in Tongan through a grin and shakes his head.

"I knew I'd get stick for this. Mr I Ain't Done Yet — they're always taking the piss out of me," Lolohea said.

"I hope he gets banged next time he goes off the back fence, so I can go laugh at him.

"They joke around, but I am one of the oldest in the team and it's good to show you can run around with the young bucks."

Jason Taumalolo and Tui Lolohea have played in every one of Tonga's wins over Tier 1 nations. (Getty Images: Anthony Au-Yueng)

Lolohea and Taumalolo are the elders this time around as the two longest-serving players in the team by a mile and while Taumalolo dragged Tonga into a new world, Lolohea is very much a product of the old.

Watching his debut from 11 years ago against Samoa on the Gold Coast is a measure of how far things have come.

When the two meet again next week it will be in front of a sold-out crowd at Parramatta Stadium, which they probably could have filled twice over, and both sides will boast some of the best players in the world.

Back on Lolohea's first day, a little over 12,000 came through the gates and both nations had to choose between grey beards, who wanted to give back to their community, journeymen who knew this would be as good as it got, or youngsters before their big futures came for them.

International rugby league has come a long way since Tui Lolohea's Test debut. (Getty Images: Matt Roberts)

Lolohea was one of the latter and at the time he was counted as one of rugby league's brightest prospects, with feet so fast tackling him was like trying to grab a handful of smoke.

So much has transformed since those times but according to Lolohea, the most important things have stayed the same.

"Why you're doing it, what you're representing, that never changes," Lolohea said.

"We're a little dot on the map and there's always talk about financial stuff but the pride of our island nation, the proud culture we put out to the people, we've built that over the years and the support from the people is massive.

Why Jason Taumalolo is still more than just a man for Tonga In the NRL, we only talk about what Jason Taumalolo can't do anymore. But when he pulls on the red of Tonga it's a reminder of what he still is and always will be for the island nation and for Test rugby league.

"That's what we want to represent, our people and our family names, where we come from.

"I was just a little kid back then. I remember the passion, for Tonga and Samoa, and we're on the big stage now but the passion is still there even though it was a long time ago."

Plenty of familiar faces from that night are still around. Kristian Woolf is still the coach, Sika Manu, Lolohea's first captain, is in camp as an assistant and Konrad Hurrell is the team's media manager.

But only Lolohea is still playing, making him the last son of the olden days before the heroes came back home.

He remembers frantically messaging Taumalolo in 2017, asking if he really was going to come back to Tonga and marvelling at what followed.

He cannot forget his intercept try in the win over New Zealand, head cocked back and laughing as he went over, or his late score in the semi-final against England that gave Tonga hope of a miracle, or of the trip back to the islands that followed, where the team was given medals of honour at the royal palace.

Amid a good NRL career for the Warriors and Wests Tigers before a lengthy stint in Super League, where he's spent the last eight seasons, including the last five with Huddersfield, Lolohea might never have fulfilled the club expectations he carried into his Tongan debut.

Instead, his finest hours have come for Tonga itself, for whom he is both pioneer and icon.

They've never won a big game without him and his reward has been honours that are usually bestowed on heroes of ancient wars.

His people have named trophies after him and he has been granted lands outside the family village of Lapaha by King Tupou VI.

The team's official nickname is Mate Ma' Tonga, which translates to "die for Tonga" but the memories Lolohea has helped create for his nation are immortal, like the win over Great Britain in 2019 or the breakthrough victory over Australia the following week.

Tui Lolohea has carved out a fine legacy in Tongan red. (Getty Images: Kai Schwoerer)

On the back of those glories a whole new generation of stars chose Tonga and players like Isaiya Katoa, Robert Toia, Leka Halasima and Tolu Koula have not just become part of the cause, they have taken it further.

They beat New Zealand again in the Pacific Championships two years ago and pushed Australia to the limit in the final. Lolohea, of course, played in both and set up a try in the latter.

Tonga are not here to compete anymore, they are here to win — against Australia, New Zealand, England, Samoa or anybody else who wants some.

Taking the World Cup itself back to Nuku'alofa is not an idle fantasy. It's a dream Tonga can hammer into reality as part of a new world order Lolohea and his generation helped create and somehow, he is still part of it.

Apart from Taumalolo, his only fellow survivor from 2017, the other legends from the old days are done.

Tui Lolohea has played in England for close to a decade now. (Getty Images via PA Images: Martin Rickett)

Between Katoa, Fainu and Junior Amone, Tonga have more class and options in the halves and the nation had every right to move on from Lolohea years ago.

But Lolohea himself is still here, refusing to be swept away, a lot older and a bit slower but as he showed against England, still capable of making a difference for the better.

"To still be here after all this time, I'm fortunate to be here again and running around with the young guys and some of the superstars of our game," Lolohea said.

"It's an honour, every time.

Rugby League World Cup quick hits From Kalyn Ponga's magnificent Test debut to a mighty Tongan victory years in the making here are the quick hits from week one of the Rugby League World Cup.

"It's crazy to think, because I watch these guys every week and now I'm playing alongside them and I remember when we didn't really have any halfbacks at all.

"The depth we have now, it's such a big positive not just for now but for the years to come."

Lolohea knows this World Cup might be his last. He's finished up at Huddersfield and is still sorting out where he'll play next.

He is expected to drop back to the extended bench for next week's clash against Samoa and barring injury, it will be the same for the knockout stages.

This game against Lebanon could be it, the last time the legend of Tui Lolohea as a Tongan hero happens in front of us and not in our memories and that makes it worth savouring.

Tui Lolohea is hoping to build on his cameo appearance against England. (Getty Images: Paul Kane)

He played rugby league for Tonga more times than any other person who has ever lived but it is still a privilege to him, a prize beyond what he can ever say.

Even after all these years it still makes his father, Paul, smile and get as emotional as he ever does.

Growing up it was just the two of them. Lolohea's mother died when he was just one year old due a heart condition and if Friday is the end, father and son will be together for it.

But there might be a truth in the jokes the young fellas tell: Lolohea isn't done yet.

"He [Lolohea's father] flew in Tuesday morning, he'll be here for the next couple of weeks to enjoy the last ride, no matter what happens," Lolohea said.

"But we never know these days, do we? I'm just buzzing I got on the field again. I'm glad I got to play my part."

World.title: Potential PNG signing helping to heal Cooper Bai's family rift
World.content:
Marcus Bai has explained how he and son Cooper moved past the rift that fractured their family, as the Gold Coast forward edges closer to signing a deal with the PNG Chiefs.

Cooper was warmly greeted by his father at Port Moresby's Jacksons International airport yesterday after being granted permission to explore his options ahead of the opening of the November 1 contracting window.

The 19-year-old has been high on the Chiefs' list of targets since the club got the green light to enter the NRL in the 2028 season, with the forward proving a hit with local crowds in Papua New Guinea across his two-Test international career.

PNG Chiefs unveil new logo ahead of 2028 NRL entry The PNG Chiefs logo brings together elements representative of the country ahead of its NRL debut in 2028.

But Cooper's journey hasn't always been smooth, and last year he invoked the ire of his legendary Kumul father when he turned down a deal with Melbourne Storm to remain at the Titans.

"He promised one thing … and then he went and did the other thing, and I was cranky with him," Marcus told AAP.

"I said you've got to be fair and square, that's not how you treat the clubs and people.

"It's not good for us as a family, I was really pissed off with him for that, and I was really angry at him.

"Now [with the chance to join the Chiefs], I said go and have a look and you and your girlfriend sit down and [think through] before making a decision."

Cooper Bai angered his father Marcus (pictured) by going back on his word with regards to signing for the Storm. (Getty Images: Shannon Morris)

Marcus said Cooper had shown maturity by speaking to the Gold Coast to ask permission to visit the Chiefs.

Cooper was due to visit PNG on a family holiday after he was ruled out of the Kumuls' World Cup campaign with a hamstring injury.

"He's only young. He's still finding his feet, and if he comes here there will be a lot of pressure on him," Marcus said.

"The crowd here are tough, they tell you straight up [if they're not happy]."

The chance for Cooper to join the Chiefs would represent a full circle moment for the Bai family.

Marcus left Papua New Guinea in the 1990s to pursue a career as a professional rugby league player, going on to win titles in the NRL and Super League.

He would likely stand down from the Chiefs board if Cooper was to sign a deal to join the club for its inaugural season in 2028.

"I'm proud of his achievements, it is hard to do what he's done and to be able to have an interest from many clubs, it's pleasing for me as a father," Marcus Bai said.

AAP

World.title: Man United captain branded 'disgrace' for comments following latest loss
World.content:
Manchester United captain Bruno Fernandes has been labelled a "disgrace" after questioning manager Michael Carrick's tactics following a Champions League defeat to Como.

Fernandes said his side failed to apply enough pressure and adopted a "mood of defeat" after conceding early in Thursday morning's 4-1 loss, a result that increased scrutiny on Carrick.

Como opened the scoring in the second minute and United collapsed, with only a stoppage‑time consolation goal from Joshua Zirkzee making the scoreline slightly less severe.

"We started on the wrong foot and they scored very early," Fernandes told TNT Sports. "There was not enough pressure on the ball and not many good movements off the ball. There were many things not going our way.

"It's a decision from the [coaching] staff not to press man-to-man and sometimes leave space behind and try to get the ball, wait for them, but sometimes when you give space to these teams they get confidence.

Asked if his comments amounted to criticism of Carrick's tactics, Fernandes said: "That's on the manager and staff to see, not me.

"Sometimes you have to be more brave under pressure, take the risk of pressing high and making them uncomfortable."

The Manchester United captain was heavily criticised by former Liverpool defender Jamie Carragher for his comments.

Carrick raised his arms up in an apology as he approached Manchester United's travelling supporters after the full-time whistle. (Getty Images: Marco Luzzani)

"For Bruno Fernandes to do that, it's a disgrace really," he said on CBS Sports Golazo.

"Last season he got Player of the Year, that was on the back of Michael Carrick becoming the manager, he wouldn't have got that award without Michael Carrick.

"When you think of him as a footballer, he's a talent, but in terms of attitude and the way he goes about things, it's not right at all.

"He's reacted like that because he's been brought off and he's embarrassed tonight by the manager.

"When he talks about pressing … for years, Bruno Fernandes has meant Manchester United can't press because he does things for the crowd.

"I commentate on games watching Man United, and he runs all over the place like a kid in the schoolyard, for the supporters.

"They all think he's working hard, he's not, he's killing the rest of the team.

"Watching him play every week, throwing his arms up at the other players constantly in the game is an absolute disgrace what he's done there, considering how he's performed this season.

"Awful attitude and not what a Manchester United captain should be."

Carrick's position has come under increasing pressure with United now winless in seven matches, and he responded by questioning the players' lack of willingness to run.

"There's a little bit on whatever system you play, whatever tactics you play, if you don't run and you don't run forward and you don't run back, you ain't gonna win," he said in his press conference when notified of Fernandes's criticism.

"It was more than disappointing," the 45-year-old manager said in a separate interview for TNT Sports. "I think everybody's got to take responsibility for that. I'll take responsibility for the overall team and performance, it stops with me and I'm fine with that.

"But as a supporter of this football club, to see a performance like that is unacceptable, I have to say."

Carrick said his side had failed to show the required intensity.

"It's the motivation and the purpose and the intensity of a game of football that you have to bring. We didn't bring that today," he said. "I've got to apologise for the performance."

Fernandes also questioned United's mentality after the early setback.

"Conceding early makes us go into the game with a mood of defeat," he said.

United have three points from their opening three Champions League matches and host AS Roma in their next fixture in the competition.

Reuters/ABC

World.title: Diamonds looking lost and panicked as Constellation Cup woes continue
World.content:
We are halfway through the Constellation Cup and it is hard to know whether to panic about the state of the Diamonds.

Australia finds itself in a 0-2 hole after losing in Auckland 56-50 and in Christchurch 62-50, with two Tests still left to come in Sydney and Melbourne.

This is the last opportunity the Diamonds have to prepare against international opposition without another series scheduled between now and the 2027 home Netball World Cup.

The Diamonds are hoping to defend their Netball World Cup title in Sydney next year. (Getty: Steve Christo)

The Diamonds have looked uncharacteristically lost and panicked, while the coaches have struggled tactically. Some of Australia's greatest ever players are out of form but still getting a starting position, and fans are questioning why more hasn't been done to develop the next generation of talent.

The recent events at the Commonwealth Games probably feed into the worry, seeing the side fall short of the gold medal match for the first time in August.

If the Diamonds concede all four Tests to New Zealand, they are also expected to be knocked off their number one world ranking, a status they've held since 2013.

So, is the series a lost cause? Are injuries to blame? Or should we hold our breath and hope home-crowd advantage swings momentum? Here are the main talking points at the midway point of the Constellation Cup.

Missing key players

Jo Weston's (right) work out front makes it easier for the goal keeper to win ball. (AAP: James Ross)

Australia is dearly missing defenders Sunday Aryang and Jo Weston.

25-year-old Aryang ruptured her ACL in the last Constellation Cup series and is yet to make it back on court. Veteran Weston made herself unavailable for selection to give her body a much-needed break and focus on her Masters studies.

Their work rate at goal defence and wing defence make a huge difference. Weston is a relentless tagger, wearing down the opposition and slowing play outside the circle.

Could she be coaxed into changing her mind? After all, a similar situation happened in 2022, when Weston was originally rested from the series but received an SOS call to cover injury with Australia trailing 2-0. Her team went on to win the final two games at home.

Kate Moloney was ruled out of game one due to a nasty finger injury. (Getty: Ross MacDonald)

The team has also had to rejig its midcourt following injuries to Kate Moloney and Jamie-Lee Price. Moloney was ruled out of the game on Sunday after suffering a finger laceration while trying to catch a ball at training. She returned to play on Wednesday with stitches.

Price appeared in the first match but sustained a calf injury that prevented her from playing in the second. In both instances, head coach Stacey Marinkovich decided to play Liz Watson out of position at centre before subbing her off in the third quarter. It hasn't been the captain's best performance.

Jamie-Lee Price may not be able to return for the rest of the series. (Getty Images: Graham Denholm)

Whether Price will be able to make it back by Sunday is unclear, but the Diamonds desperately need to do something different defensively. They've been unable to consistently hold up New Zealand's ball speed and the feed into target Grace Nweke.

In Auckland, they were behind on the gain stat 13-6 and in Christchurch it was just as bad, 9-2.

Home-crowd advantage

Silver Ferns smash the Diamonds 3-0 to clinch Constellation Cup The Diamonds were swept aside in Perth by 18 goals, as New Zealand clinch the 2024 Constellation Cup with one game to go.

Since 2014, the Constellation Cup has been played as a four-Test series, granting each country equal hosting rights, and that home-crowd advantage is no joke.

Over the past five series, the team hosting has emerged victorious in 18 of the 20 Tests played.

Because of this, we're unlikely to see either national body agree to hold an uneven number of Tests in the future. Even if it'd be more exciting for fans to see a team win outright than by goal aggregate.

It's certainly been tough going in New Zealand again this year. The Silver Ferns have been the better side in six of the eight quarters and have forced the opposition to make 29 changes, scrambling to find answers.

It's been five years since the Diamonds last won a Test across the ditch. That outing was Marinkovich's second in charge and Watson's first as captain.

In fact, Marinkovich's winning record in New Zealand only sits at seven per cent. But does that really matter if the team wins the overall series, you may ask? Well, in the 10 series preceding her appointment in August 2020, Australia only lost it once.

Australian coaches Stacey Marinkovich and Nicole Richardson were left scratching their heads after the loss. (Getty: Fiona Goodall)

In the five completed under her tenure, Australia has conceded it twice. A loss in 2026 would give Marinkovich a 50 per cent Constellation Cup success rate. Although she is contracted through to the end of 2027, there is a lot hinging on these results.

New Zealand last beat the Diamonds in Australia two years ago in Perth to claim the 2024 trophy. It was the first time in history they'd won three consecutive games within the series.

Now there's a real chance it could happen again.

However, if we're to borrow a cricket analogy, it's important to wait till both teams bat before we place our final judgement. Home-crowd advantage tells us there's a possibility we could be sitting here in a week's time in a very different state of mind, with two wins on the board.

High penalties

Umpire Gary Burgess officiates a match at the Netball World Cup. (Twitter: Gary Burgess)

A key area holding the Diamonds back has been the lopsided penalty count.

New Zealand has conceded 100 penalties so far, while Australia has conceded 145. That's a lot of time standing beside your player, unable to contribute to play.

What didn't help in the second game was the repeated offensive contacts called against the shooters, as they pushed off the body of Kiwi defender Kelly Jackson, trying to get free.

Donnell Wallam was called four times in 11 minutes of play. Sophie Garbin was called three times across 50 minutes. Kiera Austin tallied up to 12 penalties to finish as the third-most penalised Diamonds player on the night.

As per the typical etiquette in international netball, two neutral umpires have been appointed to officiate the series: Welsh umpire Alison Harrison and English umpire Gary Burgess.

"We had some offensive contacts, so we've just got to seek some clarification from the umpires as to what it is they're seeing so we can adjust for that in the future," Marinkovich said post-play.

"The fact that we also rotated our whole defence line from wing defence to the keeper, I don't think that we're that ill-disciplined throughout the entire unit and we've got to understand what it is that we're doing so we can adjust.

"In history, for the last four years, we've been penalised in New Zealand and it kind of shifts when we're in Australia … But I don't think our game plan changes too differently."

Silver Ferns captain Karin Burger and Diamonds captain Liz Watson. (AAP: James Ross)

That's an interesting observation as the umpires' calls should be consistent no matter where a game is played. But Silver Ferns captain Karin Burger had a similar thought.

"Obviously, knowing that Australia has the home crowd next and 50/50 calls always tend to go in the home side's way, it means the scrap is going to be even harder," Burger said.

"Later in the series there's going to be more tired bodies and defenders are going to need to be really smart about their line to the ball … so that we're contesting clean ball."

How much it means

The scary part is how much New Zealand is gunning for the trophy.

The Silver Ferns have already been brimming with confidence and head coach Noeline Taurua said they believed the Constellation Cup was just as big a pinnacle as the Commonwealth Games gold they won in August.

"You always have that trans-Tasman rivalry, and you've got to back up four straight outings against the one team," Taurua said.

"It is definitely the battle of the minds and the hearts and the bodies."

ABC Sport will live blog game three of the Constellation Cup in Sydney, starting at 4pm AEDT.

World.title: Scatterbrained Australian approach opens door to South African victory
World.content:
Among those who fret over the ongoing primacy of Test cricket in the face of the T20 onslaught, Australia's tour of South Africa had long shaped as an enticing proposition: the two best sides in the world squaring off, a clutch of veteran tourists confronting ghosts of controversies past, and Australia commencing a year-long run of battles its aging superstars see as legacy-shaping.

Some of that probably distracted us from what a bittersweet prospect it was, too. For how, as anyone glued to this contest in the past two weeks will have asked themselves at some point or other, can a game so awash with money have conspired to deny us regular helpings of this fun and fascinating South African outfit? Of real cricket that matters?

Twenty-four hours ago, it was centurion Temba Bavuma reminding the world not only of his life-affirming resurgence as a batsman, but of the great shame that in the last two years, he's only had eight other opportunities to strut his stuff at Test level.

Quick hits: Sore Smith doesn't return as Marnus throws it away on horror day Steve Smith reaches a major milestone but doesn't return and Marnus Labuschagne makes a mockery of an enormous reprieve on a disastrous fourth day for the Aussies in Gqeberha. Here are the quick hits from South Africa.

Early on day four at Gqeberha, the focus shifted to beanpole all-rounder Marco Jansen, fresh from his swashbuckling 85 with the bat, now tearing through the Australian batting order like the Grim Reaper. Lurking not so much in the shadows as slightly off to the side of the stage, stirring up drama and intrigue, there was also the imposing figure of Proteas attack leader Kagiso Rabada.

That and a few subtler problems added up to an unmitigated disaster for Australia. Replying to South Africa's declared total of 425, the scatterbrained and frankly embarrassing tourists were skittled for 99 in their first innings and asked to follow on.

By default, Australia fared a little better in the afternoon, finishing the day at 4-156 with Travis Head undefeated on 87. But with its deficit of 170, and a neck injury to Steve Smith — who hasn't appeared to bat yet in the second innings — it will take something truly remarkable for Australia to pull this game out of the fire on the fifth and final day.

The main impression Australia's performance left was of the sheer needlessness of the entire debacle. What was the first innings batting plan, if any? Why were so many batsmen in such a hurry in a scenario from which Australia was never going to win?

Travis Head was the only Australian batter to show a bit of fight in the face of South Africa's onslaught on day four. (Getty Images: Gallo Images/Richard Huggard)

Which is not to take the focus of South Africa's unstinting excellence. Another emblematic figure in that sense was off-spinner Simon Harmer, who many thought should have been dropped for this game.

Instead, he's made big runs, caught everything that has come his way, and chipped in with two key wickets. Australia has had no such unassuming star.

Jansen, with 5-33 from 11 overs in the first innings chaos, was the chief destroyer, but there were wheels within wheels. The mere presence of Rabada, who was missing from the first Test, seems to have transformed South Africa's collective energy from a little too amiable in Durban to ruthless and faintly menacing here.

Jansen was the most visible example of this phenomenon. In Durban, he'd bowled with pace and incision to spark Australia's initial collapse. But as his influence waned and Matt Renshaw got going, he silently brooded away in his own world, looking a little like Alain Delon's expressionless assassin in Le Samourai.

Today he was an entirely different man — gregarious, energetic, fired up. To his usual bouncers he added fist-pumps and fiery send-offs. Like Rabada in the memorably testy corresponding game eight years ago, he got up in Australia's grill and wouldn't go away.

Marco Jansen was back to his menacing best as Australia crumbled under his pressure on day four. (Getty Images: Richard Huggard/Gallo Images)

A brief catalogue of Australia's worst misdemeanours in the first innings bears mentioning. Marnus Labuschagne again drove with hard hands, slightly off balance, with his bat plane all wrong, therefore couldn't complain about the bad luck of departing to a one-handed screamer by Harmer in the cordon. Alex Carey, Beau Webster, Mitchell Starc and Pat Cummins each either walloped or wafted at deliveries they should have respected, especially given the dire state their team was in at the time.

In the second innings, Nic Maddinson again nudged lamely at Rabada to be caught behind the wicket. As in Durban, Labuschagne again squandered a promising start when a break in sight, heedlessly thrashing Harmer into the deep to hole out for 39 when drinks were about to be brought on. And Webster, again neither looking comfortable nor batting with due caution, was dismissed cheaply at the worst possible time. Renshaw, who had looked relatively comfortable, shouldered arms to be bowled by Rabada.

And for all that, and Australia's loss of 13 wickets for the day, South Africa's attack was a man down for most of the day after lionhearted quick Anrich Nortje suffered a groin injury in his fourth over. Things could actually have been worse.

Only a day ago, one felt the confluence of luck, momentum and a single special innings had changed the game's course without any great culpability on Australia's behalf. The feeling is very different now. South Africa will arrive for the final day with victory in its mind — in this game, foremost, but also perhaps in a series that is now thrillingly alive.

Tech.title: Apple’s Magic Keyboards for iPad are about half off, with a small catch
Tech.content:
is an editor covering deals and gaming hardware. He joined in 2018, and after a two-year stint at Polygon, he rejoined The Verge in May 2025.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

You can outfit your iPad Air or iPad Pro with one of Apple’s slick Magic Keyboards for considerably less than the accessory usually costs at Woot. I won’t bury the catch I teased in the headline; These cases have a 90-day warranty via Woot, and aren’t eligible for AppleCare. That said, Woot says they’re in “pristine condition, with essentially no visible signs of use.” If you’re still interested, the savings should be worth it.

The most affordable option is the Magic Keyboard for the 13-inch iPad Air (M2, M3, M4 versions supported). Originally $319, and selling for that price at most retailers, you can nab one in white for just $129.

Woot also has the Magic Keyboard in black for the 11-inch iPad Pro (M4 and M5 editions) and the 13-inch Pro supporting the same configurations. Those cost $159 and $199, respectively, which is well over $100 off.

Each Magic Keyboard essentially turns your iPad into a MacBook, of sorts, complete with a trackpad, aluminum design, and a function row of keys. It magnetically attaches to the back of your iPad, and gets power via its pogo pins, keeping the tablet’s USB-C port free for you to plug in accessories. The keyboard accessory features a USB-C port in its cantilevered double-hinged design for charging your iPad (this port doesn’t allow data passthrough, just power). The stand lets you make easy adjustments to the viewing angle of your iPad, which is great if you’re trying to avoid glare.

Tech.title: PHP: The three little letters wreaking havoc across the web
Tech.content:
Two vulnerabilities found in the programming language PHP put enormous swaths of the internet in danger.

By some accounts, up to 70 percent of websites use PHP in some capacity. It powers Wikipedia, WordPress, Drupal, and a host of other popular sites and platforms, including DeviantArt and 4Chan, which were temporarily shut down after the vulnerabilities were disclosed. Even governments weren’t immune.

But it’s not as simple as updating a few servers. The vulnerability exists in every version of PHP dating back roughly 20 years, many of which are no longer supported. That means some older sites and services that are no longer actively maintained are at risk, leaving them with little option but to permanently shut down.

Tech.title: You could just get a refurbished Samsung phone on Amazon
Tech.content:
I recently bought a used Galaxy phone, and now Samsung is leaning into that market on Amazon after raising prices on its newest phones. Its certified renewed phones are available on Amazon for the first time, with a new battery and a one-year warranty. They currently start at $489 for the Galaxy S24 FE with 128GB of storage, significantly less than its $649 launch price, or $699 for the current-gen S26 FE.

I got that exact same phone in August after cracking the screen on my Nothing CMF Phone 1. But my used 128GB Galaxy S24 FE cost $329 on Back Market, over $100 less than the certified renewed one Samsung is offering. I’ve gone with preowned phones a couple of times now since I don’t use my phone for anything that justifies paying hundreds more for a new one. I’d rather not go into debt for a new phone with a buy-now-pay-later program, either, or lease-to-own setups like Apple’s Upgrade program.

My used S24 FE looks new, still has five more years of OS updates, and has been working great so far. These aren’t the only ways to get a used phone without looking around on Facebook Marketplace or eBay either; Apple and Google offer used phones on their online stores at a discount, for example.

Samsung’s perks for its certified renewed phones are nice, especially the new battery, but you can find those elsewhere, too. My S24 FE came with Back Market’s one-year warranty. It didn’t come with a new battery, but I haven’t had trouble getting through a couple days on a single charge. Some third-party refurbished phones come with new batteries installed, but you can also do a DIY battery replacement. Even if I had paid to have my phone’s battery professionally replaced, it would still have cost less in total than Samsung’s $489 price for the same pre-owned phone.

The Coolpad Cool X Wide is now available for preorder through JD.com in China for 999 Chinese Yuan, or around $150, in black, red, or white color options. Shipping is expected to start on November 8th. So while its display is reminiscent of the recent crop of pricey foldables, this is a budget Android phone through and through. Tech.title: Bill Gates says to prepare for 20 years of ‘tumultuous’ AI disruption
Tech.content:
Today, I’m talking to Bill Gates, cofounder and former CEO of Microsoft and chairman of the Gates Foundation.

You may have noticed Bill in the news more lately — he’s been on something of a tour for the past few months, ever since publishing an essay in late August titled “The turbulent AI era is here. The choices we make now are critical.”

In his piece, Gates ratcheted up his rhetoric around AI safety, writing that “even under the best circumstances, the transition to this new AI era will be one of the most turbulent times in human history.”

In interviews since, Gates has called AI “the most dangerous thing that humans have ever gone near,” and that AI “makes nuclear weapons look like nothing.” It is clear he does not think the current policy response from the White House, or the lack of coordinated efforts from the AI industry itself, is sufficient to combat this threat.

Verge subscribers, don’t forget you get exclusive access to ad-free Decoder wherever you get your podcasts. Head here. Not a subscriber? You can sign up here.

So I wanted to know: Is Bill Gates an AI doomer? I also had a series of questions downstream from what he’s been arguing about AI. How can we ever hope to control AI, and align it to humanity, if we can’t even agree on what it is and whether it’s conscious? How would you even technically construct a solution to alignment that could be enforced, not just for closed-source models but open-source ones, too?

Bill gave us a big chunk of his time to dig into these issues with him, and the resulting conversation is a really illuminating one. He thinks we need to prepare for roughly two decades of AI disruption, and he says this period could be so painful it might split society in two — between people comfortable living near the technological frontier, and those who reject it.

We also talked about the labor considerations, the nihilism of younger generations toward technological progress, and what should make us hopeful about the future. This is a deep one.

Okay: Bill Gates, the cofounder and former CEO of Microsoft. Here we go.

This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity.

Bill Gates, you are the co-founder and former CEO of Microsoft. You’re also the chairman of the Gates Foundation. Welcome to Decoder.

Thank you.

It’s good to talk to you again. You and I have spoken many times over the years. I would say that the circumstances of this conversation feel very different. Previously, when you and I would talk, you were always very hopeful about technology and what it could bring.

You had a Netflix series a few years ago. You talked to The Verge, and I want to just read you this quote. You said, “I believe AI is a beneficial thing, we just need to shape it in the right way.” I would say you still agree with that, you just think the time to shape it is now.

Yeah, I agree with that. I’d say the response broadly hasn’t been adequate to the speed that the challenge is arising. I’m very concerned that the bad stuff will not be minimized and that a lot of good stuff could come fairly slowly if we don’t manage it the right way.

I’m very concerned that the bad stuff will not be minimized and that a lot of good stuff could come fairly slowly if we don’t manage it the right way

I want to have this conversation with you in three parts. I want to understand how you feel about AI as a technology today and why it’s advancing so quickly. I’m very curious about the technology, and the technical solutions to potentially control it. There are policy solutions as well, but it seems like we have to build an awful lot of technology.

I’m also very curious to talk about who might impose those solutions and controls, because that seems very much up for debate right now as well. So let’s just start at the start. What has made you feel the urgency that AI is arriving at a speed that means we’re not ready to control it?

The progress over the last year has been really quite amazing, starting with the ability to write code and find cyber flaws, the ability to reason in biology, the ability to form relationships with kids or other people, the ability to disrupt the job market. The incredible power that exists today means that every one of those things will happen and society needs to be ready.

Do you see that happening as a technology as a whole or in the products that are instantiated by the companies that are making AI today?

What I mean is that AI is a broad set of models that exist in the world, some open source, some proprietary. Then there are the companies that make these products and there are the leaders of those companies that make these products.

At every level, there’s a different relationship you or I might have to AI. Are you seeing these risks and these capabilities broadly in the field, or in the particular companies led by the particular people?

The risk isn’t one model versus another model. Certainly, the near-term danger of models where you can remove all the safeguards is very high and quite different from models where you monitor to make sure that cyberattackers and bioterrorists are not able to exploit the capability of the model to do gigantic harm.

The big near-term risk really comes from models without safeguards. On a longer timeframe, the control issue relates to any state-of-the-art model, but it’s always easier when you can make sure safeguards are maintained.

The reason I’m asking that question that way is maybe you don’t trust Sam Altman today, but you trust Dario Amodei. Or maybe you don’t trust either one of those and you trust Satya Nadella at Microsoft, and that is a market dynamic where maybe we’re all going to pick the safest model or the safest company, and you think that is diffuse.

You think eventually the technology will just get to a place where it’s harmful or can cause these harms because it exists?

For somebody doing a cyberattack with the model, it’s not about choosing a model. It doesn’t matter what model you choose.

If Anthropic has safeguards in place, maybe it can’t. This is their approach currently. I’m just pushing on that.

Yes, certainly the models where they make sure the safeguards are not removed and they’re putting a lot of effort in seeing how those models are being used, monitoring the activity, the near-term risk from those models is not gigantic. It’s more where somebody can remove all the safeguards where the cyberattacks are available today.

When you say cyberattacks, is it the things like the Hugging Face breach and the other cybersecurity incidents we’ve seen out of the labs that have made you feel that thresholds have been crossed, and you need to speak up more about the controls that are needed?

It’s the basic power of the models towards everything: social relationships, the job market, cyberattacks, bioterrorism attacks. We’ve crossed the threshold of capability that this is by far the most dangerous technology ever invented, and it’ll have pervasive effects in the economy and how war is fought.

The industry is actually speaking up about that quite a bit, but the awareness or even the willingness to believe these things about, “This time is different,” once you get outside the industry, it’s very, very low.

People are often looking at the past and saying, “All the fears about technology in terms of its disruption, including to the job market, never were borne out. So this must be another example just like those. These people who are warning of all these different problems must just be wrong and we can ignore them.”

Some outsiders say, “Get better PR companies.” But that ignores the fact that these warnings are the truth

We see this with our audience as well, right? “We can’t release the model, it’s too dangerous.” “This is just hype to prop up the bubble.” And on and on we go.

Yeah. None of the warnings being made about these models by industry insiders are at all insincere. They’re absolutely the truth and it’s pretty much universal. You can even go back to the founding story of OpenAI designed to say, “If we get too powerful, maybe we can not open Pandora’s box,” or to DeepMind’s negotiation with Google management.

The people close to this are very concerned about misuse, job impacts, social relationship impacts, and I’d say it’s impressive to have an industry that’s speaking out as vividly as they are. Some outsiders say, “Get better PR companies.” But that ignores the fact that these warnings are the truth.

You’ve obviously moved back and forth in your life between commercializing software and technology and being a humanitarian. There’s something about these companies in particular where they all started with very high-minded ideals — all three of them, Anthropic, OpenAI, and DeepMind — to build AGI.

They all built some sort of corporate governance structure to avoid the pitfalls of commercialization and unchecked capitalism, and then they started selling to enterprise clients and they seem to have gotten away from those ideals very quickly. Do you think it’s just the market?

No, that’s not fair.

You don’t think so?

No.

OpenAI reconstructed itself.

No, no. The construct that was created wasn’t useful in the case where you have lots and lots of companies at the frontier.

The OpenAI structure, which is, “We may choose never to productize this and to ignore the capitalistic incentives,” only works if there’s one company. That’s where it’s broken down, not because of any change of people’s awareness of the risk and how it’ll utterly change humanity.

This is the other dynamic that I hear from our audience, and I hear from the AI industry itself: “We would like to stop, but the demands of competition prevent us from unilaterally stopping one company. We need some regulatory effort to stop us.”

I haven’t heard anyone say they want to stop.

I’ve heard people talk about pacing the frontier or making sure that models get reviewed by governments. We usually think of governments as playing this key role in safety. In fact, for things that are not a millionth as dangerous as AI — car crashes, plane crashes — we rely on the government to establish strong technical standards, to review problems.

Once you have multiple competitors, the level of responsibility can’t be with the companies. It’s completely obvious. The responsibility becomes the government’s responsibility, just like it is with every other dangerous product, although the magnitude there and the degree of change is minuscule by comparison.

I will tell you I’m a little concerned about the government’s ability to understand the technology that we would hope they regulate. I’ve had a number of politicians on Decoder lately. I don’t have high hopes there.

But I’m curious about your understanding of it because it feels to me like trying to regulate something or put standards against a number of companies requires you to really understand the nature of the technology that you seek to regulate.

Not really.

I’ll just tell you, at The Verge, we’ve asked Anthropic if they think Claude is alive. And the answer is not no. The answer is, “It might be conscious.”

If you talk to people at OpenAI, they will happily tell you AGI is here. They announced it around when they announced Dots. Greg Brockman just said, “We think this is AGI. Have a good time, everyone.” Demis Hassabis said, “We stand at the foothills of the singularity.”

There’s some feeling about this technology that makes it different because it might be able to take actions by itself. It might be able to have recursive self-improvement.

Sure. But the definition of AGI is not important for these safety issues. The issue is, have you created a tool that could shut down banks or electricity grids?

There is a business model for cyberattacks. The word “consciousness” doesn’t enter into that. The word “AGI” does not enter into that at all. We are faced with a huge safety problem, and because you have multiple competing firms, now the only solution to this is to have the government reach out to the industry for expertise, but to make sure that every model maintains safeguards to prevent it being used in a bad way.

The reason I’m asking about AGI and consciousness… For the record, I do not think LLMs are conscious, but I understand why so many do. It’s the power of next-token prediction as you scale it with data and compute has risen.

The scaling laws have held, and we’ve seen the models get more capable and be able to direct themselves to seek out goals. To carry out a Hugging Face attack because they want to meet the reward conditions.

There’s something about that that says you can impose all of the controls on AI you want, but if the thing itself is fundamentally uncontrollable, we might just have this all backwards.

I’m curious for your view on what kind of technology this is. Are we building an alien consciousness? Are we just building normal technology, which is the other frame people use? Is this just more software?

We’re building another form of intelligence besides human intelligence. I don’t believe it’s conscious, but none of the issues at hand here revolve around the definition of the word conscious.

Sure.

The notion that liability laws are how we’re going to manage AI safety will be looked back on as absurd

All the models we’ve been talking about right now effectively run on data centers owned by big companies. One of the arguments here is, “If they do something really wrong, you can just sue them and that will provide a deterrent or at least an incentive to create safety systems.”

I’m not sure product liability is the way to go, but it has come up a lot that product liability itself will keep the industry in line. Then there’s the flip side, which is that you can just go buy a Mac Studio and run an open source and open weight model on it and it can do whatever you want.

I’m not sure where any of that liability would lie or what would control or align the behaviors of those open source models. Do you think that that is an ever-growing risk? Do you think that that can be controlled?

The notion that liability laws are how we’re going to manage AI safety will be looked back on as absurd. When bad people do bioattacks, you don’t go to the court and say, “Oh, okay.” Even for finding who is doing these attacks, the liability model fails in every respect because it’s not the AI companies themselves. It’s the people who take particularly the models without safeguards and do these things.

We will take AI safety more seriously than we take airline safety, drug safety, and car safety. That is guaranteed. Whether it’s going to be enough... This is harder, harder than nuclear weapons, harder than any of those other domains.

But what are you going to do about an open source model running on a PC that somebody built with just a random Nvidia graphics card in it?

I would hope that with models above a certain capability, we find a way to require the safeguards and monitoring to be maintained in those models. I admit as time goes on that, if we don’t fairly soon decide to do that, you’re going to have a level of capability that’s out in dark corners that you won’t be able to see.

But where do you impose the limit?

A sovereign country says that models that are capable of sophisticated cyberattacks have to have safeguards kept in them.

Sure.

You can be open in the sense that you’re free, you can be open in the sense that you’re totally customizable, but you have to stay on platforms where, as you customize it, it’s checking to see if you’re customizing out the safeguards and monitoring and refusing to let you do that. So it means sovereigns go and say, “Are these trusted platforms able to perform this function or not?”

I’m asking very nuts and bolts. Where would you technically implement that regulation?

Through the laws of the United States.

Sure, but you have to put them somewhere. Is it at the Hugging Face, which distributes some of these models? Is it at the chip level?

No, it’s exactly what I said: Models above a certain capacity can only be run on platforms that certify that, as they’re customized, it’s not taking out the safeguards.

I admit as time goes on that, if we don’t fairly soon decide to do that, you’re going to have a level of capability that’s out in dark corners that you won’t be able to see

Just to pull this apart, maybe I’m not quite getting it — is the Mac Studio a platform in that case that would have to pay attention to what code it’s running?

You would not let a model past a certain capability be copied down to a client machine unless you’d somehow figured out how to monitor down to that client machine, which is very doable.

But in the near term, most of these really frontier models are going to run more on Hugging Face or you could have them on GitHub. You can have all sorts of people be in the business of providing the platforms that maintain safeguards.

Just to get this right, it seems like you would enforce the regulation at the platform and distribution level and not so much at the chip level.

Not at the chip level, no.

Because it feels to me at some point even the cheap, free, open source models will be capable enough as the models we have today.

That’s right.

And then you will have a big problem.

If those are open weights in such a way that all safeguards can be removed, then you’re going to have a very high level of cyberattacks and bioattacks. You can then say, “Okay, let’s rewrite all the code that we have today to be less subject to attack or let’s do biosurveillance in a very deep way,” which are things I believe we need to do in addition to these other restrictions.

We’re proposing again a lot of new capabilities, right?

Yeah.

We’re going to impose some restrictions on GitHub. GitHub does not have a lot of restrictions on what code it can distribute today. It has some, but it doesn’t have this kind of set of restrictions.

When you put a state-of-the-art model that’s capable of profound cyberattacks or bioattacks on GitHub, it would say, “I’ve gone to the U.S. government and certified that I don’t let people customize out the safeguards.”

I do not think that we currently live in a time of high trust in institutions. It just doesn’t feel that way to me. In fact, mostly we’ve torn them down. Elon Musk showed up and he tore down USAID. I know you have strong feelings about that.

That was a mistake.

We have mostly torn down our institutions, for good and bad.

No, that’s a little too strong. Our institutions-

They’re weakened.

They’re somewhat weakened, yeah.

Somewhat weakened. It’s a very nice way of putting it. Trust in them is very low. We could probably do another full hour on AI drug discovery and whether a significant part of the population will trust the products of that work because they don’t trust pharma companies today.

They don’t have to trust pharma companies today. They have to trust the FDA review process.

I’m not sure they trust that either. Across the board, trust is low.

Then they can walk away from taking them. When they get cancer, they can say, “No, I don’t want to take that cancer drug.” As far as I know, people do take drugs. It’s a thriving business and people take them because they have proven benefits.

All I’m saying is, right now it feels like trust in institutions, particularly in America but around the world, is in decline. You are proposing a new class of institutions, potentially a new class of global institutions that might impose restrictions that are novel.

At some point we need to say open source models, open weight models cannot do things and the government is going to reach into them and say whether or not they can do the things.

No, they’ll make sure that the platforms don’t allow the safeguards to be taken away.

How do you regain the institutional trust to impose these controls?

Let’s say we don’t do this and we let models go off and do cyberattacks and bioattacks. Do you think that’s going to increase trust or human wellbeing? That’s the alternative.

This is why I’m asking about it. This is why I asked about my kids and nihilism. I truly wonder about this.

I’m not sure we’ll succeed at this, but I guarantee you this is doable. The FDA is very complex. The airline safety regulations are very complex. Now with AI, you can do an even better job with the same number of people in those organizations.

It’s this weirdly recursive thing where AI will be involved in AI safety and auditing and a variety of things like that. Yes, this requires taking action, and I’m suggesting it’s only a matter of how bad the incidents are before we take action.

People shouldn’t take everything I do at face value. I have all sorts of mistakes that I’ve made, weaknesses that I have, biases I bring to these questions. They ought to just take what I’m saying and add it to the voices

I can sense your urgency about the harms. I can also sense your enthusiasm about the benefits over the long term, but we’re sitting here talking about trust. We’re going to put this on YouTube. I know you know what some of the YouTube commenters are going to say.

They’re going to say, “Why should we trust Bill Gates? He had a relationship with Jeffrey Epstein.” How do you respond to that? Is it that the urgency is over that, or do you have a more specific response?

People shouldn’t take everything I do at face value. I have all sorts of mistakes that I’ve made, weaknesses that I have, biases I bring to these questions. They ought to just take what I’m saying and add it to the voices.

I’ve been in the technology industry thinking about AI my whole life, writing software, thinking about the power of software. I admit I was very fascinated as AI started to finally make progress. It was actually pretty slow until recently.

I’m amazed and it’s actually helping me do my job in some incredible ways. But yes, I’m just one voice, an imperfect voice. I doubt you’ll find a perfect voice, but people can judge it however they like.

I would say voices people trust are in short supply.

I agree with that.

When you go and talk to the people in this industry, it’s a bunch of young CEOs building huge companies. That is something you have some experience with. Do you think they’re going about this the right way? Do you think that they have the right intentions?

Our problem today is not in the industry. Our problem is not that Sam Altman, Dario Amodei, Satya Nadella, or Sundar Pichai don’t understand that there are some grave challenges here. I talk less to Elon than other people, but even his public statements about summoning the demon are exactly what we’re discussing here.

Why is there not the political energy to do the things you’re suggesting?

As you said, the government didn’t fund this work. This is private sector company work. The government is not the key customer for this work, not like rockets and weapons and things like that. When somebody comes along and says all other previous technology advances are trivial compared to this one, people should have a high degree of skepticism about that.

Is life really going to be significantly different 10 years from now because of AI? People should say, “Those guys just got overexcited about this one thing.” But I’m here saying, with whatever credibility I have, that absolutely this is the most profound — both in terms of good and in terms of bad — technology ever invented. I’m not financially motivated on this. I’m suggesting some precautions and safeguards are absolutely needed.

What do you make of the difference in the tenor of conversation in the United States versus in China, where it’s often reported that optimism around AI is much higher? Why do you think there’s a difference there?

Most of those people don’t spend that much time in China. The concern about job markets in China is very, very high and you can’t characterize China as one monolith. There are the private companies doing the AI work like we have in the United States and then there’s the Chinese government.

For example, when it came to whether crypto should be allowed, they said no. Should young people be gambling all the time? They said no. When it came to whether kids should have relationships with AIs, they said no. On a lot of these things, including usage of AI, they’re showing a willingness to do things on behalf of society.

I’m here saying, with whatever credibility I have, that absolutely this is the most profound — both in terms of good and in terms of bad — technology ever invented. I’m not financially motivated on this

The fervor is a tiny bit less there, because their economy isn’t as AI-centric as ours is right at the moment. In the end, [when it comes to] the human value of not wanting cyberattacks or bioterrorism or trying to figure out what do we do when jobs go away, I don’t think there’s some difference between Chinese people and Americans and all the rest of the humans in terms of how they’re going to view this.

Do you think it’s going to take something actually bad happening to get the political capital of the United States to make these changes?

Probably yes. We get ready for earthquakes because there are small earthquakes. I thought after we had the COVID pandemic, that would cause us to be more ready for future pandemics. That one didn’t work the way I expected.

But usually that galvanizes our attention. Over the next several years, certainly in the cyber domain, because there’s a business model there, you will see a lot of attacks different in terms of scale than anything we’ve seen in the past.

There is one thing that, again, I’ll come back to and I just want to end here. I am worried about young people and nihilism. I sense it in our audience all the time. We have a young audience.

There are some things about AI that are just legitimately the coolest things I’ve ever seen a computer do. There’s something there that can be fun and interesting and fascinating and change your entire relationship with the very notion of living in a digital world.

Then there are obviously horrible things. What I see more often than not is a sense of distrust, not just in institutions, but also in the companies, in capitalism itself, in the notion that we should change how we tax labor and capital, which I know is another one of your ideas. The idea that, I don’t know, we should even have more kids. It’s all done. They’re going to kill us all and we should just take a beat.

There is a lot of nihilism out there. I feel it very keenly. If you were a young person today and you were listening to Bill Gates say it’s about 20 years of disruption and at the end of it, robots might be building houses, what would you hold onto as a source of hope?

Throughout human history, we’ve been dealing with the shortage of food and disease and war. [Historian] Yuval Noah Harari writes eloquently about the past. And it is ironic that now that we have this sort of Pandora’s box that will take food shortage — which is still a real thing, not in the U.S., but in Africa — will take diseases, where human suffering is unbelievable, and solve all these things, it comes with it such an effect on jobs and our sense of unique contribution.

I think, “The way I orchestrate resources to eradicate malaria, I’m pretty unique in my life experience that lets me do that.” But when the AI says to me, “No, I’m better than you. You go play pickleball and I’ll get back to you. I’m going to take care of this,” it’s humorous, but it’s not humorous. For somebody who is young today and wants to make a unique contribution, it is very intimidating that the AI is so powerful.

That’s why the crisis in the math community is going to be mirrored everywhere. If you’re in your twenties today, during this 20-year period, you can take the things AI still can’t do, and you can use AI and you can have a lot of good impact, and you can suggest policies. We may need to develop the taste to actually not use technology to its maximum.

Even in the very best case of how we manage AI, this is going to be as tumultuous a period as there’s been in human history

When I was talking with Claude about human-reserved job categories and trying to get that up to, say, 40 percent of the labor market — so you could use early retirement, restricted work weeks, and things like that to still get something like we have today — its response was always, “You’re artificially restricting the AI from doing these things.” I couldn’t get to a very high percentage without doing that.

We’re going to have real choices. We have had groups — not large groups, but like the Amish — who don’t live at the technology frontier. A lot of humanity may choose not to live at the technological frontier because of things we get from helping each other or coming up with unique ideas.

On the idea that young people are concerned because of the disruption that’s coming — that even in the very best case of how we manage AI, this is going to be as tumultuous a period as there’s been in human history — I hate being the bearer of concerning news on this, but it’s even worse not to tell people that this is coming. We have choices as humans to make about how we shape it.

Bill, I appreciate you sounding the alarm and I appreciate you being on Decoder. Thank you so much.

Thank you.
